topics.title: Rational and Irrational Numbers
topics.summary: A rational number can be written as p/q (q ≠ 0); its decimal terminates or repeats. An irrational number cannot; its decimal neither ends nor repeats (√2, π).
notes: A rational number can be written as p/q (q ≠ 0); its decimal terminates or repeats. An irrational number cannot; its decimal neither ends nor repeats (√2, π).
Rational and irrational numbers together form the real numbers; every real number is a point on the number line.
A surd is an irrational root such as √3; like surds can be added (2√3 + 5√3 = 7√3).
Rationalising: multiply by the conjugate, e.g. 1/(√3 + 1) × (√3 − 1)/(√3 − 1) = (√3 − 1)/2.
√2 is irrational: if √2 = p/q in lowest terms, then p² = 2q², so p and then q are even — a contradiction.
√2 can be marked on the number line with a right triangle of sides 1 and 1 and a compass.
outcomes: Place rational and irrational numbers on the real number line
Simplify surds and rationalise denominators
Prove that √2 is irrational

lesson.hook: The diagonal of a square with side 1 m is √2 m. Can this length ever be written exactly as a fraction?
lesson.activity: Pupils construct √2, √3 and √5 on the number line using right triangles and a compass (the square-root spiral).

questions.q: Is 0.121121112… rational or irrational?
questions.a: Irrational: it neither terminates nor repeats.

questions.q: Simplify √50 + √18.
Rationalise 1/√5.
Find a rational number between 1/3 and 1/2.
questions.a: 5/12 (for example).

lesson.homework: Prove that √3 is irrational using the method used for √2.

topics.title: Compound Interest
topics.summary: Compound interest adds each year's interest to the principal, so the next year's interest is earned on a bigger amount.
notes: Compound interest adds each year's interest to the principal, so the next year's interest is earned on a bigger amount.
Amount A = P(1 + r/100)ⁿ; CI = A − P.
For half-yearly compounding, use r/2 per half-year and 2n half-years.
Growth (population, prices) uses the same formula; depreciation (a machine losing value) uses A = P(1 − r/100)ⁿ.
Over two years, CI − SI = P(r/100)².
Different rates in successive years: A = P(1 + r₁/100)(1 + r₂/100).
outcomes: Explain compound interest as repeated simple interest
Use A = P(1 + r/100)ⁿ, including half-yearly compounding
Solve problems on growth and depreciation

lesson.hook: Why does money in a fixed deposit grow faster than simple interest suggests?
lesson.example: ₹10 000 at 10% compound interest for 2 years: A = 10 000 × 1.1² = ₹12 100; CI = ₹2100 (SI would be ₹2000).
lesson.activity: Make a year-by-year table for ₹5000 at 8% for 3 years, first as simple and then as compound interest; compare the totals.

questions.q: Find the CI on ₹8000 for 2 years at 5% per annum.
A machine worth ₹50 000 depreciates 10% a year. Find its value after 2 years.
What rate is used for half-yearly compounding at 12% per annum?
questions.a: 6% per half-year.

questions.q: Find the difference between CI and SI on ₹5000 for 2 years at 10%.

lesson.homework: A town has 40 000 people and grows 5% a year. Find its population after 3 years.

topics.title: Expansions
topics.summary: (a + b)² = a² + 2ab + b²; (a − b)² = a² − 2ab + b²; (a + b)(a − b) = a² − b².
notes: (a + b)² = a² + 2ab + b²; (a − b)² = a² − 2ab + b²; (a + b)(a − b) = a² − b².
(x + a)(x + b) = x² + (a + b)x + ab.
(a + b)³ = a³ + b³ + 3ab(a + b); (a − b)³ = a³ − b³ − 3ab(a − b).
(a + b + c)² = a² + b² + c² + 2ab + 2bc + 2ca.
Identities are true for every value; they help with mental arithmetic and simplification.
If a + 1/a = p, then a² + 1/a² = p² − 2 and a³ + 1/a³ = p³ − 3p.
outcomes: Use standard identities to expand algebraic expressions
Expand (a ± b)², (a ± b)³, (x + a)(x + b) and (a + b + c)²
Use identities to evaluate expressions and find values like a³ + b³ from a + b and ab

lesson.hook: Can you find 103² in your head in five seconds? An identity makes it easy.
lesson.activity: Cut squares and rectangles from paper to show (a + b)² = a² + 2ab + b² as areas.

questions.q: Expand (2x − 3y)².
questions.a: 4x² − 12xy + 9y².

questions.q: If a + b = 5 and ab = 6, find a² + b².
Find 99³ using an identity.
If x + 1/x = 3, find x² + 1/x².

lesson.homework: Expand (x + 2y + 3z)² and check with x = y = z = 1.

topics.title: Factorisation
topics.summary: Take out the highest common factor first: 6x² + 9x = 3x(2x + 3).
notes: Take out the highest common factor first: 6x² + 9x = 3x(2x + 3).
Group terms: ax + ay + bx + by = (a + b)(x + y).
Difference of squares: a² − b² = (a + b)(a − b).
a³ + b³ = (a + b)(a² − ab + b²); a³ − b³ = (a − b)(a² + ab + b²).
ax² + bx + c: find two numbers whose product is ac and sum is b, split the middle term and group.
Always check by multiplying the factors back.
outcomes: Factorise by taking common factors and grouping
Factorise a² − b², a³ ± b³ and quadratic trinomials by splitting the middle term
Use factorisation to simplify expressions

lesson.hook: Factorisation is expansion in reverse. How do we find what was multiplied?
lesson.activity: Pupils race in pairs: one writes a product of two binomials and expands it, the other factorises it back.

questions.q: Factorise x² − 5x + 6.
Factorise 8a³ − 27.
Factorise 49x² − 16y².
Factorise ax − bx + ay − by.

lesson.homework: Factorise: 2x² + x − 6; a⁴ − b⁴; x³ + 64.

topics.title: Simultaneous Linear Equations
topics.summary: Two linear equations in x and y are solved together to find values satisfying both.
notes: Two linear equations in x and y are solved together to find values satisfying both.
Substitution: express one variable from one equation and put it into the other.
Elimination: multiply to make one variable's coefficients equal, then add or subtract.
Cross-multiplication for a₁x + b₁y + c₁ = 0, a₂x + b₂y + c₂ = 0: x/(b₁c₂ − b₂c₁) = y/(c₁a₂ − c₂a₁) = 1/(a₁b₂ − a₂b₁).
Word problems: choose variables, write two equations from the facts, solve and check in the original words.
The solution is the point where the two lines meet on a graph.
outcomes: Solve simultaneous linear equations by elimination, substitution and cross-multiplication
Frame equations from word problems
Check solutions

lesson.hook: A pen and a pencil cost ₹25; two pens and three pencils cost ₹60. How do we find each price?
lesson.example: x + y = 25 and 2x + 3y = 60: double the first: 2x + 2y = 50; subtract: y = 10, so x = 15 — pen ₹15, pencil ₹10.
lesson.activity: Pupils write their own "price puzzles" with two items and swap them to solve by two different methods.

questions.q: Solve x + y = 7, x − y = 1.
Solve 3x + 2y = 12, x − y = −1.
The sum of two numbers is 20 and their difference is 4. Find them.
questions.a: 12 and 8.

questions.q: When do two linear equations have no solution?
questions.a: When their lines are parallel (a₁/a₂ = b₁/b₂ ≠ c₁/c₂).

lesson.homework: A two-digit number is 4 times the sum of its digits, and the digits differ by 3. Find it (answer 36).

topics.title: Indices (Exponents)
topics.summary: aᵐ × aⁿ = aᵐ⁺ⁿ; aᵐ ÷ aⁿ = aᵐ⁻ⁿ; (aᵐ)ⁿ = aᵐⁿ; (ab)ⁿ = aⁿbⁿ.
notes: aᵐ × aⁿ = aᵐ⁺ⁿ; aᵐ ÷ aⁿ = aᵐ⁻ⁿ; (aᵐ)ⁿ = aᵐⁿ; (ab)ⁿ = aⁿbⁿ.
a^(1/n) is the nth root of a; a^(m/n) = (ⁿ√a)ᵐ.
Write numbers as powers of primes to simplify: 16 = 2⁴, 27 = 3³.
Exponential equations: make the bases equal and compare the powers (2ˣ = 32 → x = 5).
These laws make calculations with very large or small numbers easier.
outcomes: State and use the laws of indices
Simplify expressions with zero, negative and fractional indices
Solve simple exponential equations

lesson.hook: What could 2⁰, 2⁻³ or 8^(2/3) possibly mean?
lesson.activity: Build a table of powers of 2 from 2⁻³ to 2⁵ and ask pupils to spot the pattern that gives 2⁰ = 1.

questions.q: Evaluate 16^(3/4).
Simplify (x³)² × x⁻⁴.
questions.a: x².

questions.q: Solve 3ˣ⁺¹ = 81.
Evaluate 5⁰ + 2⁻¹.

lesson.homework: Simplify (27/8)^(−2/3) and 2ⁿ⁺² ÷ 2ⁿ.

topics.title: Logarithms
topics.summary: If aˣ = N then logₐ N = x (a > 0, a ≠ 1).
notes: If aˣ = N then logₐ N = x (a > 0, a ≠ 1).
logₐ 1 = 0 and logₐ a = 1.
Laws: log(mn) = log m + log n; log(m/n) = log m − log n; log mⁿ = n log m.
Common logarithms use base 10: log 100 = 2, log 1000 = 3.
Logarithms turn multiplication into addition and powers into multiplication.
Expansion example: log(a²b/c³) = 2 log a + log b − 3 log c.
outcomes: Convert between exponential and logarithmic form
Use the laws of logarithms
Expand and simplify logarithmic expressions

lesson.hook: Before calculators, how did scientists multiply huge numbers quickly?
lesson.example: log₂ 32 = 5 because 2⁵ = 32; log 20 + log 5 = log 100 = 2.
lesson.activity: Give pupils pairs of cards (2⁵ = 32 and log₂ 32 = 5) to match exponential and logarithmic forms.

questions.q: Write 3⁴ = 81 in logarithmic form.
questions.a: log₃ 81 = 4.

questions.q: Evaluate log₅ 125.
Simplify log 8 + log 125.
Expand log (x³y²).
questions.a: 3 log x + 2 log y.

lesson.homework: If log 2 = 0.3010 and log 3 = 0.4771, find log 12 and log 18.

topics.title: Triangles and Congruency
topics.summary: Two triangles are congruent if they have exactly the same shape and size; corresponding parts are equal (CPCT).
notes: Two triangles are congruent if they have exactly the same shape and size; corresponding parts are equal (CPCT).
SSS: three sides equal; SAS: two sides and the included angle equal.
ASA or AAS: two angles and a corresponding side equal.
RHS: in right triangles, hypotenuse and one side equal.
SSA and AAA do not guarantee congruency.
Proofs list equal parts with reasons, name the condition, then use CPCT.
outcomes: State the congruency conditions SSS, SAS, ASA/AAS and RHS
Prove triangles congruent and use CPCT
Apply congruency to simple geometric problems

lesson.hook: How can a carpenter be sure two triangular brackets are exactly the same shape and size without measuring every part?
lesson.example: In ΔABC with AB = AC, draw AD ⊥ BC. Then ΔABD ≅ ΔACD by RHS (AB = AC, AD common), so BD = DC.
lesson.activity: Cut out triangles with given measurements (e.g. SSS, SAS) and check by placing them on top of each other.

questions.q: Which congruency condition uses a hypotenuse?
questions.a: RHS.

questions.q: Is AAA a congruency condition?
questions.a: No — it gives similar triangles of possibly different sizes.

questions.q: What does CPCT stand for?
questions.a: Corresponding parts of congruent triangles.

questions.q: If two triangles have all three sides equal, which condition applies?
questions.a: SSS.

lesson.homework: Prove that the diagonals of a rectangle are equal using congruent triangles.

chapters.title: Isosceles Triangles and Inequalities in Triangles

topics.title: Isosceles Triangles and Inequalities in Triangles
topics.summary: In an isosceles triangle the angles opposite the equal sides are equal; conversely, sides opposite equal angles are equal.
notes: In an isosceles triangle the angles opposite the equal sides are equal; conversely, sides opposite equal angles are equal.
If two sides of a triangle are unequal, the angle opposite the greater side is greater, and conversely.
The sum of any two sides of a triangle is greater than the third side.
Of all line segments from a point to a line, the perpendicular is the shortest.
An equilateral triangle has all angles 60°.
These results help check whether three lengths can form a triangle.
outcomes: Prove and use: angles opposite equal sides are equal, and the converse
Use inequalities in a triangle: the greater side is opposite the greater angle
Use the triangle inequality and the shortest distance property

lesson.hook: Why is a straight road the shortest way between two towns?
lesson.example: Can sides 4 cm, 5 cm and 10 cm form a triangle? 4 + 5 = 9 < 10, so no.
lesson.activity: Give pupils straws of lengths 3, 4, 5, 6 and 10 cm; they test which triples form triangles and state the rule.

questions.q: In ΔPQR, PQ = PR and ∠Q = 50°. Find ∠P.
In ΔABC, AB > AC. Which angle is greater, ∠B or ∠C?
questions.a: ∠C (opposite the greater side AB).

questions.q: Can 2, 3 and 6 be the sides of a triangle?
questions.a: No, because 2 + 3 < 6.

questions.q: What is the shortest distance from a point to a line?
questions.a: The perpendicular distance.

lesson.homework: Prove that the angles of an equilateral triangle are each 60°.

topics.title: Mid-point and Equal Intercept Theorems
topics.summary: Mid-point theorem: the line joining the mid-points of two sides of a triangle is parallel to the third side and half of it.
notes: Mid-point theorem: the line joining the mid-points of two sides of a triangle is parallel to the third side and half of it.
Converse: a line through the mid-point of one side, parallel to another side, bisects the third side.
Equal intercept theorem: if a transversal makes equal intercepts on three or more parallel lines, any other transversal also makes equal intercepts.
Joining the mid-points of the sides of any quadrilateral forms a parallelogram.
The theorems are proved with congruent triangles and properties of parallelograms.
They help find unknown lengths in triangles and trapeziums.
outcomes: Prove the mid-point theorem and its converse
Prove the equal intercept theorem
Solve problems using these theorems

lesson.hook: Join the mid-points of two sides of any triangle. What do you notice about this line and the third side?
lesson.example: In ΔABC, D and E are mid-points of AB and AC and BC = 12 cm. Then DE ∥ BC and DE = 6 cm.
lesson.activity: Pupils draw three different triangles, join mid-points and measure the segments to test the theorem before proving it.

questions.q: State the mid-point theorem.
questions.a: The segment joining the mid-points of two sides is parallel to the third side and half its length.

questions.q: If DE = 7 cm joins mid-points of AB and AC, find BC.
questions.a: 14 cm.

questions.q: What figure is formed by joining mid-points of the sides of a quadrilateral?
questions.a: A parallelogram.

questions.q: State the equal intercept theorem.
questions.a: If three or more parallel lines make equal intercepts on one transversal, they make equal intercepts on every transversal.

lesson.homework: Prove that the line joining the mid-points of the diagonals of a trapezium is parallel to its parallel sides.

topics.title: Pythagoras Theorem
topics.summary: In a right triangle, the square on the hypotenuse equals the sum of the squares on the other two sides: c² = a² + b².
notes: In a right triangle, the square on the hypotenuse equals the sum of the squares on the other two sides: c² = a² + b².
Converse: if c² = a² + b² in a triangle, the angle opposite c is a right angle.
An area-based proof arranges four copies of the triangle inside a square of side a + b.
Pythagorean triplets: (3, 4, 5), (5, 12, 13), (8, 15, 17), (7, 24, 25); multiples also work.
Applications: ladder against a wall, diagonal of a rectangle, heights and distances.
If c² < a² + b² the triangle is acute; if c² > a² + b² it is obtuse.
outcomes: State and prove Pythagoras theorem using areas
Use the theorem and its converse to find lengths and test right angles
Recognise Pythagorean triplets

lesson.hook: How did ancient builders make perfect right angles with just a rope?
lesson.example: A 13 m ladder reaches 12 m up a wall. Its foot is √(169 − 144) = 5 m from the wall.
lesson.activity: Use the Pythagoras virtual lab: change the angle C and watch c² equal a² + b² only at 90°.

questions.q: Find the hypotenuse if the legs are 6 cm and 8 cm.
questions.a: 10 cm.

questions.q: Is 9, 40, 41 a Pythagorean triplet?
Find the diagonal of a rectangle 15 cm × 8 cm.
questions.a: 17 cm.

questions.q: A triangle has sides 5, 6, 7. Is it right-angled?

lesson.homework: Measure the length and width of your classroom and calculate its diagonal; check with a tape.

topics.title: Rectilinear Figures: Quadrilaterals and Parallelograms
topics.summary: The angle sum of a quadrilateral is 360°; of an n-sided polygon (n − 2) × 180°; each exterior angle of a regular polygon is 360°/n.
notes: The angle sum of a quadrilateral is 360°; of an n-sided polygon (n − 2) × 180°; each exterior angle of a regular polygon is 360°/n.
In a parallelogram opposite sides and opposite angles are equal and the diagonals bisect each other.
A quadrilateral is a parallelogram if both pairs of opposite sides are equal, or one pair is equal and parallel, or its diagonals bisect each other.
A rectangle has equal diagonals; a rhombus has diagonals that bisect at right angles; a square has both properties.
Each diagonal divides a parallelogram into two congruent triangles.
A trapezium has one pair of parallel sides; a kite has two pairs of adjacent equal sides.
outcomes: State and use properties of parallelograms, rectangles, rhombuses and squares
Prove that a quadrilateral is a parallelogram using given conditions
Use angle properties of polygons

lesson.hook: A rhombus and a square both have four equal sides. What makes them different?
lesson.example: Each interior angle of a regular hexagon: (6 − 2) × 180 ÷ 6 = 120°; each exterior angle = 60°.
lesson.activity: Pupils fold paper parallelograms, rectangles and rhombuses along diagonals and record which properties hold for each.

questions.q: Find the sum of the interior angles of an octagon.
How many sides has a regular polygon with exterior angle 40°?
Which quadrilateral has diagonals that are equal and perpendicular bisectors of each other?
questions.a: A square.

questions.q: One angle of a parallelogram is 70°. Find the others.

lesson.homework: Prove that the diagonals of a rhombus meet at right angles.

topics.title: Construction of Polygons
topics.summary: A quadrilateral needs five independent measurements to be drawn uniquely (e.g. four sides and a diagonal).
notes: A quadrilateral needs five independent measurements to be drawn uniquely (e.g. four sides and a diagonal).
Construct parallelograms using properties: opposite sides equal and parallel, diagonals bisecting each other.
A rhombus can be drawn from its diagonals, which bisect each other at right angles.
A regular hexagon: draw a circle and step the radius six times round it; the chord equals the radius.
Always draw a rough sketch first and mark the given measurements.
Keep construction arcs visible; write the steps of construction.
outcomes: Construct quadrilaterals from given measurements with ruler and compasses
Construct parallelograms and rhombuses
Construct a regular hexagon

lesson.hook: With only a ruler and compasses, how do we draw an exact regular hexagon?
lesson.example: Rhombus with diagonals 8 cm and 6 cm: draw one diagonal, its perpendicular bisector, mark 3 cm each side, join the four points; each side is 5 cm.
lesson.activity: Each pupil constructs a regular hexagon in a circle of radius 4 cm and checks that all sides are equal and each angle is 120°.

questions.q: How many measurements are needed to construct a quadrilateral?
questions.a: Five independent ones.

questions.q: Why does stepping the radius round a circle give a regular hexagon?
questions.a: Each chord equals the radius, forming six equilateral triangles.

questions.q: What property of a rhombus helps construct it from diagonals?
questions.a: Its diagonals bisect each other at right angles.

questions.q: Construct a parallelogram with sides 5 cm and 4 cm and angle 60° — which property do you use?
questions.a: Opposite sides equal and parallel.

lesson.homework: Construct a quadrilateral ABCD with AB = 5 cm, BC = 4 cm, CD = 6 cm, DA = 4.5 cm and AC = 7 cm.

topics.title: Area Theorems
topics.summary: Parallelograms on the same base and between the same parallels are equal in area.
notes: Parallelograms on the same base and between the same parallels are equal in area.
A triangle on the same base and between the same parallels as a parallelogram has half its area.
Triangles on the same base and between the same parallels are equal in area.
Triangles with equal areas on the same base have equal altitudes.
A median divides a triangle into two triangles of equal area.
Area of a parallelogram = base × height; area of a triangle = ½ × base × height.
outcomes: Prove that parallelograms on the same base and between the same parallels are equal in area
Use: a triangle has half the area of a parallelogram on the same base and between the same parallels
Solve problems on areas of triangles and parallelograms

lesson.hook: Can two very different-looking parallelograms have exactly the same area?
lesson.example: ABCD is a parallelogram of area 40 cm²; P is any point on CD. Then ΔPAB has area 20 cm².
lesson.activity: Cut a parallelogram from paper, slice off a triangle and move it to form a rectangle of the same base and height.

questions.q: What is the relation between a triangle and a parallelogram on the same base and between the same parallels?
questions.a: The triangle has half the area.

questions.q: A median of a triangle divides it into two parts. How do their areas compare?
questions.a: They are equal.

questions.q: Find the area of a parallelogram with base 12 cm and height 5 cm.
questions.a: 60 cm².

questions.q: Two triangles on the same base have equal areas. What can you say about their heights?
questions.a: They are equal.

lesson.homework: Prove that the diagonals of a parallelogram divide it into four triangles of equal area.

topics.title: Circle: Chord and Arc Properties
topics.summary: The perpendicular from the centre to a chord bisects it; the line from the centre to the mid-point of a chord is perpendicular to it.
notes: The perpendicular from the centre to a chord bisects it; the line from the centre to the mid-point of a chord is perpendicular to it.
Equal chords are equidistant from the centre, and chords equidistant from the centre are equal.
Equal chords subtend equal angles at the centre and cut off equal arcs, and conversely.
There is one and only one circle through three points not in a straight line.
The perpendicular bisectors of two chords meet at the centre.
These properties are proved with congruent triangles and Pythagoras theorem.
outcomes: Prove chord properties of a circle
Use properties of equal chords and arcs
Show that one circle passes through three non-collinear points

lesson.hook: How can you find the centre of a round plate using only a ruler and a set square?
lesson.example: A chord of length 16 cm is 6 cm from the centre. Radius = √(8² + 6²) = 10 cm.
lesson.activity: Pupils draw two chords on a paper circle, fold each to find its perpendicular bisector and see that the folds cross at the centre.

questions.q: A chord of a circle of radius 13 cm is 12 cm from the centre. Find its length.
What can you say about two chords that are equidistant from the centre?
questions.a: They are equal.

questions.q: How many circles pass through three non-collinear points?
questions.a: Exactly one.

questions.q: Does the perpendicular from the centre bisect a chord?
questions.a: Yes.

lesson.homework: Find the centre of a bangle or plate by drawing two chords and their perpendicular bisectors.

topics.title: Statistics
topics.summary: Raw data is as collected; arrayed data is arranged in order; grouped data is organised into class intervals.
notes: Raw data is as collected; arrayed data is arranged in order; grouped data is organised into class intervals.
Discrete variables take separate values (number of children); continuous variables can take any value in a range (height).
A frequency table with tally marks shows how often each value or class occurs.
Class interval, limits, boundaries, class size and class mark (mid-value) describe grouped data; discontinuous classes (10–19, 20–29) are made continuous by adjusting by 0.5.
Mean = sum of observations ÷ number of observations; median is the middle value of arrayed data.
A frequency polygon joins the mid-points of the tops of histogram bars.
outcomes: Classify data as raw, arrayed, grouped, discrete and continuous
Make frequency tables with tally marks and class intervals
Find mean and median of ungrouped data and draw frequency polygons

lesson.hook: The marks of 40 pupils are a jumble of numbers. How do we see the pattern?
lesson.example: Marks 5, 7, 8, 8, 9, 10, 12: mean = 59 ÷ 7 ≈ 8.43; median = 8 (the 4th value).
lesson.activity: Collect the heights of all pupils, group them in 5 cm intervals, make a frequency table and draw a histogram and frequency polygon.

questions.q: Is the number of students in a class discrete or continuous?
questions.a: Discrete.

questions.q: Find the median of 3, 9, 4, 7, 5.
questions.a: Arrange: 3, 4, 5, 7, 9; median = 5.

questions.q: What is the class mark of 20–30?
Convert 10–19, 20–29 into continuous classes.

lesson.homework: Record the daily temperature for two weeks and find the mean and median.

topics.title: Mensuration: Plane Figures
topics.summary: Triangle: ½ × base × height; Heron's formula A = √(s(s − a)(s − b)(s − c)) where s = (a + b + c)/2.
notes: Triangle: ½ × base × height; Heron's formula A = √(s(s − a)(s − b)(s − c)) where s = (a + b + c)/2.
Equilateral triangle of side a: area = (√3/4)a².
Rectangle lw, parallelogram bh, rhombus ½d₁d₂, trapezium ½(sum of parallel sides) × h.
Circle: circumference 2πr, area πr².
A path round a rectangle or a ring (annulus): area = outer area − inner area.
Convert units carefully: 1 m² = 10 000 cm²; 1 hectare = 10 000 m².
outcomes: Find the area and perimeter of triangles (including Heron's formula) and quadrilaterals
Find the area and circumference of circles
Solve problems with inner and outer areas (paths, rings)

lesson.hook: A farmer has a triangular plot with sides 50 m, 60 m and 70 m but no height. How can he find its area?
lesson.activity: Measure the school ground or a table top and calculate its area and the cost of covering it.

questions.q: Find the area of an equilateral triangle of side 6 cm.
Find the area of a trapezium with parallel sides 10 and 6 cm and height 4 cm.
questions.a: 32 cm².

questions.q: Find the area of a ring with outer radius 7 cm and inner radius 3.5 cm.
A rhombus has diagonals 12 cm and 16 cm. Find its area and side.
questions.a: 96 cm²; side 10 cm.

lesson.homework: A 2 m wide path runs round a 30 m × 20 m garden. Find its area and the cost of tiling at ₹50 per m².

topics.title: Mensuration: Cube and Cuboid
topics.summary: Cuboid: volume = lbh; total surface area = 2(lb + bh + hl); lateral surface area = 2h(l + b).
notes: Cuboid: volume = lbh; total surface area = 2(lb + bh + hl); lateral surface area = 2h(l + b).
Cube of side a: volume a³; total surface area 6a²; diagonal a√3.
An open box has no top: subtract one face lb.
For a hollow box or a wall, volume of material = external volume − internal volume.
Volume of any prism = area of cross-section × length.
1 litre = 1000 cm³; 1 m³ = 1000 litres.
outcomes: Find the surface area and volume of cubes and cuboids
Solve problems with internal and external dimensions, open boxes and cost
Use volume = area of cross-section × height

lesson.hook: How much paint does a water tank need, and how much water can it hold?
lesson.example: A tank 2 m × 1.5 m × 1 m holds 3 m³ = 3000 litres of water.
lesson.activity: Measure a chalk box or shoe box, find its volume and surface area, then open it out to check the surface area.

questions.q: Find the volume of a cube of side 4 cm.
questions.a: 64 cm³.

questions.q: Find the total surface area of a cuboid 5 × 4 × 3 cm.
How many litres does a 1 m³ tank hold?
questions.a: 1000 litres.

questions.q: A cube has total surface area 150 cm². Find its side.
questions.a: 5 cm.

lesson.homework: Find how many bricks of 20 cm × 10 cm × 7.5 cm make a wall 10 m long, 3 m high and 25 cm thick.

topics.title: Trigonometric Ratios
topics.summary: For an acute angle θ in a right triangle: sin θ = opposite/hypotenuse, cos θ = adjacent/hypotenuse, tan θ = opposite/adjacent.
notes: For an acute angle θ in a right triangle: sin θ = opposite/hypotenuse, cos θ = adjacent/hypotenuse, tan θ = opposite/adjacent.
Reciprocals: cosec θ = 1/sin θ, sec θ = 1/cos θ, cot θ = 1/tan θ.
The ratios depend only on the angle, not on the size of the triangle.
Given one ratio, draw a triangle, find the third side by Pythagoras and write the others.
tan θ = sin θ / cos θ.
sin θ and cos θ are never more than 1 for acute angles.
outcomes: Define sine, cosine and tangent and their reciprocals in a right triangle
Find all trigonometric ratios from one given ratio
Relate ratios to the sides of a right triangle

lesson.hook: How can surveyors find the height of a tower without climbing it?
lesson.example: If sin A = 3/5, take opposite 3, hypotenuse 5, adjacent 4: cos A = 4/5, tan A = 3/4.
lesson.activity: Pupils draw right triangles with a 30° angle of different sizes and measure sides: the ratios stay the same.

questions.q: If tan θ = 5/12, find sin θ.
What is the reciprocal of cos θ?
questions.a: sec θ.

questions.q: Can sin θ equal 1.5? Why?
questions.a: No — the opposite side cannot exceed the hypotenuse.

questions.q: In a right triangle with legs 8 and 15, find the hypotenuse and cos of the angle opposite 8.

lesson.homework: Given cos A = 12/13, find all the other trigonometric ratios of A.

chapters.title: Trigonometric Ratios of Standard and Complementary Angles

topics.title: Trigonometric Ratios of Standard and Complementary Angles
topics.summary: From an equilateral triangle: sin 30° = ½, cos 30° = √3/2, tan 30° = 1/√3; sin 60° = √3/2, cos 60° = ½, tan 60° = √3.
notes: From an equilateral triangle: sin 30° = ½, cos 30° = √3/2, tan 30° = 1/√3; sin 60° = √3/2, cos 60° = ½, tan 60° = √3.
From an isosceles right triangle: sin 45° = cos 45° = 1/√2, tan 45° = 1.
sin 0° = 0, cos 0° = 1, tan 0° = 0; sin 90° = 1, cos 90° = 0, tan 90° is not defined.
Complementary angles: sin(90° − A) = cos A, cos(90° − A) = sin A, tan(90° − A) = cot A, sec(90° − A) = cosec A.
Use a table of standard values to evaluate expressions.
Right-triangle problems: choose the ratio that links the known side and the unknown side.
outcomes: Find trigonometric ratios of 0°, 30°, 45°, 60° and 90°
Evaluate expressions using these values
Use complementary angle relations and solve simple right-triangle problems

lesson.hook: Why is sin 30° exactly ½, and why is sin 60° equal to cos 30°?
lesson.activity: Make a class chart of the standard values and a memory trick (for sin: √0/2, √1/2, √2/2, √3/2, √4/2).

questions.q: Evaluate 2 sin 30° + tan 45°.
Simplify sin 35° / cos 55°.
Find θ if cos θ = ½ (acute).
A ladder makes 60° with the ground and its foot is 2 m from the wall. Find its length.
questions.a: cos 60° = 2/L, so L = 4 m.

lesson.homework: Evaluate (tan² 60° + sec² 45°)/(cosec² 30°).

topics.title: Coordinate Geometry
topics.summary: The Cartesian plane has an x-axis and a y-axis meeting at the origin (0, 0); a point is an ordered pair (x, y).
notes: The Cartesian plane has an x-axis and a y-axis meeting at the origin (0, 0); a point is an ordered pair (x, y).
The axes divide the plane into four quadrants: (+, +), (−, +), (−, −), (+, −).
In y = mx + c, x is the independent and y the dependent variable; a linear equation gives a straight line.
The solution of two simultaneous linear equations is the point where their lines intersect.
Distance between (x₁, y₁) and (x₂, y₂) = √((x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)²).
Parallel lines have no common point; the equations then have no solution.
outcomes: Plot points on the Cartesian plane and identify quadrants
Solve simultaneous linear equations graphically
Use the distance formula

lesson.hook: How does a map app describe exactly where you are with just two numbers?
lesson.example: Distance between (1, 2) and (4, 6) = √(9 + 16) = 5.
lesson.activity: Draw y = x + 1 and y = −x + 5 on graph paper in pairs; read the meeting point (2, 3) and check it in both equations.

questions.q: In which quadrant is (−3, 4)?
questions.a: The second quadrant.

questions.q: Find the distance between (0, 0) and (6, 8).
What are the coordinates of a point on the y-axis?
Solve graphically: x + y = 4, x − y = 2.
questions.a: Lines meet at (3, 1).

lesson.homework: Show that (1, 1), (4, 5) and (7, 9) lie on a straight line using the distance formula.

topics.title: Goods and Services Tax (GST)
topics.summary: Goods and Services Tax is a tax on supply of goods and services, collected at each stage of sale.
notes: Goods and Services Tax is a tax on supply of goods and services, collected at each stage of sale.
Within a state (intra-state), GST is split equally into CGST (central) and SGST (state); between states (inter-state), IGST is charged.
Rates are slabs such as 5%, 12%, 18% and 28%.
A dealer pays GST on purchases (input tax) and collects GST on sales (output tax); tax payable = output tax − input tax (input tax credit).
The final consumer bears the full tax; the government receives it bit by bit from each dealer.
A tax invoice shows the price, the rate and the amounts of CGST, SGST or IGST.
outcomes: Explain GST: CGST, SGST and IGST, input tax credit and tax invoices
Calculate GST paid and payable along a chain of sales
Find prices including and excluding GST

lesson.hook: A shirt costs ₹1000 plus 12% GST. Who actually pays the tax, and how does it reach the government?
lesson.example: A shopkeeper buys goods for ₹5000 and sells them for ₹6000, GST 12% (intra-state). Input tax ₹600, output tax ₹720, so he pays ₹120: CGST ₹60 and SGST ₹60.
lesson.activity: Pupils prepare a tax invoice for three items from a stationery shop at 12% and 18% GST, splitting CGST and SGST.

questions.q: Find the GST on a ₹2500 item at 18%.
questions.a: ₹450 (CGST ₹225 + SGST ₹225 intra-state).

questions.q: Which tax is charged on a sale from Karnataka to Maharashtra?
questions.a: IGST.

questions.q: A dealer's input tax is ₹300 and output tax is ₹420. How much GST does he pay?
Who ultimately bears the GST?
questions.a: The final consumer.

lesson.homework: Collect a real restaurant or shop bill and check its GST calculation.

topics.title: Banking: Recurring Deposit Accounts
topics.summary: In a recurring deposit (RD) a fixed sum is deposited every month for a fixed period; the bank pays simple interest on it.
notes: In a recurring deposit (RD) a fixed sum is deposited every month for a fixed period; the bank pays simple interest on it.
Interest is calculated as if the equivalent principal for one month were kept: P × n(n + 1)/2 × 1/12.
Interest I = P × n(n + 1)/(2 × 12) × r/100, where P is the monthly instalment, n the number of months and r the rate per annum.
Maturity value = total deposit (P × n) + interest.
The formula can be rearranged to find P, n or r.
Savings bank accounts earn interest on the minimum balance between the 10th and the last day of each month.
outcomes: Explain recurring deposit accounts
Calculate interest and maturity value on a recurring deposit
Find the monthly instalment or time from given data

lesson.hook: If you save ₹500 every month in a bank, how much will you get after two years?
lesson.activity: Pupils compare two RD plans (₹400 for 2 years at 7% and ₹600 for 1 year at 8%) and decide which earns more interest per rupee saved.

questions.q: What is the maturity value of an RD of ₹200 a month for 12 months at 6%?
How much is deposited in total in an RD of ₹1000 for 36 months?
Does an RD earn simple or compound interest (in ICSE problems)?
questions.a: Simple interest.

questions.q: Write the formula for RD interest.

lesson.homework: Find the monthly instalment that gives a maturity value of ₹6325 in 12 months at 10% (answer ₹500).

topics.title: Shares and Dividends
topics.summary: A share is a part of a company's capital; its face (nominal) value is printed on it; its market value is what it sells for.
notes: A share is a part of a company's capital; its face (nominal) value is printed on it; its market value is what it sells for.
At premium: market value > face value; at discount: market value < face value; at par: equal.
Dividend is paid on the face value: dividend = number of shares × face value × rate%.
Number of shares = investment ÷ market value of one share.
Rate of return (yield) = income ÷ investment × 100.
Buying shares at a high market value lowers the real return even if the dividend rate is high.
outcomes: Explain shares, face value, market value, dividend and premium or discount
Calculate income, investment and rate of return
Compare investments

lesson.hook: A company's ₹10 share sells for ₹25. If it pays a 20% dividend, what do you really earn?
lesson.example: Invest ₹5000 in ₹10 shares at ₹25: 200 shares. Dividend 20% of ₹10 = ₹2 per share, income ₹400; return = 400/5000 = 8%.
lesson.activity: Give groups two "companies" with different face values, market prices and dividends; they calculate the return and choose the better investment.

questions.q: What is dividend calculated on?
questions.a: The face value of the shares.

questions.q: How many ₹100 shares at ₹120 can be bought for ₹6000?
questions.a: 50 shares.

questions.q: A ₹50 share sells at ₹40. Is it at a premium or discount?
questions.a: At a discount of ₹10.

questions.q: Find the return on buying ₹100 shares at ₹125 with a 10% dividend.

lesson.homework: Find the income from 300 shares of ₹20 each paying 12% dividend, and the investment needed at ₹30 per share.

topics.title: Linear Inequations
topics.summary: An inequation uses <, >, ≤ or ≥ instead of =.
notes: An inequation uses <, >, ≤ or ≥ instead of =.
Solve like an equation, but when multiplying or dividing both sides by a negative number, reverse the inequality sign.
The solution set depends on the replacement set: natural numbers N, whole numbers W, integers Z or real numbers R.
On the number line, a filled dot includes a point (≤, ≥) and an open dot excludes it (<, >); for real numbers, draw a thick line.
Combined inequations like −2 ≤ x < 3 are solved in parts and the common values taken.
Always check a value from the solution set in the original inequation.
outcomes: Solve linear inequations in one variable
Represent solution sets on the number line
Find solution sets over given replacement sets (N, W, Z, R)

lesson.hook: A lift can carry at most 8 people. How do we write "at most" in mathematics?
lesson.activity: Draw a number line on the floor; pupils stand on the points that belong to a solution set called out by the teacher.

questions.q: Solve 2x − 3 < 7, x ∈ N.
Solve −x > 4, x ∈ R.
What happens to the inequality when both sides are divided by −2?
questions.a: The sign is reversed.

questions.q: Solve −1 < 2x + 1 ≤ 7, x ∈ Z.

lesson.homework: Solve and graph on a number line: 3 − 2x ≥ x − 12, x ∈ R.

topics.title: Quadratic Equations
topics.summary: A quadratic equation has the form ax² + bx + c = 0 (a ≠ 0) and has at most two roots.
notes: A quadratic equation has the form ax² + bx + c = 0 (a ≠ 0) and has at most two roots.
Factorisation: split the middle term, then set each factor equal to zero.
Formula: x = (−b ± √(b² − 4ac)) / 2a.
Discriminant D = b² − 4ac: D > 0 two distinct real roots, D = 0 two equal roots, D < 0 no real roots.
Word problems: choose the unknown, form the equation, solve, and reject roots that make no sense (negative lengths).
Roots can be checked by substituting back.
outcomes: Solve quadratic equations by factorisation and by the formula
Use the discriminant to describe the nature of roots
Solve word problems leading to quadratic equations

lesson.hook: The area of a rectangular plot is 300 m² and its length is 5 m more than its breadth. What are its sides?
lesson.activity: Plot y = x² − 5x + 6 with the grapher and see where it crosses the x-axis; compare with the roots found by factorising.

questions.q: Solve x² − 7x + 12 = 0.
questions.a: x = 3 or 4.

questions.q: Find the discriminant of 2x² + 3x + 5 = 0 and the nature of its roots.
questions.a: D = 9 − 40 = −31 < 0: no real roots.

questions.q: Solve x² − 4x − 1 = 0 by formula.
The product of two consecutive positive integers is 132. Find them.

lesson.homework: A train covers 360 km at a uniform speed; had it been 5 km/h faster it would take 1 hour less. Find its speed (answer 40 km/h).

topics.title: Ratio and Proportion
topics.summary: a : b = c : d means a/b = c/d, so ad = bc (product of extremes = product of means).
notes: a : b = c : d means a/b = c/d, so ad = bc (product of extremes = product of means).
In a : b = b : c, b is the mean proportion (b² = ac) and c the third proportional.
Duplicate ratio of a : b is a² : b²; sub-duplicate √a : √b; triplicate a³ : b³; compound ratio of a : b and c : d is ac : bd.
If a/b = c/d: invertendo b/a = d/c; alternendo a/c = b/d; componendo (a + b)/b = (c + d)/d; dividendo (a − b)/b = (c − d)/d.
Componendo and dividendo together: (a + b)/(a − b) = (c + d)/(c − d).
Setting a/b = c/d = k simplifies many proofs.
outcomes: Use properties of ratio and proportion: continued and mean proportion
Apply componendo, dividendo, alternendo and invertendo
Solve problems with duplicate, triplicate and compound ratios

lesson.hook: If 4 books cost ₹200, what do 7 cost? Proportion answers it — but it can do much more.
lesson.example: Mean proportion of 4 and 16: b² = 64, so b = 8. Third proportional to 2 and 6: 2/6 = 6/c, c = 18.
lesson.activity: Pupils check a recipe scaled for the whole class using proportion and present the new quantities.

questions.q: Find the fourth proportional to 3, 6 and 5.
Find the compound ratio of 2 : 3 and 9 : 4.
If x : y = 3 : 4, find (x + y) : (y − x).
Find the mean proportion between 9 and 25.

lesson.homework: If a/b = c/d, prove that (a² + c²)/(b² + d²) = ac/bd.

topics.title: Remainder and Factor Theorems
topics.summary: Remainder theorem: when f(x) is divided by (x − a), the remainder is f(a).
notes: Remainder theorem: when f(x) is divided by (x − a), the remainder is f(a).
For (ax − b) the remainder is f(b/a).
Factor theorem: (x − a) is a factor of f(x) if and only if f(a) = 0.
To factorise a cubic, find one root by trying factors of the constant term, divide, then factorise the quadratic.
Unknown coefficients can be found from given remainders or factors.
These theorems save time compared with long division.
outcomes: State and use the remainder theorem
State and use the factor theorem
Factorise cubic polynomials completely

lesson.hook: Can you tell whether (x − 2) divides x³ − 3x² + 4 without doing the long division?
lesson.example: f(x) = x³ − 6x² + 11x − 6: f(1) = 0, so (x − 1) is a factor; dividing gives x² − 5x + 6 = (x − 2)(x − 3). So f(x) = (x − 1)(x − 2)(x − 3).
lesson.activity: Pupils test candidate factors ±1, ±2, ±3 of a cubic in teams and race to factorise it completely.

questions.q: Find the remainder when x³ + 2x − 5 is divided by x − 1.
Is (x + 2) a factor of x³ + 8?
Find k if (x − 3) is a factor of x² − kx + 6.
Factorise x³ − 7x + 6.

lesson.homework: Find a and b if x³ + ax² + bx − 6 has factors (x − 1) and (x + 2).

topics.title: Matrices
topics.summary: A matrix is a rectangular arrangement of numbers in rows and columns; order m × n means m rows and n columns.
notes: A matrix is a rectangular arrangement of numbers in rows and columns; order m × n means m rows and n columns.
Types: row, column, square, zero (null), identity (I) and diagonal matrices.
Matrices of the same order are added by adding corresponding elements.
A × B is defined when the number of columns of A equals the number of rows of B; element (i, j) = row i of A · column j of B.
Matrix multiplication is generally not commutative: AB ≠ BA; AI = IA = A.
Matrix equations are solved by comparing corresponding elements.
outcomes: Describe matrices: order, types and equality
Add, subtract and multiply matrices, and multiply by a scalar
Solve simple matrix equations

lesson.hook: A shop records sales of three items on two days in a table. How can such tables be added and multiplied?
lesson.activity: Use a table of prices (column) and quantities bought by three families (rows); multiply to get each family's bill.

questions.q: What is the order of a matrix with 2 rows and 3 columns?
Can a 2 × 3 matrix be multiplied by a 2 × 2 matrix (in that order)?
questions.a: No: 3 columns ≠ 2 rows.

questions.q: What is the identity matrix of order 2?
If [x 2; 3 y] = [5 2; 3 −1], find x and y.

lesson.homework: If A = [2 1; 0 3] and B = [1 0; 2 1], find AB and BA and show they are different.

topics.title: Arithmetic Progression
topics.summary: An arithmetic progression (AP) has a constant difference d between consecutive terms: a, a + d, a + 2d, …
notes: An arithmetic progression (AP) has a constant difference d between consecutive terms: a, a + d, a + 2d, …
nth term: tₙ = a + (n − 1)d.
Sum of n terms: Sₙ = n/2 [2a + (n − 1)d] = n/2 (first + last).
Three terms in AP can be taken as a − d, a, a + d.
If a, b, c are in AP then 2b = a + c.
APs model regular increases: savings, seats in rows, instalments.
outcomes: Recognise an arithmetic progression and find its nth term
Find the sum of n terms of an AP
Solve word problems with APs

lesson.hook: A pupil saves ₹10 in week 1, ₹15 in week 2, ₹20 in week 3… How much after a year?
lesson.activity: Pupils find the number of logs in a pile with 20 at the bottom, 19 above and so on to 5 at the top, by adding and by the formula.

questions.q: Find the 20th term of 3, 7, 11, …
Find the sum of the first 100 natural numbers.
Which term of 5, 8, 11, … is 50?
If 2k + 1, 13 and 5k − 3 are in AP, find k.

lesson.homework: How many three-digit numbers are divisible by 7? (Answer: 128.)

topics.title: Geometric Progression
topics.summary: A geometric progression (GP) has a constant ratio r between consecutive terms: a, ar, ar², …
notes: A geometric progression (GP) has a constant ratio r between consecutive terms: a, ar, ar², …
nth term: tₙ = arⁿ⁻¹.
Sum of n terms: Sₙ = a(rⁿ − 1)/(r − 1) for r > 1, or a(1 − rⁿ)/(1 − r) for r < 1.
Three terms in GP can be taken as a/r, a, ar; if a, b, c are in GP, b² = ac (geometric mean).
GPs model doubling and halving: bacteria, compound growth, bouncing balls.
For r = 1 all terms are equal and Sₙ = na.
outcomes: Recognise a geometric progression and find its nth term
Find the sum of n terms of a GP
Apply GPs to growth problems

lesson.hook: A rumour is told to 3 people, each of whom tells 3 more, and so on. How many know it after 6 rounds?
lesson.example: Rumour: 3 + 9 + 27 + … for 6 rounds: S₆ = 3(3⁶ − 1)/2 = 3 × 728/2 = 1092 people.
lesson.activity: Fold a sheet of paper in half again and again; record the number of layers and see the GP 1, 2, 4, 8, …

questions.q: Find the 8th term of 2, 6, 18, …
Find the sum of 1 + 2 + 4 + … to 10 terms.
Find the geometric mean of 4 and 25.
Which term of 3, 6, 12, … is 384?

lesson.homework: A ball dropped from 16 m bounces back to half its height each time. Find the total distance it travels up to its 4th touch of the ground.

topics.title: Reflection
topics.summary: Reflection in the x-axis: (x, y) → (x, −y); in the y-axis: (x, y) → (−x, y); in the origin: (x, y) → (−x, −y).
notes: Reflection in the x-axis: (x, y) → (x, −y); in the y-axis: (x, y) → (−x, y); in the origin: (x, y) → (−x, −y).
Reflection in x = a: (x, y) → (2a − x, y); in y = b: (x, y) → (x, 2b − y).
A point on the mirror line is its own image — an invariant point.
Reflection preserves size and shape; the mirror line is the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining a point and its image.
Combining reflections: reflection in the x-axis then the y-axis is the same as reflection in the origin.
Graph work: reflect points, join them, and name the figure (e.g. a kite or rhombus).
outcomes: Find the image of a point under reflection in the x-axis, y-axis, origin and lines x = a, y = b
Identify invariant points
Use reflections to find figures and their properties on graph paper

lesson.hook: Your reflection in a mirror is the same distance behind it as you are in front. How does this look with coordinates?
lesson.example: P(3, −2) reflected in the y-axis is (−3, −2); in the line x = 1 it is (2 × 1 − 3, −2) = (−1, −2).
lesson.activity: On graph paper pupils reflect a triangle in both axes and the origin, and colour the four images.

questions.q: Find the image of (4, 5) in the x-axis.
Find the image of (−2, 3) in the origin.
Is (0, 5) invariant under reflection in the y-axis?
questions.a: Yes.

questions.q: Find the image of (5, 2) in the line y = 4.

lesson.homework: A(2, 3) is reflected in the x-axis to B and B in the origin to C. Find B and C and name the single transformation from A to C.

topics.title: Section and Mid-point Formulae
topics.summary: A point dividing A(x₁, y₁) and B(x₂, y₂) internally in the ratio m : n is ((mx₂ + nx₁)/(m + n), (my₂ + ny₁)/(m + n)).
notes: A point dividing A(x₁, y₁) and B(x₂, y₂) internally in the ratio m : n is ((mx₂ + nx₁)/(m + n), (my₂ + ny₁)/(m + n)).
Mid-point: ((x₁ + x₂)/2, (y₁ + y₂)/2).
Centroid of a triangle (where the medians meet): ((x₁ + x₂ + x₃)/3, (y₁ + y₂ + y₃)/3).
The ratio in which the x-axis divides a segment is found by setting the y-coordinate of the point to zero.
Mid-points help find missing vertices of parallelograms (diagonals bisect each other).
Always write the ratio in the order of the points.
outcomes: Use the section formula for internal division
Use the mid-point formula and find coordinates of the centroid
Find the ratio in which a line divides a segment

lesson.hook: Where exactly is the point two-thirds of the way from one town to another on a map grid?
lesson.example: The point dividing A(1, 2) and B(7, 8) in the ratio 1 : 2 is ((7 + 2)/3, (8 + 4)/3) = (3, 4).
lesson.activity: Plot A(0, 0) and B(9, 6) on graph paper and mark the points dividing AB in 1 : 2 and 2 : 1; check with the formula.

questions.q: Find the mid-point of (2, 3) and (8, −1).
Find the centroid of (0, 0), (6, 0) and (0, 9).
In what ratio does the x-axis divide the join of (2, −3) and (5, 6)?
If (4, 5) is the mid-point of (2, 3) and (x, y), find x and y.

lesson.homework: ABCD is a parallelogram with A(1, 2), B(4, 3), C(6, 6). Find D.

topics.title: Equation of a Straight Line
topics.summary: Slope (gradient) m = tan θ = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁), where θ is the angle with the positive x-axis.
notes: Slope (gradient) m = tan θ = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁), where θ is the angle with the positive x-axis.
Slope-intercept form: y = mx + c, where c is the y-intercept.
Point-slope form: y − y₁ = m(x − x₁); two-point form uses the slope of the two points.
Parallel lines have equal slopes; perpendicular lines have slopes whose product is −1.
For ax + by + c = 0, slope = −a/b.
A line parallel to the x-axis has slope 0 (y = k); a line parallel to the y-axis has an undefined slope (x = k).
outcomes: Find the slope of a line and use it to test parallel and perpendicular lines
Write the equation of a line in slope-intercept and two-point forms
Find intercepts and the equation of a line through a point parallel or perpendicular to another

lesson.hook: How steep is a road that rises 3 m for every 50 m? Slope turns steepness into a number.
lesson.activity: Plot y = 2x + 1, y = 2x − 3 and y = −½x + 2 with the grapher; pupils see which are parallel and which perpendicular.

questions.q: Find the slope of 2x − 3y + 6 = 0.
Find the equation of a line with slope −2 and y-intercept 5.
Are y = 3x + 1 and x + 3y = 7 perpendicular?
questions.a: Slopes 3 and −1/3; product −1, so yes.

questions.q: Find the inclination of a line with slope √3.

lesson.homework: Find the equation of the line through (2, 3) perpendicular to 3x + 4y = 12.

topics.title: Similarity
topics.summary: Similar figures have the same shape but not necessarily the same size: corresponding angles are equal and corresponding sides are proportional.
notes: Similar figures have the same shape but not necessarily the same size: corresponding angles are equal and corresponding sides are proportional.
Triangles are similar by AA (two angles equal), SAS (two sides proportional and included angle equal) or SSS (three sides proportional).
Basic proportionality theorem: a line parallel to one side of a triangle divides the other two sides proportionally.
The ratio of the areas of two similar triangles equals the square of the ratio of their corresponding sides.
In a right triangle, the perpendicular from the right angle to the hypotenuse forms two triangles similar to it and to each other.
Scale factor k: lengths multiply by k, areas by k², volumes by k³ — used in maps and models.
outcomes: Define similar figures and state the AA, SAS and SSS similarity conditions
Use the basic proportionality theorem
Relate areas of similar triangles to the squares of corresponding sides; use scale drawings and maps

lesson.hook: How can we find the height of a tree using its shadow and the shadow of a stick?
lesson.example: A 1 m stick casts a 0.8 m shadow while a tree casts a 12 m shadow at the same time. By similar triangles, height = 12 ÷ 0.8 = 15 m.
lesson.activity: Measure the shadows of a stick and a pole outside at the same time and calculate the pole's height.

questions.q: Are congruent triangles also similar?
questions.a: Yes, with scale factor 1.

questions.q: Two similar triangles have sides in the ratio 3 : 5. Find the ratio of their areas.
In ΔABC, DE ∥ BC, AD = 2, DB = 3, AE = 4. Find EC.
A map has scale 1 : 50 000. What real distance is 4 cm on the map?
questions.a: 2 km.

lesson.homework: A model of a building is made to a scale of 1 : 100. If the model's floor area is 20 cm², find the real floor area.

topics.title: Loci
topics.summary: A locus is the path traced by a point that moves according to a given condition.
notes: A locus is the path traced by a point that moves according to a given condition.
Points at a fixed distance from a fixed point: a circle.
Points equidistant from two fixed points: the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining them.
Points equidistant from two intersecting lines: the bisectors of the angles between them.
Points at a fixed distance from a line: two lines parallel to it on both sides.
A point satisfying two conditions lies where the two loci meet (e.g. the circumcentre and incentre of a triangle).
outcomes: Describe a locus as a set of points satisfying a condition
Construct standard loci: fixed distance from a point, equidistant from two points, two lines and a line
Use loci to locate points satisfying two conditions

lesson.hook: A goat is tied to a peg with a 3 m rope. Where can it graze?
lesson.example: The point equidistant from all three vertices of a triangle is where two perpendicular bisectors of its sides meet — the circumcentre.
lesson.activity: On the playground, pupils stand equidistant from two marked points; they form a line — the perpendicular bisector.

questions.q: What is the locus of points 4 cm from a point O?
questions.a: A circle of radius 4 cm with centre O.

questions.q: What is the locus of points equidistant from A and B?
questions.a: The perpendicular bisector of AB.

questions.q: Where is the point equidistant from the three sides of a triangle?
questions.a: At the incentre, where the angle bisectors meet.

questions.q: Describe the locus of the centre of a wheel rolling on a straight road.
questions.a: A line parallel to the road at a distance equal to the radius.

lesson.homework: Construct ΔABC with AB = 6 cm, BC = 5 cm, AC = 4.5 cm; find the point equidistant from A and B and 2 cm from AC.

topics.title: Circles: Angle and Cyclic Properties
topics.summary: The angle subtended by an arc at the centre is double the angle it subtends at any point on the remaining circle.
notes: The angle subtended by an arc at the centre is double the angle it subtends at any point on the remaining circle.
Angles in the same segment are equal.
The angle in a semicircle is a right angle.
Opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral add up to 180°; an exterior angle equals the interior opposite angle.
Equal chords subtend equal angles at the centre and on the circumference.
In problems, mark every known angle and look for isosceles triangles formed by radii.
outcomes: Prove and use angle properties of circles
Prove and use properties of cyclic quadrilaterals
Solve problems with angles in circles

lesson.hook: All the angles at the edge of a circle, standing on the same arc, turn out equal. Why?
lesson.example: In a cyclic quadrilateral ABCD, ∠A = 70°, so ∠C = 110°; if AC is a diameter, ∠ABC = 90°.
lesson.activity: Pupils draw several angles standing on the same arc and measure them, then draw a triangle in a semicircle and measure the angle.

questions.q: The angle at the centre is 120°. Find the angle at the circumference on the same arc.
What is the angle in a semicircle?
In a cyclic quadrilateral, one angle is 85°. Find its opposite angle.
Are angles in the same segment equal?
questions.a: Yes.

lesson.homework: Prove that the angle at the centre is double the angle at the circumference.

topics.title: Tangents and Intersecting Chords
topics.summary: A tangent touches a circle at exactly one point and is perpendicular to the radius at that point.
notes: A tangent touches a circle at exactly one point and is perpendicular to the radius at that point.
The two tangents from an external point are equal in length and subtend equal angles at the centre.
If two chords AB and CD intersect at P (inside or outside the circle), PA × PB = PC × PD.
Tangent-secant: if PT is a tangent and PAB a secant, PT² = PA × PB.
Alternate segment theorem: the angle between a tangent and a chord equals the angle in the alternate segment.
Two circles touching each other have their centres and the point of contact in one line.
outcomes: Prove and use tangent properties: radius ⟂ tangent, equal tangents from an external point
Use the intersecting chords and secant properties
Use the alternate segment theorem

lesson.hook: Why does a bicycle wheel touch the road at only one point, and what makes that point special?
lesson.example: From P, a tangent PT = 12 cm and a secant PAB with PA = 8 cm: PT² = PA × PB → 144 = 8 × PB → PB = 18 cm.
lesson.activity: Pupils draw two tangents from a point to a circle and measure them; then check PA × PB = PC × PD for two intersecting chords.

questions.q: What is the angle between a tangent and the radius at the point of contact?
A tangent from a point 13 cm from the centre of a circle of radius 5 cm. Find its length.
questions.a: 12 cm.

questions.q: Chords AB and CD cut at P inside a circle; PA = 4, PB = 6, PC = 3. Find PD.
State the alternate segment theorem.
questions.a: The angle between a tangent and a chord equals the angle in the alternate segment.

lesson.homework: Prove that the lengths of the tangents drawn from an external point to a circle are equal.

topics.title: Constructions
topics.summary: Tangent at a point on the circle: draw a line perpendicular to the radius at that point.
notes: Tangent at a point on the circle: draw a line perpendicular to the radius at that point.
Tangents from an external point P: bisect OP, draw a circle on OP as diameter; it cuts the circle at the points of contact.
Circumcircle: centre at the meeting point of the perpendicular bisectors of the sides.
Incircle: centre at the meeting point of the angle bisectors; radius is the perpendicular to a side.
Regular hexagon in a circle: step the radius round the circle; its incircle touches the mid-points of the sides.
Show all arcs and write steps; measure and state the required lengths.
outcomes: Construct tangents to a circle from an external point
Construct circumscribed and inscribed circles of a triangle
Construct regular hexagons with circumscribed and inscribed circles

lesson.hook: How do engineers draw a belt that just touches two pulleys?
lesson.example: From P, 8 cm from O on a circle of radius 3 cm, each tangent has length √(64 − 9) = √55 ≈ 7.4 cm — measure to check the construction.
lesson.activity: Pupils construct the circumcircle and incircle of the same triangle and compare the two centres.

questions.q: Where is the centre of the circumcircle of a triangle?
questions.a: Where the perpendicular bisectors of its sides meet.

questions.q: Why does the circle on OP as diameter give the points of contact?
questions.a: The angle in a semicircle is 90°, so the radius is perpendicular to the tangent there.

questions.q: Where is the circumcentre of a right triangle?
questions.a: At the mid-point of the hypotenuse.

questions.q: How is the radius of the incircle found?
questions.a: As the perpendicular distance from the incentre to any side.

lesson.homework: Construct a regular hexagon of side 3.5 cm and its circumscribed circle.

topics.title: Mensuration: Cylinder, Cone and Sphere
topics.summary: Cylinder: curved surface 2πrh, total surface 2πr(r + h), volume πr²h.
notes: Cylinder: curved surface 2πrh, total surface 2πr(r + h), volume πr²h.
Cone: slant height l = √(r² + h²), curved surface πrl, total surface πr(l + r), volume ⅓πr²h.
Sphere: surface 4πr², volume ⁴⁄₃πr³; hemisphere: curved surface 2πr², total 3πr², volume ⅔πr³.
Melting and recasting: the volume stays the same.
Hollow solids: volume of material = outer volume − inner volume.
Combined solids: add volumes; for surface area include only the exposed surfaces.
outcomes: Find the surface area and volume of cylinders, cones and spheres
Solve problems with hollow solids, cost, and melting and recasting
Work with combinations of solids

lesson.hook: How many ice-cream cones can be filled from one cylindrical tub?
lesson.activity: Fill a cone and a cylinder of the same base and height with sand: three cones fill the cylinder, showing V = ⅓πr²h.

questions.q: Find the volume of a sphere of radius 3 cm (π = 3.14).
Find the slant height of a cone with r = 6 cm, h = 8 cm.
questions.a: 10 cm.

questions.q: A metal sphere of radius 6 cm is melted into a cylinder of radius 4 cm. Find its height.
Find the total surface area of a hemisphere of radius 7 cm.

lesson.homework: A toy is a cone on a hemisphere of radius 3.5 cm; the total height is 15.5 cm. Find its volume.

topics.title: Trigonometric Identities
topics.summary: From a right triangle and Pythagoras: sin²A + cos²A = 1 (for 0° ≤ A ≤ 90°).
notes: From a right triangle and Pythagoras: sin²A + cos²A = 1 (for 0° ≤ A ≤ 90°).
Dividing by cos²A: 1 + tan²A = sec²A; dividing by sin²A: 1 + cot²A = cosec²A.
tan A = sin A/cos A, cot A = cos A/sin A.
To prove an identity, start from the more complex side and simplify to the other; convert to sines and cosines if stuck.
Useful forms: 1 − sin²A = cos²A, sec²A − tan²A = 1.
Never "move terms across" as if solving an equation — an identity is proved, not solved.
outcomes: Prove the identities sin²A + cos²A = 1, 1 + tan²A = sec²A, 1 + cot²A = cosec²A
Use them to simplify expressions and prove further identities
Find ratios from one given ratio

lesson.hook: Is sin²A + cos²A really 1 for every angle? Why?
lesson.example: Prove (1 − cos²A) cosec²A = 1: (1 − cos²A) = sin²A, and sin²A × 1/sin²A = 1.
lesson.activity: Check sin²A + cos²A = 1 with a calculator for five angles chosen by the class.

questions.q: Simplify (sec²A − 1) cot²A.
questions.a: tan²A × cot²A = 1.

questions.q: If sin A = 0.6, find cos A (acute).
Prove sec A − tan A = 1/(sec A + tan A).
questions.a: Multiply: (sec A − tan A)(sec A + tan A) = sec²A − tan²A = 1.

questions.q: Simplify cos A tan A.
questions.a: sin A.

lesson.homework: Prove: (sin A + cos A)² + (sin A − cos A)² = 2.

topics.title: Heights and Distances
topics.summary: The angle of elevation is measured upward from the horizontal to an object; the angle of depression downward from the horizontal.
notes: The angle of elevation is measured upward from the horizontal to an object; the angle of depression downward from the horizontal.
The angle of elevation from A to B equals the angle of depression from B to A (alternate angles).
Draw a clear figure, mark the right angle and the known side, and choose tan, sin or cos accordingly.
For two positions or two objects, set up two right triangles with a common side and solve together.
Use tables (or standard values) for the ratios; give answers to the required accuracy.
Applications: heights of towers, widths of rivers, distances of ships.
outcomes: Explain angles of elevation and depression
Solve heights and distances problems with one or two right triangles
Use trigonometric tables

lesson.hook: From a boat, a lighthouse top is seen at 30°. How far away is the boat if the lighthouse is 50 m tall?
lesson.activity: Make a clinometer from a protractor, straw and thread; pupils measure the angle of elevation of a flag-pole top and calculate its height.

questions.q: What is the angle of depression?
questions.a: The angle below the horizontal from the eye to an object below.

questions.q: A kite string is 100 m long at 60° to the ground. Find the height.
The shadow of a 10 m pole is 10√3 m. Find the Sun's elevation.
Why are the angles of elevation and depression between two points equal?
questions.a: They are alternate angles between parallel horizontal lines.

lesson.homework: From the top of a 60 m building, the angles of depression of the top and foot of a tower are 30° and 60°. Find the tower's height (answer 40 m).

topics.title: Statistics
topics.summary: Mean of grouped data: direct Σfx/Σf; short-cut A + Σfd/Σf; step-deviation A + (Σft/Σf) × i.
notes: Mean of grouped data: direct Σfx/Σf; short-cut A + Σfd/Σf; step-deviation A + (Σft/Σf) × i.
Median is the middle value; for grouped data find the median class; from a cumulative frequency curve (ogive) read the value at n/2.
Quartiles Q₁ and Q₃ are read at n/4 and 3n/4; the inter-quartile range is Q₃ − Q₁.
Mode is the most frequent value; for grouped data it is estimated from a histogram.
A less-than ogive plots cumulative frequency against the upper class boundaries.
Choose the average that best represents the data: the mean is affected by extreme values, the median is not.
outcomes: Find mean, median and mode of raw and grouped data
Use direct, short-cut and step-deviation methods for the mean
Draw histograms and ogives and read median and quartiles from an ogive

lesson.hook: The class average is 72. Is that the "typical" mark? Mean, median and mode can tell different stories.
lesson.activity: Collect the pocket money or travel time of all pupils, group it, and draw a histogram and ogive; read the median and quartiles.

questions.q: Find the mode of 2, 3, 3, 5, 3, 7, 5.
What is plotted on the x-axis of a less-than ogive?
questions.a: The upper class boundaries.

questions.q: Find the median of 4, 8, 6, 10, 12, 14.
Which average is not affected by a few very large values?
questions.a: The median.

lesson.homework: Draw an ogive for given marks and find the median, Q₁, Q₃ and the number of pupils who scored above 60.

topics.title: Probability
topics.summary: A random experiment has known possible outcomes but an unpredictable result (tossing a coin, rolling a die).
notes: A random experiment has known possible outcomes but an unpredictable result (tossing a coin, rolling a die).
The sample space is the set of all possible outcomes; an event is a subset of it.
Probability of an event E = number of favourable outcomes ÷ total number of equally likely outcomes.
0 ≤ P(E) ≤ 1; an impossible event has probability 0, a sure event 1.
P(E) + P(not E) = 1.
A deck has 52 cards: 4 suits of 13, 26 red and 26 black, 12 face cards.
outcomes: Explain random experiments, outcomes, sample space and events
Calculate the probability of simple events
Use P(E) + P(not E) = 1

lesson.hook: What are the chances of drawing a king from a pack of 52 cards?
lesson.activity: Use the probability virtual lab to toss a coin 1000 times; compare the experimental probability with ½.

questions.q: A die is rolled. Find the probability of an even number.
Two coins are tossed. Find the probability of getting at least one head.
A bag has 3 red and 5 blue balls. Find P(red).
If P(E) = 0.35, find P(not E).

lesson.homework: Two dice are thrown. List the sample space and find the probability that the sum is 7.

topics.title: Measurements and Experimentation
topics.summary: Every measurement is a number with a unit; SI base units include the metre (m), kilogram (kg), second (s), kelvin (K) and ampere (A).
notes: Every measurement is a number with a unit; SI base units include the metre (m), kilogram (kg), second (s), kelvin (K) and ampere (A).
Least count is the smallest value an instrument can measure; a smaller least count gives a more accurate reading.
Vernier callipers: least count = value of 1 main-scale division ÷ number of vernier divisions; reading = main-scale reading + (coinciding vernier division × LC).
Screw gauge: least count = pitch ÷ number of circular-scale divisions; a zero error is subtracted with its sign to correct the reading.
A simple pendulum has time period T = 2π√(l/g); T² is directly proportional to l, so the graph of l against T² is a straight line through the origin.
Frequency is the number of oscillations per second: f = 1/T, measured in hertz (Hz).
outcomes: Use SI units and their symbols correctly, and convert between SI, cgs and fps units
Read a Vernier callipers and a screw gauge, including least count and zero error
Find the time period of a simple pendulum and relate it to its length

lesson.hook: A tailor measures cloth to the nearest centimetre, but an engineer checking a wire needs a hundredth of a millimetre. How do instruments measure so finely?
lesson.example: A Vernier callipers has 1 MSD = 1 mm and 10 vernier divisions, so LC = 0.1 mm. Main scale reads 2.3 cm and the 6th vernier division coincides: diameter = 2.3 + 6 × 0.01 = 2.36 cm.
lesson.activity: Time 20 oscillations of a pendulum for five different lengths (50–150 cm). Work out T and T² each time and plot l against T² on the board.

questions.q: What is the least count of a screw gauge with pitch 1 mm and 100 circular divisions?
Why is the time for 20 oscillations measured instead of one?
questions.a: It reduces the error of starting and stopping the watch; T = total time ÷ 20.

questions.q: A pendulum's length is made four times. What happens to its time period?
questions.a: T ∝ √l, so T doubles.

questions.q: Write the SI units of mass, length and temperature.
questions.a: Kilogram (kg), metre (m) and kelvin (K).

lesson.homework: Make a pendulum with a thread and a stone. Measure its time period for two lengths and check whether T² ÷ l stays nearly the same.

topics.title: Motion in One Dimension
topics.summary: A scalar has only magnitude (distance, speed, time); a vector has magnitude and direction (displacement, velocity, acceleration).
notes: A scalar has only magnitude (distance, speed, time); a vector has magnitude and direction (displacement, velocity, acceleration).
Speed = distance ÷ time; velocity = displacement ÷ time. Acceleration = change in velocity ÷ time; a negative acceleration is retardation.
On a distance-time graph the slope gives speed; a straight line means uniform speed.
On a velocity-time graph the slope gives acceleration and the area under the graph gives the displacement.
For uniform acceleration: v = u + at, S = ut + ½at², S = ½(u + v)t and v² = u² + 2aS.
A body falling freely near the Earth has acceleration g ≈ 9.8 m s⁻² downwards.
outcomes: Tell scalar and vector quantities apart, and distance from displacement
Read distance-time and velocity-time graphs and use their slopes and areas
Derive and use the three equations of uniformly accelerated motion

lesson.hook: Two friends walk from home to school: one goes straight, one goes round the market. They cover different distances — do they have the same displacement?
lesson.example: A car moving at 10 m/s accelerates at 2 m/s² for 5 s. v = 10 + 2 × 5 = 20 m/s; S = 10 × 5 + ½ × 2 × 25 = 75 m.
lesson.exampleTex: v = u + at,\quad S = ut + \tfrac12 at^2,\quad v^2 = u^2 + 2aS
lesson.activity: Draw a velocity-time graph for a bus: speeding up for 10 s, steady for 20 s, braking for 5 s. Pupils find the acceleration in each part and the total distance from the area.

questions.q: Is speed a scalar or a vector?
questions.a: A scalar: it has no direction.

questions.q: What does the area under a velocity-time graph give?
questions.a: The displacement.

questions.q: A body starts from rest with acceleration 3 m/s². How far does it go in 4 s?
Can a body have zero velocity but non-zero acceleration? Give an example.
questions.a: Yes — a ball thrown up at its highest point.

lesson.homework: Derive v² = u² + 2aS from the other two equations of motion.

topics.title: Laws of Motion
topics.summary: Contact forces act on touching bodies (friction, normal reaction, tension); non-contact forces act at a distance (gravitational, electric, magnetic).
notes: Contact forces act on touching bodies (friction, normal reaction, tension); non-contact forces act at a distance (gravitational, electric, magnetic).
First law: a body stays at rest or in uniform motion in a straight line unless an external force acts on it. The tendency to keep its state is inertia; more mass means more inertia.
Linear momentum p = mv. Second law: the rate of change of momentum equals the applied force, F = Δp ÷ Δt = ma.
The SI unit of force is the newton (N): 1 N gives a 1 kg mass an acceleration of 1 m s⁻²; the cgs unit is the dyne (1 N = 10⁵ dyne).
Third law: to every action there is an equal and opposite reaction; action and reaction act on different bodies, so they never cancel.
Gravitational units: 1 kgf = 9.8 N is the force with which the Earth pulls a 1 kg mass.
outcomes: Classify forces as contact and non-contact forces
State Newton's three laws of motion and explain inertia and momentum
Use F = ma and F = Δp ÷ Δt with the equations of motion

lesson.hook: Why do passengers in a bus fall forward when the driver brakes suddenly?
lesson.example: A 1200 kg car speeds up from 5 m/s to 15 m/s in 4 s. a = (15 − 5) ÷ 4 = 2.5 m/s², so F = 1200 × 2.5 = 3000 N.
lesson.activity: Coin on a card on a glass: flick the card away; the coin drops into the glass. Then push two skateboards (or two pupils on a smooth floor) apart to show action and reaction.

questions.q: Why does a gun recoil when fired?
questions.a: The bullet is pushed forward (action); the gun is pushed back equally (reaction).

questions.q: Define momentum and give its SI unit.
questions.a: p = mv; unit kg m s⁻¹.

questions.q: A force of 10 N acts on a 2 kg body. Find its acceleration.
questions.a: a = F ÷ m = 5 m s⁻².

questions.q: Name two non-contact forces.
questions.a: Gravitational and magnetic force (also electric).

lesson.homework: List five situations at home or on the road that show inertia, and say which law each one illustrates.

topics.title: Gravitation
topics.summary: Every body attracts every other body with a force F = G m₁m₂ ÷ r²: directly proportional to the product of the masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them.
notes: Every body attracts every other body with a force F = G m₁m₂ ÷ r²: directly proportional to the product of the masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them.
G is the universal gravitational constant, 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻²; the force is tiny for everyday objects but large for planets.
Gravity is the Earth's pull on bodies near it; it gives every freely falling body the same acceleration g ≈ 9.8 m s⁻², whatever its mass (ignoring air resistance).
Mass is the quantity of matter (kg), the same everywhere; weight is the force of gravity on it, W = mg (N), and changes from place to place.
Gravitation keeps the Moon moving round the Earth and the planets round the Sun, and causes tides.
Weight is measured with a spring balance; mass with a beam (physical) balance.
outcomes: State Newton's law of universal gravitation and explain its importance
Explain acceleration due to gravity and free fall
Compare mass and weight, and use gravitational units of force

lesson.hook: An apple falls to the ground, yet the Moon does not fall onto the Earth. Is the same force acting on both?
lesson.example: A 50 kg pupil weighs W = mg = 50 × 9.8 = 490 N (= 50 kgf) on the Earth; on the Moon, where g is about 1.6 m s⁻², the weight is about 80 N but the mass is still 50 kg.
lesson.activity: Drop a crumpled paper ball and a flat sheet from the same height, then two crumpled balls of different sizes. Discuss why air resistance, not mass, makes the flat sheet slow.

questions.q: How does the gravitational force change if the distance between two masses is doubled?
questions.a: It becomes one-fourth.

questions.q: Why does mass not change on the Moon while weight does?
questions.a: Mass is the amount of matter; weight depends on the Moon's smaller pull (g).

questions.q: What is the weight of a 2 kg bag in newtons?
Name two effects of gravitation other than falling bodies.
questions.a: The Moon's orbit round the Earth, and ocean tides.

lesson.homework: Find your weight in newtons and in kgf, and estimate what it would be on the Moon.

topics.title: Pressure in Fluids
topics.summary: Thrust is the total force acting normally on a surface; pressure = thrust ÷ area, measured in pascal (1 Pa = 1 N m⁻²).
notes: Thrust is the total force acting normally on a surface; pressure = thrust ÷ area, measured in pascal (1 Pa = 1 N m⁻²).
In a liquid, pressure increases with depth: p = hρg, where h is the depth and ρ the density; it acts equally in all directions at a point.
Pascal's law: pressure applied to an enclosed liquid is transmitted equally to every part of it — the principle of the hydraulic press and hydraulic brakes.
The air above us exerts atmospheric pressure, about 1.013 × 10⁵ Pa at sea level (76 cm of mercury).
Atmospheric pressure decreases with altitude; a falling barometer reading can warn of stormy weather, and an altimeter uses pressure to show height.
Everyday results: broad dam bases, divers' suits, sucking a drink through a straw, and nose bleeding at high altitudes.
outcomes: Distinguish thrust from pressure and use p = hρg for liquids
State Pascal's law and explain how pressure is transmitted in liquids
Explain atmospheric pressure, its measurement and its change with altitude

lesson.hook: Why is a dam built thicker at the bottom than at the top?
lesson.example: At 10 m depth in water (ρ = 1000 kg m⁻³), extra pressure p = hρg = 10 × 1000 × 9.8 = 98 000 Pa — nearly one extra atmosphere.
lesson.activity: Punch three holes at different heights in a tall plastic bottle and fill it with water. The jet from the lowest hole goes farthest: pressure rises with depth.

questions.q: Why do camels have broad feet for walking on sand?
questions.a: A larger area reduces the pressure on the sand, so they do not sink.

questions.q: State Pascal's law.
questions.a: Pressure applied to an enclosed liquid is transmitted undiminished in all directions.

questions.q: What happens to atmospheric pressure as we climb a mountain?
questions.a: It decreases.

questions.q: Find the pressure due to a 2 m column of water.

lesson.homework: Draw and label a hydraulic press and explain how a small force on the narrow piston lifts a heavy load.

chapters.title: Upthrust in Fluids, Archimedes' Principle and Floatation

topics.title: Upthrust in Fluids, Archimedes' Principle and Floatation
topics.summary: A fluid pushes up on any body immersed in it; this upward force is upthrust or buoyancy (F_B).
notes: A fluid pushes up on any body immersed in it; this upward force is upthrust or buoyancy (F_B).
Archimedes' principle: a body wholly or partly immersed in a fluid loses weight equal to the weight of the fluid it displaces.
If F_B < W the body sinks; if F_B = W it floats; a body denser than the fluid sinks, a less dense body floats.
Relative density = density of substance ÷ density of water = weight in air ÷ loss of weight in water; it has no unit.
Principle of floatation: a floating body displaces fluid equal to its own weight; the fraction immersed = density of body ÷ density of liquid.
