A ship floats because its hollow shape displaces a large volume of water; a submarine sinks or rises by filling or emptying ballast tanks.
outcomes: Explain buoyancy (upthrust) and the three cases of a body in a fluid
State Archimedes' principle and find relative density by experiment
State the principle of floatation and apply it to ships, submarines and icebergs

lesson.hook: A steel needle sinks in water, yet a steel ship weighing thousands of tonnes floats. Why?
lesson.example: A stone weighs 60 gf in air and 40 gf in water. Loss of weight = 20 gf, so relative density = 60 ÷ 20 = 3.
lesson.activity: Hang a stone from a spring balance, lower it into a full overflow can and weigh the water collected: the loss of weight equals the weight of water displaced.

questions.q: Why does an iceberg float with only a small part above water?
questions.a: Ice (density about 0.9 g cm⁻³) is only a little less dense than sea water, so most of it must be under water to displace its own weight.

questions.q: What is the SI unit of relative density?
questions.a: It has no unit; it is a ratio.

questions.q: A body weighs 10 N in air and 6 N in water. Find the upthrust.
How does a submarine dive?
questions.a: It lets water into its ballast tanks, so its weight becomes more than the upthrust.

lesson.homework: Put an egg in a glass of water, then keep adding salt and stirring. Record when the egg rises and explain why.

topics.title: Heat and Temperature
topics.summary: Heat is a form of energy that flows from a hotter body to a colder one; its SI unit is the joule (J). Temperature measures how hot a body is (°C or K).
notes: Heat is a form of energy that flows from a hotter body to a colder one; its SI unit is the joule (J). Temperature measures how hot a body is (°C or K).
Most substances expand on heating and contract on cooling; the particles move faster and further apart.
Water behaves unusually: when cooled from 4 °C to 0 °C it expands instead of contracting. This is its anomalous expansion.
Water is densest (and has the least volume) at 4 °C. Graphs of volume against temperature show a minimum at 4 °C; density shows a maximum there.
In winter the cold top water above 4 °C sinks until the whole lake is at 4 °C; colder water then stays on top and freezes, and the ice (a poor conductor) protects the water below.
The same expansion on freezing bursts water pipes in winter and cracks rocks in cold climates.
outcomes: Distinguish heat from temperature and use the joule as the unit of heat
Explain the anomalous expansion of water and its effect on aquatic life
Read the graph of volume and density of water against temperature

resources.title: Melting point of ice and boiling point of water
Specific heat by the method of mixtures

lesson.hook: In very cold countries a lake freezes on top, yet fish stay alive in the water below. How?
lesson.example: A kilogram of water at 4 °C occupies 1000 cm³; the same water frozen into ice occupies about 1090 cm³ — which is why a full, sealed bottle of water cracks in the freezer.
lesson.activity: Draw the volume-temperature graph of water from 0 °C to 10 °C with the class; mark the minimum at 4 °C and discuss what it means for a pond in winter.

questions.q: At what temperature is water densest?
questions.a: At 4 °C.

questions.q: Why do water pipes burst in severe winter?
questions.a: Water expands when it freezes, pushing the pipe apart.

questions.q: Give the SI units of heat and temperature.
questions.a: Joule and kelvin.

questions.q: Why does ice float on water?
questions.a: Ice is less dense than water because water expands on freezing.

lesson.homework: Write a paragraph on how the anomalous expansion of water helps fish survive winter in a frozen lake.

chapters.title: Energy Flow, Energy Sources and Global Warming

topics.title: Energy Flow, Energy Sources and Global Warming
topics.summary: Green plants trap solar energy by photosynthesis; the energy then flows along food chains, and only about 10% passes to each next level.
notes: Green plants trap solar energy by photosynthesis; the energy then flows along food chains, and only about 10% passes to each next level.
Renewable sources (solar, wind, hydro, tidal, biomass, geothermal) are replaced by nature; non-renewable sources (coal, petroleum, natural gas, nuclear fuel) are limited.
Burning fossil fuels releases carbon dioxide; with methane and water vapour, it traps infrared radiation from the Earth's surface — the greenhouse effect.
The natural greenhouse effect keeps the Earth warm enough for life; extra greenhouse gases cause global warming.
Consequences of global warming: melting glaciers and polar ice, rising sea levels, changing rainfall and more extreme weather.
We can reduce it by saving energy, using public transport and renewable sources, and planting and protecting forests.
outcomes: Trace energy flow through food chains and explain its importance
Compare renewable and non-renewable energy sources
Explain the greenhouse effect, global warming and ways to reduce it

lesson.hook: Almost all the energy we use — food, wood, petrol — began as sunlight. How does it reach us?
lesson.example: In a grass → deer → tiger chain, if grass stores 10 000 J, the deer gets about 1000 J and the tiger about 100 J — which is why there are far fewer tigers than deer.
lesson.activity: Keep two thermometers in the sun, one inside a closed transparent jar. After 20 minutes compare them: the jar traps heat, like greenhouse gases do.

questions.q: Name two renewable and two non-renewable energy sources.
questions.a: Solar and wind; coal and petroleum.

questions.q: Which gas contributes most to the extra greenhouse effect from human activity?
questions.a: Carbon dioxide.

questions.q: Why does energy decrease at each step of a food chain?
questions.a: Most of it is used in life processes and lost as heat.

questions.q: Give two effects of global warming.
questions.a: Melting glaciers and rising sea level (also changes in rainfall).

lesson.homework: Make a list of five ways your family can save energy at home, and estimate which one saves the most.

topics.title: Reflection of Light
topics.summary: Laws of reflection: the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, and the incident ray, the normal and the reflected ray lie in one plane.
notes: Laws of reflection: the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, and the incident ray, the normal and the reflected ray lie in one plane.
A plane mirror forms a virtual, erect image, the same size as the object, as far behind the mirror as the object is in front, and laterally inverted.
Regular reflection from smooth surfaces gives clear images; diffuse reflection from rough surfaces lets us see objects from every direction.
Two mirrors at an angle θ form n = (360 ÷ θ) − 1 images when 360 ÷ θ is even; two parallel mirrors form many images.
A periscope uses two plane mirrors at 45° to see over obstacles; mirrors are also used in kaleidoscopes and at road bends.
When a mirror turns by an angle θ, the reflected ray turns by 2θ.
outcomes: State the laws of reflection and verify them
Describe the image formed by a plane mirror and by two mirrors at an angle
Draw ray diagrams for images in a plane mirror

resources.title: Focal length of a convex lens and a concave mirror

lesson.hook: Why does the word AMBULANCE appear reversed on the front of an ambulance?
lesson.example: Two mirrors at 60°: 360 ÷ 60 = 6, so the number of images = 6 − 1 = 5.
lesson.activity: Place two mirrors hinged with tape and a coin between them. Change the angle (90°, 60°, 45°) and count the images; compare with the formula.

questions.q: State the two laws of reflection.
questions.a: i = r; the incident ray, reflected ray and normal lie in the same plane.

questions.q: How far is the image of a person standing 2 m in front of a plane mirror from the person?
What is lateral inversion?
questions.a: Left and right are interchanged in the image.

questions.q: How many images are formed by two mirrors at 90°?

lesson.homework: Make a simple periscope from a long carton and two small mirrors, and draw its ray diagram.

topics.title: Spherical Mirrors
topics.summary: A spherical mirror is part of a hollow sphere: concave if it reflects from the inside surface, convex if from the outside.
notes: A spherical mirror is part of a hollow sphere: concave if it reflects from the inside surface, convex if from the outside.
Pole (P), centre of curvature (C), radius of curvature (R) and principal focus (F); focal length f = R ÷ 2.
Rays parallel to the principal axis pass through F after reflection from a concave mirror (or appear to come from F for a convex mirror); a ray through C returns along itself.
A concave mirror forms a real, inverted image when the object is beyond F, and a virtual, erect, magnified image when the object is between P and F.
A convex mirror always forms a virtual, erect, diminished image behind the mirror, and gives a wide field of view.
Uses: concave — shaving mirrors, dentists' mirrors, torch and headlight reflectors; convex — rear-view mirrors and security mirrors.
outcomes: Describe concave and convex mirrors with pole, centre of curvature, principal focus and focal length
Draw ray diagrams for images in spherical mirrors
State the uses of concave and convex mirrors

resources.title: Focal length of a convex lens and a concave mirror

lesson.hook: Why do shops and ATMs use a small convex mirror in a corner, while a dentist uses a concave one?
lesson.example: A concave mirror has R = 30 cm, so f = 15 cm. An object 10 cm from it is between P and F: the image is virtual, erect and larger — as in a shaving mirror.
lesson.activity: Use a concave mirror to focus the image of a distant window on a sheet of paper; the distance from mirror to paper is roughly its focal length.

questions.q: What is the relation between focal length and radius of curvature?
Which mirror is used as a rear-view mirror, and why?
questions.a: A convex mirror: it gives an erect image and a wide field of view.

questions.q: Where should an object be placed for a concave mirror to give a virtual, magnified image?
questions.a: Between the pole and the principal focus.

questions.q: Can a convex mirror form a real image?
questions.a: No, its image is always virtual.

lesson.homework: Draw ray diagrams for a concave mirror with the object beyond C, at C and between P and F, and describe each image.

topics.title: Propagation of Sound Waves
topics.summary: Sound is produced by vibrating bodies — a guitar string, a drum skin, our vocal cords.
notes: Sound is produced by vibrating bodies — a guitar string, a drum skin, our vocal cords.
Sound needs a material medium; it cannot travel through a vacuum (bell-jar experiment).
In air, sound travels as a longitudinal wave: particles vibrate along the direction of travel, forming compressions and rarefactions.
Wave speed v = f λ, where f is the frequency and λ the wavelength; sound travels at about 330 m s⁻¹ in air, faster in water and fastest in solids.
Humans hear roughly 20 Hz to 20 kHz; below 20 Hz is infrasonic (elephants, earthquakes), above 20 kHz ultrasonic (bats, dolphins).
Ultrasound is used in medical scanning, cleaning delicate parts, and SONAR to find the depth of the sea.
outcomes: Explain that sound is produced by vibrations and needs a medium
Describe sound waves as longitudinal waves with compressions and rarefactions
Relate wavelength, frequency and speed, and classify infrasonic, audible and ultrasonic sound

lesson.hook: Astronauts on the Moon talk by radio even when standing side by side. Why can't they just speak?
lesson.example: A sound of frequency 330 Hz in air (v = 330 m s⁻¹) has wavelength λ = v ÷ f = 330 ÷ 330 = 1 m.
lesson.activity: Stretch a slinky on the floor and push one end back and forth: pupils see compressions and rarefactions travelling along it.

questions.q: Why can't sound travel through space?
questions.a: There is no medium (air) in a vacuum to carry the vibrations.

questions.q: What is the range of human hearing?
questions.a: About 20 Hz to 20 000 Hz.

questions.q: A wave has frequency 500 Hz and wavelength 0.66 m. Find its speed.
Give two uses of ultrasound.
questions.a: Medical scanning and SONAR (also cleaning small parts).

lesson.homework: Find out how bats use ultrasound to find their way in the dark and write five lines on it.

topics.title: Current Electricity
topics.summary: An electric current is a flow of charge; it flows only in a closed circuit. Current I = charge ÷ time, measured in ampere (A).
notes: An electric current is a flow of charge; it flows only in a closed circuit. Current I = charge ÷ time, measured in ampere (A).
Potential difference (voltage) between two points drives the current; it is measured in volt (V) with a voltmeter connected in parallel.
An ammeter measures current and is connected in series; a key (switch) opens or closes the circuit.
Resistance opposes current and is measured in ohm (Ω); conductors (metals) have low resistance, insulators (rubber, plastic) very high.
Cells in series give a larger voltage; bulbs in parallel each get the full voltage and stay lit if one fuses.
Standard circuit symbols make diagrams clear: cell, battery, key, bulb, resistor, ammeter, voltmeter.
outcomes: Draw a simple circuit with a cell, key, bulb, ammeter and voltmeter using standard symbols
Explain current, potential difference and resistance and their units
Tell conductors from insulators and connect cells and bulbs in series and parallel

lesson.hook: A torch lights only when its switch is pressed. What exactly does the switch complete?
lesson.example: A charge of 30 C flows through a bulb in 1 minute: I = 30 ÷ 60 = 0.5 A.
lesson.activity: Build a circuit with two cells, a key and two bulbs, first in series and then in parallel; remove one bulb each time and see what happens to the other.

questions.q: How is an ammeter connected in a circuit?
questions.a: In series.

questions.q: Why are household bulbs connected in parallel?
questions.a: Each gets the full voltage and can be switched independently; one failing does not switch off the others.

questions.q: Name the unit of resistance.
questions.a: Ohm (Ω).

questions.q: Give two examples of insulators.
questions.a: Rubber and plastic (also dry wood, glass).

lesson.homework: Draw the circuit diagram of a torch using standard symbols.

topics.title: Magnetism
topics.summary: A magnet attracts iron, nickel and cobalt; like poles repel and unlike poles attract.
notes: A magnet attracts iron, nickel and cobalt; like poles repel and unlike poles attract.
A magnetic material placed near a magnet becomes a magnet itself — induced magnetism; induction comes before attraction.
The Earth behaves like a huge magnet whose magnetic south pole lies near the geographic north; a freely suspended magnet (compass) points north-south.
Field lines run from the north pole to the south pole outside a magnet; at a neutral point the magnet's field and the Earth's field cancel.
A current in a coil wound round a soft iron core makes an electromagnet; its strength grows with the current and the number of turns, and it can be switched off.
Electromagnets are used in electric bells, cranes that lift scrap iron, loudspeakers and MRI machines.
outcomes: Explain induced magnetism and the magnetic field of the Earth
Describe a compass and the neutral points of a magnet
Make an electromagnet and list its uses

resources.title: Magnetic field of a bar magnet

lesson.hook: Why does an iron nail brought near a magnet start picking up pins itself?
lesson.example: Doubling the turns of wire on an electromagnet (same current) roughly doubles the number of pins it can lift.
lesson.activity: Wind 50 turns of insulated wire on an iron nail, connect a cell and count the pins it lifts; repeat with 100 turns and with two cells.

questions.q: What is induced magnetism?
questions.a: Magnetism produced in a magnetic material when it is near a magnet.

questions.q: Why is soft iron used for the core of an electromagnet?
questions.a: It becomes magnetised and demagnetised easily.

questions.q: Give two ways to make an electromagnet stronger.
questions.a: Increase the current, or increase the number of turns.

questions.q: In which direction does a freely suspended magnet rest?
questions.a: Along the north-south direction.

lesson.homework: List three devices at home that contain an electromagnet and say what the electromagnet does in each.

topics.title: Force: Moments and Circular Motion
topics.summary: The turning effect of a force is its moment: moment = force × perpendicular distance from the pivot (N m); anticlockwise moments are taken as positive by convention.
notes: The turning effect of a force is its moment: moment = force × perpendicular distance from the pivot (N m); anticlockwise moments are taken as positive by convention.
Principle of moments: a body is in equilibrium when the sum of anticlockwise moments about the pivot equals the sum of clockwise moments.
Two equal and opposite parallel forces not in one line form a couple; its moment = one force × the distance between them (e.g. turning a steering wheel or tap).
The centre of gravity is the point through which the whole weight of a body acts; for a uniform rod it is at the middle.
A body is in static equilibrium when the resultant force and resultant moment on it are both zero.
In uniform circular motion the speed is constant but the direction changes, so the body accelerates towards the centre; the force needed is centripetal force. Centrifugal force is not a real force.
outcomes: Define the moment of a force and use the principle of moments
Explain couple, centre of gravity and conditions of equilibrium
Describe uniform circular motion and centripetal force

lesson.hook: Why is a door handle fixed at the edge of the door, far from the hinges?
lesson.example: A metre rule is pivoted at its middle. A 20 g mass hangs 30 cm to the left; where must a 30 g mass hang to balance it? 20 × 30 = 30 × d, so d = 20 cm to the right.
lesson.activity: Balance a metre rule on a pencil and hang coins at different distances on both sides until it balances; check that the moments on each side are equal.

questions.q: Define the moment of a force.
questions.a: Force × perpendicular distance of its line of action from the pivot.

questions.q: Why is it easier to open a door by pushing near the handle?
questions.a: The larger distance from the hinge gives a larger moment for the same force.

questions.q: Where is the centre of gravity of a uniform circular disc?
questions.a: At its centre.

questions.q: Is a body moving in a circle at constant speed accelerated?
questions.a: Yes, its direction and so its velocity changes continuously.

lesson.homework: Find three examples of couples in everyday life and draw the two forces in each.

topics.title: Work, Energy and Power
topics.summary: Work is done when a force moves its point of application: W = F × s × cos θ; unit joule (J). No displacement means no work.
notes: Work is done when a force moves its point of application: W = F × s × cos θ; unit joule (J). No displacement means no work.
Energy is the capacity to do work, also measured in joules; 1 kWh = 3.6 × 10⁶ J.
Kinetic energy K = ½mv² is energy of motion; gravitational potential energy U = mgh is energy of position.
Power is the rate of doing work: P = W ÷ t, unit watt (W); 1 horse power = 746 W.
Energy changes form but is never created or destroyed (conservation of energy): a falling ball changes potential energy into kinetic energy.
Examples of conversions: a hydroelectric dam (potential → kinetic → electrical), a bulb (electrical → light and heat), a cell (chemical → electrical).
outcomes: Define work, energy and power with their units
Use W = Fs cos θ, kinetic energy ½mv² and potential energy mgh
State the principle of conservation of energy and trace energy changes

lesson.hook: A porter holding a heavy load still on his head feels tired — but in physics is he doing any work?
lesson.example: A 2 kg ball dropped from 5 m: U at the top = 2 × 10 × 5 = 100 J (g = 10 m s⁻²). Just before landing all of it is kinetic energy: ½ × 2 × v² = 100, so v = 10 m/s.
lesson.activity: Pupils time themselves running up a flight of stairs, measure the height, and calculate their power as (weight × height) ÷ time.

questions.q: When is the work done by a force zero?
questions.a: When there is no displacement, or the force is perpendicular to the displacement.

questions.q: Find the kinetic energy of a 1000 kg car moving at 20 m/s.
Define one watt.
questions.a: The power of doing 1 joule of work in 1 second.

questions.q: What energy change takes place when a ball rolls down a slope?
questions.a: Potential energy changes into kinetic energy.

lesson.homework: Trace the energy changes from the Sun to the light of a bulb powered by a hydroelectric dam.

topics.title: Machines
topics.summary: A machine lets a smaller effort overcome a larger load or changes the direction or speed of a force.
notes: A machine lets a smaller effort overcome a larger load or changes the direction or speed of a force.
Mechanical advantage MA = load ÷ effort; velocity ratio VR = distance moved by effort ÷ distance moved by load; efficiency η = MA ÷ VR (× 100%).
No real machine is 100% efficient because of friction and the weight of moving parts; work output is always less than work input.

Levers: class I has the fulcrum between load and effort (see-saw, scissors); class II the load between (nutcracker, wheelbarrow); class III the effort between (tongs, forearm) — class III always has MA < 1.
A single fixed pulley changes the direction of force (MA ≈ 1); a single movable pulley has VR = 2.
A block and tackle with n pulleys has VR = n; its MA is less because of friction and the weight of the lower block.
outcomes: Explain a machine as a force multiplier: load, effort, mechanical advantage, velocity ratio and efficiency
Classify levers into three classes with examples
Find MA, VR and efficiency of single and block-and-tackle pulley systems

lesson.hook: How can one person lift a car with a jack, or a heavy load with a pulley?
lesson.example: A block and tackle of 4 pulleys lifts 800 N with an effort of 250 N. VR = 4, MA = 800 ÷ 250 = 3.2, efficiency = 3.2 ÷ 4 = 80%.
lesson.activity: Classify ten tools on the table — scissors, bottle opener, tongs, stapler, broom — as class I, II or III levers by finding the fulcrum, load and effort.

questions.q: Why is the efficiency of a machine always less than 100%?
questions.a: Some work is lost against friction and in lifting the moving parts.

questions.q: Give one example each of class I, II and III levers.
questions.a: Scissors; wheelbarrow; tongs.

questions.q: What is the VR of a single movable pulley?
A lever has MA 4. What effort lifts a load of 200 N?

lesson.homework: Draw a block and tackle system with two pulleys in each block and find its velocity ratio.

chapters.title: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces

topics.title: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces
topics.summary: Light bends when it passes from one medium to another because its speed changes; this is refraction.
notes: Light bends when it passes from one medium to another because its speed changes; this is refraction.
Laws of refraction: the incident ray, refracted ray and normal lie in one plane, and sin i ÷ sin r is constant for a pair of media (Snell's law).
Refractive index μ = speed of light in vacuum ÷ speed of light in the medium = sin i ÷ sin r; glass is about 1.5 and water about 1.33.
A ray through a parallel glass block emerges parallel to the incident ray but shifted sideways (lateral displacement); a pond looks shallower than it is (real depth ÷ apparent depth = μ).
When light goes from a denser to a rarer medium at an angle greater than the critical angle, it is totally reflected back — total internal reflection (critical angle of glass about 42°).
Uses: sparkling of diamonds, total reflecting prisms in periscopes and binoculars, and optical fibres for endoscopes and internet cables.
outcomes: Describe refraction of light through a glass block and state the laws of refraction
Define refractive index and relate it to the speed of light
Explain total internal reflection, critical angle and their applications

resources.title: Focal length of a convex lens and a concave mirror

lesson.hook: Why does a straight pencil look bent where it enters a glass of water, and why do diamonds sparkle?
lesson.example: A tank of water 1.33 m deep (μ = 1.33) appears only 1.33 ÷ 1.33 = 1 m deep when viewed from above.
lesson.activity: Trace rays through a rectangular glass slab with pins at three angles of incidence; measure i and r and show sin i ÷ sin r is nearly the same.

questions.q: Why does a pond appear shallower than it is?
questions.a: Light from the bottom bends away from the normal as it leaves the water, so it seems to come from a higher point.

questions.q: State two conditions for total internal reflection.
questions.a: Light must go from a denser to a rarer medium, and the angle of incidence must exceed the critical angle.

questions.q: Light travels at 2 × 10⁸ m/s in glass. Find the refractive index of glass.
Name one use of optical fibres.
questions.a: Endoscopes to see inside the body (also telecommunication).

lesson.homework: Put a coin in an empty cup, move back until it just disappears, and ask someone to fill the cup with water. Explain why the coin reappears.

topics.title: Refraction through a Lens
topics.summary: A convex lens is thicker in the middle and converges light; a concave lens is thinner in the middle and diverges light.
notes: A convex lens is thicker in the middle and converges light; a concave lens is thinner in the middle and diverges light.
Rays parallel to the principal axis meet at (or seem to come from) the principal focus F; the distance from the optical centre to F is the focal length f.
A convex lens gives a real, inverted image when the object is beyond F, and a virtual, erect, magnified image when the object is within F (magnifying glass).
A concave lens always forms a virtual, erect, diminished image on the same side as the object.
Lens formula 1/v − 1/u = 1/f (sign convention); magnification m = v ÷ u; power P = 1 ÷ f (in metres), measured in dioptres (D).
Uses: convex — magnifying glass, camera, projector, spectacles for long sight; concave — spectacles for short sight, door peep-holes.
outcomes: Describe convex and concave lenses and their principal focus and focal length
Draw ray diagrams for images formed by lenses and describe each image
Use the lens formula and power of a lens, and list uses of lenses

resources.title: Focal length of a convex lens and a concave mirror

lesson.hook: How does a magnifying glass make small print look big, and how can it also burn paper in sunlight?
lesson.example: A convex lens of focal length 10 cm has power P = 1 ÷ 0.1 = +10 D. An object 30 cm away forms an image at v where 1/v − 1/(−30) = 1/10, so v = 15 cm, real and inverted.
lesson.activity: Focus a distant tree on a screen with a convex lens and measure the approximate focal length; then move a candle nearer and see the image grow.

questions.q: Which lens can form a real image?
questions.a: A convex (converging) lens.

questions.q: What is the power of a concave lens of focal length 50 cm?
Where must an object be placed to use a convex lens as a magnifying glass?
questions.a: Between the optical centre and the principal focus.

questions.q: What kind of image does a concave lens form?
questions.a: Virtual, erect and diminished.

lesson.homework: Draw ray diagrams for a convex lens with the object at infinity, beyond 2F, at 2F and within F.

topics.title: Spectrum
topics.summary: A prism splits white light into seven colours (VIBGYOR); this is dispersion, because each colour has a slightly different refractive index in glass.
notes: A prism splits white light into seven colours (VIBGYOR); this is dispersion, because each colour has a slightly different refractive index in glass.
Violet deviates the most and red the least; a second inverted prism can recombine the colours into white light.
Visible light is a small part of the electromagnetic spectrum: gamma rays, X-rays, ultraviolet, visible, infrared, microwaves and radio waves, all travelling at 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹ in vacuum.
Infrared rays produce heating (used in remote controls and night vision); ultraviolet rays cause sunburn and kill germs; X-rays pass through flesh but not bone.
Small particles in the air scatter short wavelengths (blue) far more than long ones (red), so the sky looks blue.
At sunrise and sunset sunlight crosses more air, blue is scattered away, and the Sun looks red; danger signals are red because red scatters least.
outcomes: Describe the dispersion of white light by a prism into a spectrum
Name the parts of the electromagnetic spectrum and their properties
Explain the scattering of light and why the sky is blue and the Sun red at sunset

resources.title: Refraction and dispersion by a prism

lesson.hook: Where do the colours of a rainbow come from, and why is the sky blue and not white?
lesson.example: Red light has wavelength about 700 nm and violet about 400 nm; since scattering varies roughly as 1 ÷ λ⁴, violet-blue light is scattered several times more than red.
lesson.activity: Send sunlight through a prism (or a glass of water on a sunny window sill) onto white paper and label the colours in order.

questions.q: Which colour deviates the most in a prism?
questions.a: Violet.

questions.q: Name two uses of infrared radiation.
questions.a: TV remote controls and night-vision cameras.

questions.q: Why are danger signals red?
questions.a: Red light is scattered least, so it can be seen from far away.

questions.q: Arrange X-rays, radio waves and visible light in order of increasing wavelength.
questions.a: X-rays, visible light, radio waves.

lesson.homework: Write a paragraph on why the sky looks blue from the Earth but black from the Moon.

topics.title: Sound
topics.summary: An echo is a reflected sound heard separately from the original; the ear keeps a sound for about 0.1 s, so the reflector must be at least about 17 m away in air.
notes: An echo is a reflected sound heard separately from the original; the ear keeps a sound for about 0.1 s, so the reflector must be at least about 17 m away in air.
Echoes are used to find distances: distance = speed × time ÷ 2 (SONAR in ships, ultrasound in medicine).
A body vibrates at its natural frequency when disturbed; damped vibrations die out due to friction; forced vibrations follow an external periodic force.
Resonance: when the forcing frequency equals the natural frequency, the amplitude becomes very large (a glass breaking, a bridge swaying with marching soldiers).
Loudness depends on amplitude; pitch depends on frequency (a shrill sound has high frequency); quality or timbre depends on the waveform (overtones).
Noise pollution — above about 80 dB — harms hearing; loudness is measured in decibels.
outcomes: Explain echoes and the minimum distance needed to hear one, and use them to find distances
Distinguish natural, damped and forced vibrations and explain resonance
Relate loudness, pitch and quality to amplitude, frequency and waveform

lesson.hook: How do ships find the depth of the sea, and why can a singer's note break a glass?
lesson.example: A ship's SONAR hears the echo from the sea bed 4 s after sending a pulse. With sound in water at 1500 m/s, depth = 1500 × 4 ÷ 2 = 3000 m.
lesson.activity: Fill glass bottles with different amounts of water and blow across them; relate the height of the air column to the pitch. Then strike a tuning fork and hold it over a resonating bottle.

questions.q: Why must the reflecting surface be at least 17 m away to hear an echo?
questions.a: So that the echo returns after 0.1 s, when the first sound has faded from the ear.

questions.q: What is resonance?
questions.a: Large vibration when the frequency of the applied force equals the natural frequency.

questions.q: Which characteristic of sound depends on frequency?
questions.a: Pitch.

questions.q: A person claps and hears the echo from a cliff after 2 s. How far is the cliff? (speed 340 m/s)

lesson.homework: List five sources of noise near your school and suggest a way to reduce each one.

topics.title: Current Electricity
topics.summary: Ohm's law: at constant temperature the current through a conductor is proportional to the potential difference across it, V = IR.
notes: Ohm's law: at constant temperature the current through a conductor is proportional to the potential difference across it, V = IR.
The emf of a cell is the p.d. across it when no current flows; when current flows, terminal voltage V = ε − Ir, where r is the internal resistance.
Resistance R = ρl ÷ A: it increases with length, decreases with cross-sectional area, and depends on the material (resistivity ρ) and temperature.
Series: R = R₁ + R₂ + … (same current); parallel: 1/R = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ + … (same p.d.); the parallel combination is smaller than the smallest resistor.
Ohmic conductors (metals at constant temperature) give a straight V-I graph; a filament lamp or a diode does not.
Good conductors (copper, silver) have low resistivity; nichrome has high resistivity and is used in heaters.
outcomes: State Ohm's law and use V = IR
Relate the emf of a cell, its terminal voltage and internal resistance
Find equivalent resistance in series and parallel, and relate resistance to length, area and material

lesson.hook: Why does a thick copper wire carry current more easily than a thin nichrome wire of the same length?
lesson.example: Resistors of 6 Ω and 3 Ω in parallel: 1/R = 1/6 + 1/3 = 1/2, so R = 2 Ω. With a 6 V supply the total current is 3 A.
lesson.activity: Set up a circuit with a battery, rheostat, ammeter, voltmeter and a resistor; take five readings and plot V against I. The slope gives the resistance.

questions.q: State Ohm's law.
questions.a: At constant temperature, V ∝ I, i.e. V = IR.

questions.q: How does the resistance of a wire change if its length is doubled?
questions.a: It doubles.

questions.q: Find the resistance of 4 Ω and 12 Ω in series and in parallel.
A cell of emf 2 V and internal resistance 0.5 Ω gives a current of 1 A. Find the terminal voltage.

lesson.homework: Measure the resistance of a pencil lead using a cell, ammeter and voltmeter at home or in the lab, and record your readings.

topics.title: Electrical Power and Household Circuits
topics.summary: Electrical energy W = VIt = I²Rt = V²t ÷ R; electrical power P = VI, measured in watt.
notes: Electrical energy W = VIt = I²Rt = V²t ÷ R; electrical power P = VI, measured in watt.
The commercial unit of energy is the kilowatt-hour: 1 kWh = 1000 W × 3600 s = 3.6 × 10⁶ J ("one unit").

Power reaches homes through the live (phase), neutral and earth wires, at 220 V a.c. and 50 Hz in India; the colour code is red or brown for live, black or blue for neutral and green or yellow-green for earth.
Switches and fuses go in the live wire; a fuse wire (low melting point) or an MCB breaks the circuit when too much current flows.
Earthing connects metal bodies of appliances to the ground so that a leak of current flows safely to earth instead of through a person.
The ring main system and a three-pin plug (thicker earth pin) keep circuits safe; never overload sockets or touch switches with wet hands.
outcomes: Calculate electrical energy and power, and cost of electricity in kWh
Describe household circuits: mains, earthing, fuse, MCB, switches and ring system
Explain the colour code and safety precautions for using electricity

lesson.hook: A 2 kW heater runs for 3 hours a day. How much does it add to the monthly bill?
lesson.example: Heater: 2 kW × 3 h × 30 days = 180 kWh per month; at ₹7 per unit that is ₹1260.
lesson.activity: Read the power rating on five appliances in the classroom or at home, estimate their daily hours of use, and work out the monthly units consumed.

questions.q: Why is a fuse connected in the live wire?
questions.a: So that when it blows the appliance is disconnected from the high voltage.

questions.q: How many joules are in 1 kWh?
What is the purpose of earthing?
questions.a: To carry leaked current safely to the ground and protect users from shock.

questions.q: Find the current drawn by a 1100 W iron on 220 V.
questions.a: I = P ÷ V = 5 A.

lesson.homework: Study your home's electricity bill: note the units used and the rate, and check the total.

topics.title: Electromagnetism
topics.summary: A current in a straight wire makes circular magnetic field lines around it; the right-hand thumb rule gives their direction.
notes: A current in a straight wire makes circular magnetic field lines around it; the right-hand thumb rule gives their direction.
A current in a solenoid makes a field like a bar magnet; with a soft iron core it becomes an electromagnet.
A current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field feels a force (Fleming's left-hand rule); this is the principle of the d.c. motor, with a split-ring commutator to keep it turning.
Electromagnetic induction: a changing magnetic field through a coil induces an emf (Faraday); the direction is given by Lenz's law and Fleming's right-hand rule.
An a.c. generator turns mechanical energy into electrical energy by rotating a coil in a magnetic field, using slip rings.
A transformer changes a.c. voltage: step-up raises it for transmission, step-down lowers it for use; Vs ÷ Vp = Ns ÷ Np.
outcomes: Describe the magnetic field around a straight wire and a solenoid (right-hand rule)
Explain the force on a current-carrying conductor and the working of a d.c. motor
Explain electromagnetic induction and the a.c. generator and transformer

resources.title: Magnetic field of a bar magnet

lesson.hook: How does electricity make a fan turn, and how does a turning generator make electricity?
lesson.example: A step-down transformer with 2000 primary turns and 100 secondary turns on 220 V gives Vs = 220 × 100 ÷ 2000 = 11 V.
lesson.activity: Move a bar magnet in and out of a coil connected to a galvanometer: the needle deflects only while the magnet moves, and reverses direction when it moves the other way.

questions.q: State Fleming's left-hand rule.
questions.a: Forefinger along the field, middle finger along the current: the thumb gives the direction of the force.

questions.q: What is the function of the commutator in a d.c. motor?
questions.a: It reverses the current in the coil every half turn so it keeps rotating one way.

questions.q: What is electromagnetic induction?
questions.a: Production of an emf in a coil by a changing magnetic field through it.

questions.q: Why is power transmitted at high voltage?
questions.a: A smaller current flows, so less energy is lost as heat in the wires.

lesson.homework: Draw a labelled diagram of a d.c. motor and explain how it turns.

topics.title: Calorimetry
topics.summary: Heat capacity is the heat needed to raise a body's temperature by 1 °C (J/°C); specific heat capacity c is that for 1 kg of a substance (J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹).
notes: Heat capacity is the heat needed to raise a body's temperature by 1 °C (J/°C); specific heat capacity c is that for 1 kg of a substance (J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹).
Heat absorbed or given out Q = m c ΔT; water has a very high specific heat capacity (4200 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹), so it warms and cools slowly.
Principle of calorimetry: when a hot and a cold body are mixed (with no loss), heat lost by the hot body = heat gained by the cold one.
During melting or boiling the temperature stays constant; the heat taken is latent heat. Specific latent heat of fusion of ice is 336 000 J kg⁻¹.
Ice at 0 °C cools a drink better than water at 0 °C because it also takes latent heat as it melts.
The high specific heat of water moderates coastal climates and makes it a good coolant in car radiators.
outcomes: Define heat capacity and specific heat capacity and use Q = mcΔT
Explain latent heat of fusion and vaporisation
Solve problems on heat lost and gained (principle of calorimetry)

resources.title: Specific heat by the method of mixtures

lesson.hook: Why does the sand on a beach get hot at noon while the sea stays cool?
lesson.example: Heat to warm 2 kg of water from 20 °C to 70 °C: Q = 2 × 4200 × 50 = 420 000 J.
lesson.activity: Mix 100 g of hot water at 60 °C with 100 g of cold water at 20 °C in an insulated cup; predict and then measure the final temperature (about 40 °C).

questions.q: Why does a coastal city have a milder climate than an inland one?
questions.a: The sea's high specific heat means it heats and cools slowly, moderating the temperature.

questions.q: Why is the temperature constant while ice melts?
questions.a: The heat supplied is used as latent heat to change the state, not to raise the temperature.

questions.q: How much heat melts 0.5 kg of ice at 0 °C?
State the principle of calorimetry.
questions.a: Heat lost by the hot body = heat gained by the cold body, if no heat is lost.

lesson.homework: Explain why steam at 100 °C causes a worse burn than water at 100 °C.

topics.title: Radioactivity and Nuclear Energy
topics.summary: An atom has a small, heavy nucleus of protons and neutrons (mass number A, atomic number Z); isotopes have the same Z but different A.
notes: An atom has a small, heavy nucleus of protons and neutrons (mass number A, atomic number Z); isotopes have the same Z but different A.
Some unstable nuclei give out radiation spontaneously — radioactivity: alpha (helium nucleus), beta (fast electron) and gamma (electromagnetic wave).
In alpha decay A falls by 4 and Z by 2; in beta decay Z rises by 1 and A is unchanged; gamma emission changes neither.
Penetrating power increases alpha → beta → gamma; ionising power decreases in the same order.

Nuclear fission splits a heavy nucleus (uranium-235) into two lighter ones with a large release of energy (power plants); fusion joins light nuclei (in the Sun) and releases even more energy per kilogram (E = mc²).
Radioisotopes are used in medicine (cancer treatment, tracers), agriculture and carbon dating; exposure must be minimised — distance, shielding, protective clothing and safe disposal.
outcomes: Describe the nucleus and radioactivity: alpha, beta and gamma radiation
Explain changes in the nucleus during radioactive decay, and nuclear fission and fusion
State uses of radioactivity and the safety precautions needed

lesson.hook: How does the Sun keep shining for billions of years, and how do nuclear power plants make electricity?
lesson.example: Radium-226 (Z = 88) emits an alpha particle and becomes radon: A = 226 − 4 = 222, Z = 88 − 2 = 86.
lesson.activity: Make a comparison chart of alpha, beta and gamma radiation (nature, charge, penetrating power, what stops each) on the board with the class.

questions.q: What is the nature of a beta particle?
questions.a: A fast-moving electron from the nucleus.

questions.q: Which radiation is most penetrating?
questions.a: Gamma radiation.

questions.q: Distinguish fission from fusion.
questions.a: Fission splits a heavy nucleus; fusion joins light nuclei — both release energy.

questions.q: Give one medical use of radioisotopes.
questions.a: Treating cancer (radiotherapy), or as tracers.

lesson.homework: Find out where India's nuclear power plants are and write how safety is maintained in one of them.

topics.title: The Language of Chemistry
topics.summary: A symbol stands for one atom of an element (H, O, Na from natrium, Fe from ferrum).
notes: A symbol stands for one atom of an element (H, O, Na from natrium, Fe from ferrum).
Valency is the combining capacity of an atom or radical: H is 1, O is 2, Al is 3, C is 4; some elements have more than one valency (Fe²⁺, Fe³⁺).
A radical is a group of atoms that acts as one unit: SO₄²⁻, NO₃⁻, CO₃²⁻, OH⁻, NH₄⁺.
To write a formula, cross over the valencies and simplify: Al³⁺ and SO₄²⁻ give Al₂(SO₄)₃.
A chemical equation must be balanced so that the atoms of each element are equal on both sides (law of conservation of mass).
Relative molecular mass is the sum of the relative atomic masses of the atoms in a molecule: H₂SO₄ = 2 + 32 + 64 = 98.
outcomes: Write symbols of elements and use valency to write chemical formulae
Name radicals and write formulae of compounds
Balance chemical equations and calculate relative molecular mass

lesson.hook: Chemists everywhere read "H₂O" the same way. How does the language of chemistry make that possible?
lesson.example: Calcium (valency 2) and chloride (valency 1) give CaCl₂; its relative molecular mass = 40 + 2 × 35.5 = 111.
lesson.activity: Give pupils cards with ions (Na⁺, Mg²⁺, Al³⁺, Cl⁻, O²⁻, SO₄²⁻, PO₄³⁻); in pairs they combine cards so the charges balance and write the formula.

questions.q: Write the formula of aluminium oxide.
questions.a: Al₂O₃.

questions.q: What is a radical? Give two examples.
questions.a: A group of atoms acting as one unit, e.g. SO₄²⁻ and NH₄⁺.

questions.q: Balance: H₂ + O₂ → H₂O.
questions.a: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O.

questions.q: Find the relative molecular mass of CaCO₃ (Ca = 40, C = 12, O = 16).

lesson.homework: Write and balance equations for: magnesium burning in oxygen; zinc with dilute sulphuric acid; sodium with water.

topics.title: Chemical Changes and Reactions
topics.summary: A chemical change forms new substances with new properties; it is usually permanent and involves energy change.
notes: A chemical change forms new substances with new properties; it is usually permanent and involves energy change.
Combination: two or more substances form one (C + O₂ → CO₂). Decomposition: one substance breaks into simpler ones (2HgO → 2Hg + O₂), by heat, light or electricity.
Displacement: a more reactive element displaces a less reactive one (Zn + CuSO₄ → ZnSO₄ + Cu). Double decomposition: two compounds exchange radicals, often forming a precipitate or neutralising.
Conditions for reaction include contact, heat, light, electricity, pressure, a catalyst and solution.
Exothermic reactions give out heat (burning, neutralisation, quicklime with water); endothermic reactions take in heat (decomposition of limestone, photosynthesis).
Signs of chemical change: gas evolved, colour change, precipitate, change of state or temperature.
outcomes: Classify chemical reactions: combination, decomposition, displacement and double decomposition
Describe energy changes: exothermic and endothermic reactions
State the conditions that bring about chemical change

lesson.hook: When you light a gas stove, mix quicklime with water, or leave iron in the rain, what changes are taking place?
lesson.example: Silver nitrate + sodium chloride → silver chloride (white precipitate) + sodium nitrate: AgNO₃ + NaCl → AgCl↓ + NaNO₃ — a double decomposition.
lesson.activity: Show three reactions: zinc in copper sulphate solution, a pinch of lead nitrate heated in a dry tube (in a fume cupboard), and quicklime with water; pupils classify each and note the signs.

questions.q: Classify: CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂.
questions.a: Thermal decomposition (endothermic).

questions.q: Why does iron displace copper from copper sulphate solution?
questions.a: Iron is more reactive than copper.

questions.q: Give one example of an exothermic reaction.
questions.a: Burning of methane (or neutralisation, quicklime with water).

questions.q: What is the role of a catalyst?
questions.a: It changes the rate of a reaction without itself being used up.

lesson.homework: Find five chemical changes in your kitchen and classify each one.

topics.title: Water
topics.summary: Water dissolves more substances than any other liquid, so it is called a universal solvent; the dissolved substance is the solute.
notes: Water dissolves more substances than any other liquid, so it is called a universal solvent; the dissolved substance is the solute.
Solubility is the amount of solute that saturates 100 g of water at a given temperature; for most solids it rises with temperature, while gases dissolve less in warm water.
Water of crystallisation is water bound in crystals (CuSO₄·5H₂O is blue; anhydrous CuSO₄ is white).

Efflorescent crystals lose water to air (washing soda); deliquescent substances absorb so much moisture they dissolve (NaOH, CaCl₂); hygroscopic ones absorb moisture without dissolving (conc. H₂SO₄, quicklime) — used as drying agents.
Hard water contains calcium and magnesium salts and does not lather with soap. Temporary hardness (bicarbonates) is removed by boiling; permanent hardness (sulphates and chlorides) by washing soda.
Hard water wastes soap and forms scale in kettles and boilers.
outcomes: Explain why water is called a universal solvent and describe solutions
Distinguish hydrated and anhydrous substances, efflorescence, deliquescence and hygroscopic substances
Explain hard and soft water and the methods of removing hardness

lesson.hook: Why does soap lather easily in rain water but form scum in some well water?
lesson.example: Boiling removes temporary hardness: Ca(HCO₃)₂ → CaCO₃↓ + H₂O + CO₂; the insoluble CaCO₃ is the scale in a kettle.
lesson.activity: Heat blue copper sulphate crystals in a dry test tube: they turn white and water collects on the cooler part; add the water back and the blue colour returns.

questions.q: Why is water called a universal solvent?
questions.a: It dissolves a very large number of substances.

questions.q: What happens when washing soda crystals are left in air?
questions.a: They lose water of crystallisation and become powdery (efflorescence).

questions.q: How is permanent hardness removed?
questions.a: By adding washing soda, which precipitates calcium and magnesium as carbonates.

questions.q: Name a deliquescent substance.
questions.a: Sodium hydroxide (or calcium chloride).

lesson.homework: Test tap water, filtered water and rain water with a few drops of soap solution and compare the lather.

topics.title: Atomic Structure and Chemical Bonding
topics.summary: An atom has a nucleus of protons (+) and neutrons (no charge) with electrons (−) in shells around it; atomic number Z = protons, mass number A = protons + neutrons.
notes: An atom has a nucleus of protons (+) and neutrons (no charge) with electrons (−) in shells around it; atomic number Z = protons, mass number A = protons + neutrons.
Isotopes have the same atomic number but different mass numbers (¹²C and ¹⁴C; ³⁵Cl and ³⁷Cl).
Electrons fill shells K, L, M… holding 2, 8, 8 in the first twenty elements; atoms react to reach a stable octet (or duplet).

Electrovalent (ionic) bonds form when electrons transfer from a metal to a non-metal: Na → Na⁺ + e⁻, Cl + e⁻ → Cl⁻; ionic compounds are hard, have high melting points and conduct when molten or dissolved.
Covalent bonds form when atoms share electron pairs (H₂, Cl₂, H₂O, CH₄, NH₃); covalent compounds usually have low melting points and do not conduct.
Valency = number of electrons an atom gains, loses or shares to complete its octet.
outcomes: Describe the structure of an atom: protons, neutrons, electrons, atomic and mass number, isotopes
Arrange electrons in shells (2, 8, 8) and explain valency
Explain electrovalent and covalent bonding with electron-dot diagrams

lesson.hook: Why does sodium, a soft metal, and chlorine, a poisonous gas, join to make harmless table salt?
lesson.example: Magnesium (2, 8, 2) gives two electrons to oxygen (2, 6): Mg²⁺ (2, 8) and O²⁻ (2, 8) attract to form MgO.
lesson.activity: Draw electron-dot structures of NaCl, MgCl₂, H₂O and CH₄ with the class; colour-code each atom's electrons to show transfer and sharing.

questions.q: An atom has 11 protons and 12 neutrons. Find Z and A.
What are isotopes?
questions.a: Atoms of an element with the same atomic number but different mass numbers.

questions.q: Why does an ionic compound conduct electricity when molten?
questions.a: Its ions are free to move.

questions.q: How many shared pairs are there in a methane molecule?
questions.a: Four.

lesson.homework: Write the electronic configuration of the first 20 elements and mark their valencies.

topics.title: The Periodic Table
topics.summary: Dobereiner grouped elements in triads; Newlands noticed that every eighth element was similar (law of octaves).
notes: Dobereiner grouped elements in triads; Newlands noticed that every eighth element was similar (law of octaves).
Mendeleev arranged elements by atomic mass, left gaps for undiscovered elements and predicted their properties.
Moseley showed atomic number is the true basis: the modern periodic law says properties are periodic functions of atomic number.
The modern table has 18 vertical groups and 7 horizontal periods; elements in a group have the same number of valence electrons and similar properties.
The period number is the number of electron shells; e.g. sodium (2, 8, 1) is in period 3, group 1.
Group 1 alkali metals, group 17 halogens and group 18 noble gases are important families.
outcomes: Trace the development of the periodic table from Dobereiner and Newlands to Mendeleev and Moseley
State the modern periodic law and describe groups and periods
Relate an element's position to its electronic configuration

lesson.hook: With over a hundred elements, how can chemists predict how a new one will behave?
lesson.example: Chlorine (Z = 17) has configuration 2, 8, 7: three shells → period 3; seven valence electrons → group 17 (halogens).
lesson.activity: Give each pupil an element card with its atomic number; the class arranges itself into rows and columns by electron shells and valence electrons to rebuild part of the table.

questions.q: State the modern periodic law.
questions.a: The properties of elements are periodic functions of their atomic numbers.

questions.q: What do elements in the same group have in common?
questions.a: The same number of valence electrons and similar properties.

questions.q: Where is an element with configuration 2, 8, 2 placed?
questions.a: Period 3, group 2.

questions.q: Why did Mendeleev leave gaps in his table?
questions.a: For elements not yet discovered, whose properties he predicted.

lesson.homework: Pick one group and find the names, symbols and one use of each of its first four elements.

chapters.title: Study of the First Element: Hydrogen

topics.title: Study of the First Element: Hydrogen
topics.summary: Active metals give hydrogen with water: sodium with cold water, magnesium with steam, iron with steam (reversible).
notes: Active metals give hydrogen with water: sodium with cold water, magnesium with steam, iron with steam (reversible).
In the laboratory, zinc granules and dilute hydrochloric or sulphuric acid give hydrogen, collected by downward displacement of water.
Zinc or aluminium with hot concentrated sodium hydroxide also gives hydrogen.
Industrially, steam is passed over hot coke (water gas), then hydrogen is separated (Bosch process).
Hydrogen is colourless, odourless, lighter than air and burns with a pop; it is used to make ammonia, hydrogenate oils and as fuel.
Oxidation is gain of oxygen, loss of hydrogen or loss of electrons; reduction is the opposite. Hydrogen is a reducing agent: CuO + H₂ → Cu + H₂O.
outcomes: Describe the preparation of hydrogen from water, dilute acids and alkalis
State the properties and uses of hydrogen and its industrial manufacture (Bosch process)
Explain oxidation and reduction in terms of oxygen, hydrogen and electrons

lesson.hook: Hydrogen is the lightest element and fuels rockets. How do we make it, and why must it be handled carefully?
lesson.example: Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂: 65 g of zinc gives 2 g (about 22.4 L at STP) of hydrogen.
lesson.activity: Collect a test tube of hydrogen from zinc and dilute acid (teacher demonstration) and bring a lighted splint near its mouth: a squeaky pop shows hydrogen.

questions.q: Why is hydrogen collected by downward displacement of water?
questions.a: It is nearly insoluble in water and lighter than air.

questions.q: Identify the substance oxidised: CuO + H₂ → Cu + H₂O.
questions.a: Hydrogen is oxidised (copper oxide is reduced).

questions.q: Why is nitric acid not used to prepare hydrogen?
questions.a: It is an oxidising agent and oxidises the hydrogen formed to water.

questions.q: Give two uses of hydrogen.
questions.a: Making ammonia; hydrogenation of oils (also rocket fuel).

lesson.homework: Draw and label the apparatus for the laboratory preparation of hydrogen.

topics.title: Study of Gas Laws
topics.summary: Gases can be compressed and expand to fill their container because their particles are far apart and move randomly.
notes: Gases can be compressed and expand to fill their container because their particles are far apart and move randomly.
Boyle's law: at constant temperature the volume of a fixed mass of gas is inversely proportional to its pressure, P₁V₁ = P₂V₂.
Charles's law: at constant pressure the volume of a fixed mass of gas is directly proportional to its absolute temperature, V₁ ÷ T₁ = V₂ ÷ T₂.
Absolute (Kelvin) temperature: T (K) = t (°C) + 273; absolute zero is 0 K (−273 °C).
Combined gas equation: P₁V₁ ÷ T₁ = P₂V₂ ÷ T₂; standard temperature and pressure (STP) is 273 K and 760 mm of mercury.
Kinetic theory: faster particles at higher temperature hit the walls harder and more often, which is why pressure rises when a gas is heated in a closed container.
outcomes: State Boyle's law and Charles's law and use them in calculations
Relate the Kelvin and Celsius scales and use the gas equation
Explain the gas laws using the kinetic theory of gases

lesson.hook: Why does a bicycle tyre pumped hard in the morning feel harder in the afternoon sun?
lesson.example: A gas occupies 300 cm³ at 27 °C (300 K). At 127 °C (400 K) and the same pressure, V₂ = 300 × 400 ÷ 300 = 400 cm³.
lesson.activity: Close the nozzle of a syringe with your finger and push the plunger: pupils feel the pressure rise as the volume falls. Warm a balloon on a bottle neck in hot water and watch it grow.

questions.q: Convert 27 °C to kelvin.
The pressure on a gas is doubled at constant temperature. What happens to its volume?
questions.a: It is halved.

questions.q: What is absolute zero?
questions.a: 0 K or −273 °C, the lowest possible temperature.

questions.q: Define STP.
questions.a: 273 K and 760 mm of mercury pressure.

lesson.homework: Solve: a gas has volume 500 cm³ at 760 mm and 0 °C. Find its volume at 380 mm and 273 °C.

topics.title: Atmospheric Pollution
topics.summary: Major air pollutants: carbon monoxide, sulphur dioxide, oxides of nitrogen, hydrocarbons and particulate matter, mainly from vehicles, industries and burning waste.
notes: Major air pollutants: carbon monoxide, sulphur dioxide, oxides of nitrogen, hydrocarbons and particulate matter, mainly from vehicles, industries and burning waste.
Sulphur dioxide and nitrogen oxides dissolve in rain to form acids — acid rain damages buildings (marble), soil, lakes and plants.
Carbon monoxide is poisonous because it binds to haemoglobin and stops the blood carrying oxygen.
CFCs from old refrigerators and sprays break down the ozone layer, which protects us from ultraviolet rays.
Extra carbon dioxide and methane increase the greenhouse effect, causing global warming.
Remedies: cleaner fuels (CNG), catalytic converters, planting trees, public transport, and not burning garbage or crop stubble.
outcomes: Name the main air pollutants and their sources
Explain acid rain, ozone depletion and the extra greenhouse effect
Suggest measures to reduce air pollution

lesson.hook: Why is the Taj Mahal's marble turning yellow, and why do cities issue air-quality warnings in winter?
lesson.example: Marble (CaCO₃) reacts with sulphuric acid from acid rain: CaCO₃ + H₂SO₄ → CaSO₄ + H₂O + CO₂, slowly eating away the stone.
lesson.activity: Stick petroleum-jelly-coated cards in different places around school for a week; compare how much dust each collects and discuss the sources.

questions.q: Name two gases that cause acid rain.
questions.a: Sulphur dioxide and nitrogen dioxide.

questions.q: Why is carbon monoxide dangerous?
questions.a: It combines with haemoglobin, reducing oxygen supply to the body.

questions.q: What harm does ozone depletion cause?
questions.a: More ultraviolet radiation reaches the Earth, causing skin cancer and eye damage.

questions.q: Suggest two ways to reduce vehicle pollution.
questions.a: Use CNG or electric vehicles; use public transport and car pools.

lesson.homework: Check the air quality index of your city for a week (news or an app) and relate the changes to weather and festivals.

topics.title: Periodic Properties and their Variations
topics.summary: Across a period (left to right) the nuclear charge increases, so atomic size decreases; down a group new shells are added, so size increases.
notes: Across a period (left to right) the nuclear charge increases, so atomic size decreases; down a group new shells are added, so size increases.
Ionisation potential (energy to remove an electron) increases across a period and decreases down a group.
Electron affinity and electronegativity increase across a period and decrease down a group; fluorine is the most electronegative element.
Metallic character decreases across a period and increases down a group; non-metallic character does the opposite.
Alkali metals become more reactive down group 1 (easier to lose the outer electron); halogens become less reactive down group 17 (harder to gain an electron).
Elements in the same group have similar properties because they have the same number of valence electrons.
outcomes: Explain how atomic size, metallic character, ionisation potential, electron affinity and electronegativity vary in a period and a group
Relate these trends to the electronic configuration of elements
Compare the reactivity of alkali metals and halogens down their groups

lesson.hook: Why is caesium so reactive that it explodes in water, while lithium only fizzes?
lesson.example: Sodium (2, 8, 1) and chlorine (2, 8, 7) are in period 3: sodium is larger, loses its electron easily (low ionisation potential) and is metallic; chlorine is smaller, gains an electron easily and is non-metallic.
lesson.activity: Draw a blank periodic table outline and have pupils add arrows showing how each property changes across a period and down a group.

questions.q: How does atomic size change down a group, and why?
questions.a: It increases, because a new electron shell is added each time.

questions.q: Which element is the most electronegative?
questions.a: Fluorine.

questions.q: Why is potassium more reactive than sodium?
questions.a: Its outer electron is farther from the nucleus and more easily lost.

questions.q: Across period 3, which way does ionisation potential change?
questions.a: It increases from sodium to argon.

lesson.homework: Make a table of the first 20 elements with their configuration, group, period and whether they are metals or non-metals.

topics.title: Chemical Bonding
topics.summary: An electrovalent (ionic) bond forms by transfer of electrons from a metal to a non-metal; oppositely charged ions attract (NaCl, MgCl₂, CaO).
notes: An electrovalent (ionic) bond forms by transfer of electrons from a metal to a non-metal; oppositely charged ions attract (NaCl, MgCl₂, CaO).
A covalent bond forms by sharing electron pairs; single, double and triple bonds share one, two and three pairs (Cl₂, O₂, N₂; CH₄, H₂O, NH₃).
Polar covalent molecules (H₂O, HCl) have uneven sharing because one atom is more electronegative; non-polar ones (CH₄, Cl₂) share evenly.
A coordinate bond is a covalent bond where both electrons come from one atom's lone pair: NH₃ + H⁺ → NH₄⁺; H₂O + H⁺ → H₃O⁺.
Ionic compounds are crystalline solids, have high melting points, dissolve in water and conduct when molten or in solution.
Covalent compounds are often gases or liquids, have low melting points, dissolve in organic solvents and generally do not conduct.
outcomes: Explain electrovalent, covalent and coordinate bonding with electron-dot diagrams
Compare properties of ionic and covalent compounds
Explain the formation of the hydronium and ammonium ions

lesson.hook: Water and table salt are both compounds, yet one melts at 0 °C and the other at 801 °C. Why so different?
lesson.example: In NH₄⁺ the nitrogen's lone pair is donated to H⁺, forming a coordinate bond; all four N–H bonds then become identical.
lesson.activity: Pupils build models of NaCl and H₂O with beads or clay, then test (or watch) salt solution and sugar solution with a bulb circuit.

questions.q: Why does molten NaCl conduct electricity?
questions.a: Its ions are free to move.

questions.q: What is a lone pair?
questions.a: A pair of valence electrons not used in bonding.

questions.q: Draw or describe the bonding in a nitrogen molecule.
questions.a: A triple covalent bond: three shared pairs.

questions.q: How is the hydronium ion formed?
questions.a: Water donates a lone pair to H⁺: H₂O + H⁺ → H₃O⁺.

lesson.homework: Draw electron-dot structures of CO₂, N₂, NH₃ and MgO, and label each bond type.

topics.title: Acids, Bases and Salts
topics.summary: An acid gives H⁺ (as H₃O⁺) ions in water; a base neutralises an acid; a soluble base is an alkali and gives OH⁻ ions.
notes: An acid gives H⁺ (as H₃O⁺) ions in water; a base neutralises an acid; a soluble base is an alkali and gives OH⁻ ions.
The pH scale runs from 0 to 14: below 7 acidic, 7 neutral, above 7 basic; strong acids are fully ionised, weak acids only partly.
Neutralisation: acid + base → salt + water (H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O).
Normal salts (NaCl), acid salts with replaceable hydrogen (NaHCO₃, NaHSO₄) and basic salts (Pb(OH)Cl) are formed by partial or complete replacement.
Dilute acids react with carbonates and bicarbonates (CO₂), sulphites (SO₂) and sulphides (H₂S).
Salts are prepared by direct combination (Fe + Cl₂), metal + acid (Zn + H₂SO₄), neutralisation/titration (NaOH + HCl) and precipitation (BaCl₂ + Na₂SO₄ → BaSO₄↓).
outcomes: Define acids, bases and alkalis in terms of ions, and measure pH
Classify salts (normal, acid, basic) and describe the action of dilute acids on salts
Describe methods of preparing salts: direct combination, displacement, neutralisation, precipitation

lesson.hook: Why does an antacid relieve acidity, and how are salts like copper sulphate made in a laboratory?
lesson.example: Insoluble lead chloride is made by precipitation: Pb(NO₃)₂ + 2HCl → PbCl₂↓ + 2HNO₃; filter, wash and dry the precipitate.
lesson.activity: Test lemon juice, soap solution, vinegar, baking soda and tap water with universal indicator paper and arrange them on a pH line on the board.

questions.q: What ions does an alkali produce in water?
questions.a: Hydroxide ions (OH⁻).

questions.q: Is NaHCO₃ a normal, acid or basic salt?
questions.a: An acid salt.

questions.q: What gas is formed when dilute HCl reacts with sodium sulphite?
questions.a: Sulphur dioxide.

questions.q: Which method would you use to prepare barium sulphate?
questions.a: Precipitation (double decomposition).

lesson.homework: Write equations for preparing: zinc sulphate from zinc; sodium chloride by neutralisation; lead chloride by precipitation.

topics.title: Analytical Chemistry
topics.summary: Analytical chemistry identifies substances by their reactions. Adding NaOH or NH₄OH to a salt solution precipitates many metal hydroxides with typical colours.
notes: Analytical chemistry identifies substances by their reactions. Adding NaOH or NH₄OH to a salt solution precipitates many metal hydroxides with typical colours.
With NaOH: Cu²⁺ gives a pale blue precipitate, Fe²⁺ dirty green, Fe³⁺ reddish brown, Ca²⁺ white (insoluble in excess), Zn²⁺ and Pb²⁺ white (soluble in excess).
With NH₄OH: Cu(OH)₂ dissolves in excess to form a deep blue solution; Zn(OH)₂ also dissolves in excess (colourless); Pb(OH)₂ does not.
Zinc, aluminium and lead are amphoteric: their oxides and hydroxides react with both acids and alkalis.
Hot concentrated NaOH reacts with zinc and aluminium to release hydrogen (Zn + 2NaOH → Na₂ZnO₂ + H₂).
Ammonium salts warmed with NaOH give ammonia, which turns moist red litmus blue.
outcomes: Identify cations by the colour of precipitates with sodium hydroxide and ammonium hydroxide
Describe the action of alkalis on metals and amphoteric oxides and hydroxides
Use these tests to identify an unknown salt

lesson.hook: A pale blue precipitate turns deep blue with excess ammonia. Which metal ion gives this clue?
lesson.example: An unknown solution gives a white precipitate with NaOH that dissolves in excess, and a white precipitate with NH₄OH that also dissolves in excess: it contains Zn²⁺.
lesson.activity: Give groups four unlabelled solutions (copper, iron(II), iron(III) and zinc salts) and the two reagents; they identify each by the colour and behaviour of the precipitate.

questions.q: What colour precipitate does Fe³⁺ give with NaOH?
questions.a: Reddish brown.

questions.q: How can you tell Zn²⁺ from Pb²⁺ using ammonium hydroxide?
questions.a: The zinc hydroxide precipitate dissolves in excess NH₄OH; lead hydroxide does not.

questions.q: What is an amphoteric oxide? Give an example.
questions.a: One that reacts with both acids and bases, e.g. ZnO or Al₂O₃.

questions.q: Describe the test for an ammonium salt.
questions.a: Warm with NaOH: ammonia is given off, turning moist red litmus blue.

lesson.homework: Prepare a flow chart for identifying Cu²⁺, Fe²⁺, Fe³⁺, Zn²⁺, Pb²⁺ and Ca²⁺ with NaOH and NH₄OH.

topics.title: Mole Concept and Stoichiometry
topics.summary: Gay-Lussac's law: gases react in volumes that bear a simple whole-number ratio to each other and to the gaseous products (at the same T and P).
notes: Gay-Lussac's law: gases react in volumes that bear a simple whole-number ratio to each other and to the gaseous products (at the same T and P).
Avogadro's law: equal volumes of all gases at the same temperature and pressure contain equal numbers of molecules.
One mole contains 6.022 × 10²³ particles (Avogadro's number); its mass in grams is the molar mass; one mole of any gas occupies 22.4 L at STP.
Vapour density = mass of a volume of gas ÷ mass of the same volume of hydrogen; relative molecular mass = 2 × vapour density.
Percentage composition, empirical formula (simplest ratio) and molecular formula are found from masses and moles.
Balanced equations give mole, mass and volume relationships (stoichiometry).
outcomes: State Gay-Lussac's law of combining volumes and Avogadro's law
Define the mole, molar mass, molar volume and vapour density
Calculate masses, volumes and percentage composition from equations and formulae

lesson.hook: How many molecules are in a glass of water — and how can chemists count particles they cannot see?
lesson.example: Mass of CO₂ from burning 12 g of carbon: C + O₂ → CO₂, 1 mol C gives 1 mol CO₂, so 12 g gives 44 g of CO₂ (22.4 L at STP).
lesson.activity: Weigh out one mole each of salt (58.5 g), sugar (342 g) and water (18 g) and show them side by side: same number of particles, very different masses.

questions.q: What is the volume of 2 moles of oxygen at STP?
The vapour density of a gas is 32. Find its relative molecular mass.
How many molecules are in 18 g of water?
questions.a: 6.022 × 10²³ (one mole).

questions.q: Find the percentage of nitrogen in NH₃ (N = 14, H = 1).

lesson.homework: A compound has 40% carbon, 6.67% hydrogen and 53.3% oxygen. Find its empirical formula (answer: CH₂O).

topics.title: Electrolysis
topics.summary: Electrolytes conduct electricity when molten or dissolved and are decomposed by it; non-electrolytes (sugar, alcohol) do not conduct.
notes: Electrolytes conduct electricity when molten or dissolved and are decomposed by it; non-electrolytes (sugar, alcohol) do not conduct.
Strong electrolytes are fully ionised (NaCl, HCl); weak electrolytes only partly (acetic acid, ammonium hydroxide).
In electrolysis, cations move to the cathode (−) and gain electrons (reduction); anions move to the anode (+) and lose electrons (oxidation).
Molten lead bromide gives lead at the cathode and bromine vapour at the anode; acidified water gives hydrogen and oxygen in the ratio 2 : 1.
Copper sulphate with copper electrodes: copper dissolves from the anode and deposits on the cathode — used to refine copper.
Applications: electroplating (object as cathode), electrorefining and extracting reactive metals such as aluminium and sodium.
outcomes: Distinguish electrolytes and non-electrolytes, strong and weak electrolytes
Explain electrolysis and the migration of ions to electrodes
Describe electrolysis of molten lead bromide, acidified water and copper sulphate, and applications of electrolysis

lesson.hook: How are spoons silver-plated, and how is pure copper made for electric wires?
lesson.example: At the cathode in electrolysis of molten PbBr₂: Pb²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Pb; at the anode: 2Br⁻ − 2e⁻ → Br₂.
lesson.activity: Electrolyse copper sulphate solution with two carbon rods and a 6 V battery; after ten minutes pupils see pink copper on the cathode.

questions.q: Why is electrolysis called a redox reaction?
questions.a: Reduction happens at the cathode and oxidation at the anode.

questions.q: Name a weak electrolyte.
questions.a: Acetic acid (or ammonium hydroxide).

questions.q: In electroplating a spoon with silver, what is the cathode?
questions.a: The spoon.

questions.q: What are the products of electrolysis of acidified water?
questions.a: Hydrogen at the cathode and oxygen at the anode, 2 : 1 by volume.

lesson.homework: Draw the set-up for electroplating an iron key with nickel and label the anode, cathode and electrolyte.

topics.title: Metallurgy
topics.summary: Metals occur free (gold) or combined as minerals; an ore is a mineral from which a metal can be extracted profitably.
notes: Metals occur free (gold) or combined as minerals; an ore is a mineral from which a metal can be extracted profitably.

The activity series (K, Na, Ca, Mg, Al, Zn, Fe, Pb, H, Cu, Ag, Au) decides the method: very reactive metals by electrolysis, middle ones by reduction with carbon, least reactive found free or by heating.
Stages: concentration of the ore (hydraulic washing, magnetic separation, froth floatation, leaching), conversion to oxide (roasting or calcination), reduction and refining.
Aluminium: bauxite is purified to alumina (Baeyer's process); alumina dissolved in molten cryolite is electrolysed (Hall-Héroult process) with carbon electrodes; aluminium collects at the cathode.
Cryolite lowers the melting point and improves conduction; the carbon anodes burn away and must be replaced.
Alloys: brass (Cu + Zn), bronze (Cu + Sn), duralumin (Al + Cu + Mg + Mn), stainless steel (Fe + Cr + Ni + C), solder (Pb + Sn); an amalgam is an alloy of mercury.
outcomes: Describe the occurrence of metals as minerals and ores and the activity series
Explain the stages of extracting metals: concentration, reduction and refining
Describe the extraction of aluminium and state the composition and uses of common alloys

lesson.hook: Aluminium is the most common metal in the Earth's crust, yet it was once more costly than gold. Why?
lesson.example: In the Hall-Héroult process: at the cathode Al³⁺ + 3e⁻ → Al; at the anode O²⁻ ions give oxygen, which reacts with the carbon anode to form CO₂.
lesson.activity: Show samples or pictures of bauxite, haematite and copper pyrites, and objects made of brass, bronze, steel and solder; pupils match each alloy to its metals and uses.

questions.q: Why can aluminium not be extracted by heating its oxide with carbon?
questions.a: Aluminium is more reactive than carbon, so carbon cannot reduce alumina.

questions.q: What is the role of cryolite?
questions.a: It lowers the melting point of alumina and increases conductivity.

questions.q: What is the difference between roasting and calcination?
questions.a: Roasting heats a sulphide ore in air; calcination heats a carbonate ore in little or no air.

questions.q: Name the metals in bronze.
questions.a: Copper and tin.

lesson.homework: Find three alloys used at home or in school and state their components and why an alloy is used instead of the pure metal.

topics.title: Study of Compounds: Hydrogen Chloride
topics.summary: In the laboratory, sodium chloride is heated with concentrated sulphuric acid: NaCl + H₂SO₄ → NaHSO₄ + HCl (below 200 °C).
notes: In the laboratory, sodium chloride is heated with concentrated sulphuric acid: NaCl + H₂SO₄ → NaHSO₄ + HCl (below 200 °C).
The gas is dried by passing through concentrated sulphuric acid and collected by upward displacement of air, as it is heavier than air.
Hydrogen chloride is extremely soluble in water — the fountain experiment shows water rushing into a flask of the gas.
With ammonia it forms dense white fumes of ammonium chloride: NH₃ + HCl → NH₄Cl (a test for either gas).
Its solution, hydrochloric acid, is a strong acid: it turns blue litmus red, reacts with metals (hydrogen), bases (salt + water) and carbonates (CO₂).
With silver nitrate solution, HCl gives a white precipitate of silver chloride — a test for chloride ions.
outcomes: Describe the laboratory preparation of hydrogen chloride from sodium chloride
State the properties of hydrogen chloride: density, solubility (fountain experiment) and reaction with ammonia
Describe the acidic properties of hydrochloric acid

lesson.hook: A gas that makes a "fountain" when water rushes into its flask — what makes hydrogen chloride so soluble?
lesson.example: Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂; CaCO₃ + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂; AgNO₃ + HCl → AgCl↓ (white) + HNO₃.
lesson.activity: Teacher demonstration: bring a glass rod dipped in ammonia near the mouth of a hydrochloric acid bottle; dense white fumes of ammonium chloride form.

questions.q: Why is hydrogen chloride collected by upward displacement of air?
questions.a: It is heavier than air and very soluble in water.

questions.q: Why is concentrated sulphuric acid used to dry HCl gas?
questions.a: It absorbs moisture and does not react with HCl.

questions.q: What does the fountain experiment show?
questions.a: That hydrogen chloride is highly soluble in water.

questions.q: How do you test for chloride ions?
questions.a: Add silver nitrate solution: a white precipitate of AgCl forms.

lesson.homework: Draw the apparatus for preparing and collecting dry hydrogen chloride, labelling each part.

topics.title: Study of Compounds: Ammonia
topics.summary: In the laboratory, ammonium chloride is heated with slaked lime: 2NH₄Cl + Ca(OH)₂ → CaCl₂ + 2H₂O + 2NH₃; the gas is dried over quicklime and collected by downward displacement of air.
notes: In the laboratory, ammonium chloride is heated with slaked lime: 2NH₄Cl + Ca(OH)₂ → CaCl₂ + 2H₂O + 2NH₃; the gas is dried over quicklime and collected by downward displacement of air.
Nitrides such as Mg₃N₂ and AlN give ammonia with warm water; ammonium salts give ammonia with alkalis.
Haber's process: N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃, at about 450–500 °C and 200–900 atm, with finely divided iron (molybdenum promoter); ammonia is removed by cooling.
Ammonia is lighter than air and extremely soluble (fountain experiment); its solution is weakly alkaline (NH₄OH).
It burns in oxygen with a yellowish-green flame (4NH₃ + 3O₂ → 2N₂ + 6H₂O); with a platinum catalyst at 800 °C it is oxidised to nitric oxide — the first step of making nitric acid.
It reduces hot copper(II) oxide to copper, forms white fumes with HCl, and reacts with chlorine (products depend on which is in excess).
outcomes: Describe the laboratory preparation of ammonia and its preparation from nitrides
Explain the manufacture of ammonia by Haber's process
State the properties of ammonia: solubility, burning in oxygen, catalytic oxidation and reactions with acids, metal oxides and chlorine
