lesson.hook: Most of the world's fertiliser starts as ammonia made from nitrogen in the air. How is air turned into fertiliser?
lesson.example: 3CuO + 2NH₃ → 3Cu + 3H₂O + N₂: black copper oxide turns reddish brown, showing ammonia is a reducing agent.
lesson.activity: Teacher demonstration of the ammonia fountain using a flask of dry ammonia and water with phenolphthalein: pink water rushes up.

questions.q: Why is ammonia not dried with concentrated sulphuric acid?
questions.a: It is basic and reacts with the acid.

questions.q: State the conditions of Haber's process.
questions.a: About 450–500 °C, high pressure (200–900 atm), iron catalyst with molybdenum promoter.

questions.q: Why is ammonia collected by downward displacement of air?
questions.a: It is lighter than air and very soluble in water.

questions.q: What does the reaction of ammonia with hot copper(II) oxide show?
questions.a: That ammonia is a reducing agent.

lesson.homework: Draw a flow chart of Haber's process from raw materials to liquid ammonia.

topics.title: Study of Compounds: Nitric Acid
topics.summary: In the laboratory, potassium nitrate is heated with concentrated sulphuric acid in an all-glass apparatus: KNO₃ + H₂SO₄ → KHSO₄ + HNO₃; the acid vapour is condensed.
notes: In the laboratory, potassium nitrate is heated with concentrated sulphuric acid in an all-glass apparatus: KNO₃ + H₂SO₄ → KHSO₄ + HNO₃; the acid vapour is condensed.
All-glass apparatus is used because nitric acid vapour attacks rubber and cork.
Ostwald process: ammonia is oxidised with air over platinum at about 800 °C to nitric oxide, which forms nitrogen dioxide; this is absorbed in water with air to give nitric acid.
Concentrated nitric acid decomposes in light to NO₂, which dissolves in it and makes it yellow — so it is stored in brown bottles.
It is a strong oxidising agent: it oxidises carbon to CO₂ and sulphur to H₂SO₄, and reacts with copper to give NO₂ (concentrated) or NO (dilute) instead of hydrogen.
Uses: fertilisers (ammonium nitrate), explosives, dyes and in purifying gold and silver.
outcomes: Describe the laboratory preparation of nitric acid from potassium or sodium nitrate
Outline the large-scale manufacture of nitric acid (Ostwald process)
Explain the oxidising properties of nitric acid with metals and non-metals

lesson.hook: Why is concentrated nitric acid kept in brown bottles, and why does it turn yellow over time?
lesson.example: Cu + 4HNO₃ (conc.) → Cu(NO₃)₂ + 2H₂O + 2NO₂: reddish-brown fumes and a blue-green solution.
lesson.activity: Discuss with a diagram why an all-glass retort is used, and compare the reaction of copper with concentrated and dilute nitric acid.

questions.q: Why does nitric acid not give hydrogen with most metals?
questions.a: It oxidises the hydrogen formed to water.

questions.q: Why is commercial nitric acid yellow?
questions.a: Dissolved NO₂ from its decomposition in light.

questions.q: Name the catalyst in the Ostwald process.
questions.a: Platinum.

questions.q: Give two uses of nitric acid.
questions.a: Making fertilisers and explosives (also dyes).

lesson.homework: Write equations for the three steps of the Ostwald process.

topics.title: Study of Compounds: Sulphuric Acid
topics.summary: Contact process: sulphur burns to SO₂; SO₂ + O₂ ⇌ SO₃ over vanadium pentoxide at about 450 °C; SO₃ is absorbed in concentrated H₂SO₄ to give oleum, which is diluted to H₂SO₄.
notes: Contact process: sulphur burns to SO₂; SO₂ + O₂ ⇌ SO₃ over vanadium pentoxide at about 450 °C; SO₃ is absorbed in concentrated H₂SO₄ to give oleum, which is diluted to H₂SO₄.
SO₃ is not dissolved directly in water because it forms a dense acid mist.
Dilute sulphuric acid is a strong acid: it reacts with metals, oxides, hydroxides, carbonates, sulphites and sulphides.
Hot concentrated acid is an oxidising agent: it oxidises carbon to CO₂ and sulphur to SO₂.
It is a strong dehydrating agent: it chars sugar to carbon and turns blue copper sulphate crystals white. Always add acid to water, never water to acid.
Being non-volatile, it displaces volatile acids from their salts (making HCl and HNO₃); it is used for fertilisers, detergents, batteries and in refining petroleum.
outcomes: Outline the manufacture of sulphuric acid by the contact process
Describe sulphuric acid as an acid, an oxidising agent and a dehydrating agent
Explain its non-volatile nature and state its uses

lesson.hook: Sulphuric acid is called the "king of chemicals". What makes it so important?
lesson.example: C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁ (sugar) + conc. H₂SO₄ → 12C + 11H₂O: the sugar swells into a black column of carbon.
lesson.activity: Teacher demonstration (with safety screen): add concentrated sulphuric acid to sugar in a beaker; pupils record colour, heat and volume changes.

questions.q: Why is SO₃ not dissolved directly in water in the contact process?
questions.a: It forms a fog of acid droplets that is hard to condense.

questions.q: Name the catalyst in the contact process.
questions.a: Vanadium pentoxide (V₂O₅).

questions.q: Why must acid be added to water and not water to acid?
questions.a: The mixing gives out a lot of heat; adding water to acid can make it boil and splash.

questions.q: How does sulphuric acid help to make hydrochloric acid?
questions.a: Being non-volatile, it displaces volatile HCl from sodium chloride.

lesson.homework: List five everyday products made using sulphuric acid.

topics.title: Organic Chemistry
topics.summary: Carbon is tetravalent and can bond to itself in chains, branches and rings (catenation), giving a huge variety of organic compounds.
notes: Carbon is tetravalent and can bond to itself in chains, branches and rings (catenation), giving a huge variety of organic compounds.
A homologous series has the same general formula and functional group, with neighbours differing by CH₂ (alkanes CₙH₂ₙ₊₂, alkenes CₙH₂ₙ, alkynes CₙH₂ₙ₋₂).
Isomers have the same molecular formula but different structures (butane and isobutane); IUPAC names use a root (meth-, eth-, prop-, but-) and a suffix (-ane, -ene, -yne, -ol, -oic acid).
Alkanes are saturated and undergo substitution (methane + chlorine in sunlight); alkenes and alkynes are unsaturated and undergo addition (ethene + bromine decolourises bromine water).
Ethanol (C₂H₅OH) is made by fermentation or hydration of ethene; it burns cleanly, reacts with sodium, and is used as a solvent and fuel.
Ethanoic acid (CH₃COOH) is a weak acid (vinegar); with ethanol and concentrated sulphuric acid it forms a sweet-smelling ester (esterification).
outcomes: Explain why carbon forms so many compounds (catenation and tetravalency)
Describe homologous series, isomerism and IUPAC naming of simple compounds
Study alkanes, alkenes and alkynes, ethanol and ethanoic acid: preparation, properties and uses

lesson.hook: From LPG to vinegar to plastic bags — how can one element, carbon, form millions of compounds?
lesson.example: Propane (C₃H₈), propene (C₃H₆) and propyne (C₃H₄) are the three-carbon members of the alkane, alkene and alkyne series.
lesson.activity: Make ball-and-stick models (clay and toothpicks) of methane, ethane, ethene and ethyne, and of butane and isobutane to show isomerism.

questions.q: What is a homologous series?
questions.a: A family of organic compounds with the same functional group and general formula, differing by CH₂.

questions.q: How can you tell ethene from ethane in the laboratory?
questions.a: Ethene decolourises bromine water; ethane does not.

questions.q: Give the IUPAC name of CH₃COOH.
questions.a: Ethanoic acid.

questions.q: What is formed when ethanol reacts with ethanoic acid?
questions.a: An ester (ethyl ethanoate) and water.

lesson.homework: Write the structures and IUPAC names of the first four alkanes and alkenes.

topics.title: Cell: The Unit of Life
topics.summary: The cell is the structural and functional unit of life; cell theory: all living things are made of cells, and new cells come from existing cells.
notes: The cell is the structural and functional unit of life; cell theory: all living things are made of cells, and new cells come from existing cells.
Protoplasm is the living substance of the cell: cytoplasm plus nucleus.
The cell membrane controls what enters and leaves; the plant cell also has a rigid cellulose cell wall.

The nucleus controls the cell and carries hereditary material (chromosomes); mitochondria release energy by respiration; ribosomes make proteins; the endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi body transport and package materials.
Plant cells have chloroplasts (photosynthesis) and a large central vacuole; animal cells have small vacuoles and a centrosome.
Cells vary in shape and size according to their function: long nerve cells, disc-shaped red blood cells, guard cells.
outcomes: Describe the cell as the unit of life and the cell theory
Name the parts of plant and animal cells and state their functions
Compare plant and animal cells

lesson.hook: Every living thing, from an amoeba to an elephant, is built from tiny units. What are they, and how do they work?
lesson.example: An onion peel cell shows a clear cell wall, a nucleus at the side and a big vacuole; a cheek cell has no wall, a central nucleus and no large vacuole.
lesson.activity: Prepare stained slides of onion peel (iodine) and cheek cells (methylene blue); pupils draw and label both and list three differences.

questions.q: Which organelle is called the powerhouse of the cell?
questions.a: The mitochondrion.

questions.q: Name two structures found in plant cells but not in animal cells.
questions.a: Cell wall and chloroplasts (also a large central vacuole).

questions.q: What is the function of the cell membrane?
questions.a: It controls the movement of substances into and out of the cell.

questions.q: State the cell theory.
questions.a: All living things are made of cells, and new cells arise from existing cells.

lesson.homework: Make a model of a plant cell or an animal cell with household materials and label its parts.

topics.title: Tissues: Plant and Animal Tissues
topics.summary: A tissue is a group of similar cells doing a particular job.
notes: A tissue is a group of similar cells doing a particular job.
Meristematic tissue has actively dividing cells at the tips of roots and shoots and in the cambium; it makes the plant grow.
Permanent tissues: simple (parenchyma for storage, collenchyma for flexibility, sclerenchyma for strength) and complex (xylem carries water, phloem carries food).
Epithelial tissue covers surfaces and lines organs; connective tissue (bone, cartilage, blood, tendons, ligaments) supports and links.
Muscular tissue: striated (voluntary, in limbs), unstriated (involuntary, in the gut) and cardiac (heart, never tires).
Nervous tissue is made of neurons that carry messages as electrical impulses.
outcomes: Describe the main types of plant tissues: meristematic and permanent (simple and complex)
Describe the main types of animal tissues: epithelial, connective, muscular and nervous
Relate the structure of each tissue to its function

lesson.hook: A plant has no bones or muscles, yet stands upright and carries water to its top leaves. Which tissues do this?
lesson.example: The husk of a coconut is sclerenchyma — dead, thick-walled cells that make it hard and fibrous.
lesson.activity: Place a celery stalk or a white flower in coloured water for a few hours; cut across the stem and look for the coloured xylem strands.

questions.q: Which plant tissue carries water from roots to leaves?
questions.a: Xylem.

questions.q: Where is meristematic tissue found?
questions.a: At the tips of roots and shoots, and in the cambium.

questions.q: Name the three types of muscle.
questions.a: Striated, unstriated and cardiac.

questions.q: What does connective tissue do? Give an example.
questions.a: It supports and binds other tissues, e.g. bone or tendon.

lesson.homework: Draw a table of plant and animal tissues with one example of where each is found.

topics.title: The Flower
topics.summary: A flower is the reproductive part of a plant; a typical bisexual flower has four whorls on the thalamus: calyx, corolla, androecium and gynoecium.
notes: A flower is the reproductive part of a plant; a typical bisexual flower has four whorls on the thalamus: calyx, corolla, androecium and gynoecium.
Sepals (calyx) protect the bud; petals (corolla) attract insects with colour and scent.
The androecium is made of stamens, each with a filament and an anther that produces pollen grains (male).
The gynoecium has carpels (pistil): stigma receives pollen, style joins it to the ovary, and the ovary contains ovules with the egg.
Bisexual flowers have both stamens and pistil (hibiscus, mustard); unisexual flowers have only one (papaya, cucumber).
The flower's parts later form the fruit (ovary) and seeds (ovules).
outcomes: Name the parts of a typical bisexual flower and state their functions
Describe the stamen and pistil in detail
Distinguish bisexual and unisexual flowers

lesson.hook: Why does a flower have such bright petals and a sweet smell — whom is it trying to attract?
lesson.example: In a hibiscus flower: 5 green sepals, 5 red petals, many stamens fused into a tube around the style, and a 5-lobed stigma at the top.
lesson.activity: Dissect a hibiscus or datura flower; pupils separate the whorls, stick them on paper and label each part.

questions.q: Which part of a flower produces pollen grains?
questions.a: The anther.

questions.q: Name the three parts of a pistil.
questions.a: Stigma, style and ovary.

questions.q: What is a unisexual flower? Give an example.
questions.a: A flower with only stamens or only a pistil, e.g. papaya.

questions.q: What is the function of the sepals?
questions.a: They protect the flower in the bud stage.

lesson.homework: Collect three different flowers and write whether each is bisexual or unisexual, with reasons.

topics.title: Pollination and Fertilisation
topics.summary: Pollination is the transfer of pollen from an anther to a stigma; self-pollination is within the same flower or plant, cross-pollination between plants.
notes: Pollination is the transfer of pollen from an anther to a stigma; self-pollination is within the same flower or plant, cross-pollination between plants.
Cross-pollination gives more variety and healthier offspring; self-pollination is sure but reduces variation.
Agents: insects (bright, scented flowers with nectar and sticky pollen), wind (small dull flowers, light dry pollen, feathery stigmas), water and birds.
After pollination a pollen tube grows down the style to the ovule; a male gamete fuses with the egg — fertilisation — forming a zygote.
After fertilisation the ovule becomes the seed, the ovary becomes the fruit, and the petals and sepals usually fall off.
In flowering plants a second male gamete fuses with the polar nuclei to form the endosperm (double fertilisation).
outcomes: Distinguish self-pollination and cross-pollination and their advantages
Describe agents of pollination and the adaptations of flowers for each
Explain fertilisation and the formation of fruit and seed

lesson.hook: Bees buzz from flower to flower. How does their visit lead to fruit and seeds?
lesson.example: Maize is wind-pollinated: its tassels release huge amounts of light pollen, and the long silky "hairs" are its stigmas that catch it.
lesson.activity: Compare an insect-pollinated flower (hibiscus) and a wind-pollinated one (grass or maize tassel) with a hand lens; list their differences in a table.

questions.q: What is cross-pollination?
questions.a: Transfer of pollen from a flower of one plant to the stigma of a flower on another plant of the same kind.

questions.q: Give two features of wind-pollinated flowers.
questions.a: Light, dry pollen in large amounts; feathery stigmas (also small, dull flowers).

questions.q: What does the ovary become after fertilisation?
questions.a: The fruit.

questions.q: Where does fertilisation take place in a flower?
questions.a: In the ovule inside the ovary.

lesson.homework: Write the steps from pollination to seed formation as a flow chart.

topics.title: Seeds: Structure and Germination
topics.summary: A seed has a seed coat (testa), an embryo (radicle, plumule and one or two cotyledons) and stored food.
notes: A seed has a seed coat (testa), an embryo (radicle, plumule and one or two cotyledons) and stored food.
A dicot seed like bean or gram has two cotyledons storing food; a monocot seed like maize has one cotyledon and stored food in the endosperm.
Germination is the growth of the embryo into a seedling: the radicle forms the root and the plumule the shoot.
Seeds need water, oxygen and a suitable temperature to germinate; light is not needed for most seeds.
In epigeal germination the cotyledons come above the soil (bean, castor); in hypogeal germination they stay below (pea, maize).
The stored food is used up during germination, which is why sprouts shrink the cotyledons.
outcomes: Describe the structure of dicot (bean) and monocot (maize) seeds
Explain the conditions needed for germination
Distinguish epigeal and hypogeal germination

lesson.hook: A tiny seed holds a whole baby plant and its lunch box. What is inside, and what wakes it up?
lesson.example: A soaked bean seed splits easily into two cotyledons, with the tiny radicle and plumule attached between them; a maize grain cannot be split this way.
lesson.activity: Set up three jars of moong seeds: dry, moist and fully under boiled water; observe for a week and record which germinate (compare with the virtual germination lab).

questions.q: Name the three conditions needed for germination.
questions.a: Water, oxygen (air) and a suitable temperature.

questions.q: Where is food stored in a maize grain?
questions.a: In the endosperm.

questions.q: What is epigeal germination? Give an example.
questions.a: Cotyledons are pushed above the soil, e.g. bean.

questions.q: Which part of the embryo becomes the root?
questions.a: The radicle.

lesson.homework: Grow beans and peas in a pot; draw the seedlings on day 3 and day 7 and say which shows epigeal germination.

topics.title: Respiration in Plants
topics.summary: Respiration is the breakdown of food (glucose) in cells to release energy stored as ATP; it goes on all the time in every living cell, day and night.
notes: Respiration is the breakdown of food (glucose) in cells to release energy stored as ATP; it goes on all the time in every living cell, day and night.
Aerobic respiration uses oxygen: C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O + energy. Glycolysis (in the cytoplasm) splits glucose into pyruvic acid; the Krebs cycle (in mitochondria) completes the breakdown.
Anaerobic respiration happens without oxygen and releases less energy: in yeast C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂ + a little energy.
Germinating seeds respire fast: they give out carbon dioxide (turns lime water milky) and heat (a thermometer in a flask of germinating seeds shows a rise).
Plants exchange gases through stomata and lenticels; at night they only respire.
Respiration differs from photosynthesis: it releases energy and CO₂; photosynthesis stores energy and releases O₂.
outcomes: Describe respiration as the release of energy from food
Outline aerobic respiration (glycolysis and Krebs cycle) and anaerobic respiration with equations
Describe experiments to show gaseous exchange and heat production in germinating seeds

lesson.hook: Do plants breathe? If they make oxygen in sunlight, do they also use it?
lesson.example: 1 molecule of glucose gives about 38 ATP in aerobic respiration but only 2 ATP in anaerobic respiration.
lesson.activity: Put germinating seeds in one thermos flask and boiled (dead) seeds in another, each with a thermometer; record the temperature for three days.

questions.q: Write the word equation for aerobic respiration.
questions.a: Glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water + energy.

questions.q: Where does glycolysis take place?
questions.a: In the cytoplasm.

questions.q: Why are boiled seeds used as a control?
questions.a: They are dead and do not respire, so any change in the other flask is due to respiration.

questions.q: What is formed by anaerobic respiration in yeast?
questions.a: Ethanol and carbon dioxide.

lesson.homework: Explain why dough rises when yeast is added and left in a warm place.

topics.title: Five Kingdom Classification
topics.summary: Classification groups organisms by similarities and differences, making them easier to study; Whittaker's five kingdoms are Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae and Animalia.
notes: Classification groups organisms by similarities and differences, making them easier to study; Whittaker's five kingdoms are Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae and Animalia.
Monera: single-celled prokaryotes without a true nucleus (bacteria, blue-green algae).
Protista: single-celled eukaryotes (Amoeba, Paramecium, Euglena).
Fungi: eukaryotes without chlorophyll that absorb food, with cell walls of chitin (mushroom, yeast, bread mould).

Plantae: Thallophyta (algae, no true body parts), Bryophyta (mosses, amphibians of the plant world), Pteridophyta (ferns, with vascular tissue but no seeds) and Spermatophyta (seed plants: gymnosperms and angiosperms).
Animalia: multicellular heterotrophs without cell walls, from sponges to mammals.
outcomes: Explain the need for classification and the five kingdom system
State the main characteristics of Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae and Animalia with examples
Classify the plant kingdom into Thallophyta, Bryophyta, Pteridophyta and Spermatophyta

lesson.hook: How do scientists keep track of millions of kinds of living things?
lesson.example: A fern has roots, stems, leaves and vascular tissue but produces spores, not seeds, so it belongs to Pteridophyta.
lesson.activity: Show pictures or specimens of bacteria (curd), yeast, a moss, a fern, a pine cone and a flowering plant; groups place each in its kingdom and division.

questions.q: What is a prokaryote?
questions.a: An organism whose cells have no true nucleus, e.g. bacteria.

questions.q: To which kingdom does yeast belong?
questions.a: Fungi.

questions.q: Why are bryophytes called amphibians of the plant kingdom?
questions.a: They live on land but need water for reproduction.

questions.q: Name the two groups of seed plants.
questions.a: Gymnosperms and angiosperms.

lesson.homework: Find five organisms around your home and place each in its kingdom.

chapters.title: Economic Importance of Bacteria and Fungi

topics.title: Economic Importance of Bacteria and Fungi
topics.summary: Useful bacteria: Lactobacillus turns milk into curd; nitrogen-fixing bacteria (Rhizobium in root nodules) enrich soil; decomposers recycle nutrients; some bacteria make vitamins and antibiotics.
notes: Useful bacteria: Lactobacillus turns milk into curd; nitrogen-fixing bacteria (Rhizobium in root nodules) enrich soil; decomposers recycle nutrients; some bacteria make vitamins and antibiotics.
Bacteria are used in retting of fibres, curing tea and tobacco, and making vinegar.
Harmful bacteria cause diseases (cholera, tuberculosis, typhoid, tetanus) and spoil food.
Useful fungi: yeast in baking and brewing; Penicillium gives penicillin; mushrooms are food; fungi decompose dead matter.
Harmful fungi cause ringworm, athlete's foot and plant diseases (rust of wheat) and spoil bread and pickles.
Food is preserved against microbes by refrigeration, boiling, drying, salting, sugar and pasteurisation.
outcomes: Describe useful and harmful roles of bacteria
Describe useful and harmful roles of fungi
Relate microbes to food, agriculture, medicine and disease

lesson.hook: Curd, bread, antibiotics and compost all depend on microbes. Are germs only harmful?
lesson.example: Alexander Fleming noticed in 1928 that Penicillium mould stopped bacteria growing around it — the discovery of the first antibiotic, penicillin.
lesson.activity: Leave a slice of moist bread in a closed box for four days; observe the mould with a hand lens and discuss what conditions helped it grow.

questions.q: Which bacterium changes milk into curd?
questions.a: Lactobacillus.

questions.q: How do nitrogen-fixing bacteria help farmers?
questions.a: They convert atmospheric nitrogen into compounds plants can use.

questions.q: Name an antibiotic obtained from a fungus.
questions.a: Penicillin, from Penicillium.

questions.q: Give two ways of preserving food from microbes.
questions.a: Refrigeration and salting (also drying, boiling, pasteurisation).

lesson.homework: Make a two-column chart: "microbes that help us" and "microbes that harm us", with five examples each.

topics.title: Nutrition and a Balanced Diet
topics.summary: Carbohydrates (rice, wheat) and fats (ghee, oil) give energy; proteins (pulses, eggs, milk) build and repair the body.
notes: Carbohydrates (rice, wheat) and fats (ghee, oil) give energy; proteins (pulses, eggs, milk) build and repair the body.
Minerals: calcium for bones and teeth, iron for haemoglobin, iodine for thyroxine, sodium for nerve and muscle function.
Vitamins protect against disease: A (night blindness), B₁ (beriberi), C (scurvy), D (rickets), K (blood clotting).
Water carries materials and controls body temperature; roughage (cellulose) helps bowel movement and prevents constipation.
A balanced diet has all nutrients in the right amounts for a person's age, work and health.
Protein-energy malnutrition causes kwashiorkor (protein lack: swollen belly) and marasmus (lack of protein and energy: very thin body).
outcomes: Name the classes of food and state the functions of carbohydrates, fats, proteins, minerals, vitamins and water
Explain a balanced diet and the role of roughage
Describe deficiency diseases such as kwashiorkor, marasmus, scurvy, rickets and anaemia

lesson.hook: Two children eat the same amount of food; one is healthy, the other weak and sick. What could be missing?
lesson.example: Iron deficiency causes anaemia: less haemoglobin means less oxygen reaches the tissues, so the person tires quickly. Green leafy vegetables, jaggery and pulses supply iron.
lesson.activity: Pupils list everything they ate yesterday, sort it into nutrient groups and judge whether the day's diet was balanced.

questions.q: Which vitamin deficiency causes scurvy?
questions.a: Vitamin C.

questions.q: What is the role of roughage?
questions.a: It adds bulk and helps the movement of food, preventing constipation.

questions.q: Distinguish kwashiorkor and marasmus.
questions.a: Kwashiorkor is due to lack of protein; marasmus to lack of both protein and energy.

questions.q: Why is iodised salt recommended?
questions.a: Iodine is needed for thyroxine; its lack causes goitre.

lesson.homework: Plan a balanced one-day menu for a Class 9 pupil using local foods.

topics.title: Teeth and the Digestive System
topics.summary: A tooth has a crown (enamel — the hardest substance in the body), neck and root; inside are dentine and the pulp cavity with nerves and blood vessels.
notes: A tooth has a crown (enamel — the hardest substance in the body), neck and root; inside are dentine and the pulp cavity with nerves and blood vessels.
Adults have incisors (cutting), canines (tearing), premolars and molars (grinding); the adult dental formula is 2123/2123, 32 teeth.
The alimentary canal: mouth → oesophagus → stomach → small intestine → large intestine; food is pushed along by waves of muscle contraction (peristalsis).
Salivary amylase starts starch digestion in the mouth; pepsin digests proteins in the acidic stomach; bile from the liver emulsifies fats; pancreatic and intestinal enzymes complete digestion.
Digested food is absorbed through villi in the small intestine into blood and lymph; assimilation is its use by body cells.
The large intestine absorbs water; undigested food leaves as faeces.
outcomes: Describe the structure of a tooth and the types of teeth with their functions and dental formula
Name the organs and glands of the digestive system and their functions
Explain digestion by enzymes, absorption, assimilation and peristalsis

lesson.hook: A chapati becomes energy in your muscles. What happens to it on the way?
lesson.example: Chew plain rice for two minutes: it starts tasting sweet because salivary amylase turns starch into maltose.
lesson.activity: Starch-iodine test with saliva: add saliva to starch solution in one tube and water in another; after 15 minutes add iodine — only the water tube turns blue-black.

questions.q: Which is the hardest substance in the human body?
questions.a: Enamel.

questions.q: What is the function of bile?
questions.a: It emulsifies fats, breaking them into small droplets.

questions.q: Where is most digested food absorbed?
questions.a: In the small intestine, through the villi.

questions.q: Write the dental formula of an adult human.

lesson.homework: Draw and label the human digestive system and write one enzyme and its action for each part.

topics.title: Skeleton: Movement and Locomotion
topics.summary: The skeleton supports the body, protects organs (skull protects the brain, ribs the heart and lungs), allows movement, makes blood cells in bone marrow and stores calcium.
notes: The skeleton supports the body, protects organs (skull protects the brain, ribs the heart and lungs), allows movement, makes blood cells in bone marrow and stores calcium.
The axial skeleton is the skull, vertebral column, ribs and sternum; the appendicular skeleton is the girdles and limbs. An adult has 206 bones.
Immovable joints are fixed (sutures of the skull); slightly movable joints allow a little movement (between vertebrae).
Freely movable (synovial) joints: hinge (elbow, knee), ball and socket (shoulder, hip), gliding (wrist), pivot (neck, between atlas and axis).
Muscles work in antagonistic pairs: the biceps contracts to bend the arm; the triceps contracts to straighten it.
Ligaments join bone to bone; tendons join muscle to bone; cartilage cushions joints.
outcomes: State the functions of the human skeleton and name the axial and appendicular skeleton
Classify joints by their movement with examples
Explain how bones and muscles work together in movement

lesson.hook: Your elbow bends only one way but your shoulder swings round in a circle. Why?
lesson.example: The ball-shaped head of the femur fits in the socket of the hip girdle, letting the leg move in many directions; the knee is a hinge and moves in one plane.
lesson.activity: Pupils move their neck, elbow, shoulder and wrist and classify each joint; then feel the biceps and triceps as they bend and straighten the arm.

questions.q: Give one example each of a hinge joint and a ball and socket joint.
questions.a: Knee (or elbow); shoulder (or hip).

questions.q: What connects a muscle to a bone?
questions.a: A tendon.

questions.q: Which bones form the axial skeleton?
questions.a: Skull, vertebral column, ribs and sternum.

questions.q: Why are the biceps and triceps called antagonistic muscles?
questions.a: They work in opposite directions: one bends the joint, the other straightens it.

lesson.homework: Make a model of the elbow joint with cardboard strips and rubber bands to show how the biceps and triceps work.

topics.title: Skin: Structure and Functions
topics.summary: The skin is the largest organ: the epidermis (outer, with a dead protective layer and pigment melanin) and the dermis (inner, with blood vessels, nerves, glands and hair roots).
notes: The skin is the largest organ: the epidermis (outer, with a dead protective layer and pigment melanin) and the dermis (inner, with blood vessels, nerves, glands and hair roots).
The skin protects against germs, water loss and ultraviolet light; it senses touch, pain, heat and cold; it makes vitamin D in sunlight.
Sweat glands give out sweat, which cools the body as it evaporates and removes some salts and urea.
Sebaceous glands secrete sebum that keeps hair and skin soft and waterproof; hair and nails are made of keratin.
In heat, skin blood vessels widen (vasodilation) and sweating increases so more heat is lost; in cold they narrow (vasoconstriction) and hairs stand up.
Mammary glands are modified sweat glands that produce milk.
outcomes: Name the layers and parts of the skin and state their functions
Describe skin derivatives: sweat and sebaceous glands, hair, nails and mammary glands
Explain how the skin helps to regulate body temperature

lesson.hook: Why do we sweat on a hot day and get goose bumps in the cold?
lesson.example: After running, your face is flushed (vasodilation brings warm blood to the surface) and sweaty (evaporation of sweat takes away heat).
lesson.activity: Put a drop of water and a drop of spirit on the back of the hand: the spirit feels colder because it evaporates faster, just as sweat cools the skin.

questions.q: Name the pigment that gives colour to the skin.
questions.a: Melanin.

questions.q: How does sweating cool the body?
questions.a: Sweat evaporates, taking heat from the skin.

questions.q: What is vasoconstriction?
questions.a: Narrowing of blood vessels near the skin surface to reduce heat loss.

questions.q: Give two functions of the skin.
questions.a: Protection and temperature regulation (also sensation, vitamin D).

lesson.homework: Draw and label a section of human skin.

topics.title: The Respiratory System
topics.summary: Air enters through the nostrils and passes the pharynx, larynx, trachea, bronchi and bronchioles to the alveoli in the lungs.
notes: Air enters through the nostrils and passes the pharynx, larynx, trachea, bronchi and bronchioles to the alveoli in the lungs.
Alveoli are tiny thin-walled air sacs surrounded by capillaries: oxygen diffuses into the blood and carbon dioxide diffuses out.
Inhalation: the diaphragm contracts and flattens and the ribs move up and out, the chest volume increases and air is drawn in. Exhalation is the reverse.
Breathing is the physical movement of air; respiration is the chemical breakdown of food in cells to release energy (tissue respiration), which also produces body heat.
Exhaled air has less oxygen and more carbon dioxide and water vapour than inhaled air.
The nose filters, warms and moistens air; cilia and mucus trap dust and germs.
outcomes: Name the organs of the human respiratory system
Explain the mechanism of breathing (inhalation and exhalation)
Distinguish breathing from respiration and explain tissue respiration and heat production

lesson.hook: You breathe about 15 times a minute without thinking. What makes air rush in and out?
lesson.example: Inhaled air has about 21% oxygen and 0.04% carbon dioxide; exhaled air has about 16% oxygen and 4% carbon dioxide.
lesson.activity: Build a bell-jar lung model with a plastic bottle, two balloons and a rubber sheet; pull the sheet (diaphragm) down and watch the "lungs" fill.

questions.q: Where does gaseous exchange take place in the lungs?
questions.a: In the alveoli.

questions.q: What happens to the diaphragm during inhalation?
questions.a: It contracts and flattens, increasing the chest volume.

questions.q: How is breathing different from respiration?
questions.a: Breathing moves air in and out; respiration releases energy from food in cells.

questions.q: Why should we breathe through the nose?
questions.a: It filters, warms and moistens the air.

lesson.homework: Count your breaths per minute at rest and after skipping for one minute; explain the difference.

topics.title: Health and Hygiene
topics.summary: Good health is physical, mental and social well-being; personal hygiene (clean body, hands, food) and public hygiene (clean water, drains, waste disposal) prevent disease.
notes: Good health is physical, mental and social well-being; personal hygiene (clean body, hands, food) and public hygiene (clean water, drains, waste disposal) prevent disease.
Communicable diseases spread from person to person through air, water, food, contact or vectors (mosquitoes, flies); non-communicable ones (diabetes, heart disease) do not spread.
Endemic diseases are always present in an area; epidemic ones spread widely in a region for a time; pandemic ones spread across countries; sporadic cases occur here and there.

Examples: bacterial — cholera, typhoid, tuberculosis, tetanus; viral — influenza, polio, hepatitis, AIDS; protozoan — malaria, amoebic dysentery, sleeping sickness; helminthic — filariasis, ascariasis, taeniasis.
Active immunity is made by the body after infection or vaccination; passive immunity is given ready-made antibodies (anti-tetanus serum, mother's milk).
The Red Cross gives relief in wars and disasters and runs blood banks; WHO leads world health work, such as eradicating smallpox.
outcomes: Explain personal and public hygiene and sanitation
Classify diseases as communicable, non-communicable, endemic, epidemic, pandemic and sporadic, with modes of transmission
Describe bacterial, viral, protozoan and helminthic diseases, immunity, and the work of the Red Cross and WHO

lesson.hook: Why can a disease like influenza spread through a whole city in weeks, while diabetes cannot spread at all?
lesson.example: Malaria is caused by the protozoan Plasmodium and spread by the female Anopheles mosquito; removing standing water breaks the chain.
lesson.activity: Map the class's ideas on how diseases spread (air, water, food, contact, vectors) and add one disease and one prevention for each route.

questions.q: What is an epidemic?
questions.a: A disease that spreads quickly to many people in an area for a time.

questions.q: Name a disease caused by a virus.
questions.a: Influenza (or polio, hepatitis, AIDS).

questions.q: Distinguish active and passive immunity.
questions.a: Active immunity is produced by the body; passive immunity is given as ready-made antibodies.

questions.q: Give two activities of the WHO.
questions.a: Controlling epidemics and running vaccination programmes (also setting health standards).

lesson.homework: Survey your locality for places where mosquitoes can breed and suggest how to remove them.

topics.title: Waste Generation and Management
topics.summary: Waste comes from homes (kitchen and packaging waste), industries (chemicals, fly ash), agriculture (crop stubble, pesticides), hospitals (biomedical waste) and electronics (e-waste).
notes: Waste comes from homes (kitchen and packaging waste), industries (chemicals, fly ash), agriculture (crop stubble, pesticides), hospitals (biomedical waste) and electronics (e-waste).
Biodegradable waste (food, paper, leaves) is broken down by microbes; non-biodegradable waste (plastics, glass, metals) lasts for years.
Poorly managed waste spreads disease, pollutes soil and water, blocks drains and releases methane and toxic gases.
Segregation at source into wet and dry (green and blue bins) makes treatment easier; composting and vermicomposting turn wet waste into manure.
Sanitary landfills, incineration (for biomedical waste) and recycling handle the rest; e-waste needs special recycling to recover metals safely.
The 3 Rs — reduce, reuse, recycle — cut the amount of waste made in the first place.
outcomes: Identify sources of waste: domestic, industrial, agricultural, biomedical and e-waste
Distinguish biodegradable and non-biodegradable waste and explain their effects
Describe methods of waste management: segregation, composting, landfill, incineration and the 3 Rs

lesson.hook: Where does the bag of garbage from your home go after the truck takes it away?
lesson.example: A school canteen producing 20 kg of vegetable peelings a week can compost it into about 7–8 kg of manure for the school garden.
lesson.activity: Audit one day's waste from the classroom: sort it into biodegradable, recyclable and other, weigh each pile and discuss how to reduce it.

questions.q: Give two examples of non-biodegradable waste.
questions.a: Plastic bottles and glass (also metal cans).

questions.q: What is vermicomposting?
questions.a: Using earthworms to turn organic waste into compost.

questions.q: Why must biomedical waste be handled separately?
questions.a: It may carry infections and harmful chemicals.

questions.q: What are the 3 Rs?
questions.a: Reduce, reuse and recycle.

lesson.homework: Set up a small compost pot at home with kitchen peelings and record the changes every week.

topics.title: Cell Cycle and Cell Division
topics.summary: The cell cycle has interphase (the cell grows and copies its DNA) and the division phase (M phase).
notes: The cell cycle has interphase (the cell grows and copies its DNA) and the division phase (M phase).
Mitosis produces two daughter cells identical to the parent, each with the same number of chromosomes; it happens in body (somatic) cells for growth and repair.
Stages of mitosis: prophase (chromosomes condense, nuclear membrane disappears), metaphase (chromosomes line up at the equator), anaphase (chromatids move to the poles), telophase (new nuclei form).
Cytokinesis divides the cytoplasm: by furrowing in animal cells and a cell plate in plant cells.
Meiosis happens in reproductive cells; it has two divisions and produces four cells, each with half the chromosome number (haploid), and new combinations of genes.
Meiosis keeps the chromosome number constant from generation to generation when gametes fuse at fertilisation.
outcomes: Describe the cell cycle: interphase and cell division
Explain the stages of mitosis and their significance
Compare mitosis and meiosis

lesson.hook: A cut on your finger heals in a few days, and you grew from one cell into trillions. How do cells multiply?
lesson.example: A human body cell has 46 chromosomes (diploid); mitosis gives two cells with 46 each, while meiosis gives four gametes with 23 each.
lesson.activity: Pupils model mitosis with pairs of pipe cleaners or wool for chromosomes, moving them through each stage on a large paper cell.

questions.q: In which stage do chromosomes line up at the equator?
questions.a: Metaphase.

questions.q: How many cells does meiosis produce from one parent cell?
questions.a: Four.

questions.q: Where does meiosis take place in humans?
questions.a: In the testes and ovaries (reproductive organs).

questions.q: Give one difference between mitosis and meiosis.
questions.a: Mitosis keeps the chromosome number the same; meiosis halves it.

lesson.homework: Draw the four stages of mitosis in an animal cell and label the chromosomes and spindle.

topics.title: Structure of Chromosomes
topics.summary: Chromosomes are thread-like structures in the nucleus made of DNA and proteins; they carry genes.
notes: Chromosomes are thread-like structures in the nucleus made of DNA and proteins; they carry genes.
A chromosome has two identical sister chromatids joined at the centromere before division.
DNA is a double helix of two strands of nucleotides; a gene is a segment of DNA that controls a particular trait.
Humans have 23 pairs of chromosomes: 22 pairs of autosomes and one pair of sex chromosomes (XX in females, XY in males).
Alternative forms of a gene are alleles; they sit at the same place (locus) on a pair of homologous chromosomes.
A child's sex is decided by the father: an X-carrying sperm gives a girl (XX), a Y-carrying sperm a boy (XY).
outcomes: Describe the structure of a chromosome: chromatids, centromere, DNA and genes
Explain the terms gene, allele and chromosome number
Describe sex chromosomes and how sex is determined in humans

lesson.hook: Where exactly is the information that decides your eye colour stored?
lesson.example: The mother always gives an X; if the father's sperm carries X the child is XX (girl), if Y the child is XY (boy), so the chance of either is 1 in 2.
lesson.activity: Build a paper-strip double helix, or draw a chromosome with its chromatids, centromere and genes marked as bands.

questions.q: How many pairs of chromosomes are there in a human body cell?
questions.a: 23 pairs (46 chromosomes).

questions.q: What is a gene?
questions.a: A segment of DNA that controls a trait.

questions.q: What are the sex chromosomes of a human male?
questions.a: XY.

questions.q: What joins the two chromatids of a chromosome?
questions.a: The centromere.

lesson.homework: Write a short note on why the belief that a mother decides the sex of her child is wrong.

topics.title: Genetics: Mendel's Laws of Inheritance
topics.summary: Mendel crossed garden peas with contrasting traits and found patterns of inheritance.
notes: Mendel crossed garden peas with contrasting traits and found patterns of inheritance.
Dominant traits show when one allele is present (T for tall); recessive traits show only when both alleles are recessive (tt short).
Genotype is the genetic make-up (TT, Tt, tt); phenotype is the visible trait. TT and tt are homozygous, Tt heterozygous.
Monohybrid cross Tt × Tt gives phenotypes 3 tall : 1 short and genotypes 1 TT : 2 Tt : 1 tt.
Mendel's laws: dominance, segregation (alleles separate into gametes) and independent assortment (dihybrid ratio 9 : 3 : 3 : 1).
Sex-linked disorders like haemophilia and red-green colour blindness are carried on the X chromosome, so they are commoner in males.
outcomes: Explain Mendel's monohybrid and dihybrid crosses and his laws
Use the terms dominant, recessive, genotype, phenotype, homozygous and heterozygous
Explain sex-linked inheritance with haemophilia and colour blindness

lesson.hook: Two tall pea plants produced a short one. How can a trait skip a generation?
lesson.example: Tt × Tt: gametes T and t from each parent give TT, Tt, Tt and tt in a Punnett square — three tall to one short.
lesson.activity: Flip two coins (T/t for each parent) 40 times as a class and record the combinations; compare with the expected 1 : 2 : 1 ratio.

questions.q: What is the phenotypic ratio of a monohybrid cross in F2?
Define a recessive trait.
questions.a: One that shows only when both alleles are recessive.

questions.q: State the law of segregation.
questions.a: The two alleles of a gene separate during gamete formation, each gamete getting one.

questions.q: Why is colour blindness commoner in men?
questions.a: The gene is on the X chromosome and men have only one X.

lesson.homework: Draw a Punnett square for a cross between a homozygous round-seeded and a wrinkled-seeded pea plant, and give the F1 and F2 results.

topics.title: Absorption by Roots
topics.summary: Imbibition is the absorption of water by solid particles such as dry seeds and wood (swelling of seeds).
notes: Imbibition is the absorption of water by solid particles such as dry seeds and wood (swelling of seeds).
Diffusion is the movement of particles from higher to lower concentration; osmosis is the movement of water through a semi-permeable membrane from a dilute to a concentrated solution.
Root hairs increase the surface area; soil water enters them by osmosis because cell sap is more concentrated; minerals are taken up by active transport using energy.
A cell full of water is turgid; one that has lost water is flaccid. In a strong salt solution the cytoplasm shrinks from the wall (plasmolysis); in water it recovers (deplasmolysis).
Water moves from cell to cell to the xylem and rises in the stem by root pressure and mainly by the transpiration pull.
Too much fertiliser near roots can plasmolyse root cells and wilt the plant.
outcomes: Explain absorption of water by roots: imbibition, diffusion, osmosis and active transport
Describe turgidity, flaccidity, plasmolysis and deplasmolysis
Explain root pressure and the upward movement of water

lesson.hook: Why do salted cucumber slices go limp, and how does water get from the soil into a root?
lesson.example: Raisins in water swell (endosmosis); swollen raisins in strong sugar syrup shrink (exosmosis) — the osmosis virtual lab shows the same with a balance.
lesson.activity: Potato osmoscope: scoop a hollow in a peeled potato, fill it with sugar solution and stand it in water; the level inside rises over a day.

questions.q: Define osmosis.
questions.a: Movement of water through a semi-permeable membrane from a dilute to a concentrated solution.

questions.q: What is plasmolysis?
questions.a: Shrinking of the cytoplasm away from the cell wall when a cell loses water in a strong solution.

questions.q: How do root hairs help absorption?
questions.a: They greatly increase the surface area in contact with soil water.

questions.q: Why do dry seeds swell when soaked?
questions.a: They absorb water by imbibition.

lesson.homework: Explain why sprinkling salt on a lawn kills the grass.

topics.title: Transpiration
topics.summary: Transpiration is the loss of water as vapour from the aerial parts of a plant, mostly through stomata.
notes: Transpiration is the loss of water as vapour from the aerial parts of a plant, mostly through stomata.
Stomata open when guard cells are turgid (usually in light) and close when they are flaccid.
The rate increases with light, temperature and wind, and decreases with high humidity and poor water supply.
Transpiration creates a pull that draws water up the xylem, carries minerals, and cools the leaves.
The potometer measures water uptake; a cobalt chloride paper turns from blue to pink with water vapour from a leaf surface (more on the lower surface).
Desert plants reduce transpiration with thick cuticles, sunken stomata, fewer leaves or leaves turned into spines (cactus); guttation is loss of liquid water through hydathodes.
outcomes: Explain transpiration and its types (stomatal, cuticular, lenticular)
Describe factors affecting the rate of transpiration and experiments to show it
State the significance of transpiration and adaptations to reduce it

resources.title: How fast does a shoot lose water?

lesson.hook: A big banyan tree gives off hundreds of litres of water every day. Why does it lose so much water?
lesson.example: Cover a potted plant's leaves with a transparent bag: in an hour droplets collect inside. Weighing the pot shows the water lost.
lesson.activity: Tie polythene bags over leafy twigs in sun, shade and wind; compare the water collected after two hours.

questions.q: Where are most stomata found on a dicot leaf?
questions.a: On the lower surface.

questions.q: Give two factors that increase transpiration.
questions.a: High temperature and wind (also bright light, low humidity).

questions.q: What is the use of a potometer?
questions.a: To measure the rate of water uptake (and so transpiration) by a shoot.

questions.q: How does a cactus reduce water loss?
questions.a: Its leaves are spines, it has a thick cuticle and sunken stomata.

lesson.homework: Explain why transpiration is called a necessary evil.

topics.title: Photosynthesis
topics.summary: Photosynthesis: 6CO₂ + 12H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ + 6H₂O in the presence of sunlight and chlorophyll.
notes: Photosynthesis: 6CO₂ + 12H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ + 6H₂O in the presence of sunlight and chlorophyll.
It takes place in chloroplasts: the light reaction (in the grana) splits water, releases oxygen and makes ATP and NADPH; the dark reaction (in the stroma) fixes carbon dioxide into glucose.
The oxygen released comes from water, not from carbon dioxide.
Starch test: a leaf is boiled, decolourised in alcohol and tested with iodine; experiments show light, chlorophyll and CO₂ are all needed (covered leaf, variegated leaf, KOH to absorb CO₂).
Factors: light intensity, CO₂ concentration, temperature and water.
Photosynthesis makes food for almost all living things, keeps oxygen and carbon dioxide balanced in the air, and stored the energy now in fossil fuels.
outcomes: Describe the process of photosynthesis with its equation
Explain the light and dark reactions and the role of chlorophyll
Describe experiments on the need for light, chlorophyll and carbon dioxide, and the significance of photosynthesis

resources.title: Starch test: light and chlorophyll for photosynthesis

lesson.hook: Every breath of oxygen you take and every grain you eat depends on leaves. How do leaves make food from air and water?
lesson.example: In a variegated leaf only the green parts turn blue-black with iodine, showing chlorophyll is needed (see the starch-test virtual lab).
lesson.activity: Put a water plant (Hydrilla) under an inverted funnel and test tube in sunlight; count bubbles per minute at different distances from a lamp.

questions.q: Write the balanced equation for photosynthesis.
questions.a: 6CO₂ + 12H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ + 6H₂O (with light and chlorophyll).

questions.q: Where does the dark reaction take place?
questions.a: In the stroma of the chloroplast.

questions.q: Why is the leaf boiled in alcohol before the iodine test?
questions.a: To remove chlorophyll so the colour change can be seen.

questions.q: What is the source of oxygen released in photosynthesis?
questions.a: Water.

lesson.homework: Design an experiment to show that carbon dioxide is needed for photosynthesis, naming the control.

topics.title: Chemical Coordination in Plants
topics.summary: Plants coordinate growth with chemicals called phytohormones.
notes: Plants coordinate growth with chemicals called phytohormones.
Auxins promote cell elongation and cause bending towards light; gibberellins cause stem elongation and seed germination; cytokinins promote cell division.
Abscisic acid is a growth inhibitor: it closes stomata in drought and keeps seeds dormant; ethylene ripens fruits.
Tropisms are growth movements in response to a stimulus: stems show positive phototropism, roots positive geotropism and hydrotropism, pollen tubes chemotropism, tendrils thigmotropism.
In a shoot lit from one side, auxin collects on the shaded side, which grows faster, so the shoot bends towards light.
Uses: auxins for rooting cuttings and weed killers, gibberellins for bigger grapes, ethylene (from ethephon or calcium carbide — the latter unsafe) for ripening.
outcomes: Describe plant hormones: auxins, gibberellins, cytokinins, abscisic acid and ethylene
Explain tropisms: phototropism, geotropism, hydrotropism, chemotropism and thigmotropism
State the uses of plant hormones in agriculture

lesson.hook: Why does a plant on a window sill bend towards the light, and how do farmers ripen mangoes quickly?
lesson.example: A seedling in a box with one hole bends towards the hole: auxin moves to the shaded side and those cells elongate more.
lesson.activity: Grow bean seedlings in a shoe box with a hole at one end and a maze of card inside; after a week the shoots find their way to the light.

questions.q: Which hormone ripens fruits?
questions.a: Ethylene.

questions.q: What is geotropism? How do roots respond?
questions.a: Growth in response to gravity; roots grow towards gravity (positive geotropism).

questions.q: Why does a shoot bend towards light?
questions.a: Auxin collects on the shaded side and makes those cells grow longer.

questions.q: Name a hormone that closes stomata during drought.
questions.a: Abscisic acid.

lesson.homework: Plant a seed in a transparent cup and turn it on its side after the root appears; record how the root and shoot respond over five days.

topics.title: The Circulatory System
topics.summary: Blood has plasma and cells: red blood cells (haemoglobin carries oxygen, no nucleus in mammals), white blood cells (fight infection) and platelets (clotting).
notes: Blood has plasma and cells: red blood cells (haemoglobin carries oxygen, no nucleus in mammals), white blood cells (fight infection) and platelets (clotting).
The heart has four chambers: right atrium and ventricle pump deoxygenated blood to the lungs; left atrium and ventricle pump oxygenated blood to the body. Valves stop backflow.
Double circulation: blood passes through the heart twice in one round — pulmonary circulation (heart–lungs) and systemic circulation (heart–body).
Arteries carry blood away from the heart under high pressure (thick elastic walls); veins return blood (thin walls, valves); capillaries are one cell thick for exchange.
The heartbeat (lub-dub) is the closing of valves; a normal pulse is about 72 per minute; blood pressure is about 120/80 mm Hg.
ABO blood groups (A, B, AB, O) and the Rh factor matter for transfusion; lymph returns tissue fluid to the blood and helps fight infection.
outcomes: Describe blood and lymph and the functions of their components
Describe the structure and working of the heart, and double circulation
Distinguish arteries, veins and capillaries; explain blood groups, blood pressure and heartbeat

lesson.hook: Your heart beats about 1 lakh times a day without rest. What is it pumping, and where to?
lesson.example: The left ventricle has the thickest wall because it pumps blood to the whole body; the right ventricle pumps only to the nearby lungs.
lesson.activity: Pupils find their pulse at the wrist, count for a minute at rest and after jumping; the class plots the results and discusses why the rate rises.

questions.q: Which blood cells help in clotting?
questions.a: Platelets.

questions.q: Why is it called double circulation?
questions.a: Blood passes through the heart twice in each complete round.

questions.q: Why do veins have valves?
questions.a: To stop blood flowing backwards as it returns to the heart under low pressure.

questions.q: Which blood group is called the universal donor?
questions.a: O negative (O).

lesson.homework: Draw and label the human heart and trace the path of blood with arrows.

topics.title: The Excretory System
topics.summary: Excretion removes metabolic wastes (urea, carbon dioxide, excess salts and water); the kidneys, lungs, skin and liver are excretory organs.
notes: Excretion removes metabolic wastes (urea, carbon dioxide, excess salts and water); the kidneys, lungs, skin and liver are excretory organs.
The urinary system: two kidneys, two ureters, the urinary bladder and the urethra; the renal artery brings blood and the renal vein takes it away.
Each kidney has about a million nephrons; a nephron has Bowman's capsule around a glomerulus, and a long tubule with Henle's loop.
Urine forms in three steps: ultrafiltration in the glomerulus, selective reabsorption of glucose, salts and water in the tubule, and tubular secretion of some wastes.
Kidneys also control the water and salt balance of the body (osmoregulation) with the help of ADH from the pituitary.
When kidneys fail, dialysis (artificial kidney) or a transplant removes wastes from the blood.
outcomes: Describe the organs of the human urinary system and their functions
Explain the structure of a nephron and urine formation (ultrafiltration, selective reabsorption, tubular secretion)
Explain osmoregulation and the role of the kidneys and dialysis

lesson.hook: How do two bean-shaped organs clean about 180 litres of blood filtrate every day?
lesson.example: About 180 L of filtrate forms each day, but only about 1.5 L of urine is passed; the rest is reabsorbed in the tubules.
lesson.activity: Draw a nephron on the board as a "filter and recycle" machine; pupils add labels and arrows for filtration, reabsorption and secretion.

questions.q: Where does ultrafiltration take place?
questions.a: In the glomerulus, into Bowman's capsule.

questions.q: Which substances are reabsorbed in the tubule?
questions.a: Glucose, amino acids, salts and most of the water.

questions.q: What is osmoregulation?
questions.a: Keeping the water and salt balance of the body constant.

questions.q: What is dialysis?
questions.a: Artificial removal of wastes from blood when the kidneys fail.

lesson.homework: Find out how much water you drink in a day and how the colour of urine changes with water intake.

topics.title: The Nervous System
topics.summary: A neuron has a cell body (cyton), dendrites that receive messages and an axon that carries impulses away; synapses link neurons.
notes: A neuron has a cell body (cyton), dendrites that receive messages and an axon that carries impulses away; synapses link neurons.
The central nervous system is the brain and spinal cord; the peripheral nervous system is the cranial and spinal nerves; the autonomic system controls involuntary organs.

Cerebrum: thinking, memory, voluntary actions and senses; cerebellum: balance and coordination; medulla oblongata: heartbeat, breathing, swallowing; thalamus and hypothalamus: relay, hunger, thirst and temperature; pons: connects parts.
In the brain grey matter is outside and white matter inside; in the spinal cord it is the reverse.
A reflex action is a quick, automatic response to a stimulus controlled by the spinal cord: receptor → sensory neuron → spinal cord → motor neuron → effector (reflex arc).
Voluntary actions are under conscious control of the cerebrum; involuntary ones are not; conditioned reflexes are learnt (mouth watering at the smell of food).
outcomes: Describe the structure of a neuron and the central, peripheral and autonomic nervous systems
Name the parts of the brain and their functions, and the structure of the spinal cord
Explain reflex action and the reflex arc, and compare voluntary and involuntary actions

lesson.hook: You pull your hand away from a hot pan before you even feel the pain. How is that possible?
lesson.example: Knee-jerk: a tap below the kneecap stretches a tendon; the message goes to the spinal cord and straight back to the thigh muscle, which kicks — the brain is told afterwards.
lesson.activity: Ruler-drop test for reaction time: one pupil drops a ruler, the other catches it; the distance fallen gives the reaction time. Compare with a knee-jerk reflex.

questions.q: Which part of the brain controls balance?
questions.a: The cerebellum.

questions.q: What is a reflex action?
questions.a: A quick, automatic response to a stimulus, controlled by the spinal cord.

questions.q: Trace the path of a reflex arc.
questions.a: Receptor → sensory neuron → spinal cord (relay neuron) → motor neuron → effector.

questions.q: Which part of the brain controls heartbeat and breathing?
questions.a: The medulla oblongata.

lesson.homework: Draw a labelled diagram of the human brain and write one function of each part.

chapters.title: Sense Organs: The Eye and the Ear

topics.title: Sense Organs: The Eye and the Ear
topics.summary: Eye parts: cornea (bends light), iris and pupil (control light), lens (focuses), retina (rods for dim light, cones for colour), optic nerve (to the brain); the blind spot has no receptors.
notes: Eye parts: cornea (bends light), iris and pupil (control light), lens (focuses), retina (rods for dim light, cones for colour), optic nerve (to the brain); the blind spot has no receptors.
Accommodation: ciliary muscles change the thickness of the lens to focus near and far objects.
Myopia (short sight): distant objects blur because the image forms in front of the retina — corrected with a concave lens. Hypermetropia (long sight) — convex lens.
Presbyopia comes with age as the lens stiffens; astigmatism (uneven cornea) uses cylindrical lenses; cataract is a cloudy lens, treated by surgery.
The ear: outer ear (pinna and ear canal), middle ear (eardrum and three ossicles — malleus, incus, stapes), inner ear (cochlea for hearing; semicircular canals and utriculus for balance).
Sound vibrates the eardrum; the ossicles amplify it; hair cells in the cochlea change it into nerve impulses to the brain.
outcomes: Describe the structure and functions of the human eye
Explain defects of vision and their correction
Describe the parts of the ear and their roles in hearing and balance

lesson.hook: How does the eye focus on a book and then on a distant bus in a split second?
lesson.example: A student who sees the blackboard blurred but reads a book clearly has myopia; a concave lens moves the image back onto the retina.
lesson.activity: Find the blind spot: draw a dot and a cross 6 cm apart, close the left eye, look at the cross and move the card slowly until the dot vanishes.

questions.q: Which cells of the retina detect colour?
questions.a: Cones.

questions.q: Which lens corrects myopia?
questions.a: A concave lens.

questions.q: Name the three ear ossicles.
questions.a: Malleus, incus and stapes.

questions.q: Which part of the ear helps us keep balance?
questions.a: The semicircular canals (and utriculus) of the inner ear.

lesson.homework: Draw and label the human eye and ear.

topics.title: The Endocrine System
topics.summary: Endocrine (ductless) glands release hormones straight into the blood; exocrine glands use ducts (salivary, sweat). The pancreas is both.
notes: Endocrine (ductless) glands release hormones straight into the blood; exocrine glands use ducts (salivary, sweat). The pancreas is both.
Pancreas (islets of Langerhans): insulin lowers blood sugar; glucagon raises it. Too little insulin causes diabetes mellitus.
Thyroid: thyroxine controls metabolism; too little causes goitre, cretinism in children and myxoedema in adults; too much causes exophthalmic goitre.
Adrenal glands: cortical hormones control salts and sugar; adrenaline prepares the body for emergencies ("fight or flight") — faster heart and breathing.
Pituitary (the master gland): growth hormone (too little — dwarfism, too much — gigantism), tropic hormones that control other glands, ADH (water reabsorption) and oxytocin.
Feedback: when thyroxine is high, the pituitary makes less TSH, so the thyroid slows down.
outcomes: Distinguish endocrine and exocrine glands
Name the hormones of the pituitary, thyroid, adrenal and pancreas and their effects
Describe effects of too little or too much hormone and the feedback mechanism

lesson.hook: Why does your heart race and your mouth go dry just before an exam?
lesson.example: Before a race adrenaline raises the heart rate and blood sugar and sends blood to the muscles — the body gets ready to act fast.
lesson.activity: Make a body outline chart: pupils place cards of the glands in the right positions and write each gland's hormone and one effect.

questions.q: Which hormone lowers blood sugar?
questions.a: Insulin.

questions.q: Why is the pituitary called the master gland?
questions.a: Its tropic hormones control several other endocrine glands.

questions.q: What causes goitre?
questions.a: Lack of iodine, so too little thyroxine is made.

questions.q: Name the emergency hormone.
questions.a: Adrenaline.

lesson.homework: Write about why iodised salt is used across India.

topics.title: The Reproductive System
topics.summary: Male: testes make sperm and testosterone; sperm travel through the vas deferens and urethra; seminal vesicles, prostate and Cowper's glands add fluid.
notes: Male: testes make sperm and testosterone; sperm travel through the vas deferens and urethra; seminal vesicles, prostate and Cowper's glands add fluid.
Female: ovaries release an egg (ovum) each month and make oestrogen and progesterone; the oviduct (fallopian tube) carries the egg; the uterus holds the baby.
Secondary sexual characters appear at puberty under the control of these hormones.
A sperm has a head (nucleus and acrosome), middle piece (mitochondria) and tail; fertilisation in the oviduct forms a zygote, which implants in the uterus wall.
The placenta supplies oxygen and food and removes wastes; gestation in humans is about 280 days, ending in birth (parturition).

The menstrual cycle (about 28 days) prepares the uterus lining; if no fertilisation occurs it breaks down (menstruation). Family planning uses barriers, pills, IUDs and surgery (vasectomy, tubectomy).
outcomes: Describe the male and female reproductive organs and their functions
Explain the structure of sperm and egg, fertilisation, implantation, placenta, gestation and parturition
Describe the menstrual cycle and methods of family planning

lesson.hook: How does a single fertilised cell grow into a baby in nine months?
lesson.example: Ovulation happens around day 14 of a 28-day cycle; the egg lives about a day, so fertilisation usually happens in the oviduct soon after.
lesson.activity: Use labelled diagrams to follow the path of a sperm and an egg to fertilisation and implantation; discuss respectfully with scientific terms only.

questions.q: Where does fertilisation take place in humans?
questions.a: In the oviduct (fallopian tube).

questions.q: Give two functions of the placenta.
questions.a: Supplying oxygen and nutrients to the foetus and removing its wastes.

questions.q: What is the role of the acrosome in a sperm?
questions.a: Its enzymes help the sperm enter the egg.

questions.q: Name two methods of family planning.
questions.a: Barrier methods and oral pills (also IUDs, vasectomy, tubectomy).

lesson.homework: Make a table comparing male and female reproductive organs and their functions.

topics.title: Human Population
topics.summary: Demography is the study of human populations; population density is the number of people per square kilometre.
notes: Demography is the study of human populations; population density is the number of people per square kilometre.
Birth rate and death rate are counted per 1000 people per year; growth rate = birth rate − death rate (ignoring migration).
A rapid rise in population (population explosion) happened as the death rate fell with better medicine, sanitation and food, while the birth rate stayed high.
Effects: pressure on food, water, housing, jobs, schools, health care and the environment.
Population control: education (especially of girls), later marriage (legal age), awareness of small families, family-planning methods and health care that reduces infant deaths.
Balanced population policies aim at a healthy, well-educated population rather than only numbers.
outcomes: Explain population growth, population explosion and its causes in India and the world
Define demography, population density, birth rate, death rate and growth rate
Discuss the need for and methods of population control

lesson.hook: India is now the most populous country in the world. What does that mean for food, water and jobs?
lesson.example: If a town has a birth rate of 20 and a death rate of 7 per 1000, its growth rate is 13 per 1000, or 1.3% a year.
lesson.activity: Groups use census data for their state (or given figures) to calculate density and growth rate, and list local effects of population growth.

questions.q: What is demography?
questions.a: The statistical study of human populations.

questions.q: Give two causes of population explosion in India.
questions.a: Falling death rate due to medical care; continuing high birth rate.

questions.q: Define population density.
questions.a: The number of people living per square kilometre.

questions.q: Suggest two measures to control population growth.
questions.a: Educating girls and promoting family planning (also later marriage).

lesson.homework: Interview elders at home about family sizes in their time and today; write what has changed and why.

topics.title: Human Evolution
topics.summary: Evolution is the gradual change of living things over many generations, producing new species.
notes: Evolution is the gradual change of living things over many generations, producing new species.
Lamarck proposed that characters acquired by use and disuse are passed on (a stretching giraffe) — later shown to be wrong, since acquired characters are not inherited.
Darwin's natural selection: organisms overproduce, compete (struggle for existence), vary, and those best suited survive and reproduce (survival of the fittest).
Evidence of evolution comes from fossils, homologous organs (a human arm, a whale flipper and a bat wing), vestigial organs (appendix) and embryos.
Human ancestors in order: Australopithecus, Homo habilis (tool maker), Homo erectus (used fire), Neanderthals, Cro-Magnon and Homo sapiens sapiens (modern humans).
Human evolution included upright walking, a larger brain, smaller jaws and the use of tools, fire and language.
outcomes: Explain theories of evolution: Lamarck's inheritance of acquired characters and Darwin's natural selection
Describe the main stages of human ancestors
Relate evidence and examples to the theories

lesson.hook: Did the giraffe get its long neck by stretching, or were long-necked giraffes simply the ones that survived?
lesson.example: Peppered moths in industrial England: when soot darkened tree trunks, dark moths survived birds better and became common — natural selection in action.
lesson.activity: Give each group a set of cards (pictures of skulls or descriptions of hominins) to arrange in order and justify their sequence.

questions.q: Why was Lamarck's theory rejected?
questions.a: Characters acquired during life are not passed on to offspring.

questions.q: What is survival of the fittest?
questions.a: Individuals best suited to their environment survive and reproduce more.

questions.q: Give one example of a vestigial organ in humans.
questions.a: The vermiform appendix (or wisdom teeth).

questions.q: Which human ancestor first used fire?
questions.a: Homo erectus.

lesson.homework: Write two paragraphs comparing Lamarck's and Darwin's explanations of the long neck of the giraffe.

topics.title: Pollution
topics.summary: Pollution is the harmful change in air, water or soil due to human activity; pollutants include gases, chemicals, plastics, radiation and noise.
notes: Pollution is the harmful change in air, water or soil due to human activity; pollutants include gases, chemicals, plastics, radiation and noise.

Air: vehicles and industries release CO, SO₂, NOₓ and particles; water: sewage, industrial effluents, fertilisers (eutrophication); soil: pesticides and plastics; noise above about 80 dB harms hearing.
Biodegradable pollutants (sewage) are broken down by microbes; non-biodegradable ones (DDT, plastics, heavy metals) persist and build up in food chains (biomagnification).
Effects on climate: acid rain, ozone depletion and global warming; on health: respiratory diseases, poisoning, hearing loss.
Radioactive pollution from nuclear accidents or waste can cause cancer and genetic damage.
Prevention: cleaner fuels, sewage treatment, integrated pest management, the 3 Rs, silence zones and laws such as the Environment Protection Act.
outcomes: Describe types and sources of air, water, soil, radioactive and noise pollution
Distinguish biodegradable and non-biodegradable pollutants
Explain effects of pollution on climate, health and ecosystems, and ways to prevent it

lesson.hook: Why are rivers foaming, city air hazy and tigers' forests shrinking — and what can we do?
lesson.example: DDT sprayed on crops passes from water to plankton to fish to fish-eating birds, becoming more concentrated at each step and thinning the birds' eggshells.
lesson.activity: Groups survey pollution near the school (smoke, drains, plastic, noise) and present one problem with its cause, effect and a practical solution.

questions.q: What is biomagnification?
questions.a: The increase in concentration of a non-biodegradable pollutant at each level of a food chain.

questions.q: What is eutrophication?
questions.a: Over-growth of algae in water bodies due to fertiliser nutrients, reducing oxygen for fish.

questions.q: Name two effects of noise pollution.
questions.a: Hearing loss and stress (also sleeplessness, high blood pressure).

questions.q: Give two ways to reduce water pollution.
questions.a: Treating sewage and industrial waste before release; using fewer chemical fertilisers.

lesson.homework: Write a letter to your municipal commissioner about one pollution problem in your area and a solution.

topics.title: Introduction to Object Oriented Programming
topics.summary: Procedure-oriented programming organises a program as functions acting on data; object-oriented programming (OOP) organises it as objects that combine data and behaviour.
notes: Procedure-oriented programming organises a program as functions acting on data; object-oriented programming (OOP) organises it as objects that combine data and behaviour.
Abstraction shows only essential features and hides details; encapsulation wraps data and methods together in a class.
Inheritance lets a class acquire features of another; polymorphism lets one name take many forms (method overloading).
Java source code (.java) is compiled by javac into bytecode (.class), which the Java Virtual Machine (JVM) runs — so Java is platform-independent ("write once, run anywhere").
Java is object-oriented, robust, secure and case-sensitive; BlueJ is a simple environment used in schools.
Programs can be written as applications (with main) and run from the command line or an IDE.
outcomes: Contrast procedure-oriented and object-oriented programming
Explain the principles of OOP: abstraction, encapsulation, inheritance and polymorphism
Describe how Java programs are compiled and run (bytecode, JVM)

lesson.hook: A school has students, teachers and books, each with details and actions. How can a program be organised the same way?
lesson.example: A Car object has data (colour, speed) and behaviour (accelerate, brake). The class Car is the blueprint; each car on the road is an object.
lesson.activity: Pupils list real-world objects in the classroom and write their data (attributes) and behaviour (methods) in two columns.

questions.q: What is bytecode?
questions.a: The intermediate code produced by the Java compiler, run by the JVM.

questions.q: Name the four principles of OOP.
questions.a: Abstraction, encapsulation, inheritance and polymorphism.

questions.q: Why is Java called platform-independent?
questions.a: Its bytecode runs on any computer that has a JVM.

questions.q: What is the difference between a compiler and an interpreter?
questions.a: A compiler translates the whole program at once; an interpreter translates and runs line by line.

lesson.homework: Describe a mobile phone as an object: list five attributes and five methods.

chapters.title: Elementary Concept of Objects and Classes

topics.title: Elementary Concept of Objects and Classes
topics.summary: A class is a user-defined blueprint that describes the data and methods of its objects.
notes: A class is a user-defined blueprint that describes the data and methods of its objects.
An object is an instance of a class with its own values (state) and actions (behaviour).
Objects are created with new: Student s1 = new Student();
The dot operator calls a method or reaches a member: s1.display();
A class is an object factory and a composite data type.
Messages are passed between objects by calling methods.
outcomes: Explain a class as a blueprint and an object as its instance
Identify state (data members) and behaviour (methods) of objects
Create objects with new and call their methods

lesson.hook: If "Student" is the plan, who are the actual students?
lesson.example: class Box { int l, b, h; int volume() { return l * b * h; } } — Box b1 = new Box(); b1.l = 2; b1.b = 3; b1.h = 4; b1.volume() gives 24.
lesson.activity: Pupils write a class Book with title, author and price, create two objects and print their details.

questions.q: What is an instance of a class?
questions.a: An object created from that class.

questions.q: Which keyword creates an object?
questions.a: new.

questions.q: Why is a class called an object factory?
questions.a: Any number of objects can be created from one class.

questions.q: How do you call a method display() of object x?
questions.a: x.display();

lesson.homework: Write a class Rectangle with length and breadth and a method area(); create an object and print its area.

topics.title: Values and Data Types
topics.summary: Java uses the Unicode character set; tokens are keywords, identifiers, literals, operators and separators.
notes: Java uses the Unicode character set; tokens are keywords, identifiers, literals, operators and separators.
Identifiers name variables, methods and classes: they start with a letter, $ or _, cannot be keywords and are case-sensitive.
Primitive types: byte (1 byte), short (2), int (4), long (8), float (4), double (8), char (2), boolean.
