topics.summary: Waste is any unwanted material: domestic, industrial, agricultural, biomedical, construction and e-waste; it may be biodegradable or non-biodegradable.
notes: Waste is any unwanted material: domestic, industrial, agricultural, biomedical, construction and e-waste; it may be biodegradable or non-biodegradable.
Improper disposal spreads diseases, pollutes water and soil, blocks drains (causing floods) and releases methane from dumps.
Segregation at source into wet and dry waste is the first step; wet waste can be composted or used for biogas.
Recycling turns paper, plastic, glass and metals into new products; e-waste needs special recycling to recover metals safely.
Sanitary landfills are lined and covered; incineration burns waste (used for biomedical waste) and can generate energy.
Citizens help by following the 3 Rs, refusing single-use plastics and supporting programmes like the Swachh Bharat Mission.
outcomes: Identify types of waste and their sources
Explain the effects of improper waste disposal
Describe waste management: segregation, composting, recycling, landfills, incineration, and the role of citizens

lesson.hook: Where does India's 1.5 lakh tonnes of daily city garbage go?
lesson.example: Indore has been rated India's cleanest city for several years through strict door-to-door segregation and processing of wet and dry waste.
lesson.activity: Organise a "waste audit" of one class for a week: segregate, weigh and plan how to cut the largest category by half.

questions.q: Why is waste segregated at source?
questions.a: It makes composting and recycling easier and reduces what goes to landfills.

questions.q: What is e-waste?
questions.a: Discarded electronic items such as phones and computers.

questions.q: Give one harmful effect of open dumping.
questions.a: It spreads disease (also pollutes groundwater, releases methane).

questions.q: What is a sanitary landfill?
questions.a: A lined, covered site where waste is buried safely to prevent pollution.

lesson.homework: Write a short speech for the school assembly on reducing plastic waste.

topics.title: Civics: Our Constitution
topics.summary: A constitution is the basic law of a country: it sets up the government, divides powers and guarantees rights.
notes: A constitution is the basic law of a country: it sets up the government, divides powers and guarantees rights.
The Constituent Assembly adopted India's Constitution on 26 November 1949; it came into force on 26 January 1950 (Republic Day).
Features: single citizenship for all Indians, universal adult franchise (every citizen aged 18 or more can vote), and a written, detailed constitution.
Fundamental Rights (equality, freedom, against exploitation, religion, cultural and educational, constitutional remedies) are justiciable — courts enforce them.
Directive Principles guide the government to build a welfare state (equal pay, free education, health); they are not enforceable in court.
Fundamental Duties remind citizens of their responsibilities, such as respecting the national flag and protecting the environment.
outcomes: Define a constitution and state the dates of adoption and enforcement of India's Constitution
Describe its key features: single citizenship, universal adult franchise, Fundamental Rights and Duties, Directive Principles
Distinguish Fundamental Rights from Directive Principles and explain a welfare state

lesson.hook: Why do we celebrate both 26 November and 26 January?
lesson.example: If a school refuses admission to a child only because of caste, the family can go to court under the Right to Equality — a Fundamental Right.
lesson.activity: Groups read short cases and decide which Fundamental Right or Directive Principle each relates to.

questions.q: When did the Constitution of India come into force?
questions.a: 26 January 1950.

questions.q: What is universal adult franchise?
questions.a: The right of every adult citizen (18 years and above) to vote.

questions.q: How do Fundamental Rights differ from Directive Principles?
questions.a: Fundamental Rights are enforceable in courts; Directive Principles are not.

questions.q: What is a welfare state?
questions.a: A state that works for the social and economic well-being of all its people.

lesson.homework: Write five Fundamental Duties and say how a Class 9 student can follow each.

topics.title: Civics: Elections
topics.summary: Elections let citizens choose their representatives and hold them accountable; they are the heart of democracy.
notes: Elections let citizens choose their representatives and hold them accountable; they are the heart of democracy.
The Election Commission of India is an independent body: a Chief Election Commissioner and other Election Commissioners appointed by the President.
Its functions: preparing electoral rolls, delimitation support, recognising parties and allotting symbols, conducting elections, enforcing the Model Code of Conduct.
Direct elections: voters elect representatives directly (Lok Sabha, Vidhan Sabha); indirect elections: elected members choose (President, Rajya Sabha).
A general election is held for all seats at the end of the full term; a mid-term election is held when a house is dissolved early; a by-election fills a single vacant seat.
Secret ballot, EVMs with VVPAT, and independent officials help keep elections free and fair.
outcomes: Explain the meaning and importance of elections in a democracy
Describe the composition and functions of the Election Commission of India
Distinguish direct and indirect elections, general, mid-term and by-elections

lesson.hook: How do nearly a billion voters choose their government peacefully?
lesson.example: When an MLA resigns or dies, a by-election is held only in that constituency; the rest of the assembly continues.
lesson.activity: Hold a mock class election: form a "commission", prepare a voter list, conduct a secret ballot and count votes.

questions.q: Who appoints the Chief Election Commissioner?
questions.a: The President of India.

questions.q: Is the President elected directly or indirectly?
questions.a: Indirectly, by an electoral college of elected members.

questions.q: What is a by-election?
questions.a: An election held to fill a single seat that has fallen vacant.

questions.q: Give two functions of the Election Commission.
questions.a: Preparing electoral rolls and conducting elections (also allotting symbols).

lesson.homework: Find out when the last general and state elections were held in your state and the voter turnout.

topics.title: Civics: The State Legislature
topics.summary: A unicameral legislature has one house; a bicameral legislature has two. Most states are unicameral; a few (Karnataka, Maharashtra, Bihar, Uttar Pradesh, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana) have Legislative Councils.
notes: A unicameral legislature has one house; a bicameral legislature has two. Most states are unicameral; a few (Karnataka, Maharashtra, Bihar, Uttar Pradesh, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana) have Legislative Councils.
The Legislative Assembly (Vidhan Sabha) is the lower house, directly elected for five years; members must be citizens aged at least 25.

The Legislative Council (Vidhan Parishad) is a permanent house; one-third of members retire every two years; members are elected partly by MLAs, local bodies, graduates and teachers, and some are nominated; minimum age 30.
The State Legislature makes laws on State List and Concurrent List subjects, passes the state budget, and controls the state government through questions and motions.
Money bills can be introduced only in the Assembly; the Council can only delay ordinary bills.
The Speaker presides over the Assembly; the Chairman over the Council.
outcomes: Distinguish unicameral and bicameral legislatures
Describe the Legislative Assembly and Legislative Council: term, composition, qualifications
State the powers and functions of the State Legislature

lesson.hook: Karnataka has two houses of legislature, but Tamil Nadu has only one. Why the difference?
lesson.example: A state budget (a money bill) is introduced in the Vidhan Sabha; the Vidhan Parishad can only suggest changes within 14 days.
lesson.activity: Compare the two houses of the Karnataka legislature in a class chart: election, term, age, powers.

questions.q: What is the term of a Legislative Assembly?
questions.a: Five years (unless dissolved earlier).

questions.q: What is the minimum age to be a member of a Legislative Council?
questions.a: 30 years.

questions.q: Where can a money bill be introduced in a state?
questions.a: Only in the Legislative Assembly.

questions.q: Name two states with bicameral legislatures.
questions.a: Karnataka and Maharashtra (also Bihar, Uttar Pradesh, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana).

lesson.homework: Find the names of your constituency's MLA and the Speaker of your State Assembly.

topics.title: The Harappan Civilisation
topics.summary: The Harappan (Indus Valley) Civilisation flourished about 2600–1900 BCE at sites like Harappa, Mohenjo-daro, Lothal, Kalibangan and Dholavira.
notes: The Harappan (Indus Valley) Civilisation flourished about 2600–1900 BCE at sites like Harappa, Mohenjo-daro, Lothal, Kalibangan and Dholavira.
Sources: the Great Bath, the Citadel, granaries, a dockyard at Lothal, seals, the bronze "dancing girl", the stone "bearded man" and a still-undeciphered script.
Towns were planned on a grid with baked-brick houses, wells, bathrooms and covered drains — among the best sanitation of the ancient world.
People farmed wheat and barley, spun cotton and traded with Mesopotamia using standard weights and seals.
Crafts included beads, pottery, metal work and seal carving.
Possible causes of decline: floods, shifting rivers, drying climate, decline of trade and over-use of land.
outcomes: Describe sources of the Harappan Civilisation
Explain its town planning, trade, art and craft
Discuss the causes of its decline

lesson.hook: Over 4500 years ago, a city in the Indus valley had covered drains and a great public bath. Who built it?
lesson.example: Lothal in Gujarat had a brick dockyard connected to a river, showing sea trade — beads from Harappan sites have been found in Mesopotamia.
lesson.activity: Pupils design a "Harappan town plan" on grid paper with a citadel, lower town, drains and granary.

questions.q: Where was the Great Bath found?
questions.a: Mohenjo-daro.

questions.q: What was special about Harappan drains?
questions.a: They were covered and connected to every house.

questions.q: Why can we not read Harappan writing?
questions.a: The script has not yet been deciphered.

questions.q: Give two possible causes of the decline of the Harappan Civilisation.
questions.a: Floods and drying of rivers (also decline in trade).

lesson.homework: Draw and describe one Harappan seal and explain what it tells us.

topics.title: The Vedic Period
topics.summary: The Vedic period (about 1500–600 BCE) is known from the four Vedas — Rig, Sama, Yajur and Atharva — and later the epics Ramayana and Mahabharata.
notes: The Vedic period (about 1500–600 BCE) is known from the four Vedas — Rig, Sama, Yajur and Atharva — and later the epics Ramayana and Mahabharata.
Early Vedic society was organised in families and tribes; the king (rajan) led in war and protected people; assemblies — sabha, samiti and vidatha — advised him.
Women in the Early Vedic period took part in assemblies and education; their position declined in the Later Vedic period.
The Early Vedic economy was mainly pastoral (cattle); the Later Vedic economy was based on agriculture with iron tools and settled villages.
Society became divided into four varnas (Brahmins, Kshatriyas, Vaishyas, Shudras), which later became rigid.
Life was divided into four ashramas (Brahmacharya, Grihastha, Vanaprastha, Sanyasa); education was given in gurukuls.
outcomes: Name the four Vedas and the epics as sources
Describe society, the king and assemblies of the Early Vedic period
Compare women's position and the economy in the Early and Later Vedic periods; describe varnas, ashramas and education

lesson.hook: What can hymns composed over 3000 years ago tell us about how people lived?
lesson.example: In the Rig Veda cattle were counted as wealth — the word "gavishti" (search for cows) was used for war.
lesson.activity: Make a comparison chart of the Early and Later Vedic periods under society, women, economy and religion.

questions.q: Name the four Vedas.
questions.a: Rig, Sama, Yajur and Atharva.

questions.q: What were the sabha and samiti?
questions.a: Assemblies that advised the Vedic king.

questions.q: How did women's position change in the Later Vedic period?
questions.a: It declined; they lost access to assemblies and education.

questions.q: Name the four ashramas.
questions.a: Brahmacharya, Grihastha, Vanaprastha and Sanyasa.

lesson.homework: Write a paragraph on education in the gurukul system.

topics.title: Jainism and Buddhism
topics.summary: Sources: Jain Angas; Buddhist Tripitakas and Jataka stories.
notes: Sources: Jain Angas; Buddhist Tripitakas and Jataka stories.
Causes of rise: rigid varna system, costly rituals and sacrifices, Sanskrit texts people could not understand, and the growth of trade and towns that wanted a simpler faith.
Mahavira (the 24th Tirthankara) taught the Tri-ratnas — right faith, right knowledge and right conduct — non-violence (ahimsa), and freedom from karma to reach moksha.
Gautama Buddha taught the Four Noble Truths (life has suffering, desire causes it, it can end, the Eightfold Path ends it).
The Eightfold Path: right view, resolve, speech, action, livelihood, effort, mindfulness and concentration — leading to nirvana.
Both taught equality, non-violence and ethical living in the people's languages (Prakrit, Pali).
outcomes: State the sources for Jainism and Buddhism
Explain the causes of their rise in the 6th century BCE
Describe the teachings of Mahavira and Buddha

lesson.hook: Why did two princes give up their palaces to seek the truth about suffering?
lesson.example: Buddha preached in Pali, the language of ordinary people, and welcomed all castes into the sangha — one reason his teachings spread widely.
lesson.activity: Pupils read a short Jataka-style story (retold) and identify the moral lesson and which teaching it reflects.

questions.q: What are the Tri-ratnas of Jainism?
questions.a: Right faith, right knowledge and right conduct.

questions.q: State the Four Noble Truths.
questions.a: Life has suffering; desire causes suffering; suffering can end; the Eightfold Path ends it.

questions.q: Name the Buddhist scriptures.
questions.a: The Tripitakas.

questions.q: Give two causes for the rise of these religions.
questions.a: Rigid caste system and costly rituals (also use of Sanskrit).

lesson.homework: Compare the teachings of Mahavira and Buddha in a table.

topics.title: The Mauryan Empire
topics.summary: Sources: Kautilya's Arthashastra, Megasthenes' Indika, Ashoka's edicts on rocks and pillars, and the Sanchi Stupa.
notes: Sources: Kautilya's Arthashastra, Megasthenes' Indika, Ashoka's edicts on rocks and pillars, and the Sanchi Stupa.
Kings in order: Chandragupta Maurya (founder, with Chanakya's help), Bindusara and Ashoka.
Administration was centralised: the king at the top, a council of ministers, provinces under princes, officials for revenue, trade and justice, and spies; Pataliputra was the capital.
After the Kalinga war (about 261 BCE), Ashoka was moved by its suffering and adopted Dhamma.
Dhamma: respect for elders, kindness to servants and animals, tolerance of all religions, non-violence and welfare works such as roads, wells and hospitals.
Impact: peace and unity, spread of Buddhism to Sri Lanka and beyond; the Lion Capital of Sarnath is India's national emblem.
outcomes: Describe sources for the Mauryan Empire
Name the Mauryan kings in order and describe their administration
Explain Ashoka's Dhamma and its impact

lesson.hook: Why did an emperor who won a great war turn to peace and non-violence?
lesson.example: Ashoka's edicts were written in Prakrit, mostly in the Brahmi script, so ordinary people could hear and understand his message.
lesson.activity: Pupils write a modern "edict" for their school with five principles in the spirit of Ashoka's Dhamma.

questions.q: Who wrote the Arthashastra?
questions.a: Kautilya (Chanakya).

questions.q: What changed Ashoka's outlook?
questions.a: The suffering caused by the Kalinga war.

questions.q: What was the capital of the Mauryan Empire?
questions.a: Pataliputra.

questions.q: Give two principles of Ashoka's Dhamma.
questions.a: Religious tolerance and non-violence (also respect for elders).

lesson.homework: Find out where the Lion Capital of Ashoka is used today and what its parts symbolise.

topics.title: The Sangam Age
topics.summary: The Sangam Age (about 300 BCE–300 CE) is named after assemblies of Tamil poets in Madurai.
notes: The Sangam Age (about 300 BCE–300 CE) is named after assemblies of Tamil poets in Madurai.
Sources: Sangam poems, the Tirukkural of Thiruvalluvar (couplets on ethics, wealth and love), and megalithic burials.
Three kingdoms ruled: the Cheras, Cholas and Pandyas.
Society was organised by occupation and landscape (hills, forests, farmland, coast, desert); women poets such as Avvaiyar wrote, though widow life was hard.
Agriculture (rice, sugarcane, cotton) and crafts flourished.
Trade with Rome and South-East Asia through ports like Muziris, Puhar and Korkai exported pepper, pearls and muslin; Roman coins have been found in Tamil Nadu.
outcomes: Describe the Sangam Age and its sources: the Sangam literature, Tirukkural and megaliths
Explain society and the position of women
Describe the economy: agriculture and trade

lesson.hook: What do ancient Tamil poems tell us about life in south India 2000 years ago?
lesson.example: Hoards of Roman gold coins found in Tamil Nadu show that Roman traders paid for Indian pepper, called "black gold".
lesson.activity: Pupils read a few couplets of the Tirukkural in English translation and discuss their meaning today.

questions.q: Who wrote the Tirukkural?
questions.a: Thiruvalluvar.

questions.q: Name the three kingdoms of the Sangam Age.
questions.a: Chera, Chola and Pandya.

questions.q: What is a megalith?
questions.a: A large stone structure, often marking a burial.

questions.q: Name a Sangam port that traded with Rome.
questions.a: Muziris (or Puhar, Korkai).

lesson.homework: On a map of south India, mark the three Sangam kingdoms and two ports.

topics.title: The Age of the Guptas
topics.summary: Sources: the Chinese pilgrim Fa-hien's account and Harisena's Allahabad Pillar Inscription praising Samudragupta.
notes: Sources: the Chinese pilgrim Fa-hien's account and Harisena's Allahabad Pillar Inscription praising Samudragupta.
Kings in order: Chandragupta I, Samudragupta (the conqueror), Chandragupta II (Vikramaditya) and later rulers.
Administration: the king had wide powers, helped by ministers; provinces (bhuktis) and districts (vishayas) were governed by officials; land revenue was the main income.
Education: Nalanda became a great centre of learning.
Science and medicine: Aryabhata (the Earth rotates, value of π, place value and zero) and Sushruta (surgery, with Sushruta Samhita).
Culture: Kalidasa's works (Abhijnanashakuntalam, Meghaduta), the Deogarh temple, Ajanta paintings and the iron pillar at Mehrauli.
outcomes: Describe sources: Fa-hien's account and the Allahabad Pillar Inscription
Name the Gupta kings in order and describe their administration
Explain contributions to education, science, medicine and culture

lesson.hook: Why is the Gupta period often called the Golden Age of ancient India?
lesson.example: The iron pillar at Mehrauli, made in the Gupta period, has stood for about 1600 years with hardly any rust — a sign of advanced metallurgy.
lesson.activity: Groups prepare a "Gupta hall of fame" with short notes on Aryabhata, Sushruta, Kalidasa and Nalanda.

questions.q: Who composed the Allahabad Pillar Inscription?
questions.a: Harisena.

questions.q: Name two works of Kalidasa.
questions.a: Abhijnanashakuntalam and Meghaduta.

questions.q: What did Aryabhata say about the Earth?
questions.a: That it rotates on its axis.

questions.q: Why is the Gupta age called the Golden Age?
questions.a: Because of great progress in art, literature, science and learning.

lesson.homework: Write about Fa-hien's description of Gupta India.

topics.title: Medieval India: The Cholas
topics.summary: Sources: copper-plate and temple inscriptions (such as at Uttaramerur) and the Brihadishwara temple at Thanjavur.
notes: Sources: copper-plate and temple inscriptions (such as at Uttaramerur) and the Brihadishwara temple at Thanjavur.
Kings: Vijayalaya (founder, 9th century), Rajaraja I and his son Rajendra I, the greatest rulers.
Rajendra I conquered up to the Ganga ("Gangaikonda Chola") and sent naval expeditions to South-East Asia.
Administration: the empire was divided into mandalams, valanadus and nadus; village assemblies (sabha and ur) managed local affairs through elected committees chosen by lot (kudavolai).
Chola art: grand Dravida temples with tall vimanas (Brihadishwara), and bronze sculptures such as Nataraja.
Temples were centres of worship, education, trade and culture.
outcomes: Describe sources for the Cholas: inscriptions and the Brihadishwara temple
Name the Chola kings in order and describe their administration
Describe Chola art and architecture

lesson.hook: How did a south Indian kingdom build a navy that reached South-East Asia?
lesson.example: The Uttaramerur inscription describes how village committee members were chosen by drawing names from a pot — an early local election system.
lesson.activity: Show pictures of the Brihadishwara temple and a Nataraja bronze; pupils describe features of Dravida architecture.

questions.q: Who built the Brihadishwara temple?
questions.a: Rajaraja I.

questions.q: What title did Rajendra I take after reaching the Ganga?
questions.a: Gangaikonda Chola.

questions.q: How were members of Chola village committees chosen?
questions.a: By drawing lots (kudavolai).

questions.q: Name a famous Chola bronze.
questions.a: Nataraja.

lesson.homework: Write a note on local self-government under the Cholas.

topics.title: Medieval India: The Delhi Sultanate
topics.summary: Sources: inscriptions, coins, chronicles and monuments such as the Qutub Minar.
notes: Sources: inscriptions, coins, chronicles and monuments such as the Qutub Minar.
Dynasties in order: Slave (Mamluk), Khilji, Tughlaq, Sayyid and Lodi (1206–1526).

Alauddin Khilji: market regulations with fixed prices, the Deccan expeditions (Malik Kafur), measures against nobles (spies, no marriage alliances without permission), a standing army with branding of horses, and revenue based on measured land.
Muhammad bin Tughlaq: transfer of capital to Daulatabad, token currency of copper and brass, higher taxes in the Doab during famine, and ambitious plans of conquest.
Tughlaq's plans failed because of poor planning, forgery of token coins and hardship to people.
The Sultanate ended when Babur defeated Ibrahim Lodi at Panipat in 1526.
outcomes: Describe sources for the Delhi Sultanate: inscriptions and the Qutub Minar
Name the dynasties in order
Explain the reforms of Alauddin Khilji and Muhammad bin Tughlaq

lesson.hook: A sultan once moved his whole capital from Delhi to Daulatabad and back again. Why?
lesson.example: Tughlaq's token copper coins had the value of silver ones, but they were easy to forge — people made them at home and the currency collapsed.
lesson.activity: Debate in class: "Muhammad bin Tughlaq's ideas were good but badly carried out." Groups argue for and against.

questions.q: Name the dynasties of the Delhi Sultanate in order.
questions.a: Slave, Khilji, Tughlaq, Sayyid, Lodi.

questions.q: Why did Alauddin Khilji regulate markets?
questions.a: To keep prices low so he could maintain a large army cheaply.

questions.q: Why did the token currency fail?
questions.a: Coins were widely forged.

questions.q: Who started building the Qutub Minar?
questions.a: Qutbuddin Aibak.

lesson.homework: Write a short biography of Alauddin Khilji focusing on his reforms.

chapters.title: The Mughal Empire and Composite Culture

topics.title: The Mughal Empire and Composite Culture
topics.summary: Sources: Abul Fazl's Ain-i-Akbari and monuments — the Taj Mahal, Jama Masjid and Red Fort.
notes: Sources: Abul Fazl's Ain-i-Akbari and monuments — the Taj Mahal, Jama Masjid and Red Fort.
Kings in order: Babur, Humayun, Akbar, Jahangir, Shah Jahan, Aurangzeb.
Babur consolidated power by the battles of Panipat (1526), Khanwa (1527) and Ghaghra (1529).
Akbar: Rajput policy of alliances and marriages, abolition of jizya and pilgrim tax, Sulh-i-kul (peace with all), social reforms, and the mansabdari system ranking officers by number of soldiers.
Composite culture grew from the mixing of Indian, Persian and Central Asian traditions in language (Urdu), music, painting, architecture and food.
The Bhakti movement (Kabir, Nanak, Mirabai) and Sufi movement (Nizamuddin Auliya) preached love of God, equality and harmony; Christian missionaries later added schools and printing.
outcomes: Describe sources: Ain-i-Akbari, Taj Mahal, Jama Masjid, Red Fort
Name the Mughal kings in order; describe Babur's battles and Akbar's policies
Explain composite culture and the Bhakti and Sufi movements

lesson.hook: How did India develop a culture that mixed Persian, Turkish and Indian traditions?
lesson.example: Akbar's Ibadat Khana at Fatehpur Sikri hosted debates among scholars of many faiths — an example of Sulh-i-kul.
lesson.activity: Pupils find everyday examples of composite culture (words, foods, clothes, music) and present them in a class chart.

questions.q: Who wrote the Ain-i-Akbari?
questions.a: Abul Fazl.

questions.q: Name Babur's three major battles.
questions.a: Panipat, Khanwa and Ghaghra.

questions.q: What was the mansabdari system?
questions.a: A system of ranks for officers based on the number of soldiers they maintained.

questions.q: Name two saints of the Bhakti movement.
questions.a: Kabir and Guru Nanak (also Mirabai, Chaitanya).

lesson.homework: Write about how Akbar tried to unite his diverse empire.

topics.title: The Renaissance and the Reformation
topics.summary: Renaissance means "rebirth" — a revival of learning and art in Europe from the 14th to 16th centuries, beginning in Italy.
notes: Renaissance means "rebirth" — a revival of learning and art in Europe from the 14th to 16th centuries, beginning in Italy.
Causes: the fall of Constantinople (1453) sent Greek scholars west, feudalism declined, new trade routes brought wealth, a spirit of enquiry grew, and the printing press spread books.
Leonardo da Vinci painted the Mona Lisa and made scientific drawings; Shakespeare wrote plays in English; Copernicus showed that the Earth goes round the Sun.
Consequences: humanism, science based on observation, vernacular literature and voyages of discovery.
The Reformation challenged the Catholic Church's practices, such as the sale of indulgences; Martin Luther's 95 Theses (1517) began Protestantism.
The Counter-Reformation reformed the Catholic Church from within (Council of Trent, Jesuits).
outcomes: Explain the meaning, causes and impact of the Renaissance
Describe contributions of Leonardo da Vinci, Shakespeare and Copernicus
Explain the causes of the Reformation, Martin Luther's role and the Counter-Reformation

lesson.hook: What made Europe suddenly burst into new art, science and ideas in the 15th century?
lesson.example: Gutenberg's printing press made books cheap; Luther's ideas spread across Germany in weeks because they were printed and read widely.
lesson.activity: Pupils design a "Renaissance newspaper" front page with reports on a painting, a scientific idea and the printing press.

questions.q: What does "Renaissance" mean?
questions.a: Rebirth (of learning and art).

questions.q: How did the printing press help the Renaissance?
questions.a: It made books cheap and spread new ideas quickly.

questions.q: What did Copernicus propose?
questions.a: That the Earth and planets revolve round the Sun.

questions.q: Who started the Reformation?
questions.a: Martin Luther.

lesson.homework: Write about one Renaissance figure and his lasting contribution.

chapters.title: The Industrial Revolution, Capitalism and Socialism

topics.title: The Industrial Revolution, Capitalism and Socialism
topics.summary: The Industrial Revolution was the shift from hand production to machine production, starting in Britain in the 18th century.
notes: The Industrial Revolution was the shift from hand production to machine production, starting in Britain in the 18th century.
Causes in Britain: coal and iron, inventions (spinning jenny, steam engine), capital from trade and colonies, markets and raw materials from colonies, and a large labour force.
Capitalism: an economic system in which private owners control factories and trade for profit; it grew with industrial wealth and free markets.
Industrialisation also brought long working hours, child labour, crowded slums and pollution.
Socialism: a system in which the means of production are owned by society or the state and wealth is shared more equally; it rose as a response to workers' hardships (Karl Marx).
Effects: new cities, railways, factory laws, trade unions and a changed world economy.
outcomes: Define the Industrial Revolution and explain its causes
Explain capitalism and the causes of its rise
Explain socialism and the causes of its rise

lesson.hook: How did machines change the way people worked and lived, and why did some thinkers want a fairer system?
lesson.example: James Watt's improved steam engine (1769) powered mills, mines and later railways, freeing factories from rivers and water wheels.
lesson.activity: Role play: a factory owner, a child worker and a reformer in 1830s Manchester each describe their day.

questions.q: Where did the Industrial Revolution begin?
questions.a: In Britain.

questions.q: Give two causes of the Industrial Revolution.
questions.a: Availability of coal and iron; new inventions (also capital, colonies).

questions.q: What is capitalism?
questions.a: A system where private owners control production for profit.

questions.q: Why did socialism arise?
questions.a: To oppose the exploitation of workers and unequal wealth under capitalism.

lesson.homework: Compare capitalism and socialism in a table under ownership, aim and role of the state.

topics.title: Civics: The Union Legislature
topics.summary: India is a federal union: powers are divided between the Union and the states (Union, State and Concurrent Lists).
notes: India is a federal union: powers are divided between the Union and the states (Union, State and Concurrent Lists).
Lok Sabha (House of the People): up to 550 elected members (currently 543), term five years, minimum age 25; presided over by the Speaker, elected by its members.

Rajya Sabha (Council of States): up to 250 members (238 elected by state legislatures, 12 nominated), a permanent house with one-third retiring every two years, minimum age 30; the Vice-President is its Chairman.

Procedures: sessions, quorum (one-tenth of members), question hour (starred questions need oral answers, unstarred ones written answers, short-notice questions on urgent matters), zero hour, adjournment and no-confidence motions.
An ordinary bill passes both houses and needs the President's assent; a money bill starts only in the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha can only delay it for 14 days.

Parliament makes laws, controls finance and the executive, elects the President and Vice-President, amends the Constitution and can impeach the President; the anti-defection law disqualifies members who switch parties.
outcomes: Explain India's federal set-up and the composition, term and qualifications of the Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha
Describe parliamentary procedures: sessions, quorum, question hour, zero hour, motions; the Speaker
State the powers of Parliament, the anti-defection law and how ordinary and money bills are passed

lesson.hook: How does a proposal become a law that applies to 140 crore people?
lesson.example: The Union Budget is a money bill: it is introduced in the Lok Sabha; if the Rajya Sabha does not return it in 14 days, it is deemed passed.
lesson.activity: Run a mock Parliament: a question hour with starred and unstarred questions and a short debate on a bill about school safety.

questions.q: What is the quorum of the Lok Sabha?
questions.a: One-tenth of its total members.

questions.q: Who presides over the Rajya Sabha?
questions.a: The Vice-President (as Chairman).

questions.q: How long can the Rajya Sabha delay a money bill?
questions.a: 14 days.

questions.q: What is a no-confidence motion?
questions.a: A motion stating that the House has no confidence in the Council of Ministers; if passed, the government must resign.

lesson.homework: Make a flow chart of how an ordinary bill becomes law.

chapters.title: Civics: The President and the Vice-President

topics.title: Civics: The President and the Vice-President
topics.summary: The President is the constitutional head of the Union; qualifications: citizen, 35 years or older, qualified to be a Lok Sabha member, holding no office of profit.
notes: The President is the constitutional head of the Union; qualifications: citizen, 35 years or older, qualified to be a Lok Sabha member, holding no office of profit.

Elected indirectly by an electoral college of elected MPs and MLAs, so the head of a parliamentary system does not rival the Prime Minister; term five years; removed by impeachment for violating the Constitution.

Powers: executive (appointing the PM, ministers, governors, judges), legislative (summoning Parliament, assent to bills, ordinances), financial (money bills need his recommendation), judicial (pardons).
Discretionary powers: choosing a PM when no party has a majority, sending a bill back once for reconsideration.
Emergency powers: national emergency (war or armed rebellion), President's rule in a state, financial emergency — each with effects such as suspension of some rights or central control of states.
The Vice-President (age 35+, elected by all MPs, term five years) is Chairman of the Rajya Sabha and acts as President when needed.
outcomes: Describe the election, qualifications and term of the President and why the election is indirect
Explain the President's powers: executive, legislative, financial, judicial, discretionary and emergency
Describe the Vice-President: election, term, removal and powers

lesson.hook: India's President signs every law, yet is called a "nominal" head. Why?
lesson.example: When Parliament is not in session, the President can issue an ordinance that has the force of law, but it must be approved within six weeks of Parliament meeting again.
lesson.activity: Groups read short scenarios (a hung Parliament, a state crisis, a mercy petition) and decide which of the President's powers applies.

questions.q: What is the minimum age to become President?
questions.a: 35 years.

questions.q: Why is the President elected indirectly?
questions.a: To keep the office a constitutional head, not a rival centre of power to the elected government.

questions.q: What is an ordinance?
questions.a: A law issued by the President when Parliament is not in session.

questions.q: Who acts as President if the office falls vacant?
questions.a: The Vice-President.

lesson.homework: Write two effects each of a national emergency and President's rule in a state.

chapters.title: Civics: The Prime Minister and the Council of Ministers

topics.title: Civics: The Prime Minister and the Council of Ministers
topics.summary: The President appoints as Prime Minister the leader of the majority party (or coalition) in the Lok Sabha; other ministers are appointed on the PM's advice.
notes: The President appoints as Prime Minister the leader of the majority party (or coalition) in the Lok Sabha; other ministers are appointed on the PM's advice.
The Council of Ministers has Cabinet ministers, Ministers of State and Deputy Ministers; a minister must become an MP within six months.
Functions: making policy, running administration, preparing legislation and the budget, and handling emergencies.
The Cabinet is a smaller inner group of senior ministers who take major decisions; the Council of Ministers is the larger body.

Collective responsibility: the whole Council is responsible to the Lok Sabha and resigns together if it loses a no-confidence vote; individual responsibility: each minister answers for their department.
The Prime Minister is the head of government, leader of the Lok Sabha and chief adviser to the President — the real executive.
outcomes: Describe the appointment of the Prime Minister and the formation and tenure of the Council of Ministers
Explain the functions of the Council of Ministers and the position and powers of the Prime Minister
Distinguish the Cabinet from the Council of Ministers; explain collective and individual responsibility

lesson.hook: Who really runs the government of India day to day?
lesson.example: If a Lok Sabha vote of no confidence passes, the whole Council of Ministers resigns — even ministers not involved in the dispute — because of collective responsibility.
lesson.activity: Draw a diagram showing the President, Prime Minister, Cabinet and Council of Ministers and the arrows of appointment and responsibility.

questions.q: Who appoints the Prime Minister?
questions.a: The President.

questions.q: Within how long must a non-member minister enter Parliament?
questions.a: Six months.

questions.q: What is collective responsibility?
questions.a: The Council of Ministers is jointly responsible to the Lok Sabha.

questions.q: How is the Cabinet different from the Council of Ministers?
questions.a: The Cabinet is a smaller body of senior ministers within the Council.

lesson.homework: Write a paragraph on why the Prime Minister is called the real executive.

topics.title: Civics: The Supreme Court
topics.summary: The Supreme Court in Delhi has the Chief Justice of India and other judges, appointed by the President (on the collegium's recommendation); judges serve until 65.
notes: The Supreme Court in Delhi has the Chief Justice of India and other judges, appointed by the President (on the collegium's recommendation); judges serve until 65.
Qualifications: citizen and a High Court judge for 5 years, or an advocate for 10 years, or a distinguished jurist.
Independence is ensured by security of tenure (removal only by Parliament for proven misbehaviour), fixed salaries, and a ban on practising law after retirement.
Original jurisdiction: disputes between the Union and states or between states; appellate: appeals from High Courts; advisory: opinions when the President asks.
Judicial review lets the Court strike down laws that violate the Constitution; as a court of record its decisions are binding precedents and it can punish contempt.
It protects Fundamental Rights through writs: habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, certiorari and quo warranto.
outcomes: Describe the composition of the Supreme Court and the qualifications and appointment of judges
Explain the independence of the judiciary
Explain its jurisdiction: original, appellate, advisory, revisory, judicial review, court of record, and writs for Fundamental Rights

lesson.hook: Can a court strike down a law passed by Parliament?
lesson.example: If a person is detained illegally, a writ of habeas corpus orders the authorities to produce the person in court and justify the detention.
lesson.activity: Groups match five situations (illegal arrest, official refusing a duty, a state–state dispute) to the right writ or jurisdiction.

questions.q: What is judicial review?
questions.a: The power of courts to declare laws or orders unconstitutional.

questions.q: What does habeas corpus mean?
questions.a: "You may have the body" — produce the detained person before the court.

questions.q: At what age do Supreme Court judges retire?
Give two ways the independence of judges is ensured.
questions.a: Security of tenure and fixed salaries (also no practice after retirement).

lesson.homework: Write about one landmark Supreme Court judgment and its importance.

chapters.title: Civics: The High Courts and Subordinate Courts

topics.title: Civics: The High Courts and Subordinate Courts
topics.summary: Each state (or group of states) has a High Court with a Chief Justice and other judges appointed by the President; they retire at 62.
notes: Each state (or group of states) has a High Court with a Chief Justice and other judges appointed by the President; they retire at 62.
Qualifications: citizen who has held judicial office for 10 years or been a High Court advocate for 10 years.

Jurisdiction: original (writs for Fundamental Rights, some cases), appellate (appeals from lower courts), revisory (checking lower courts' decisions), judicial review and court of record; it supervises subordinate courts.
Subordinate courts: the District Judge's court hears civil cases; the Sessions Court hears criminal cases; the same judge is called District and Sessions Judge.
Lok Adalats (people's courts) settle cases quickly by compromise, without fees; their decisions are final and binding.
Lok Adalats reduce the burden of cases on courts and help the poor get justice.
outcomes: Describe the composition, qualifications and appointment of High Court judges
Explain the jurisdiction and functions of High Courts
Distinguish the District Judge's court and the Sessions Court; explain Lok Adalats

lesson.hook: Where does a citizen go first when there is a dispute over land or a crime in the district?
lesson.example: A dispute over a road accident compensation can be settled at a Lok Adalat in a single day, instead of years in a regular court.
lesson.activity: Pupils draw the structure of courts in India from the Supreme Court down to the subordinate courts and Lok Adalats.

questions.q: At what age do High Court judges retire?
Which court hears criminal cases at the district level?
questions.a: The Sessions Court.

questions.q: Give two advantages of Lok Adalats.
questions.a: Quick justice and no court fees.

questions.q: What is revisory jurisdiction?
questions.a: The power of a higher court to examine the records and decisions of lower courts.

lesson.homework: Find out the name of the High Court that serves your state and where it sits.

topics.title: The First War of Independence, 1857
topics.summary: Political causes: Doctrine of Lapse, annexation of Awadh, and ill-treatment of rulers such as the Mughal emperor.
notes: Political causes: Doctrine of Lapse, annexation of Awadh, and ill-treatment of rulers such as the Mughal emperor.
Socio-religious causes: fear of forced conversion, interference in customs, and social reforms seen as attacks on tradition.
Economic causes: heavy land revenue, ruin of Indian handicrafts by British goods, and loss of jobs for nobles and soldiers.
Military causes: low pay and poor promotion for Indian sepoys, service overseas, and the greased cartridges of the Enfield rifle (the immediate cause).
Consequences: the East India Company's rule ended and the Crown took over (Government of India Act 1858); Queen Victoria's Proclamation promised religious tolerance and no further annexations.
Princely states were assured of their territory; the army was reorganised with more British soldiers and "divide and rule" among regiments.
outcomes: Explain the political, socio-religious, economic and military causes of the revolt of 1857
Describe its consequences: administrative changes, Queen Victoria's Proclamation, princely states and the army
Recognise its significance as the First War of Independence

lesson.hook: Why did soldiers, peasants and princes rise together against the British in 1857?
lesson.example: Mangal Pandey's protest at Barrackpore in March 1857 and the rising at Meerut on 10 May 1857 began the revolt; the rebels marched to Delhi.
lesson.activity: Groups prepare a cause-and-consequence chart for 1857 using coloured cards for political, social, economic and military factors.

questions.q: What was the immediate cause of the revolt of 1857?
questions.a: The greased cartridges of the new Enfield rifle.

questions.q: What was the Doctrine of Lapse?
questions.a: A policy of annexing states whose rulers died without a natural heir.

questions.q: Give two changes after 1857.
questions.a: The Crown took over from the Company; the army was reorganised.

questions.q: What did Queen Victoria's Proclamation promise?
questions.a: Religious tolerance, respect for princes and no further annexations.

lesson.homework: Write a paragraph on why 1857 is called the First War of Independence.

chapters.title: Growth of Nationalism and the Indian National Congress

topics.title: Growth of Nationalism and the Indian National Congress
topics.summary: Economic exploitation (drain of wealth, ruin of industries, famines) made Indians see British rule as harmful.
notes: Economic exploitation (drain of wealth, ruin of industries, famines) made Indians see British rule as harmful.
Repressive policies of Lord Lytton (Vernacular Press Act, Arms Act) and the Ilbert Bill controversy caused anger.

Reformers: Raja Rammohan Roy (Brahmo Samaj, fought sati), Jyotiba Phule (Satyashodhak Samaj, education for women and lower castes), Swami Dayananda Saraswati (Arya Samaj, "back to the Vedas"), Swami Vivekananda (Ramakrishna Mission, pride in Indian culture).
The press (Amrita Bazar Patrika, The Hindu, Kesari) spread ideas of nationalism.
The Indian National Congress was founded in 1885 by A. O. Hume; its first session in Bombay was presided over by W. C. Bonnerjee and the second by Dadabhai Naoroji.
Its early aims: national unity, a platform for Indian demands, and training in political work.
outcomes: Explain the factors behind the growth of nationalism: economic exploitation, repressive policies, reform movements and the press
Describe contributions of Raja Rammohan Roy, Jyotiba Phule, Swami Dayananda Saraswati and Swami Vivekananda
Describe the foundation and early objectives of the Indian National Congress

lesson.hook: How did people from many regions and languages begin to think of themselves as one nation, India?
lesson.example: Dadabhai Naoroji's "drain theory" showed how India's wealth flowed to Britain as salaries, pensions and profits, making Indians poorer.
lesson.activity: Pupils make "reformer cards" with each reformer's organisation, two contributions and one quote-free summary of his message.

questions.q: Who founded the Indian National Congress?
questions.a: A. O. Hume (1885).

questions.q: Who presided over the first session of the Congress?
questions.a: W. C. Bonnerjee.

questions.q: Name the organisation founded by Swami Dayananda Saraswati.
questions.a: Arya Samaj.

questions.q: How did the press help nationalism?
questions.a: It spread political ideas and criticism of British policies.

lesson.homework: Write two contributions each of Jyotiba Phule and Raja Rammohan Roy.

topics.title: Early Nationalists and Assertive Nationalists
topics.summary: Early Nationalists (1885–1905) believed in British justice; they used petitions, prayers and speeches (constitutional methods) to seek reforms such as more Indians in councils and services.
notes: Early Nationalists (1885–1905) believed in British justice; they used petitions, prayers and speeches (constitutional methods) to seek reforms such as more Indians in councils and services.
Dadabhai Naoroji explained the drain of wealth; Surendranath Banerjee founded the Indian Association; Gokhale worked for education and founded the Servants of India Society.
The partition of Bengal (1905) by Lord Curzon, aimed at dividing Hindus and Muslims, was seen by nationalists as "divide and rule" and sparked the Swadeshi and Boycott movement.
Differences over methods led to the Surat Split (1907) between Moderates and Extremists (Assertive Nationalists).
Assertive Nationalists aimed at swaraj and used boycott, swadeshi, national education and mass protest.

Bal Gangadhar Tilak ("Swaraj is my birthright"; Kesari; Ganapati and Shivaji festivals), Bipin Chandra Pal (swadeshi, national education) and Lala Lajpat Rai (Punjab leader, opposed the Simon Commission) — Lal-Bal-Pal.
outcomes: Describe the objectives and methods of the Early Nationalists and the contributions of Dadabhai Naoroji, Surendranath Banerjee and G. K. Gokhale
Explain the partition of Bengal (1905), the Surat Split (1907) and the objectives and methods of the Assertive Nationalists
Describe the contributions of Tilak, Bipin Chandra Pal and Lala Lajpat Rai

lesson.hook: Should India ask the British politely for reforms, or demand swaraj boldly?
lesson.example: During the Swadeshi movement people made bonfires of foreign cloth and set up swadeshi stores and national schools.
lesson.activity: Debate: "The Moderates' methods were more useful than the Extremists'" — pupils argue both sides using facts.

questions.q: Why did Curzon partition Bengal?
questions.a: Officially for administration; nationalists saw it as a plan to divide Hindus and Muslims.

questions.q: What was the Surat Split?
questions.a: The 1907 division of the Congress into Moderates and Extremists.

questions.q: Give two methods of the Assertive Nationalists.
questions.a: Boycott of foreign goods and swadeshi (also national education).

questions.q: Who said "Swaraj is my birthright"?
questions.a: Bal Gangadhar Tilak.

lesson.homework: Compare the Early and Assertive Nationalists in a table: aims, methods, leaders.

chapters.title: The Muslim League and the Lucknow Pact

topics.title: The Muslim League and the Lucknow Pact
topics.summary: The All-India Muslim League was formed in 1906 at Dacca.
notes: The All-India Muslim League was formed in 1906 at Dacca.
Factors: British policy of divide and rule, the partition of Bengal, fears among some Muslims of being a minority, and educational backwardness.
Objectives: to promote loyalty to the British, protect the political rights of Muslims and prevent hostility towards other communities.
The Lucknow Pact (1916) was an agreement between the Congress and the Muslim League to demand self-government together; the League's demand for separate electorates was accepted.
It was signed at a joint session led by Ambika Charan Mazumdar (Congress president) and Muhammad Ali Jinnah (League); Tilak played a key role.
Impact: Moderates and Extremists reunited and Hindu-Muslim unity grew, but acceptance of separate electorates later encouraged communal politics.
outcomes: Explain the factors leading to the formation of the Muslim League (1906) and its objectives
Describe the Lucknow Pact of 1916: signatories and impact
Assess its role in the national movement

lesson.hook: How did the Congress and the Muslim League come together in 1916?
lesson.example: In 1916 the Congress and the League met together at Lucknow and presented a joint scheme of reforms to the British — the first formal Hindu-Muslim political agreement.
lesson.activity: Pupils make a timeline from 1905 to 1916 with the partition of Bengal, the Muslim League, the Surat Split, the reunion and the Lucknow Pact.

questions.q: When and where was the Muslim League formed?
questions.a: 1906, at Dacca.

questions.q: What was the Lucknow Pact?
questions.a: The 1916 agreement between the Congress and the Muslim League to demand self-government together.

questions.q: Give one positive and one negative impact of the Lucknow Pact.
questions.a: It brought unity; accepting separate electorates encouraged communal politics.

questions.q: Name two leaders connected with the Lucknow Pact.
questions.a: Tilak and Jinnah.

lesson.homework: Write a short note on the objectives of the Muslim League.

chapters.title: Mahatma Gandhi and the Non-Cooperation Movement

topics.title: Mahatma Gandhi and the Non-Cooperation Movement
topics.summary: Mahatma Gandhi returned from South Africa in 1915 and used satyagraha (truth and non-violence) in Champaran, Kheda and Ahmedabad.
notes: Mahatma Gandhi returned from South Africa in 1915 and used satyagraha (truth and non-violence) in Champaran, Kheda and Ahmedabad.
The Rowlatt Act (1919) allowed arrest and detention without trial; protests followed.
At Jallianwala Bagh, Amritsar (13 April 1919), General Dyer's troops fired on a peaceful crowd, killing hundreds.
The Khilafat Movement protested against the treatment of the Ottoman Caliph after the First World War; Gandhi joined it to unite Hindus and Muslims.
Programme (1920): surrender of titles, boycott of government schools, courts, councils and foreign goods; promotion of swadeshi, khadi and national schools.
After a mob burned a police station at Chauri Chaura (February 1922), Gandhi suspended the movement; still, it made the freedom struggle a mass movement.
outcomes: Explain the causes of the Non-Cooperation Movement: the Khilafat issue, the Rowlatt Act and the Jallianwala Bagh tragedy
Describe its programme and the reasons for its suspension (Chauri Chaura)
Assess its impact

lesson.hook: How did a movement of peaceful non-cooperation shake the British Empire?
lesson.example: Rabindranath Tagore gave up his knighthood in protest against the Jallianwala Bagh massacre.
lesson.activity: Pupils write a newspaper report from 1920 announcing the Non-Cooperation programme and how people responded in their region.

questions.q: What was the Rowlatt Act?
questions.a: A 1919 law allowing arrest and imprisonment without trial.

questions.q: Why did Gandhi suspend the Non-Cooperation Movement?
questions.a: Because of the violence at Chauri Chaura in 1922.

questions.q: Give two items of the Non-Cooperation programme.
questions.a: Boycott of foreign goods and government schools (also surrender of titles).

questions.q: Why did Gandhi support the Khilafat Movement?
questions.a: To build Hindu-Muslim unity against British rule.

lesson.homework: Write on the impact of the Jallianwala Bagh tragedy on the freedom struggle.

topics.title: Civil Disobedience and Quit India
topics.summary: The all-British Simon Commission (1927) was boycotted with the slogan "Simon, go back".
notes: The all-British Simon Commission (1927) was boycotted with the slogan "Simon, go back".
At the Lahore session (1929), under Jawaharlal Nehru, the Congress declared Poorna Swaraj (complete independence) as its goal; 26 January 1930 was celebrated as Independence Day.
Gandhi's Dandi March (12 March – 6 April 1930) broke the salt law and began the Civil Disobedience Movement: making salt, boycotting foreign cloth and liquor, not paying taxes.
The Gandhi-Irwin Pact (1931) paused the movement; Gandhi attended the Second Round Table Conference in London, which failed; the movement was renewed.
The Quit India Movement (August 1942) followed the failure of the Cripps Mission and the Japanese threat; Gandhi gave the call "Do or Die".
Leaders were arrested, but people carried on the struggle; it showed the British that India could no longer be held.
outcomes: Explain the causes of the Civil Disobedience Movement: the Simon Commission and Poorna Swaraj
Describe the Dandi March, the programme, the Gandhi-Irwin Pact and the Second Round Table Conference
Explain the causes and significance of the Quit India Movement

lesson.hook: How could a march to make salt become a challenge to an empire?
lesson.example: Gandhi and 78 volunteers walked about 385 km from Sabarmati to Dandi and picked up salt from the sea shore, defying the salt tax.
lesson.activity: Trace the route of the Dandi March on a map of Gujarat and discuss why salt was a powerful symbol.

questions.q: Why was the Simon Commission boycotted?
questions.a: It had no Indian members.

questions.q: At which session was Poorna Swaraj declared?
questions.a: The Lahore session of 1929.

questions.q: What was the Gandhi-Irwin Pact?
questions.a: A 1931 agreement that suspended Civil Disobedience and released prisoners.

questions.q: What were the causes of the Quit India Movement?
questions.a: The failure of the Cripps Mission and the threat of a Japanese invasion.

lesson.homework: Write the significance of the Quit India Movement in five points.

chapters.title: Forward Bloc and the Indian National Army

topics.title: Forward Bloc and the Indian National Army
topics.summary: Subhas Chandra Bose was elected Congress president in 1938 and 1939 but differed with Gandhi over methods; he resigned and formed the Forward Bloc in 1939.
notes: Subhas Chandra Bose was elected Congress president in 1938 and 1939 but differed with Gandhi over methods; he resigned and formed the Forward Bloc in 1939.
Forward Bloc aims: complete independence, a radical programme, and uniting all left forces against British rule.
Bose escaped from house arrest in 1941 and reached Germany and then South-East Asia.
The Indian National Army (Azad Hind Fauj), first formed by Captain Mohan Singh and Rash Behari Bose, was led by Subhas Bose from 1943; he set up the Provisional Government of Free India in Singapore.
The INA fought alongside Japan in Burma and on India's north-eastern border; slogans were "Dilli Chalo" and "Jai Hind"; the Rani of Jhansi regiment was made of women.
The INA trials at the Red Fort (1945) roused national feeling and influenced Indian soldiers in the British army, hastening independence.
outcomes: Explain the objectives of the Forward Bloc
Describe the formation, objectives and contribution of the Indian National Army
Assess the role of Subhas Chandra Bose

lesson.hook: Why did a former Congress president form an army abroad to fight for India's freedom?
lesson.example: The INA trials of 1945 saw Hindu, Muslim and Sikh officers tried together, and the whole country rallied in their support.
lesson.activity: Pupils write a diary entry of an INA soldier in 1944 based on facts from the lesson.

questions.q: Who formed the Forward Bloc?
questions.a: Subhas Chandra Bose, in 1939.

questions.q: What was the slogan of the INA?
questions.a: "Dilli Chalo" (also "Jai Hind").

questions.q: Where did Bose set up the Provisional Government of Free India?
questions.a: In Singapore.

questions.q: How did the INA trials affect the freedom struggle?
questions.a: They united people and influenced Indians in the British forces, hastening independence.

lesson.homework: Write about the Rani of Jhansi regiment of the INA.

topics.title: Independence and Partition of India
topics.summary: After the Second World War, Britain was weakened and the demand for freedom was strong.
notes: After the Second World War, Britain was weakened and the demand for freedom was strong.

The Cabinet Mission (1946) proposed a united India with a weak centre, groups of provinces, a Constituent Assembly and an interim government; it failed as the League turned to Direct Action for Pakistan.
Communal violence spread, and the Mountbatten Plan (3 June 1947) proposed partition into India and Pakistan; Punjab and Bengal would be divided; princely states could join either or stay independent.
The Congress and the League accepted the plan to avoid civil war.

The Indian Independence Act (July 1947): two dominions from 15 August 1947, the end of British rule and of the Crown's paramountcy over princely states, and Constituent Assemblies to make constitutions.
Partition brought freedom along with mass migration and violence; the Constitution came into force in 1950.
outcomes: Describe the Cabinet Mission Plan (1946)
Describe the Mountbatten Plan and its acceptance
State the main clauses of the Indian Independence Act 1947

lesson.hook: How did India finally become free — and why was it divided?
lesson.example: Under the Indian Independence Act, the British Crown's paramountcy over more than 500 princely states lapsed; most joined India through the efforts of Sardar Patel.
lesson.activity: Pupils make a timeline of 1945–1947 with key events and discuss why partition was accepted.

questions.q: What did the Cabinet Mission Plan propose?
questions.a: A united India with a weak centre, groups of provinces and a Constituent Assembly.

questions.q: When was the Mountbatten Plan announced?
questions.a: 3 June 1947.

questions.q: Give two clauses of the Indian Independence Act.
questions.a: Two dominions from 15 August 1947; British paramountcy over princely states ended.

questions.q: Who led the integration of princely states?
questions.a: Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel.

lesson.homework: Write a paragraph on the human cost of partition.

topics.title: The First World War
topics.summary: Causes: aggressive nationalism, imperialist competition for colonies, an arms race (especially naval), and the division of Europe into the Triple Alliance and the Triple Entente.
notes: Causes: aggressive nationalism, imperialist competition for colonies, an arms race (especially naval), and the division of Europe into the Triple Alliance and the Triple Entente.
The immediate cause: the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand of Austria-Hungary at Sarajevo (28 June 1914); Austria attacked Serbia and the alliances drew others in.
The war (1914–1918) was fought in trenches with new weapons — machine guns, poison gas, tanks and aircraft — and killed millions.
The Treaty of Versailles (1919) blamed Germany: it lost territory and colonies, its army was limited, and it had to pay heavy reparations.
The League of Nations (1920) was formed to keep peace.
Objectives of the League: prevent war through collective security, settle disputes peacefully, and promote international cooperation.
outcomes: Explain the causes of the First World War: nationalism, imperialism, the arms race, alliances and the Sarajevo crisis
Describe its results: the Treaty of Versailles and the League of Nations
State the objectives of the League of Nations

lesson.hook: How did one assassination in Sarajevo drag the whole world into war?
lesson.example: The "war guilt" clause of the Treaty of Versailles made Germany accept full blame, leaving a deep resentment that Hitler later used.
lesson.activity: Pupils map the two alliances of 1914 on an outline map of Europe and mark Sarajevo.

questions.q: What was the immediate cause of the First World War?
questions.a: The assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand at Sarajevo.

questions.q: Name the countries of the Triple Entente.
questions.a: Britain, France and Russia.

questions.q: Give two terms of the Treaty of Versailles.
questions.a: Germany lost territory and colonies; it had to pay reparations (also army limits).

questions.q: What was the aim of the League of Nations?
questions.a: To maintain world peace through collective security.

lesson.homework: Write on why the Treaty of Versailles is said to have sown the seeds of the Second World War.

topics.title: Rise of Dictatorships
topics.summary: After the First World War, Italy felt cheated at Versailles, faced unemployment and strikes, and feared communism; Mussolini's Fascists promised order and national glory (March on Rome, 1922).
notes: After the First World War, Italy felt cheated at Versailles, faced unemployment and strikes, and feared communism; Mussolini's Fascists promised order and national glory (March on Rome, 1922).

Germany suffered from the humiliating Treaty of Versailles, reparations, inflation, the Great Depression and weak governments; Hitler's Nazi party blamed Jews and communists and promised a strong Germany (1933).
Both used propaganda, youth organisations and fear to gain support.
Similarities: a single leader with total power, one party and no opposition, extreme nationalism, glorification of war, and suppression of free speech and trade unions.
Nazism also preached racial superiority and anti-Semitism, leading to the Holocaust.
Dictatorships ended civil liberties and pushed their nations towards aggression.
outcomes: Explain the causes of the rise of Fascism in Italy and Nazism in Germany
Describe the similarities between Fascism and Nazism
Explain how dictators came to power

lesson.hook: How did people in Italy and Germany come to support leaders who ended democracy?
lesson.example: In 1923 German money lost value so fast that a loaf of bread cost billions of marks — conditions that made people desperate for strong leaders.
lesson.activity: Pupils examine how propaganda posters work (without reproducing real ones) and discuss how to recognise propaganda today.

questions.q: When did Mussolini come to power?
questions.a: 1922 (after the March on Rome).

questions.q: Give two causes of the rise of Nazism.
questions.a: The harsh Treaty of Versailles and the economic crisis (Great Depression).

questions.q: Give two common features of Fascism and Nazism.
questions.a: Rule by one party and one leader; extreme nationalism (also glorification of war).

questions.q: What was anti-Semitism in Nazi Germany?
questions.a: Hatred and persecution of Jews.

lesson.homework: Write why democracy is safer than dictatorship, with examples from this chapter.

topics.title: The Second World War
topics.summary: Causes: dissatisfaction with the Treaty of Versailles, the rise of Fascism and Nazism, the policy of appeasement by Britain and France, the Japanese invasion of China, and the failure of the League of Nations.
notes: Causes: dissatisfaction with the Treaty of Versailles, the rise of Fascism and Nazism, the policy of appeasement by Britain and France, the Japanese invasion of China, and the failure of the League of Nations.
The immediate cause: Hitler's invasion of Poland on 1 September 1939; Britain and France declared war.
The Axis (Germany, Italy, Japan) fought the Allies (Britain, France, the USSR, the USA, China and others).
Japan attacked the US naval base at Pearl Harbour (December 1941), bringing the USA into the war; the USA dropped atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki (August 1945), and Japan surrendered.
Consequences: the Axis was defeated, millions died, the United Nations was formed (1945), colonies moved towards freedom, and the world split into two blocs.
The Cold War was a rivalry between the USA and the USSR without direct war; NATO and the Warsaw Pact were the two military alliances.
outcomes: Explain the causes of the Second World War
Describe key events: Pearl Harbour, Hiroshima and Nagasaki
Explain its consequences: defeat of the Axis, formation of the UN and the Cold War

lesson.hook: Why did the world go to war again only 21 years after the "war to end all wars"?
lesson.example: At Munich (1938) Britain and France allowed Hitler to take part of Czechoslovakia, hoping to avoid war — appeasement only encouraged him.
lesson.activity: Pupils make a cause-and-consequence diagram of the Second World War and link it to the United Nations.

questions.q: What was the policy of appeasement?
questions.a: Giving in to Hitler's demands to avoid war.

questions.q: Which event brought the USA into the war?
questions.a: The Japanese attack on Pearl Harbour.

questions.q: What was the Cold War?
questions.a: A rivalry between the USA and the USSR without direct fighting.

questions.q: Name the two military alliances of the Cold War.
questions.a: NATO and the Warsaw Pact.

lesson.homework: Write a paragraph on why the League of Nations failed to prevent the Second World War.

topics.title: The United Nations
topics.summary: The United Nations was set up on 24 October 1945 to maintain peace, develop friendly relations, promote human rights and solve international problems.
notes: The United Nations was set up on 24 October 1945 to maintain peace, develop friendly relations, promote human rights and solve international problems.
General Assembly: all member states, one vote each; discusses world issues, admits members and approves the budget.

Security Council: 15 members — 5 permanent with veto power (USA, UK, France, Russia, China) and 10 elected for two years; responsible for peace and security, can impose sanctions or send peacekeepers.
International Court of Justice (The Hague): 15 judges settle legal disputes between states and give advisory opinions.
Agencies: UNICEF (New York) for children, WHO (Geneva) for health, UNESCO (Paris) for education, science and culture.
The Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948) sets out basic rights and freedoms for everyone.
outcomes: State the objectives of the United Nations
Describe the composition and functions of the General Assembly, the Security Council and the International Court of Justice
Describe UNICEF, WHO and UNESCO and the Universal Declaration of Human Rights

lesson.hook: Who helps when a pandemic spreads, children need vaccines, or heritage sites need protection?
lesson.example: UNESCO lists World Heritage Sites — India has over 40, including the Ajanta caves, the Taj Mahal and Hampi.
lesson.activity: Model UN: groups represent countries in a General Assembly debate on clean oceans and vote on a resolution.

questions.q: When was the United Nations formed?
questions.a: 24 October 1945.

questions.q: Name the five permanent members of the Security Council.
questions.a: USA, UK, France, Russia and China.

questions.q: Where is the International Court of Justice?
questions.a: The Hague (Netherlands).

questions.q: What does UNICEF do?
questions.a: It works for the welfare of children.

lesson.homework: Find out about one UN peacekeeping mission in which Indian soldiers served.

topics.title: The Non-Aligned Movement
topics.summary: Non-alignment means not joining either military bloc of the Cold War while keeping friendly relations with all and deciding each issue on its merits.
notes: Non-alignment means not joining either military bloc of the Cold War while keeping friendly relations with all and deciding each issue on its merits.
Objectives: peace and disarmament, an end to colonialism and racial discrimination, independence of foreign policy, and economic cooperation among developing countries.
Panchsheel (1954, India and China): mutual respect for territory and sovereignty, non-aggression, non-interference, equality and mutual benefit, and peaceful coexistence.
Jawaharlal Nehru shaped India's policy of non-alignment and helped bring newly independent nations together.
Architects of NAM: Nehru (India), Tito (Yugoslavia), Nasser (Egypt), Sukarno (Indonesia) and Nkrumah (Ghana); the first summit was held at Belgrade in 1961.
NAM gave newly independent countries a common voice in world affairs.
outcomes: Explain the meaning and objectives of the Non-Aligned Movement
Explain Panchsheel
Describe the role of Jawaharlal Nehru and the architects of NAM

lesson.hook: During the Cold War, why did India refuse to join either the US or the Soviet camp?
lesson.example: The first NAM summit at Belgrade in 1961 had 25 member countries; today NAM has around 120 members.
lesson.activity: Pupils list the five Panchsheel principles and apply each to relations between two neighbouring schools in a playful role play.

questions.q: What is non-alignment?
questions.a: A policy of not joining either power bloc and keeping an independent foreign policy.

questions.q: Name three architects of NAM.
questions.a: Nehru, Tito and Nasser (also Sukarno, Nkrumah).

questions.q: Where was the first NAM summit held?
questions.a: Belgrade, 1961.

questions.q: Give two principles of Panchsheel.
questions.a: Non-aggression and peaceful coexistence (also non-interference).

lesson.homework: Write about the relevance of the Non-Aligned Movement today.

topics.title: Introduction to Economics
topics.summary: Economics studies how people and societies use scarce resources to satisfy unlimited wants.
notes: Economics studies how people and societies use scarce resources to satisfy unlimited wants.
Scarcity forces choice; every choice has an opportunity cost — the next best alternative given up.
Goods are tangible things (free goods like air, economic goods that have a price); services are intangible (teaching, banking).
Utility is the power of a good to satisfy a want; value in use differs from value in exchange; price is value expressed in money.
Wealth is a stock of assets at a point of time; income is a flow of earnings over a period of time.
Microeconomics studies individual units (a consumer, a firm, a market); macroeconomics studies the whole economy (national income, inflation, unemployment).
outcomes: Define economics and explain the basic economic problem of unlimited wants and scarce resources
Explain the concepts of goods, services, utility, value, price, wealth and income
Distinguish microeconomics from macroeconomics

lesson.hook: You have ₹100 and a list of five things you want. What do you do?
lesson.example: If a farmer grows wheat on a field instead of sugarcane, the sugarcane crop she could have earned from is the opportunity cost.
lesson.activity: Each pupil lists five wants and a budget; they rank the wants, choose, and write the opportunity cost of each choice.

questions.q: What is the basic economic problem?
questions.a: Unlimited wants but scarce resources, which forces choice.

questions.q: What is opportunity cost?
questions.a: The value of the next best alternative given up.

questions.q: Distinguish wealth and income.
questions.a: Wealth is a stock at a point of time; income is a flow over a period.

questions.q: Is the study of inflation micro or macro?
questions.a: Macroeconomics.

lesson.homework: Write three examples each of free goods, economic goods and services.

topics.title: Types of Economies
topics.summary: An economy is a system through which people earn their living by producing, exchanging and consuming goods and services.
notes: An economy is a system through which people earn their living by producing, exchanging and consuming goods and services.
Capitalist (market) economy: private property, profit motive, free competition and the price mechanism decide what, how and for whom to produce (for example the USA).
Merits of capitalism: efficiency, innovation and consumer choice; demerits: inequality, monopolies and neglect of the poor.
Socialist (command) economy: the state owns the means of production and central planning decides production; aims at equality and welfare.
Merits of socialism: less inequality, planned growth; demerits: bureaucracy, lack of incentive and little consumer choice.
Mixed economy: public and private sectors exist together with government regulation; India adopted it after independence through Five-Year Plans.
outcomes: Describe the features, merits and demerits of a capitalist economy
Describe the features, merits and demerits of a socialist economy
Explain the mixed economy and why India chose it

lesson.hook: Who should decide what a country produces — the market, the government, or both?
lesson.example: In India, railways and defence are run by the state, while most shops, farms and software firms are private — a mixed economy.
lesson.activity: Pupils sort a list of 12 Indian enterprises (railways, a local bakery, SBI, a private hospital…) into public and private sectors.

questions.q: Who decides production in a capitalist economy?
questions.a: The market, through the price mechanism.

questions.q: Give one merit and one demerit of socialism.
questions.a: Less inequality; lack of incentive.

questions.q: What is a mixed economy?
questions.a: An economy where public and private sectors exist together under government regulation.

questions.q: Why did India adopt a mixed economy?
questions.a: To combine growth through private enterprise with welfare and planning by the state.

lesson.homework: Compare capitalist, socialist and mixed economies in a table.

topics.title: Problems of an Economy
topics.summary: What to produce: which goods and in what quantities, since resources cannot produce everything.
notes: What to produce: which goods and in what quantities, since resources cannot produce everything.
How to produce: the choice of technique — labour-intensive or capital-intensive.
For whom to produce: how output is distributed among people — the problem of distribution of income.
Full use of resources: an economy must avoid unemployment of labour and idle machines.
Growth of resources: an economy must increase its productive capacity over time through investment and technology.
A production possibility curve shows the combinations of two goods an economy can produce with given resources; moving along it shows opportunity cost.
outcomes: Explain the central problems of an economy: what, how and for whom to produce
Explain the problem of the full use and growth of resources
Use a production possibility curve idea to show choice

lesson.hook: Every country must decide whether to build more schools or more roads. How?
lesson.example: A country with many workers and little capital may choose labour-intensive techniques, such as handloom weaving, to create jobs.
lesson.activity: Pupils plot a simple production possibility curve for "wheat" and "cloth" from a given table and mark points inside, on and outside the curve.

questions.q: Name the three central problems of an economy.
questions.a: What, how and for whom to produce.

questions.q: What is a labour-intensive technique?
questions.a: One that uses more labour and less capital.

questions.q: What does a point inside the production possibility curve show?
questions.a: Under-use or unemployment of resources.

questions.q: How can an economy grow?
questions.a: By increasing resources and technology through investment.

lesson.homework: Explain with an example why "how to produce" matters for a country like India.

topics.title: The Indian Economy: Its Sectors
topics.summary: Primary sector: activities that use natural resources directly — agriculture, fishing, forestry, mining.
notes: Primary sector: activities that use natural resources directly — agriculture, fishing, forestry, mining.
Secondary sector: manufacturing and construction, turning raw materials into goods.
Tertiary (service) sector: services such as transport, banking, trade, education, health and IT; its share of GDP has grown the most in India.
The organised sector has registered enterprises, regular jobs and legal protection; the unorganised sector has small, scattered units with irregular jobs and low security.
Most Indian workers are in the unorganised sector, especially in agriculture.
Public sector: owned by the government, aims at welfare (railways, post); private sector: owned by individuals, aims at profit.
outcomes: Describe the primary, secondary and tertiary sectors with examples
Explain the organised and unorganised sectors
Describe the public and private sectors and their role in the Indian economy

lesson.hook: Trace a cotton shirt: from the farm, to the mill, to the shop. Which sectors did it pass through?
lesson.example: A farmer (primary) grows cotton, a mill (secondary) makes cloth, and a lorry and a shop (tertiary) take the shirt to the buyer.
lesson.activity: Pupils interview five people (family, neighbours) about their work and classify each job by sector and as organised or unorganised.

questions.q: Give two primary sector activities.
questions.a: Agriculture and fishing (also mining).

questions.q: Which sector has grown most in India's GDP?
questions.a: The tertiary (service) sector.

questions.q: Give one feature of the unorganised sector.
questions.a: Irregular jobs with little legal protection.

questions.q: What is the aim of the public sector?
questions.a: Public welfare rather than profit.

lesson.homework: Make a chart of the three sectors with five examples each from your town.

topics.title: Poverty and Unemployment in India
