topics.summary: Poverty is the inability to meet basic needs such as food, clothing, shelter, health and education.
notes: Poverty is the inability to meet basic needs such as food, clothing, shelter, health and education.
The poverty line is a minimum level of income or consumption; people below it are counted as poor; absolute poverty is falling below this minimum, relative poverty is being poor compared with others.
Causes of poverty: rapid population growth, unemployment, low productivity in agriculture, inequality, illiteracy and inflation.
Unemployment exists when people willing and able to work at the current wage cannot find work.
Types: disguised unemployment (more people on a farm than needed), seasonal unemployment (farm work only in some months), educated unemployment, and structural unemployment.
Measures: employment schemes (MGNREGA guarantees 100 days of rural work), skill development, self-employment loans, food security and education.
outcomes: Explain the meaning of poverty, the poverty line and absolute and relative poverty
Explain the causes of poverty in India and measures to remove it
Describe the types and causes of unemployment and the steps taken to reduce it

lesson.hook: What does it mean to be poor — and why can't everyone who wants a job find one?
lesson.example: If five family members work on a farm that needs only three, two are in disguised unemployment — removing them would not reduce output.
lesson.activity: Pupils design a poster for one government scheme that fights poverty or unemployment, stating who it helps and how.

questions.q: What is the poverty line?
questions.a: A minimum income or consumption level needed to meet basic needs.

questions.q: What is disguised unemployment?
questions.a: More people working than needed, so some add nothing to output.

questions.q: Give two causes of poverty in India.
questions.a: Rapid population growth and unemployment (also illiteracy).

questions.q: What does MGNREGA provide?
questions.a: 100 days of guaranteed wage employment to rural households.

lesson.homework: Write about seasonal unemployment and suggest two ways to reduce it in villages.

chapters.title: Reforms and Emerging Trends in the Indian Economy

topics.title: Reforms and Emerging Trends in the Indian Economy
topics.summary: In 1991 India faced a balance of payments crisis; the government introduced the New Economic Policy.
notes: In 1991 India faced a balance of payments crisis; the government introduced the New Economic Policy.
Liberalisation removed many controls such as industrial licensing and reduced trade barriers.
Privatisation reduced the role of the public sector through disinvestment and opened sectors to private firms.
Globalisation linked India's economy with the world through trade, foreign investment and technology.
Effects: faster growth, more foreign investment, growth of IT and services, more consumer choice; concerns include inequality and pressure on small producers.
Emerging trends: digital payments (UPI), e-commerce, start-ups, the gig economy, and schemes like Make in India and Digital India.
outcomes: Explain the economic reforms of 1991: liberalisation, privatisation and globalisation
Describe their effects on the Indian economy
Describe emerging trends: digital economy, start-ups and the services boom

lesson.hook: Why did India open its economy to the world in 1991, and how has it changed the way you shop and pay?
lesson.example: Paying a vendor by scanning a QR code with UPI is an example of the digital economy that grew rapidly after 2016.
lesson.activity: Pupils list ten products at home, find which were made abroad or by foreign companies, and discuss globalisation.

questions.q: What does LPG stand for?
questions.a: Liberalisation, privatisation and globalisation.

questions.q: Why were reforms introduced in 1991?
questions.a: Because of a balance of payments crisis.

questions.q: What is disinvestment?
questions.a: Selling part of the government's share in public sector units.

questions.q: Give two emerging trends in the Indian economy.
questions.a: Digital payments and start-ups (also e-commerce, gig work).

lesson.homework: Write the advantages and disadvantages of globalisation for Indian consumers and small producers.

chapters.title: Factors of Production: Land and Labour

topics.title: Factors of Production: Land and Labour
topics.summary: Production needs four factors: land, labour, capital and the entrepreneur; their rewards are rent, wages, interest and profit.
notes: Production needs four factors: land, labour, capital and the entrepreneur; their rewards are rent, wages, interest and profit.
Land means all free gifts of nature — soil, water, minerals, forests; it is fixed in supply, immobile, and varies in fertility.
Productivity of land depends on fertility, location, irrigation, use of fertilisers and good methods.
Labour is human effort, mental or physical, done for a reward; labour is perishable, cannot be separated from the labourer and has weak bargaining power.
Division of labour splits work into parts done by specialists; it raises efficiency and skill but causes monotony and dependence.
Efficiency of labour depends on health, education and training, working conditions, wages and tools.
outcomes: Define land as a factor of production and state its characteristics and the factors affecting its productivity
Define labour and state its characteristics
Explain the division of labour and the factors affecting the efficiency of labour

lesson.hook: What does it take to produce a loaf of bread?
lesson.example: In a garment factory, one worker cuts cloth, another stitches, and another irons — division of labour increases output.
lesson.activity: Groups make paper boats: first each pupil makes whole boats alone, then with division of labour; compare the output in five minutes.

questions.q: Name the four factors of production and their rewards.
questions.a: Land–rent, labour–wages, capital–interest, entrepreneur–profit.

questions.q: Why is land said to be fixed in supply?
questions.a: Its total quantity cannot be increased by human effort.

questions.q: Give two characteristics of labour.
questions.a: It is perishable; it cannot be separated from the labourer.

questions.q: Give one merit and one demerit of division of labour.
questions.a: Higher efficiency; monotony of work.

lesson.homework: Write how health and education affect the efficiency of labour.

chapters.title: Factors of Production: Capital and the Entrepreneur

topics.title: Factors of Production: Capital and the Entrepreneur
topics.summary: Capital is man-made wealth used to produce more wealth, such as machines, tools, buildings and raw materials.
notes: Capital is man-made wealth used to produce more wealth, such as machines, tools, buildings and raw materials.
Fixed capital lasts many production cycles (machines, buildings); working capital is used up in one cycle (raw materials, fuel).
Capital is productive, man-made and depreciates with use; human capital is the skills and knowledge of workers.
Capital formation is the increase in the stock of capital; it needs saving, mobilising savings through banks, and investment.
An entrepreneur organises the other factors, takes risks and decisions and introduces innovations; the reward is profit.
Entrepreneurs create jobs, raise output and bring new products and methods.
outcomes: Define capital and distinguish its forms: fixed and working capital, physical and human capital
Explain capital formation and its stages
Describe the functions and role of an entrepreneur

lesson.hook: Why does a tailor with a sewing machine earn more than one who sews by hand?
lesson.example: A bakery owner saves, borrows from a bank and buys a bigger oven — that is capital formation.
lesson.activity: Pupils plan a small school stall: list the fixed and working capital needed and the entrepreneur's risks.

questions.q: Distinguish fixed and working capital.
questions.a: Fixed capital is used in many production cycles; working capital is used up in one.

questions.q: What are the stages of capital formation?
questions.a: Saving, mobilising savings and investment.

questions.q: What is human capital?
questions.a: The skills, knowledge and health of workers.

questions.q: Give two functions of an entrepreneur.
questions.a: Bearing risk and organising other factors (also innovating).

lesson.homework: Write about an entrepreneur from your area and the risks they took.

topics.title: Demand and Supply
topics.summary: Demand is the quantity of a good consumers are willing and able to buy at a given price during a period.
notes: Demand is the quantity of a good consumers are willing and able to buy at a given price during a period.
Law of demand: other things remaining the same, when price rises quantity demanded falls, and when price falls it rises — the demand curve slopes downwards.
Determinants of demand: price of the good, income, prices of related goods (substitutes and complements), tastes and expectations.
A movement along the curve (extension or contraction) is caused by a change in the good's own price; a shift of the curve (increase or decrease) is caused by other factors.
Law of supply: other things remaining the same, when price rises the quantity supplied rises — the supply curve slopes upwards.
Determinants of supply: price, cost of inputs, technology, prices of other goods, taxes and subsidies, and the number of sellers.
outcomes: State the law of demand and explain the demand schedule and curve
Explain the determinants of demand and the difference between change in quantity demanded and change in demand
State the law of supply and explain its determinants

lesson.hook: Why do mango prices fall in May and rise in December?
lesson.example: When tea prices rise, people buy more coffee (a substitute); when petrol prices rise, demand for cars (a complement) may fall.
lesson.activity: Pupils make a demand schedule for samosas in class at prices ₹5 to ₹25 and plot the demand curve.

questions.q: State the law of demand.
questions.a: Other things equal, quantity demanded rises when price falls and falls when price rises.

questions.q: What causes a shift of the demand curve?
questions.a: A change in factors other than price, such as income or tastes.

questions.q: Give two determinants of supply.
questions.a: Cost of inputs and technology.

questions.q: Why does the supply curve slope upwards?
questions.a: Higher prices make it profitable to supply more.

lesson.homework: Draw and explain the difference between an extension of demand and an increase in demand.

topics.title: Elasticity of Demand and Supply
topics.summary: Price elasticity of demand measures how much quantity demanded responds to a change in price.
notes: Price elasticity of demand measures how much quantity demanded responds to a change in price.
Percentage method: Ed = percentage change in quantity demanded ÷ percentage change in price.
Types: perfectly elastic (∞), relatively elastic (> 1), unitary (= 1), relatively inelastic (< 1), perfectly inelastic (0).
Total expenditure method: if spending rises when price falls, demand is elastic; if unchanged, unitary; if it falls, inelastic.
Factors: availability of substitutes, nature of the good (necessity or luxury), share of income spent, number of uses and time.
Elasticity of supply measures how quantity supplied responds to price; it depends on time, costs and the nature of the good.
outcomes: Define price elasticity of demand and its types
Measure elasticity using the percentage method and the total expenditure method
Explain the factors affecting elasticity of demand and define elasticity of supply

lesson.hook: If the price of salt doubles, do you buy much less salt? What about cinema tickets?
lesson.example: Price of a pen falls from ₹20 to ₹16 (−20%) and sales rise from 100 to 130 (+30%): Ed = 30/20 = 1.5, so demand is elastic.
lesson.activity: Pupils calculate elasticity for five given price–quantity changes and classify each good as elastic or inelastic.

questions.q: Write the formula for price elasticity of demand.
questions.a: Ed = % change in quantity demanded ÷ % change in price.

questions.q: Is the demand for salt elastic or inelastic? Why?
questions.a: Inelastic, because it is a necessity with few substitutes and a small share of income.

questions.q: Price falls and total spending stays the same. What is the elasticity?
questions.a: Unitary (= 1).

questions.q: Give two factors affecting elasticity of demand.
questions.a: Availability of substitutes and nature of the good.

lesson.homework: Price rises from ₹10 to ₹12 and quantity falls from 50 to 45. Calculate Ed and classify.

topics.title: Market
topics.summary: A market is any arrangement through which buyers and sellers deal with each other; it need not be a place.
notes: A market is any arrangement through which buyers and sellers deal with each other; it need not be a place.
By area: local, national and international markets; by time: very short, short and long period markets.
Perfect competition: many buyers and sellers, identical products, free entry and exit, perfect knowledge — the firm is a price taker.
Monopoly: a single seller, no close substitutes, barriers to entry — the firm is a price maker and may practise price discrimination.
Monopolistic competition: many sellers with differentiated products (brands) and advertising, for example soaps and toothpastes.
Oligopoly: a few large sellers who watch one another (telecom, airlines); competition keeps prices fair and quality high.
outcomes: Define a market and classify markets by area, time and competition
Describe perfect competition, monopoly and monopolistic competition
Explain oligopoly and the role of competition

lesson.hook: Why can a local vegetable seller not charge much more than the next seller, while a railway can fix its fares?
lesson.example: Toothpaste brands sell similar products but differ in taste, packaging and advertising — monopolistic competition.
lesson.activity: Groups classify ten markets (vegetables, railways, soaps, mobile networks, electricity supply…) into market forms, with reasons.

questions.q: Give two features of perfect competition.
questions.a: Many buyers and sellers; identical products (also free entry).

questions.q: Why is a monopolist a price maker?
questions.a: Because it is the only seller with no close substitutes.

questions.q: What is product differentiation?
questions.a: Making a product appear different from rivals' by brand, design or packaging.

questions.q: Give an example of oligopoly in India.
questions.a: Mobile telecom services (or airlines).

lesson.homework: Compare perfect competition and monopoly in a table.

topics.title: Money and Commercial Banks
topics.summary: Barter is the direct exchange of goods; its difficulties include lack of double coincidence of wants, no common measure of value, indivisibility and difficulty in storing wealth.
notes: Barter is the direct exchange of goods; its difficulties include lack of double coincidence of wants, no common measure of value, indivisibility and difficulty in storing wealth.
Money solves these problems; its primary functions are medium of exchange and measure of value; secondary functions are store of value, standard of deferred payments and transfer of value.
A commercial bank accepts deposits: savings, current, fixed (term) and recurring deposits.
It lends money through loans, cash credit, overdrafts and discounting bills of exchange.
Agency functions: collecting cheques, paying bills, buying and selling shares; utility functions: lockers, drafts, ATMs, net banking and UPI.
Banks create credit: they lend out most of their deposits, and loans return as new deposits, multiplying the money supply.
outcomes: Explain the barter system and its difficulties
Describe the functions of money
Explain the functions of commercial banks: accepting deposits, lending and agency and utility services, and credit creation

lesson.hook: Imagine paying for a haircut with a sack of rice. What problems would you face?
lesson.example: If a bank must keep 10% of deposits as reserves, a ₹1000 deposit can eventually support up to ₹10,000 of deposits in the system.
lesson.activity: Pupils fill in a model deposit slip and cheque (using a sample form with no real account numbers) and explain each field.

questions.q: What is double coincidence of wants?
questions.a: Each party must want what the other has — a condition needed for barter.

questions.q: Give the two primary functions of money.
questions.a: Medium of exchange and measure of value.

questions.q: Distinguish a savings and a fixed deposit.
questions.a: Savings deposits can be withdrawn any time; fixed deposits are for a fixed period at a higher interest rate.

questions.q: How do banks create credit?
questions.a: By lending most of their deposits, which return to banks as new deposits.

lesson.homework: List four utility services of banks you or your family have used.

chapters.title: The Central Bank and Monetary Policy

topics.title: The Central Bank and Monetary Policy
topics.summary: The Reserve Bank of India (1935) is India's central bank.
notes: The Reserve Bank of India (1935) is India's central bank.
Functions: issuing currency notes (except ₹1), banker to the government, bankers' bank, lender of last resort, custodian of foreign exchange reserves and controller of credit.
Quantitative instruments: bank rate and repo rate (raising them makes loans costlier), open market operations (buying or selling government securities), and CRR and SLR (reserves banks must keep).
To control inflation, the RBI raises rates, sells securities and raises reserve ratios; to boost growth, it does the opposite.
Qualitative (selective) instruments: margin requirements, credit rationing, moral suasion and direct action.
Monetary policy aims at price stability, growth and financial stability.
outcomes: Explain the functions of the Reserve Bank of India as the central bank
Describe quantitative instruments of credit control: bank rate, repo rate, open market operations and reserve ratios
Describe qualitative instruments and the role of monetary policy

lesson.hook: Who decides how much money flows through India's banks?
lesson.example: When the RBI raises the repo rate, banks pay more to borrow, so home and car loan rates rise and spending slows.
lesson.activity: Pupils role-play the RBI's monetary policy committee: given inflation of 7%, they choose tools and explain their decision.

questions.q: When was the RBI established?
What is the repo rate?
questions.a: The rate at which the RBI lends short-term funds to banks.

questions.q: What does the RBI do to control inflation?
questions.a: Raises the repo rate and reserve ratios and sells securities.

questions.q: What is moral suasion?
questions.a: Persuading banks through advice and appeals to follow its policy.

lesson.homework: Write the difference between quantitative and qualitative credit control.

topics.title: Public Finance
topics.summary: Public finance studies the income and expenditure of the government.
notes: Public finance studies the income and expenditure of the government.
A tax is a compulsory payment to the government with no direct return; direct taxes (income tax, corporate tax) fall on those who pay them; indirect taxes (GST, customs) can be shifted to others.
Taxes can be proportional (same rate), progressive (rate rises with income) or regressive (heavier burden on the poor).
Non-tax revenue: fees, fines, licence fees, profits of public enterprises and grants.
Public expenditure: defence, infrastructure, education, health, subsidies and welfare schemes — it promotes growth and reduces inequality.
Public debt is money the government borrows, internal (from citizens and banks) or external (from abroad).
outcomes: Define public finance and distinguish public and private finance
Explain the sources of public revenue: tax and non-tax revenue; direct and indirect taxes
Describe public expenditure and public debt

lesson.hook: Where does the government get money to build roads, and on what does it spend it?
lesson.example: GST is paid by the shopkeeper to the government but passed on to buyers in the price — so it is an indirect tax.
lesson.activity: Pupils read a shop bill with GST, find the tax amount and explain who bears it.

questions.q: Give two differences between direct and indirect taxes.
questions.a: Direct taxes cannot be shifted and fall on the payer; indirect taxes can be shifted to buyers.

questions.q: What is a progressive tax?
questions.a: A tax whose rate rises as income rises.

questions.q: Give two sources of non-tax revenue.
questions.a: Fees and fines (also profits of public enterprises).

questions.q: Distinguish internal and external debt.
questions.a: Internal debt is borrowed within the country; external debt is borrowed from abroad.

lesson.homework: Write the merits and demerits of indirect taxes.

topics.title: Inflation
topics.summary: Inflation is a sustained rise in the general price level, which reduces the purchasing power of money.
notes: Inflation is a sustained rise in the general price level, which reduces the purchasing power of money.
Types by speed: creeping (mild), walking, running and hyperinflation (prices rising extremely fast).
Demand-pull inflation: total demand is greater than supply ("too much money chasing too few goods").
Cost-push inflation: rising costs of production (wages, fuel, raw materials) push prices up.
Effects: fixed-income earners, pensioners and lenders lose; borrowers and producers may gain; savings fall and inequality grows.
Controls: monetary measures (higher repo rate, CRR, selling securities) and fiscal measures (less government spending, higher taxes, more public borrowing), plus raising supply.
outcomes: Define inflation and its types: creeping, walking, running and hyperinflation
Explain demand-pull and cost-push inflation
Describe the effects of inflation and the monetary and fiscal measures to control it

lesson.hook: Why did your grandparents pay ₹2 for a cup of tea that now costs ₹15?
lesson.example: If fuel prices rise sharply, transport costs rise, and the prices of vegetables and goods rise too — cost-push inflation.
lesson.activity: Pupils compare prices of five common goods from a family member's memory of ten years ago with today and calculate the percentage rise.

questions.q: What is inflation?
questions.a: A sustained rise in the general price level.

questions.q: Distinguish demand-pull and cost-push inflation.
questions.a: Demand-pull comes from excess demand; cost-push comes from rising production costs.

questions.q: Who loses during inflation?
questions.a: Fixed-income earners, pensioners and lenders.

questions.q: Give one monetary and one fiscal measure to control inflation.
questions.a: Raising the repo rate; cutting government spending.

lesson.homework: Explain why moderate inflation may help producers but hurt pensioners.

topics.title: Consumer Awareness
topics.summary: Consumer exploitation happens through underweighing, adulteration, poor quality, high prices, false advertising and unsafe products.
notes: Consumer exploitation happens through underweighing, adulteration, poor quality, high prices, false advertising and unsafe products.
Consumer rights: right to safety, to be informed, to choose, to be heard, to seek redressal and to consumer education.
Consumer responsibilities: check labels and marks, ask for bills, avoid wasteful use and file genuine complaints.

The Consumer Protection Act 2019 set up the Central Consumer Protection Authority and consumer commissions at district, state and national levels; it also covers e-commerce and misleading advertisements.
Complaints can be filed online (e-Daakhil); commissions can order replacement, refund or compensation.
Standard marks: ISI (industrial products), Agmark (agricultural products), BIS hallmark (gold), FSSAI (food) guide consumers.
outcomes: Explain the meaning of consumer exploitation and its forms
State consumer rights and responsibilities
Describe the Consumer Protection Act 2019, consumer commissions and standardisation marks

lesson.hook: You bought a packet that weighs less than printed. What can you do?
lesson.example: A buyer who got a defective phone can approach the District Consumer Commission for a replacement or refund if the seller refuses.
lesson.activity: Pupils bring five packaged items and check the label: MRP, weight, dates, standard mark and customer-care details.

questions.q: Name four consumer rights.
questions.a: Safety, information, choice and redressal (also to be heard, consumer education).

questions.q: Which mark is used on agricultural products?
questions.a: Agmark.

questions.q: Name the three levels of consumer commissions.
questions.a: District, state and national.

questions.q: Give two responsibilities of a consumer.
questions.a: Ask for a bill; check labels and standard marks.

lesson.homework: Write a sample complaint letter about a defective product (use made-up details).

courses.title: English: Treasure Chest: Stories and Poems (Class 9), Class 9

topics.title: Bonku Babu's Friend
topics.summary: Bonku Babu, a gentle, timid teacher of Geography and Bengali in the village of Kankurgachhi, is teased every evening by the men at the local gathering (adda).
notes: Bonku Babu, a gentle, timid teacher of Geography and Bengali in the village of Kankurgachhi, is teased every evening by the men at the local gathering (adda).
One evening, walking home through a bamboo grove, he sees a glowing spacecraft land; a friendly alien called Ang, from the planet Craneus, steps out.
Ang, who had meant to go elsewhere, speaks with him kindly and shows him wonders of the Earth through a special instrument — places Bonku Babu had only taught about.
Ang tells him that meekness is wrong: one must protest when one is insulted without reason.
Inspired, Bonku Babu returns to the gathering and finally stands up to his tormentors, astonishing them.
Satyajit Ray mixes science fiction with village life to make a point about dignity and self-respect.
outcomes: Retell the story of Bonku Babu's meeting with a visitor from space
Analyse the character of Bonku Babu and how he changes
Discuss the theme of standing up against bullying

lesson.hook: Have you ever kept quiet when someone mocked you? What would give you the courage to speak?
lesson.example: The men at the gathering believe Bonku Babu will never answer back; the story's ending surprises them because the alien has changed how he sees himself.
lesson.activity: Pairs write a short dialogue between Bonku Babu and Ang in their own words, then act it out for the class.

questions.q: Where did Bonku Babu teach and what subjects?
questions.a: In the village school of Kankurgachhi; Geography and Bengali.

questions.q: Who was Ang and where did he come from?
questions.a: A friendly alien from the planet Craneus.

questions.q: What advice did Ang give Bonku Babu?
questions.a: That he should protest when people insult or hurt him without reason.

questions.q: How does Bonku Babu change by the end?
questions.a: He becomes confident and stands up to those who mocked him.

lesson.homework: Write a character sketch of Bonku Babu before and after meeting Ang.

topics.title: Oliver Asks for More
topics.summary: Oliver Twist is born in a workhouse; his mother dies at his birth, and he is raised in a branch-workhouse where the children are neglected and underfed.
notes: Oliver Twist is born in a workhouse; his mother dies at his birth, and he is raised in a branch-workhouse where the children are neglected and underfed.
At nine he is brought back to the workhouse by Mr Bumble, the beadle, and presented to the board of gentlemen who run it.
The board feeds the poor on thin gruel so that only the truly desperate will stay — Dickens mocks this as "wise" policy with bitter irony.
The starving boys cast lots, and Oliver is chosen to ask the master for more gruel.

The master strikes him with the ladle; the board is outraged, a gentleman in a white waistcoat predicts that Oliver will be hanged, and a notice offers money to anyone who will take Oliver away as an apprentice.
Dickens uses satire to attack the cruelty of the Poor Law and society's treatment of the poor.
outcomes: Narrate the events of "Oliver Asks for More" from Oliver Twist
Describe life in the workhouse and the treatment of orphans
Identify Dickens's satire and irony against the Poor Law system

lesson.hook: What would happen if a hungry child simply asked for a second helping?
lesson.example: The narrator calls the board "philosophical" while showing them starving children — the praise is ironic and exposes their cruelty.
lesson.activity: Groups prepare a news report on the workhouse from the point of view of a reporter who wants to expose conditions there.

questions.q: Who was Mr Bumble?
questions.a: The parish beadle who brought Oliver back to the workhouse.

questions.q: Why was Oliver chosen to ask for more?
questions.a: The hungry boys cast lots and the lot fell on him.

questions.q: How did the board react to Oliver's request?
questions.a: They were outraged; one member predicted he would be hanged, and they offered money to anyone who would take him away.

questions.q: What is Dickens criticising in this story?
questions.a: The cruel treatment of the poor under the workhouse system.

lesson.homework: Write a diary entry by Oliver on the night after he asked for more.

topics.title: The Model Millionaire
topics.summary: Hughie Erskine is charming and good-looking but poor; he loves Laura Merton, but her father, a retired Colonel, will not allow the marriage until Hughie has ten thousand pounds.
notes: Hughie Erskine is charming and good-looking but poor; he loves Laura Merton, but her father, a retired Colonel, will not allow the marriage until Hughie has ten thousand pounds.
Visiting his friend Alan Trevor, a painter, Hughie sees a ragged old beggar posing as a model and, moved with pity, gives him his only sovereign.
Later Trevor reveals that the "beggar" was Baron Hausberg, one of the richest men in Europe, who wanted a portrait of himself as a beggar.
Hughie is embarrassed, but the Baron is touched by his kindness.
The next day Hughie receives a wedding present for himself and Laura: a cheque for ten thousand pounds, "from an old beggar".
Wilde plays with words in the title: a millionaire who posed as a model, and a millionaire who is a model of generosity.
outcomes: Narrate the story of Hughie Erskine and the beggar-model
Analyse the characters of Hughie, Alan Trevor and Baron Hausberg
Explain the irony and wordplay in the title

lesson.hook: Would you give your last coin to a stranger who looked poorer than you?
lesson.example: Hughie's kindness seems foolish when he gives away his last coin, yet it is exactly what brings him happiness — situational irony.
lesson.activity: Pupils rewrite the ending as a short scene in which Hughie opens the envelope and tells Laura the news.

questions.q: Why could Hughie not marry Laura?
questions.a: Her father wanted him to have ten thousand pounds first.

questions.q: What did Hughie give the beggar?
questions.a: A sovereign — his only coin.

questions.q: Who was the beggar really?
questions.a: Baron Hausberg, one of the richest men in Europe.

questions.q: Explain the title "The Model Millionaire".
questions.a: The Baron was a millionaire who posed as a model and was also a model of generosity.

lesson.homework: Write a character sketch of Hughie Erskine.

topics.title: Home-coming
topics.summary: Phatik, a fourteen-year-old village boy, is the leader of the local boys and often clashes with his younger brother Makhan.
notes: Phatik, a fourteen-year-old village boy, is the leader of the local boys and often clashes with his younger brother Makhan.
After a quarrel over a prank with a log, his tired mother agrees when her brother Bishamber offers to take Phatik to Calcutta to study.
In Calcutta Phatik is unwelcome: his aunt treats him as a burden, he is slow at school and laughed at, and he longs for his village and mother.
Afraid after losing a schoolbook, he tries to go home in the rain, falls ill with fever and is brought back by the police.
In his delirium he repeats the chants of boatmen measuring the river's depth, and when his mother arrives he says that his holidays have come — and passes away.
Tagore shows sympathetically how a boy at an awkward age suffers for want of love and a sense of home.
outcomes: Narrate the story of Phatik Chakravorti in "Home-coming"
Explore the feelings of a teenager who feels unwanted
Discuss Tagore's treatment of adolescence and belonging

lesson.hook: Is fourteen an awkward age? Why do teenagers sometimes feel that no one understands them?
lesson.example: The title refers both to Phatik's wish to go home and, painfully, to his final "going home" at the end.
lesson.activity: Pupils write a letter Phatik might have wanted to send to his mother from Calcutta, expressing his feelings in their own words.

questions.q: Why did Phatik go to Calcutta?
questions.a: His uncle Bishamber offered to take him there to study, and his mother agreed.

questions.q: How did his aunt treat him?
questions.a: Coldly, as an unwanted burden.

questions.q: Why did Phatik run away in the rain?
questions.a: He had lost his book, feared punishment and longed to go home.

questions.q: What is the double meaning of the title?
questions.a: His longing to go home, and his death as the final "home-coming".

lesson.homework: Write about what Phatik's family could have done differently.

chapters.title: The Boy who Broke the Bank

topics.title: The Boy who Broke the Bank
topics.summary: Nathu, the sweeper at the Pipalnagar Bank, grumbles to Sitaram's wife that he has not been paid for two months.
notes: Nathu, the sweeper at the Pipalnagar Bank, grumbles to Sitaram's wife that he has not been paid for two months.
She passes the remark on to Mrs Srivastava, who tells Mrs Bhushan in the market that the bank cannot pay its staff.
As the gossip spreads through shops, the barber's chair and the tea-stalls, it grows into a story that the bank is failing.
Worried people rush to withdraw their savings; the manager, Seth Govind Ram, cannot meet the sudden demand, and the bank collapses.
Ironically, Nathu, who started the rumour, blames the manager and goes off to look for a new job, never realising his role.
Bond gently mocks small-town gossip and shows how rumours can cause real damage.
outcomes: Narrate how a rumour led to the collapse of the Pipalnagar bank
Examine how gossip changes as it passes from person to person
Appreciate Ruskin Bond's humour and irony

lesson.hook: Play "Chinese whispers": how much does a message change after passing through ten people?
lesson.example: Each person adds a little to the story until "a sweeper was not paid" becomes "the bank is going to fail" — a chain reaction of gossip.
lesson.activity: Play a whisper chain with a one-line message; compare the first and last versions and link it to the story.

questions.q: Why did Nathu complain?
questions.a: He had not been paid for two months.

questions.q: How did the rumour spread?
questions.a: From Sitaram's wife to Mrs Srivastava, Mrs Bhushan and then through the market and town.

questions.q: What happened to the bank?
questions.a: People withdrew their money in panic and the bank collapsed.

questions.q: What is ironic about the ending?
questions.a: Nathu, who started it all, blames the manager and never knows he caused the collapse.

lesson.homework: Write about a time a rumour caused trouble in your school or neighbourhood, and how it could have been stopped.

topics.title: The Night Mail
topics.summary: The poem was written for a 1936 documentary film about the mail train that carried letters overnight from London to Scotland.
notes: The poem was written for a 1936 documentary film about the mail train that carried letters overnight from London to Scotland.
The first part describes the train's journey through the night, past farms and hills, while the countryside sleeps.
The rhythm of the lines imitates the beat of the wheels, speeding up as the train rushes on and slowing as it nears the end.
The train carries every kind of letter — business letters, bills, news, love letters, letters of condolence and gossip.
The poem ends with people asleep and dreaming, and the idea that everyone hopes for a letter because no one wishes to be forgotten.
Auden celebrates both the working machine and the human feelings it carries.
outcomes: Understand the subject and purpose of W. H. Auden's "The Night Mail"
Identify how rhythm and sound imitate the moving train
Discuss the importance of letters in people's lives

lesson.hook: Before e-mail and phones, how did news travel overnight from one city to another?
lesson.example: When lines speed up with short, beating stresses, the reader "hears" the wheels of the train — sound matching sense.
lesson.activity: Pupils read a stanza aloud while tapping the beat on the desk, then describe how the pace changes across the poem.

questions.q: What is the "Night Mail"?
questions.a: A mail train that carried letters overnight from London to Scotland.

questions.q: How does the poem's rhythm help its meaning?
questions.a: It imitates the beat of the train's wheels.

questions.q: Name three kinds of letters the train carries.
questions.a: Business letters, love letters and letters of condolence (also bills, gossip).

questions.q: What human feeling does the poem end with?
questions.a: Everyone longs to receive a letter because no one wants to be forgotten.

lesson.homework: Write a paragraph on why letters still matter in the age of instant messages.

topics.title: Skimbleshanks: The Railway Cat
topics.summary: The poem comes from Eliot's collection of light verse about cats (1939).
notes: The poem comes from Eliot's collection of light verse about cats (1939).
Skimbleshanks travels on the night mail train to Scotland; the train, the staff say, cannot leave until he is found.
Once aboard, he acts like a guard: he patrols the corridors, checks the sleeping cars, keeps order and keeps mice away.
Passengers feel safe because he is watching over them; he seems to know everything that happens on the train.
At the end of the journey he sees the passengers off, proud of his work.
Personification, a bouncy rhyme and a repeated refrain make the poem playful and musical.
outcomes: Understand T. S. Eliot's portrait of Skimbleshanks the railway cat
Identify humour, rhyme and personification in the poem
Discuss the qualities of responsibility and pride in one's work

lesson.hook: If a cat had a job on a train, what would it be?
lesson.example: By describing a cat as a railway official who inspects and supervises, Eliot gives an animal human duties and pride — personification.
lesson.activity: Pupils write a short job description for Skimbleshanks listing his duties, in their own words.

questions.q: On which train does Skimbleshanks travel?
questions.a: The night mail train to Scotland.

questions.q: Why can the train not start without him?
questions.a: Because the staff believe he is essential to the journey.

questions.q: Give two things Skimbleshanks does on the train.
questions.a: He patrols the corridors and keeps mice away (also checks passengers).

questions.q: Name one poetic device in the poem.
questions.a: Personification (or refrain, rhyme).

lesson.homework: Compare "Skimbleshanks" with "The Night Mail": how do both poems show the same journey differently?

topics.title: I Remember, I Remember
topics.summary: The poet recalls the house where he was born, with its little window where the morning sun peeped in.
notes: The poet recalls the house where he was born, with its little window where the morning sun peeped in.
He remembers the flowers he loved — roses, lilies, violets, lilac and the laburnum planted by his brother.
He recalls swinging and feeling as light as a bird, and the fir trees whose tops he believed touched the sky.
Each stanza begins with the repeated phrase of the title, like a return to memory.
The contrast: as a child he felt light, joyful and close to heaven; as an adult he feels burdened and farther from heaven than when he was a boy.
The mood is nostalgic and melancholy — a longing for the innocence of childhood.
outcomes: Understand the memories described in Thomas Hood's "I Remember, I Remember"
Identify the contrast between childhood and adulthood
Appreciate imagery, repetition and nostalgia

lesson.hook: What is your earliest happy memory of the house you grew up in?
lesson.example: A child thinks tall fir trees touch the sky; the adult knows better — yet the adult feels farther from heaven than the child did.
lesson.activity: Pupils draw the scenes described in each stanza and label the images, then share one of their own childhood memories.

questions.q: What did the poet remember about the window?
questions.a: The morning sun came in through the little window where he was born.

questions.q: Which tree did his brother plant?
questions.a: The laburnum.

questions.q: What did he believe about the fir trees as a child?
questions.a: That their tops were close to the sky.

questions.q: What is the mood of the poem?
questions.a: Nostalgic and melancholy.

lesson.homework: Write a short poem or paragraph beginning "I remember" about your own childhood home.

chapters.title: A Doctor's Journal Entry for August 6, 1945

topics.title: A Doctor's Journal Entry for August 6, 1945
topics.summary: The poem is based on the diary of a Japanese doctor who survived the atomic bomb dropped on Hiroshima on 6 August 1945.
notes: The poem is based on the diary of a Japanese doctor who survived the atomic bomb dropped on Hiroshima on 6 August 1945.
It opens on a calm, bright morning as the doctor rests at home — a peaceful scene that makes the horror more striking.
A sudden flash of light is followed by destruction; he finds himself injured, his house wrecked.
He and his wife stumble out through the ruins; he sees injured, silent people moving like shadows and the city in ruins.
Weak from loss of blood, he struggles on, asking why they had been hurt so terribly.
Contrast, vivid imagery and a calm, factual voice make the poem a powerful message against war and nuclear weapons.
outcomes: Understand the events described in Vikram Seth's "A Doctor's Journal Entry for August 6, 1945"
Analyse imagery that conveys the horror of the atomic bombing of Hiroshima
Discuss the poem's message about war and peace

lesson.hook: What do we lose when a whole city is destroyed in a moment?
lesson.example: The quiet beginning and the calm tone of a doctor describing terrible sights make the reader feel the shock more deeply.
lesson.activity: Class discussion: pupils list the images of destruction in the poem and discuss why the poet avoids loud, emotional language.

questions.q: Whose experience is the poem based on?
questions.a: A Japanese doctor who survived the bombing of Hiroshima.

questions.q: How does the poem begin?
questions.a: On a calm, peaceful morning.

questions.q: What happens suddenly?
questions.a: A flash of light and the destruction caused by the atomic bomb.

questions.q: What is the message of the poem?
questions.a: War and nuclear weapons bring terrible suffering to ordinary people.

lesson.homework: Write a speech for Hiroshima Day (6 August) on the need for peace.

topics.title: A Work of Artifice
topics.summary: The poem describes a bonsai tree that could have grown tall on a mountainside but has been kept small in a pot by a gardener who prunes it.
notes: The poem describes a bonsai tree that could have grown tall on a mountainside but has been kept small in a pot by a gardener who prunes it.
The gardener soothingly tells the tree that being small and pretty is its nature and its good fortune.
The bonsai is an extended metaphor for women whose growth is restricted by society to fit ideas of beauty and domestic roles.
The poet links it to practices that have limited women, such as binding feet and discouraging their minds and ambitions.
The title is ironic: the bonsai is a "work of artifice" — something artificially shaped, not natural.
The poem asks readers to question the "gentle" control that stops people from reaching their full potential.
outcomes: Understand the extended metaphor of the bonsai tree in Marge Piercy's "A Work of Artifice"
Relate the poem to the way society limits women
Identify irony and the poet's tone

lesson.hook: Why is a bonsai tree small? Is it by nature, or because someone made it so?
lesson.example: The gardener's soothing words are like social messages that persuade people that their limits are natural and good.
lesson.activity: Groups discuss other examples of how people might be "pruned" by expectations and suggest how to encourage full growth.

questions.q: What could the bonsai have become?
questions.a: A tall tree on a mountainside.

questions.q: What does the gardener do to the tree?
questions.a: Prunes it to keep it small and tells it that this is its nature.

questions.q: What does the bonsai stand for?
questions.a: Women whose growth is limited by society.

questions.q: Why is the title ironic?
questions.a: The tree's smallness is artificial, not natural — a work of artifice.

lesson.homework: Write a paragraph on how schools and families can help everyone grow to their full potential.

courses.title: English: Julius Caesar: Acts I and II, Class 9

topics.title: Act I, Scene 1
topics.summary: The play opens on a street in Rome; commoners are on holiday to celebrate Caesar's triumph over the sons of Pompey.
notes: The play opens on a street in Rome; commoners are on holiday to celebrate Caesar's triumph over the sons of Pompey.
The tribunes Flavius and Marullus scold them; a cobbler answers with puns ("a mender of bad soles") that annoy the tribunes.
Marullus reminds the crowd that they once cheered Pompey and now cheer his defeat — showing how fickle the mob is.
The tribunes send the crowd home and decide to remove decorations from Caesar's statues.
Flavius wants to stop Caesar from "flying too high" — the first hint of fear of his ambition.
The scene takes place on the feast of Lupercal and prepares for the political conflict to come.
outcomes: Summarise Act I, Scene 1 of Julius Caesar
Explain the conflict between the tribunes and the commoners
Identify the play's opening themes: the fickle mob and fear of Caesar's power

lesson.hook: Why might leaders be worried when crowds celebrate one man too much?
lesson.example: The cobbler's word "soles" also sounds like "souls" — Shakespeare uses a pun to add humour and to show the commoners' cheekiness.
lesson.activity: Pupils read the scene aloud in parts, then list three things it tells us about the Roman crowd.

questions.q: Why are the commoners on holiday?
questions.a: To celebrate Caesar's triumph over the sons of Pompey.

questions.q: Who are Flavius and Marullus?
questions.a: Tribunes of Rome who oppose Caesar.

questions.q: How does Marullus show the mob is fickle?
questions.a: He reminds them they once cheered Pompey, whom Caesar has now defeated.

questions.q: What do the tribunes decide to do?
questions.a: Remove decorations from Caesar's statues and disperse the crowds.

lesson.homework: Write a note on the importance of the opening scene.

topics.title: Act I, Scene 2
topics.summary: A soothsayer warns Caesar to "beware the ides of March" (15 March); Caesar dismisses him as a dreamer.
notes: A soothsayer warns Caesar to "beware the ides of March" (15 March); Caesar dismisses him as a dreamer.
Cassius works on Brutus, flattering him and telling stories of Caesar's physical weakness (nearly drowning in the Tiber, fever in Spain) to show that Caesar is only a man.
Brutus admits he fears the people may choose Caesar as king, though he loves him.
Caesar tells Antony that he distrusts Cassius, who has a "lean and hungry look" and thinks too much.
Casca reports that Antony offered Caesar a crown three times, that Caesar refused it each time, and that he then fell down in a fit.
In a soliloquy, Cassius plans to throw forged letters into Brutus's window to win him over.
outcomes: Summarise Act I, Scene 2
Analyse how Cassius persuades Brutus
Examine Caesar's character and the report of the offered crown

lesson.hook: How does one person persuade another to act against a friend?
lesson.example: Cassius asks why "Caesar" should be a greater name than "Brutus" — he uses Brutus's pride and sense of honour to persuade him.
lesson.activity: Pupils map Cassius's arguments to Brutus on a chart: flattery, examples of Caesar's weakness, appeal to honour.

questions.q: What does the soothsayer warn Caesar about?
questions.a: To beware the ides of March.

questions.q: Give one story Cassius tells about Caesar's weakness.
questions.a: Caesar nearly drowned in the Tiber and needed Cassius's help (or his fever in Spain).

questions.q: Why does Caesar distrust Cassius?
questions.a: Cassius thinks too much, rarely smiles and has a lean and hungry look.

questions.q: What does Casca report about the crown?
questions.a: Antony offered it three times and Caesar refused it each time.

lesson.homework: Write a character sketch of Cassius based on this scene.

topics.title: Act I, Scene 3
topics.summary: A violent storm rages over Rome at night; Casca describes strange sights — a man whose hand burned without hurting, a lion near the Capitol, men on fire walking the streets.
notes: A violent storm rages over Rome at night; Casca describes strange sights — a man whose hand burned without hurting, a lion near the Capitol, men on fire walking the streets.
Cicero calmly says that people interpret events as they wish.
Cassius welcomes the storm and explains that the omens are warnings against Caesar's tyranny.
Casca reveals that the Senate plans to crown Caesar the next day; Cassius says he would rather die than live under a tyrant.
Casca joins the conspiracy.
Cinna is given the forged letters to place where Brutus will find them; the conspirators know they need Brutus's good name.
outcomes: Summarise Act I, Scene 3
Interpret the storm and the omens
Explain how Cassius wins over Casca and plans to win Brutus

lesson.hook: Why do writers often use storms at important moments in a story?
lesson.example: The disorder in nature mirrors the disorder about to happen in Rome's politics — a device called pathetic fallacy.
lesson.activity: Groups list the omens in the scene and write how Casca and Cassius interpret each differently.

questions.q: Name two strange sights Casca describes.
questions.a: A lion near the Capitol and a man whose hand burned without harm.

questions.q: How does Cassius interpret the storm?
questions.a: As a warning against Caesar's tyranny.

questions.q: What does the Senate plan for the next day?
questions.a: To crown Caesar king.

questions.q: Why do the conspirators want Brutus?
questions.a: His good name will make their deed look noble to the people.

lesson.homework: Explain how the storm scene adds to the atmosphere of the play.

topics.title: Act II, Scene 1
topics.summary: At night in his orchard, Brutus reasons that Caesar must die — not for what he has done, but for what power might make him (the serpent's egg).
notes: At night in his orchard, Brutus reasons that Caesar must die — not for what he has done, but for what power might make him (the serpent's egg).
Lucius brings him a forged letter urging him to act; Brutus takes it as Rome's call.
The conspirators arrive; Brutus refuses to let them swear an oath, refuses to include Cicero and refuses to kill Antony — they should be "sacrificers, but not butchers".
Decius promises to bring Caesar to the Senate by flattering him.
Portia, his wife, pleads to know his secret; she shows a wound she gave herself to prove her strength.
Brutus's decisions reveal his idealism and poor judgement, which will cost the conspirators later.
outcomes: Summarise Act II, Scene 1
Analyse Brutus's reasoning in his soliloquy and his decisions as leader of the conspiracy
Examine the relationship between Brutus and Portia

lesson.hook: Can you justify harming someone for what they might do in the future?
lesson.example: By sparing Antony, Brutus makes his greatest mistake: Antony later turns Rome against the conspirators.
lesson.activity: Debate: "Brutus's reasons for killing Caesar are sound." Pupils argue using lines from the soliloquy in their own words.

questions.q: What does Brutus compare Caesar to in his soliloquy?
questions.a: A serpent's egg that must be killed before it hatches.

questions.q: Why does Brutus refuse to have Antony killed?
questions.a: He thinks it would make them look like butchers, and Antony is harmless without Caesar.

questions.q: How does Portia prove her strength?
questions.a: She shows a wound she gave herself in the thigh.

questions.q: What does Decius promise?
questions.a: To bring Caesar to the Senate by flattering him.

lesson.homework: Write a character sketch of Brutus from this scene.

topics.title: Act II, Scene 2
topics.summary: On the morning of the ides of March, Calphurnia begs Caesar to stay home after dreaming that his statue ran with blood while Romans washed their hands in it.
notes: On the morning of the ides of March, Calphurnia begs Caesar to stay home after dreaming that his statue ran with blood while Romans washed their hands in it.
The augurers find no heart inside the animal they sacrificed — another bad sign.
Caesar first boasts that he is more dangerous than danger itself, but then agrees to stay home for Calphurnia's sake.
Decius reinterprets the dream as a sign that Rome will draw new life from Caesar, and says the Senate will crown him today and might mock him if he stays away.
Caesar's pride wins; he decides to go.
The conspirators and Antony arrive to escort him — dramatic irony, as Caesar greets them as friends.
outcomes: Summarise Act II, Scene 2
Examine Calphurnia's dream and Decius's reinterpretation
Analyse Caesar's pride and superstition

lesson.hook: Would you listen to a loved one's nightmare as a warning?
lesson.example: Caesar invites the conspirators to share wine "like friends", while the audience knows they plan to kill him — dramatic irony.
lesson.activity: Pupils compare Calphurnia's and Decius's readings of the dream in a two-column chart.

questions.q: What did Calphurnia dream?
questions.a: That Caesar's statue ran with blood and Romans washed their hands in it.

questions.q: What did the augurers find?
questions.a: No heart in the sacrificed animal.

questions.q: How does Decius change Caesar's mind?
questions.a: By reinterpreting the dream favourably and saying the Senate will crown him.

questions.q: What does this scene show about Caesar?
questions.a: He is proud and can be swayed by flattery.

lesson.homework: Write a character sketch of Calphurnia.

topics.title: Act II, Scene 3
topics.summary: Artemidorus, a teacher of rhetoric, stands in a street near the Capitol.
notes: Artemidorus, a teacher of rhetoric, stands in a street near the Capitol.
He reads aloud a letter he has written to warn Caesar, naming the conspirators: Brutus, Cassius, Casca, Cinna, Trebonius, Metellus Cimber, Decius Brutus and Caius Ligarius.
He plans to hand it to Caesar as he passes.
He reflects that virtue cannot live free from the bite of envy.
The scene raises the hope that Caesar might still be saved, building suspense.
It also shows that the plot is no longer a secret.
outcomes: Summarise Act II, Scene 3
Explain the role of Artemidorus
Discuss how the scene builds suspense

lesson.hook: If you knew someone was in danger, how would you warn them?
lesson.example: The audience wonders whether Caesar will read the letter in time — the short scene increases tension before the assassination.
lesson.activity: Pupils write the warning note in modern English in their own words.

questions.q: Who is Artemidorus?
questions.a: A teacher of rhetoric who wants to warn Caesar.

questions.q: What does his letter contain?
questions.a: The names of the conspirators and a warning to Caesar.

questions.q: How does the scene build suspense?
questions.a: It raises the hope that Caesar might be warned in time.

questions.q: Name four conspirators listed in the letter.
questions.a: Brutus, Cassius, Casca and Cinna.

lesson.homework: Write what you think would happen if Caesar read the letter.

topics.title: Act II, Scene 4
topics.summary: Portia is anxious and sends Lucius to the Capitol, but forgets to tell him what to do there.
notes: Portia is anxious and sends Lucius to the Capitol, but forgets to tell him what to do there.
She thinks she hears noise from the Capitol and grows more nervous; her anxiety shows she knows of the plot.
She admits that it is hard for a woman to keep a secret while having a man's mind but a woman's might.
The Soothsayer passes by, on his way to warn Caesar again.
Portia nearly gives the plot away, then covers herself.
The scene heightens suspense before the assassination.
outcomes: Summarise Act II, Scene 4
Analyse Portia's anxiety
Examine the role of the Soothsayer

lesson.hook: How do you behave when you know something worrying but cannot tell anyone?
lesson.example: Portia sends Lucius off without instructions — a small detail that shows how disturbed she is.
lesson.activity: Pupils perform Portia's lines showing her anxiety through voice and movement.

questions.q: Why is Portia anxious?
questions.a: She knows about the conspiracy and fears for Brutus.

questions.q: Why does Lucius not know what to do?
questions.a: Portia forgets to tell him what to do at the Capitol.

questions.q: Where is the Soothsayer going?
questions.a: To the Capitol to warn Caesar again.

questions.q: What does this scene add to the play?
questions.a: Suspense before the assassination.

lesson.homework: Compare Portia and Calphurnia as wives.

topics.title: Composition
topics.summary: The examination asks for one composition of about 300–350 words chosen from several topics.
notes: The examination asks for one composition of about 300–350 words chosen from several topics.
Narrative compositions tell a story in sequence; descriptive ones paint a picture of a person, place or event with sensory detail.
Argumentative compositions take a side and support it with reasons; expository ones explain a topic clearly.
Picture-based topics allow any interpretation that is clearly linked to the picture.
Plan first: jot down ideas, arrange them into an opening, three or four body paragraphs and a conclusion.
Good compositions use varied sentences, precise vocabulary, linking words (however, moreover, as a result) and correct grammar.
outcomes: Identify the kinds of composition: narrative, descriptive, argumentative, picture-based and expository
Plan a composition of about 300–350 words with an introduction, body and conclusion
Use paragraphs, linking words and varied sentences

lesson.hook: Two pupils write about "A rainy day": one gets 8/20, the other 18/20. What made the difference?
lesson.example: For "A Journey I Will Never Forget": open with a gripping moment, narrate events in order, describe sights and feelings, and end with what you learnt.
lesson.activity: Pupils plan (not write) three compositions in ten minutes each, using a mind map for each topic type.

questions.q: What is the word limit for the composition?
questions.a: About 300–350 words.

questions.q: How is a descriptive composition different from a narrative one?
questions.a: It paints a picture with detail rather than telling a sequence of events.

questions.q: Why should you plan before writing?
questions.a: To organise ideas logically and stay relevant.

questions.q: Give three linking words.
questions.a: However, moreover, as a result.

lesson.homework: Write a descriptive composition on "A busy market in the evening" (300–350 words).

topics.title: Letter Writing
topics.summary: Informal (friendly) letters are written to friends and family; the tone is warm and personal.
notes: Informal (friendly) letters are written to friends and family; the tone is warm and personal.
Formal letters are written to officials, editors, principals or companies for complaints, requests, applications or opinions.
Formal format: sender's address, date, receiver's designation and address, subject line, salutation (Sir/Madam), body in clear paragraphs, closing (Yours faithfully) and name.
Informal format: sender's address, date, salutation (Dear …), body, closing (Yours lovingly / affectionately) and name.
Formal letters come to the point quickly, stay polite and avoid slang; informal letters may share feelings and news.
Format carries marks in the examination, so it must be accurate.
outcomes: Distinguish formal and informal letters
Use the correct format: address, date, salutation, subject, body, closing and signature
Choose tone and vocabulary suited to the purpose

lesson.hook: Would you write to the Principal the way you write to your cousin?
lesson.example: A letter to the municipal commissioner about uncollected garbage uses a subject line, states the problem, its effects and a clear request for action.
lesson.activity: Pupils rewrite an informal note as a formal letter, changing format, tone and vocabulary.

questions.q: Give two differences between formal and informal letters.
questions.a: Formal letters have a subject line and formal tone; informal letters are personal and warm.

questions.q: How do you close a formal letter to an unknown official?
questions.a: Yours faithfully.

questions.q: What goes in a subject line?
questions.a: A short statement of the letter's purpose.

questions.q: Why does format matter?
questions.a: It is part of the assessment and shows the letter is properly organised.

lesson.homework: Write a letter to your friend describing your school's annual day.

topics.title: Notice and E-mail
topics.summary: The examination gives a situation and asks for (a) a notice and (b) an e-mail on the same content.
notes: The examination gives a situation and asks for (a) a notice and (b) an e-mail on the same content.
Notice format: name of the institution, the word NOTICE, date, a heading, the body (what, when, where, who, how) and the name and designation of the writer.
A notice is brief, factual and written in the third person or passive voice; it may be boxed.
E-mail format: To, Cc/Bcc if needed, Subject, salutation, body, closing and name.
An e-mail is slightly more personal but remains clear and to the point.
Both must include all key details: date, time, venue, and contact person.
outcomes: Write a notice of about 50 words with the correct format
Write an e-mail on the same content
Use a clear, concise and polite style

lesson.hook: How do you tell 800 pupils about a change in exam dates in fewer than 60 words?
lesson.example: A notice about a book fair gives dates, timings, venue and a contact teacher; the e-mail to parents gives the same details with a friendly opening.
lesson.activity: Pupils write a notice and an e-mail on a school cleanliness drive, then swap and check them against a checklist.

questions.q: What should a notice include?
questions.a: Institution name, NOTICE, date, heading, body and writer's name and designation.

questions.q: Give two features of the language of a notice.
questions.a: It is brief and factual (often in passive voice).

questions.q: What goes in the subject line of an e-mail?
questions.a: A short statement of what the e-mail is about.

questions.q: How is an e-mail different from a notice?
questions.a: It is addressed to specific people and is slightly more personal.

lesson.homework: Write a notice and an e-mail about an inter-house quiz competition.

topics.title: Comprehension and Summary
topics.summary: Read the passage twice: first for the general idea, then for details.
notes: Read the passage twice: first for the general idea, then for details.
Vocabulary questions ask for meanings in the context of the passage; use surrounding words as clues.
Short-answer questions should be answered in your own words, in full sentences, using only the passage.
A summary gives the main points on a stated aspect, within a given word limit.
Steps: underline relevant points, note them briefly, join them into a paragraph using your own words, and count words.
Avoid examples, repetition and personal opinion in a summary.
outcomes: Read an unseen passage of about 500 words and answer vocabulary and short-answer questions
Find the meanings of words from context
Write a summary within a word limit

lesson.hook: How can you understand a word you have never seen before without a dictionary?
lesson.example: In "The drought had left the earth parched and cracked", "parched" can be guessed as "very dry" from "drought" and "cracked".
lesson.activity: Pupils read a short passage (written by the teacher), guess the meanings of five words from context and then check.

questions.q: How long is the unseen passage in the examination?
questions.a: About 500 words.

questions.q: How should vocabulary questions be answered?
questions.a: By giving the meaning of the word as used in the passage.

questions.q: Give two things to avoid in a summary.
questions.a: Examples and personal opinions (also repetition).

questions.q: What should you do after writing a summary?
questions.a: Check that it covers the main points and stays within the word limit.

lesson.homework: Summarise a newspaper article of your choice in about 60 words.

topics.title: Grammar: Prepositions, Conjunctions and Verbs
topics.summary: Prepositions show relations of time (at 5 o'clock, on Monday, in May), place (at the gate, in the room, on the table) and direction (into, towards, through).
notes: Prepositions show relations of time (at 5 o'clock, on Monday, in May), place (at the gate, in the room, on the table) and direction (into, towards, through).
Some words take fixed prepositions: fond of, good at, afraid of, agree with a person, agree to a proposal.
Conjunctions join words and clauses: coordinating (and, but, or, so) and subordinating (because, although, unless, when, if).
Verbs must agree with their subjects: "Each of the boys is present"; "The news is good".
Choose the correct tense for time and sequence: "When I reached, the train had left".
The examination tests these through fill-in-the-blanks and short answers.
outcomes: Use prepositions correctly, including prepositions of time, place and direction
Use conjunctions to join clauses and sentences
Use correct verb forms: tense, subject–verb agreement and participles

lesson.hook: Is it "angry with" or "angry at" a person?
lesson.example: "He has been working here since 2020" — use "since" with a point of time and "for" with a period of time.
lesson.activity: Pupils fill a worksheet of 20 blanks with prepositions, conjunctions and verb forms, then correct each other's work.

questions.q: Fill in: She is good ___ mathematics.
questions.a: at

questions.q: Join using "although": It was raining. We went out.
questions.a: Although it was raining, we went out.

questions.q: Correct: Neither of them are ready.
questions.a: Neither of them is ready.

questions.q: Fill in: I have lived here ___ five years.
questions.a: for

lesson.homework: Write ten sentences using ten different fixed prepositions.

topics.title: Grammar: Transforming Sentences
topics.summary: Sentence transformation means rewriting a sentence in a new structure while keeping its meaning.
notes: Sentence transformation means rewriting a sentence in a new structure while keeping its meaning.
Active to passive: "The teacher praised Ravi" becomes "Ravi was praised by the teacher".
Direct to indirect speech: "I am tired," she said becomes She said that she was tired.
Degrees of comparison: "No other boy is as tall as Arun" = "Arun is the tallest boy".
Useful patterns: too…to / so…that; no sooner…than; hardly…when; unless = if…not; as soon as.
Check tense, pronouns and punctuation after every transformation.
outcomes: Transform sentences without changing meaning
Use active and passive voice, direct and indirect speech, and degrees of comparison
Use "too…to", "so…that", "no sooner…than", "hardly…when" and "unless"

lesson.hook: Can you say the same thing in three different ways?
lesson.example: "He is too weak to walk" = "He is so weak that he cannot walk."
lesson.activity: Relay game: teams transform sentences at each station; the next pupil checks and continues.

questions.q: Change to passive: The boy broke the window.
questions.a: The window was broken by the boy.

questions.q: Rewrite using "unless": If you do not hurry, you will miss the bus.
questions.a: Unless you hurry, you will miss the bus.

questions.q: Rewrite using "no sooner": As soon as he arrived, it began to rain.
questions.a: No sooner had he arrived than it began to rain.

questions.q: Change to indirect speech: He said, "I like music."
questions.a: He said that he liked music.

lesson.homework: Transform ten sentences from a newspaper using at least four different patterns.

courses.title: English: Treasure Chest: Stories and Poems (Class 10), Class 10

topics.title: With the Photographer
topics.summary: The narrator goes to a photographer for a portrait and has to wait a long time while the photographer reads a magazine.
notes: The narrator goes to a photographer for a portrait and has to wait a long time while the photographer reads a magazine.
The photographer treats his face as a problem: he criticises the narrator's features, turns his head this way and that, and tells him to change his expression.
When the proofs arrive a week later, the photographer has "retouched" the picture: features have been removed or changed.
The narrator is angry because the portrait no longer shows his real face; he wanted to be seen as he is.
Leacock uses exaggeration and comic dialogue to satirise photographers who care more for their art than for the customer.
Underneath the humour is a point about self-respect: people want to be accepted as they are.
outcomes: Narrate Stephen Leacock's "With the Photographer"
Identify the humour and satire in the photographer's behaviour
Discuss vanity, identity and honest self-image

lesson.hook: Would you be happy with a photograph of yourself that looked nothing like you?
lesson.example: The photographer's professional talk makes simple acts sound grand, while he insults his customer — comic contrast.
lesson.activity: Pupils act out the studio scene with a "photographer" and a "customer", using their own words.

questions.q: Why did the narrator go to the photographer?
questions.a: To have his portrait taken.

questions.q: How did the photographer treat him?
questions.a: Rudely; he criticised his features and kept changing his pose.

questions.q: Why was the narrator angry with the final photograph?
questions.a: It had been retouched so much that it no longer looked like him.

questions.q: What does Leacock satirise?
questions.a: Photographers who value their idea of art over the customer's real face.

lesson.homework: Write about how filters on social media relate to the ideas in this story.

topics.title: The Elevator
topics.summary: Martin, a thin twelve-year-old, has moved with his father into an old apartment building and must use its small, old elevator.
notes: Martin, a thin twelve-year-old, has moved with his father into an old apartment building and must use its small, old elevator.
He is afraid of the elevator, but his large, confident father makes fun of his fears, so Martin hides them.
A large, strange woman in a green coat begins to appear in the elevator, always silent, chewing gum and staring at him.
She seems to know about his fear; her presence grows more menacing each time, and no one else seems to notice her.
Suspense builds through the small space, the flickering lights, the creaking ride and her unexplained appearances.
The story ends on an unresolved, frightening note, leaving readers to decide whether she is real or born of Martin's fear.
outcomes: Narrate William Sleator's "The Elevator"
Analyse how suspense and fear are built
Discuss Martin's fear and his relationship with his father

lesson.hook: Is there anything you are afraid of that others laugh at?
lesson.example: The writer never explains who the woman is; this ambiguity makes her more frightening than any explanation could.
lesson.activity: Pupils mark three moments in the story where suspense rises and explain which details create it.

questions.q: Why is Martin afraid of the elevator?
questions.a: It is old and small, and he feels trapped and uneasy in it.

questions.q: How does his father react to his fear?
questions.a: He mocks it, so Martin hides his feelings.

questions.q: Describe the woman in the elevator.
questions.a: A large, silent woman in a green coat who chews gum and stares at Martin.

questions.q: Why is the ending effective?
questions.a: It is left unresolved, keeping the fear and mystery alive.

lesson.homework: Write a paragraph on how parents can help children face their fears.

topics.title: The Girl Who Can
topics.summary: The story is told by Adjoa, a seven-year-old girl in a village in Ghana, who lives with her mother and grandmother.
notes: The story is told by Adjoa, a seven-year-old girl in a village in Ghana, who lives with her mother and grandmother.
Her grandmother, Nana, often says Adjoa's thin legs are not good for anything important in a woman's life, reflecting traditional ideas about women's bodies.
Her mother, Maami, defends her and insists that Adjoa go to school — a quieter, modern voice.
At school Adjoa's thin but strong legs make her a fast runner; she wins races and a cup for her school.
Nana's attitude changes: she proudly takes charge of the cup and cares for it, showing new respect for her granddaughter.
Through a child's innocent voice, Aidoo challenges stereotypes and celebrates what girls can do.
outcomes: Narrate Ama Ata Aidoo's "The Girl Who Can"
Analyse the three generations of women and their attitudes
Discuss gender stereotypes and how Adjoa challenges them

lesson.hook: Who decides what a girl's body is "good for"?
lesson.example: The legs Nana thought useless are exactly what bring the family honour — the story's gentle irony.
lesson.activity: Groups list the stereotypes Nana expresses and discuss how each is disproved in the story.

questions.q: Who narrates the story?
questions.a: Adjoa, a seven-year-old girl.

questions.q: What did Nana think of Adjoa's legs?
questions.a: That they were too thin and not useful for a woman's traditional role.

questions.q: How does Adjoa prove herself?
questions.a: She becomes a fast runner and wins a cup at school.

questions.q: How does Nana change?
questions.a: She becomes proud of Adjoa and cares for the cup herself.

lesson.homework: Write about a girl or woman you admire who broke a stereotype.

topics.title: The Pedestrian
topics.summary: In a future city in 2053, Leonard Mead loves to walk alone through the silent streets at night.
notes: In a future city in 2053, Leonard Mead loves to walk alone through the silent streets at night.
Every house is dark except for the flicker of screens; people sit indoors like the dead, watching television.
In all his years of walking he has never met another person on foot.
A robot police car — the only one left in a city where crime has almost vanished — stops him and questions him; his job as a writer means nothing in a world where no one reads.
Because walking without purpose seems abnormal, he is taken away to a psychiatric centre for "regressive tendencies".
Bradbury warns of a society where technology and conformity make ordinary human curiosity look like a crime.
outcomes: Narrate Ray Bradbury's "The Pedestrian"
Analyse the setting of a future city dominated by screens
Discuss the themes of conformity, technology and loss of human connection

lesson.hook: When did you last go for a walk without a phone?
lesson.example: Mead's house is the only one with its lights on — a sign that he is the only one truly alive in the city.
lesson.activity: Pupils list three details that show the city is lifeless and suggest what each says about the society.

questions.q: What does Leonard Mead like to do?
questions.a: Walk alone through the city streets at night.

questions.q: Why is the city described like a graveyard?
questions.a: People sit in dark houses watching screens and never go out.

questions.q: Why does the police car arrest him?
questions.a: His walking alone at night without purpose seems abnormal.

questions.q: What is Bradbury warning about?
questions.a: Over-dependence on technology and loss of individuality.

lesson.homework: Write a paragraph comparing Mead's world with ours today.

topics.title: The Last Lesson
topics.summary: Franz, a schoolboy in Alsace, is late for school and has not learnt his lesson on participles; he expects to be scolded.
notes: Franz, a schoolboy in Alsace, is late for school and has not learnt his lesson on participles; he expects to be scolded.
Instead, the school is unusually quiet; the teacher, M. Hamel, is in his best clothes, and village elders sit at the back.
M. Hamel announces that orders have come from Berlin: after the war, only German is to be taught in the schools of Alsace and Lorraine; this is the last French lesson.
Franz regrets wasting time and suddenly loves his books and his teacher; M. Hamel says that people who keep their language hold the key to their freedom.
The lesson ends as church bells and the Prussian soldiers' trumpets sound; M. Hamel, too moved to speak, writes a patriotic message to France on the board.
The story is about the loss of language and identity under foreign rule and the value of what we take for granted.
outcomes: Narrate Alphonse Daudet's "The Last Lesson"
Analyse the change in Franz and M. Hamel
Discuss the importance of one's language and identity

lesson.hook: How would you feel if you were told that tomorrow you could no longer learn your own language at school?
lesson.example: Franz's change from dreading grammar to wishing he could learn more shows how we value things only when we are about to lose them.
lesson.activity: Pupils write about a word, song or saying in their home language that they would never want to lose.

questions.q: Why was Franz afraid of going to school?
questions.a: He had not learnt his lesson on participles.

questions.q: What order had come from Berlin?
questions.a: Only German was to be taught in the schools of Alsace and Lorraine.

questions.q: Why were the village elders in class?
questions.a: To show respect for M. Hamel and their language on the last French lesson.

questions.q: What does M. Hamel say about language?
questions.a: That keeping one's language is like holding the key to freedom.

lesson.homework: Write a diary entry by M. Hamel on the evening of the last lesson.

topics.title: Haunted Houses
topics.summary: The poet says that all houses in which people have lived and died are haunted.
notes: The poet says that all houses in which people have lived and died are haunted.
The "ghosts" are harmless: they move silently through doors and along stairs, a quiet presence of the past.
Guests at the table and the spirits of the past share the same rooms; the living and the dead mingle.
The poem contrasts the visible, material world with an invisible spiritual world that surrounds it.
Our lives, he suggests, are divided between the world of the body and the world of the spirit.
The tone is calm and reflective rather than frightening; the images of mist and moonlight add mystery.
outcomes: Understand Longfellow's idea that every house where people have lived is "haunted"
