ನುಡಿಗಟ್ಟುಗಳು ವಿಶೇಷ ಅರ್ಥ ನೀಡುತ್ತವೆ: "ತಲೆ ತಗ್ಗಿಸು" (ನಾಚಿಕೆ ಪಡು), "ಕಣ್ಣು ಕೆಂಪಗೆ ಮಾಡು" (ಕೋಪಗೊಳ್ಳು).
outcomes: ಸಮಾನಾರ್ಥಕ, ವಿರುದ್ಧಾರ್ಥಕ ಮತ್ತು ನಾನಾರ್ಥ ಪದಗಳನ್ನು ಬಳಸುವುದು
ತತ್ಸಮ-ತದ್ಭವ ಪದಗಳನ್ನು ಗುರುತಿಸುವುದು
ಗಾದೆ ಮತ್ತು ನುಡಿಗಟ್ಟುಗಳ ಅರ್ಥ ತಿಳಿದು ವಾಕ್ಯದಲ್ಲಿ ಬಳಸುವುದು

lesson.hook: "ಆಕಾಶ" ಮತ್ತು "ಆಗಸ" — ಎರಡೂ ಒಂದೇ ಅರ್ಥವೇ? ಹಾಗಾದರೆ ವ್ಯತ್ಯಾಸವೇನು?
lesson.example: "ತಪ್ಪು ತಿಳಿದ ಮೇಲೆ ಅವನು ತಲೆ ತಗ್ಗಿಸಿದನು" — ವಾಕ್ಯದಿಂದ ನುಡಿಗಟ್ಟಿನ ಅರ್ಥ (ನಾಚಿಕೆ ಪಡು) ಸ್ಪಷ್ಟವಾಗುತ್ತದೆ.
lesson.activity: ಪದ ಆಟ: ಒಂದು ಗುಂಪು ಪದ ಹೇಳಲಿ, ಇನ್ನೊಂದು ಸಮಾನಾರ್ಥಕ, ಮೂರನೆಯದು ವಿರುದ್ಧಾರ್ಥಕ ಹೇಳಲಿ.

questions.q: "ಸುಖ" ಪದದ ವಿರುದ್ಧಾರ್ಥಕ ಬರೆಯಿರಿ.
questions.a: ದುಃಖ.

questions.q: "ಆಕಾಶ" ಪದದ ತದ್ಭವ ಬರೆಯಿರಿ.
questions.a: ಆಗಸ.

questions.q: "ಕರ" ಪದದ ಎರಡು ಅರ್ಥಗಳನ್ನು ಬರೆಯಿರಿ.
questions.a: ಕೈ ಮತ್ತು ತೆರಿಗೆ (ಕಿರಣ ಎಂದೂ).

questions.q: "ಕೈ ಕೆಸರಾದರೆ ಬಾಯಿ ಮೊಸರು" ಗಾದೆಯ ಅರ್ಥವೇನು?
questions.a: ಕಷ್ಟಪಟ್ಟು ದುಡಿದರೆ ಫಲ ಸಿಗುತ್ತದೆ.

lesson.homework: ಹತ್ತು ನುಡಿಗಟ್ಟುಗಳ ಅರ್ಥ ಬರೆದು ವಾಕ್ಯಗಳಲ್ಲಿ ಬಳಸಿ.

topics.title: ವ್ಯಾಕರಣ: ವಾಕ್ಯ ರಚನೆ
topics.summary: ವಾಕ್ಯದಲ್ಲಿ ಕರ್ತೃವಿಗೂ ಕ್ರಿಯಾಪದಕ್ಕೂ ಲಿಂಗ-ವಚನಗಳಲ್ಲಿ ಹೊಂದಾಣಿಕೆ ಇರಬೇಕು: "ಹುಡುಗಿಯರು ಆಡುತ್ತಿದ್ದಾರೆ".
notes: ವಾಕ್ಯದಲ್ಲಿ ಕರ್ತೃವಿಗೂ ಕ್ರಿಯಾಪದಕ್ಕೂ ಲಿಂಗ-ವಚನಗಳಲ್ಲಿ ಹೊಂದಾಣಿಕೆ ಇರಬೇಕು: "ಹುಡುಗಿಯರು ಆಡುತ್ತಿದ್ದಾರೆ".
ಕಾಲಗಳು: ವರ್ತಮಾನ (ಓದುತ್ತಾನೆ), ಭೂತ (ಓದಿದನು), ಭವಿಷ್ಯತ್ (ಓದುವನು).
ವಿಭಕ್ತಿ ಪ್ರತ್ಯಯಗಳು: ಪ್ರಥಮಾ (ಉ), ದ್ವಿತೀಯಾ (ಅನ್ನು), ತೃತೀಯಾ (ಇಂದ), ಚತುರ್ಥೀ (ಗೆ, ಇಗೆ, ಕ್ಕೆ), ಪಂಚಮೀ (ದೆಸೆಯಿಂದ), ಷಷ್ಠೀ (ಅ), ಸಪ್ತಮೀ (ಅಲ್ಲಿ).
ಬಿಟ್ಟ ಸ್ಥಳ ತುಂಬುವಾಗ ವಾಕ್ಯದ ಅರ್ಥಕ್ಕೆ ತಕ್ಕ ವಿಭಕ್ತಿ ಆರಿಸಿ: "ಅವನು ಶಾಲೆ___ ಹೋದನು" — ಶಾಲೆಗೆ.
ಎರಡು ವಾಕ್ಯಗಳನ್ನು "ಮತ್ತು", "ಆದರೆ", "ಆದ್ದರಿಂದ" ಮುಂತಾದ ಪದಗಳಿಂದ ಜೋಡಿಸಬಹುದು.
ಉತ್ತರ ಬರೆದ ಮೇಲೆ ಪೂರ್ಣ ವಾಕ್ಯ ಓದಿ ಅರ್ಥ ಬದಲಾಗಿಲ್ಲ ಎಂದು ಖಚಿತಪಡಿಸಿಕೊಳ್ಳಿ.
outcomes: ವಾಕ್ಯಗಳನ್ನು ಶುದ್ಧಗೊಳಿಸುವುದು
ಲಿಂಗ, ವಚನ ಮತ್ತು ಕಾಲಗಳ ಹೊಂದಾಣಿಕೆಯನ್ನು ಸರಿಯಾಗಿ ಬಳಸುವುದು
ವಿಭಕ್ತಿ ಪ್ರತ್ಯಯಗಳನ್ನು ಸರಿಯಾಗಿ ಬಳಸಿ ವಾಕ್ಯ ರಚಿಸುವುದು

lesson.hook: "ಹುಡುಗಿಯರು ಆಟ ಆಡುತ್ತಿದ್ದಾನೆ" — ಈ ವಾಕ್ಯದಲ್ಲಿ ತಪ್ಪೇನು?
lesson.example: "ಮಳೆ ಬಂತು. ನಾವು ಆಟ ನಿಲ್ಲಿಸಿದೆವು." → "ಮಳೆ ಬಂದುದರಿಂದ ನಾವು ಆಟ ನಿಲ್ಲಿಸಿದೆವು."
lesson.activity: ಜೋಡಿಗಳಲ್ಲಿ ಹತ್ತು ಅಶುದ್ಧ ವಾಕ್ಯಗಳನ್ನು ಶುದ್ಧಗೊಳಿಸಿ, ತಪ್ಪು ಯಾವ ಬಗೆಯದು ಎಂದು ತಿಳಿಸಿ.

questions.q: ಶುದ್ಧಗೊಳಿಸಿ: ಹುಡುಗಿಯರು ಆಡುತ್ತಿದ್ದಾನೆ.
questions.a: ಹುಡುಗಿಯರು ಆಡುತ್ತಿದ್ದಾರೆ.

questions.q: ಬಿಟ್ಟ ಸ್ಥಳ ತುಂಬಿ: ಅವನು ಶಾಲೆ___ ಹೋದನು.
questions.a: ಶಾಲೆಗೆ.

questions.q: ದ್ವಿತೀಯಾ ವಿಭಕ್ತಿ ಪ್ರತ್ಯಯ ಯಾವುದು?
questions.a: ಅನ್ನು.

questions.q: ಭೂತಕಾಲಕ್ಕೆ ಬದಲಿಸಿ: ಅವನು ಪುಸ್ತಕ ಓದುತ್ತಾನೆ.
questions.a: ಅವನು ಪುಸ್ತಕ ಓದಿದನು.

lesson.homework: ಏಳು ವಿಭಕ್ತಿಗಳಿಗೆ ಒಂದೊಂದು ವಾಕ್ಯ ರಚಿಸಿ.

topics.title: ಪ್ರಬಂಧ ರಚನೆ
topics.summary: ನಿಮ್ಮಲ್ಲಿ ಹೆಚ್ಚು ವಿಚಾರಗಳು, ಉದಾಹರಣೆಗಳು ಮತ್ತು ಸ್ಪಷ್ಟ ರೂಪರೇಖೆ ಇರುವ ವಿಷಯವನ್ನೇ ಆರಿಸಿ.
notes: ನಿಮ್ಮಲ್ಲಿ ಹೆಚ್ಚು ವಿಚಾರಗಳು, ಉದಾಹರಣೆಗಳು ಮತ್ತು ಸ್ಪಷ್ಟ ರೂಪರೇಖೆ ಇರುವ ವಿಷಯವನ್ನೇ ಆರಿಸಿ.
ವಿಚಾರಾತ್ಮಕ ಪ್ರಬಂಧದಲ್ಲಿ ಸ್ಪಷ್ಟ ನಿಲುವು, ಉದಾಹರಣೆ ಸಹಿತ ಕನಿಷ್ಠ ಮೂರು ವಾದಗಳು, ವಿರೋಧ ಪಕ್ಷದ ಉಲ್ಲೇಖ ಮತ್ತು ದೃಢ ತೀರ್ಮಾನ ಇರಲಿ.
ಕತೆಯಲ್ಲಿ ಆಕರ್ಷಕ ಆರಂಭ, ತರ್ಕಬದ್ಧ ಘಟನಾಕ್ರಮ, ಹಿತಮಿತ ಸಂಭಾಷಣೆ ಮತ್ತು ಅರ್ಥಪೂರ್ಣ ಮುಕ್ತಾಯ ಇರಲಿ.
ಚಿತ್ರಾಧಾರಿತ ವಿಷಯದಲ್ಲಿ ಚಿತ್ರದೊಂದಿಗೆ ಸ್ಪಷ್ಟ ಸಂಬಂಧ ಇರಲಿ; ರೂಪ (ಕತೆ, ವರ್ಣನೆ, ಪ್ರಬಂಧ) ನಿಮ್ಮ ಆಯ್ಕೆ.
ಸಮಯ ಹಂಚಿಕೆ: ಐದು ನಿಮಿಷ ರೂಪರೇಖೆ, ಇಪ್ಪತ್ತೈದು ನಿಮಿಷ ಬರವಣಿಗೆ, ಐದು ನಿಮಿಷ ಪರಿಷ್ಕರಣೆ.
ವಿಷಯಕ್ಕೆ ಹೊಂದಿಕೆ, ಕ್ರಮಬದ್ಧತೆ, ಭಾಷಾ ಶುದ್ಧಿ ಮತ್ತು ಸ್ವಂತಿಕೆಗೆ ಅಂಕಗಳು — ಉದ್ದಕ್ಕಲ್ಲ.
outcomes: ಬೋರ್ಡ್ ಪರೀಕ್ಷೆಗೆ ತಕ್ಕ ಪ್ರಬಂಧ ವಿಷಯ ಆರಿಸುವುದು
ವಿಚಾರಾತ್ಮಕ, ವರ್ಣನಾತ್ಮಕ ಮತ್ತು ಕಥನಾತ್ಮಕ ರಚನೆಗಳನ್ನು ಸಮತೋಲನದಿಂದ ಬರೆಯುವುದು
ಸಮಯದ ಮಿತಿಯಲ್ಲಿ ಬರೆದು ಪರಿಷ್ಕರಿಸುವುದು

lesson.hook: ಐದು ವಿಷಯಗಳಲ್ಲಿ ಯಾವುದನ್ನು ಆರಿಸಬೇಕು — ಸುಲಭವೆನಿಸುವುದನ್ನೋ, ಹೆಚ್ಚು ವಿಚಾರಗಳಿರುವುದನ್ನೋ?
lesson.example: "ಮೊಬೈಲ್ ಫೋನ್: ವರವೋ ಶಾಪವೋ" — ಪೀಠಿಕೆ, ಮೂರು ಲಾಭಗಳು, ಮೂರು ಹಾನಿಗಳು, ಸಮತೋಲಿತ ತೀರ್ಮಾನ.
lesson.activity: ಶಿಕ್ಷಕರು ನೀಡಿದ ತಪ್ಪುಗಳಿರುವ ಪ್ರಬಂಧದಲ್ಲಿ ಹದಿನೈದು ತಪ್ಪುಗಳನ್ನು ಗುರುತಿಸಿ ಸರಿಪಡಿಸಿ.

questions.q: ಪ್ರಬಂಧದ ವಿಷಯ ಆರಿಸುವುದು ಹೇಗೆ?
questions.a: ಹೆಚ್ಚು ವಿಚಾರಗಳು, ಉದಾಹರಣೆಗಳು ಮತ್ತು ಸ್ಪಷ್ಟ ರೂಪರೇಖೆ ಇರುವ ವಿಷಯವನ್ನು.

questions.q: ವಿಚಾರಾತ್ಮಕ ಪ್ರಬಂಧದಲ್ಲಿ ಏನೇನಿರಬೇಕು?
questions.a: ಸ್ಪಷ್ಟ ನಿಲುವು, ಉದಾಹರಣೆ ಸಹಿತ ವಾದಗಳು, ವಿರೋಧ ಪಕ್ಷ ಮತ್ತು ತೀರ್ಮಾನ.

questions.q: ಸಮಯವನ್ನು ಹೇಗೆ ಹಂಚಬೇಕು?
questions.a: ಸುಮಾರು ಐದು ನಿಮಿಷ ರೂಪರೇಖೆ, ಇಪ್ಪತ್ತೈದು ನಿಮಿಷ ಬರವಣಿಗೆ, ಐದು ನಿಮಿಷ ಪರಿಷ್ಕರಣೆ.

questions.q: ಅಂಕಗಳು ಯಾವುದಕ್ಕೆ ಸಿಗುತ್ತವೆ?
questions.a: ವಿಷಯ ಹೊಂದಿಕೆ, ಕ್ರಮಬದ್ಧತೆ, ಭಾಷಾ ಶುದ್ಧಿ ಮತ್ತು ಸ್ವಂತಿಕೆಗೆ.

lesson.homework: "ಪರೀಕ್ಷೆಯೇ ಸಾಮರ್ಥ್ಯದ ನಿಜವಾದ ಅಳತೆ" ವಿಷಯದ ಪರ ಅಥವಾ ವಿರೋಧವಾಗಿ ಪ್ರಬಂಧ ಬರೆಯಿರಿ.

topics.title: ಪತ್ರ ಲೇಖನ
topics.summary: ಸಂಪಾದಕರಿಗೆ ಬರೆಯುವ ಪತ್ರದಲ್ಲಿ ಸಾರ್ವಜನಿಕ ಸಮಸ್ಯೆ, ಅದರ ಪರಿಣಾಮ ಮತ್ತು ಸಲಹೆಗಳು ಇರುತ್ತವೆ.
notes: ಸಂಪಾದಕರಿಗೆ ಬರೆಯುವ ಪತ್ರದಲ್ಲಿ ಸಾರ್ವಜನಿಕ ಸಮಸ್ಯೆ, ಅದರ ಪರಿಣಾಮ ಮತ್ತು ಸಲಹೆಗಳು ಇರುತ್ತವೆ.
ದೂರು ಪತ್ರದಲ್ಲಿ ಸಮಸ್ಯೆಯ ಸ್ಪಷ್ಟ ವಿವರ (ಸ್ಥಳ, ಸಮಯ), ಅದರಿಂದಾಗುವ ತೊಂದರೆ ಮತ್ತು ನಿರ್ದಿಷ್ಟ ಕ್ರಮಕ್ಕಾಗಿ ಮನವಿ ಇರಲಿ.
ಅರ್ಜಿಯಲ್ಲಿ ಉದ್ದೇಶ ಮೊದಲ ಪರಿಚ್ಛೇದದಲ್ಲೇ ಇರಲಿ; ಅಗತ್ಯ ವಿವರಗಳು ಸಂಕ್ಷಿಪ್ತವಾಗಿರಲಿ.
ಖಾಸಗಿ ಪತ್ರಗಳಲ್ಲಿ ಅಭಿನಂದನೆ, ಸಾಂತ್ವನ, ಸಲಹೆ ಅಥವಾ ಅನುಭವ ಹಂಚಿಕೆ ಇರಬಹುದು; ಭಾವ ಪ್ರಾಮಾಣಿಕವಾಗಿರಲಿ.
ನಮೂನೆ: ಇಂದ, ಗೆ, ಸ್ಥಳ-ದಿನಾಂಕ, ವಿಷಯ, ಸಂಬೋಧನೆ, ಒಡಲು, ಮುಕ್ತಾಯ, ಹೆಸರು — ಸರಿಯಾದ ಕ್ರಮದಲ್ಲಿ.
ವ್ಯಾವಹಾರಿಕ ಪತ್ರದ ಧ್ವನಿ ವಿನಯಪೂರ್ಣ ಆದರೆ ದೃಢವಾಗಿರಲಿ; ಅನಗತ್ಯ ವಿಷಯಗಳು ಬೇಡ.
outcomes: ದೂರು ಪತ್ರ, ಮನವಿ ಪತ್ರ, ಅರ್ಜಿ ಮತ್ತು ಸಂಪಾದಕರಿಗೆ ಪತ್ರ ಬರೆಯುವುದು
ಖಾಸಗಿ ಪತ್ರಗಳಲ್ಲಿ ಸೂಕ್ತ ಭಾವ ಮತ್ತು ಶೈಲಿ ಬಳಸುವುದು
ಬೋರ್ಡ್ ಪರೀಕ್ಷೆಯ ನಮೂನೆಯನ್ನು ಸರಿಯಾಗಿ ಪಾಲಿಸುವುದು

lesson.hook: ಯಾವ ರೀತಿಯ ದೂರು ಪತ್ರ ನಿಜವಾಗಿಯೂ ಫಲ ನೀಡುತ್ತದೆ?
lesson.example: ಸಂಪಾದಕರಿಗೆ ಪತ್ರ: ರಾತ್ರಿ ತಡವಾಗಿ ಧ್ವನಿವರ್ಧಕದ ಶಬ್ದದಿಂದ ವಿದ್ಯಾರ್ಥಿಗಳಿಗೆ ಮತ್ತು ರೋಗಿಗಳಿಗೆ ತೊಂದರೆ, ಸಮಯ ಮಿತಿ ಜಾರಿಗೆ ತರುವ ಸಲಹೆ.
lesson.activity: ಇಪ್ಪತ್ತು ನಿಮಿಷಗಳಲ್ಲಿ ಒಂದು ವ್ಯಾವಹಾರಿಕ ಪತ್ರ ಬರೆದು, ಸಹಪಾಠಿಯ ಪತ್ರವನ್ನು ಪರಿಶೀಲನಾ ಪಟ್ಟಿಯಿಂದ ಪರೀಕ್ಷಿಸಿ.

questions.q: ಸಂಪಾದಕರಿಗೆ ಪತ್ರದಲ್ಲಿ ಏನೇನಿರಬೇಕು?
questions.a: ಸಮಸ್ಯೆ, ಅದರ ಪರಿಣಾಮ ಮತ್ತು ಸಲಹೆಗಳು.

questions.q: ದೂರು ಪತ್ರವನ್ನು ಪರಿಣಾಮಕಾರಿಯಾಗಿಸುವುದು ಹೇಗೆ?
questions.a: ಸ್ಪಷ್ಟ ವಿವರ, ತೊಂದರೆ ಮತ್ತು ನಿರ್ದಿಷ್ಟ ಕ್ರಮಕ್ಕಾಗಿ ಮನವಿಯಿಂದ.

questions.q: ಸಾಂತ್ವನ ಪತ್ರದ ಭಾಷೆ ಹೇಗಿರಬೇಕು?
questions.a: ಸಹಾನುಭೂತಿಯುಳ್ಳ, ಪ್ರಾಮಾಣಿಕ ಮತ್ತು ಸರಳ.

questions.q: ವ್ಯಾವಹಾರಿಕ ಪತ್ರದ ಧ್ವನಿ ಹೇಗಿರಬೇಕು?
questions.a: ವಿನಯಪೂರ್ಣ ಆದರೆ ದೃಢ.

lesson.homework: ನಿಮ್ಮ ಊರಿನಲ್ಲಿ ಸಾರ್ವಜನಿಕ ಗ್ರಂಥಾಲಯ ತೆರೆಯುವಂತೆ ಸಲಹೆ ನೀಡಿ ಸಂಪಾದಕರಿಗೆ ಪತ್ರ ಬರೆಯಿರಿ.

topics.title: ಅಪರಿಚಿತ ಗದ್ಯಭಾಗ
topics.summary: ಪ್ರಶ್ನೆಗಳು ಮೂರು ಬಗೆ: ನೇರ ಮಾಹಿತಿ, ಆಶಯ/ತೀರ್ಮಾನ, ಮತ್ತು ಪದಾರ್ಥ.
notes: ಪ್ರಶ್ನೆಗಳು ಮೂರು ಬಗೆ: ನೇರ ಮಾಹಿತಿ, ಆಶಯ/ತೀರ್ಮಾನ, ಮತ್ತು ಪದಾರ್ಥ.
ಆಶಯದ ಪ್ರಶ್ನೆಗಳಲ್ಲಿ ಲೇಖಕರು ನೇರವಾಗಿ ಹೇಳದ ವಿಚಾರವನ್ನು ಅರಿಯಬೇಕು; ಉತ್ತರವನ್ನು ಗದ್ಯಭಾಗದ ಆಧಾರದೊಂದಿಗೆ ಜೋಡಿಸಿ.
ಉತ್ತರಗಳು ಸಂಕ್ಷಿಪ್ತ ಮತ್ತು ನಿಖರವಾಗಿರಲಿ; ಇಡೀ ಪರಿಚ್ಛೇದ ನಕಲು ಮಾಡಿದರೆ ಅಂಕ ಹೆಚ್ಚುವುದಿಲ್ಲ.
ಪದಗಳ ಅರ್ಥವನ್ನು ಗದ್ಯಭಾಗದಲ್ಲಿ ಅವು ಬಳಕೆಯಾದ ಸಂದರ್ಭಕ್ಕೆ ತಕ್ಕಂತೆ ಕೊಡಿ.
ಸಾಮಾನ್ಯ ತಪ್ಪುಗಳು: ಪ್ರಶ್ನೆ ಪೂರ್ತಿ ಓದದಿರುವುದು, ಸ್ವಂತ ಅಭಿಪ್ರಾಯ ಸೇರಿಸುವುದು, ವಾಕ್ಯ ನಕಲು ಮಾಡುವುದು.
ಕೊನೆಯಲ್ಲಿ ಎಲ್ಲ ಉತ್ತರಗಳನ್ನು ಗದ್ಯಭಾಗದೊಂದಿಗೆ ಹೋಲಿಸಿ ನೋಡಿ.
outcomes: ಬೋರ್ಡ್ ಮಟ್ಟದ ಅಪರಿಚಿತ ಗದ್ಯಭಾಗದ ಪ್ರಶ್ನೆಗಳಿಗೆ ನಿಖರ ಉತ್ತರ ಬರೆಯುವುದು
ಆಶಯ ಮತ್ತು ತೀರ್ಮಾನದ ಪ್ರಶ್ನೆಗಳನ್ನು ಅರಿಯುವುದು
ಸ್ವಂತ ಮಾತಿನಲ್ಲಿ ಸಂಕ್ಷಿಪ್ತ ಉತ್ತರ ಬರೆಯುವುದು

lesson.hook: ಚೆನ್ನಾಗಿ ಓದುವವರೂ ಗದ್ಯಭಾಗದಲ್ಲಿ ಅಂಕ ಕಳೆದುಕೊಳ್ಳುವುದೇಕೆ?
lesson.example: ಪ್ರಶ್ನೆ: "ಲೇಖಕರು ವಿಜ್ಞಾನವನ್ನು ಎರಡು ಅಲಗಿನ ಕತ್ತಿ ಎಂದು ಏಕೆ ಕರೆದಿದ್ದಾರೆ?" — ಉತ್ತರ: ಗದ್ಯಭಾಗದ ಪ್ರಕಾರ ವಿಜ್ಞಾನದಿಂದ ಲಾಭವೂ ಇದೆ, ದುರುಪಯೋಗದಿಂದ ಹಾನಿಯೂ ಇದೆ.
lesson.activity: ಒಂದು ಗದ್ಯಭಾಗದ ಮೇಲೆ ಮೂರು ಬಗೆಯ ತಲಾ ಒಂದು ಪ್ರಶ್ನೆ ರಚಿಸಿ ಸಹಪಾಠಿಯಿಂದ ಉತ್ತರಿಸಿ.

questions.q: ಗದ್ಯಭಾಗದ ಪ್ರಶ್ನೆಗಳ ಮೂರು ಬಗೆಗಳು ಯಾವುವು?
questions.a: ನೇರ ಮಾಹಿತಿ, ಆಶಯ/ತೀರ್ಮಾನ ಮತ್ತು ಪದಾರ್ಥ.

questions.q: ಆಶಯದ ಪ್ರಶ್ನೆಗೆ ಹೇಗೆ ಉತ್ತರಿಸಬೇಕು?
questions.a: ಲೇಖಕರ ಹೇಳದ ಭಾವವನ್ನು ಗದ್ಯಭಾಗದ ಆಧಾರದೊಂದಿಗೆ ಜೋಡಿಸಿ.

questions.q: ಎರಡು ಸಾಮಾನ್ಯ ತಪ್ಪುಗಳನ್ನು ತಿಳಿಸಿ.
questions.a: ಸ್ವಂತ ಅಭಿಪ್ರಾಯ ಸೇರಿಸುವುದು ಮತ್ತು ವಾಕ್ಯ ನಕಲು ಮಾಡುವುದು.

questions.q: ಪದಾರ್ಥವನ್ನು ಯಾವ ಆಧಾರದಲ್ಲಿ ಬರೆಯಬೇಕು?
questions.a: ಗದ್ಯಭಾಗದಲ್ಲಿ ಆ ಪದ ಬಳಕೆಯಾದ ಸಂದರ್ಭಕ್ಕೆ ತಕ್ಕಂತೆ.

lesson.homework: ಒಂದು ಸಂಪಾದಕೀಯ ಓದಿ ಅದರ ಮುಖ್ಯ ವಿಚಾರವನ್ನು ಮೂರು ವಾಕ್ಯಗಳಲ್ಲಿ ಬರೆಯಿರಿ.

topics.title: ವ್ಯಾಕರಣ: ಪದ ಸಂಪತ್ತು
topics.summary: ಕನ್ನಡ ಸಂಧಿಗಳು: ಲೋಪ (ಊರು + ಅಲ್ಲಿ = ಊರಲ್ಲಿ), ಆಗಮ (ಮನೆ + ಅನ್ನು = ಮನೆಯನ್ನು; ಗುರು + ಅನ್ನು = ಗುರುವನ್ನು), ಆದೇಶ (ಮಳೆ + ಕಾಲ = ಮಳೆಗಾಲ).
notes: ಕನ್ನಡ ಸಂಧಿಗಳು: ಲೋಪ (ಊರು + ಅಲ್ಲಿ = ಊರಲ್ಲಿ), ಆಗಮ (ಮನೆ + ಅನ್ನು = ಮನೆಯನ್ನು; ಗುರು + ಅನ್ನು = ಗುರುವನ್ನು), ಆದೇಶ (ಮಳೆ + ಕಾಲ = ಮಳೆಗಾಲ).
ಸಂಸ್ಕೃತ ಸಂಧಿಗಳು: ಸವರ್ಣದೀರ್ಘ (ದೇವ + ಆಲಯ = ದೇವಾಲಯ), ಗುಣ (ದೇವ + ಇಂದ್ರ = ದೇವೇಂದ್ರ), ವೃದ್ಧಿ (ಏಕ + ಏಕ = ಏಕೈಕ), ಯಣ್ (ಅತಿ + ಅಂತ = ಅತ್ಯಂತ).
ಸಮಾಸ ಎಂದರೆ ಎರಡು ಅಥವಾ ಹೆಚ್ಚು ಪದಗಳು ಸೇರಿ ಒಂದು ಪದವಾಗುವುದು; ಬಿಡಿಸಿ ಬರೆಯುವುದೇ ವಿಗ್ರಹ ವಾಕ್ಯ.
ತತ್ಪುರುಷ (ತಲೆಯ + ನೋವು = ತಲೆನೋವು), ಕರ್ಮಧಾರಯ (ಕೆಂಪು + ತಾವರೆ = ಕೆಂದಾವರೆ), ದ್ವಿಗು (ಎರಡು + ಬಗೆ = ಇಬ್ಬಗೆ), ದ್ವಂದ್ವ (ಗಿಡವೂ + ಮರವೂ = ಗಿಡಮರಗಳು).
ಬಹುವ್ರೀಹಿ: ಸಮಾಸ ಪದ ಬೇರೊಂದು ವಸ್ತುವನ್ನು ಸೂಚಿಸುತ್ತದೆ — ಚಕ್ರವನ್ನು ಪಾಣಿಯಲ್ಲಿ ಉಳ್ಳವನು ಯಾರೋ ಅವನು = ಚಕ್ರಪಾಣಿ (ವಿಷ್ಣು).
ಗಾದೆ ಮತ್ತು ನುಡಿಗಟ್ಟುಗಳನ್ನು ಅರ್ಥ ಸ್ಪಷ್ಟವಾಗುವ ವಾಕ್ಯದಲ್ಲಿ ಬಳಸಿ; ಕಾಗುಣಿತದ ಬಗ್ಗೆ ವಿಶೇಷ ಗಮನ ಕೊಡಿ.
outcomes: ಸಂಧಿಗಳನ್ನು ಗುರುತಿಸಿ ಬಿಡಿಸುವುದು: ಲೋಪ, ಆಗಮ, ಆದೇಶ ಮತ್ತು ಸಂಸ್ಕೃತ ಸಂಧಿಗಳು
ಸಮಾಸಗಳನ್ನು ಗುರುತಿಸಿ ವಿಗ್ರಹ ವಾಕ್ಯ ಬರೆಯುವುದು
ಗಾದೆ ಮತ್ತು ನುಡಿಗಟ್ಟುಗಳನ್ನು ನಿಖರವಾಗಿ ಬಳಸುವುದು

lesson.hook: "ಮಳೆ + ಕಾಲ" ಸೇರಿದಾಗ "ಮಳೆಕಾಲ" ಏಕೆ ಆಗುವುದಿಲ್ಲ, "ಮಳೆಗಾಲ" ಏಕೆ ಆಗುತ್ತದೆ?
lesson.example: "ದೇವಾಲಯ" = ದೇವ + ಆಲಯ: ಅ + ಆ ಸೇರಿ ದೀರ್ಘ "ಆ" ಆಯಿತು — ಇದು ಸವರ್ಣದೀರ್ಘ ಸಂಧಿ.
lesson.activity: ಹತ್ತು ಪದಗಳನ್ನು ಕೊಟ್ಟು, ಗುಂಪುಗಳು ಅವುಗಳ ಸಂಧಿ ಅಥವಾ ಸಮಾಸ ಗುರುತಿಸಿ ಬಿಡಿಸಲಿ.

questions.q: ಸಂಧಿ ಬಿಡಿಸಿ ಹೆಸರಿಸಿ: ಮಳೆಗಾಲ.
questions.a: ಮಳೆ + ಕಾಲ — ಆದೇಶ ಸಂಧಿ.

questions.q: ಸಂಧಿ ಬಿಡಿಸಿ ಹೆಸರಿಸಿ: ದೇವೇಂದ್ರ.
questions.a: ದೇವ + ಇಂದ್ರ — ಗುಣ ಸಂಧಿ.

questions.q: ವಿಗ್ರಹ ವಾಕ್ಯ ಬರೆದು ಸಮಾಸ ಹೆಸರಿಸಿ: ತಲೆನೋವು.
questions.a: ತಲೆಯ + ನೋವು — ತತ್ಪುರುಷ ಸಮಾಸ.

questions.q: ಬಹುವ್ರೀಹಿ ಸಮಾಸಕ್ಕೆ ಒಂದು ಉದಾಹರಣೆ ಕೊಡಿ.
questions.a: ಚಕ್ರಪಾಣಿ — ಚಕ್ರವನ್ನು ಪಾಣಿಯಲ್ಲಿ ಉಳ್ಳವನು ಯಾರೋ ಅವನು.

lesson.homework: ಪ್ರತಿ ಸಂಧಿ ಮತ್ತು ಸಮಾಸಕ್ಕೆ ಎರಡೆರಡು ಉದಾಹರಣೆಗಳನ್ನು ಬರೆಯಿರಿ.

topics.title: ವ್ಯಾಕರಣ: ವಾಕ್ಯ ರಚನೆ
topics.summary: ಸಾಮಾನ್ಯ ವಾಕ್ಯ: ಒಂದೇ ಕ್ರಿಯಾಪದ — "ಮಳೆ ಬಂದುದರಿಂದ ಆಟ ನಿಂತಿತು."
notes: ಸಾಮಾನ್ಯ ವಾಕ್ಯ: ಒಂದೇ ಕ್ರಿಯಾಪದ — "ಮಳೆ ಬಂದುದರಿಂದ ಆಟ ನಿಂತಿತು."
ಸಂಯೋಜಿತ ವಾಕ್ಯ: ಎರಡು ಸ್ವತಂತ್ರ ವಾಕ್ಯಗಳು "ಮತ್ತು, ಆದರೆ, ಆದ್ದರಿಂದ" ಮೂಲಕ — "ಮಳೆ ಬಂತು, ಆದ್ದರಿಂದ ಆಟ ನಿಂತಿತು."
ಮಿಶ್ರ ವಾಕ್ಯ: ಒಂದು ಪ್ರಧಾನ ಮತ್ತು ಒಂದು ಅಧೀನ ವಾಕ್ಯ — "ಯಾವಾಗ ಮಳೆ ಬಂತೋ ಆಗ ಆಟ ನಿಂತಿತು."
ಪ್ರಶ್ನಾರ್ಥಕ, ನಿಷೇಧಾರ್ಥಕ, ಆಶ್ಚರ್ಯಾರ್ಥಕ ರೂಪಗಳು: "ಇದು ತುಂಬಾ ಸುಂದರವಾಗಿದೆ" → "ಎಷ್ಟು ಸುಂದರವಾಗಿದೆ!"
ಕರ್ತರಿ-ಕರ್ಮಣಿ ಪ್ರಯೋಗ: "ರಾಮನು ಪತ್ರ ಬರೆದನು" → "ರಾಮನಿಂದ ಪತ್ರ ಬರೆಯಲ್ಪಟ್ಟಿತು."
ಪ್ರತಿ ಬದಲಾವಣೆಯ ನಂತರ ಲಿಂಗ, ವಚನ, ಕಾಲ ಮತ್ತು ವಿರಾಮ ಚಿಹ್ನೆಗಳನ್ನು ಪರಿಶೀಲಿಸಿ.
outcomes: ಸಾಮಾನ್ಯ, ಸಂಯೋಜಿತ ಮತ್ತು ಮಿಶ್ರ ವಾಕ್ಯಗಳನ್ನು ರಚಿಸುವುದು ಮತ್ತು ಬದಲಿಸುವುದು
ಕಾಲ, ಪ್ರಯೋಗ ಮತ್ತು ವಾಕ್ಯ ಪ್ರಕಾರಗಳನ್ನು ಸೂಚನೆಯಂತೆ ಬದಲಿಸುವುದು
ಕೊಟ್ಟ ಪದಗಳನ್ನು ಬಳಸಿ ಶುದ್ಧ ವಾಕ್ಯ ರಚಿಸುವುದು

lesson.hook: ಒಂದೇ ವಿಷಯವನ್ನು ಎಷ್ಟು ರೀತಿಯಲ್ಲಿ ಹೇಳಬಹುದು?
lesson.example: "ಗಂಟೆ ಬಾರಿಸಿತು. ಮಕ್ಕಳು ಹೊರಗೆ ಓಡಿದರು." → "ಗಂಟೆ ಬಾರಿಸಿದ ಕೂಡಲೇ ಮಕ್ಕಳು ಹೊರಗೆ ಓಡಿದರು."
lesson.activity: ರಿಲೇ ಆಟ: ಪ್ರತಿ ಗುಂಪಿಗೆ ಒಂದು ವಾಕ್ಯ; ಪ್ರತಿ ಸದಸ್ಯ ಹೊಸ ಸೂಚನೆಯಂತೆ ಅದನ್ನು ಬದಲಿಸಲಿ.

questions.q: ಸಂಯೋಜಿತ ವಾಕ್ಯವಾಗಿಸಿ: ಮಳೆ ಬಂತು. ಆಟ ನಿಂತಿತು.
questions.a: ಮಳೆ ಬಂತು, ಆದ್ದರಿಂದ ಆಟ ನಿಂತಿತು.

questions.q: ಕರ್ಮಣಿ ಪ್ರಯೋಗಕ್ಕೆ ಬದಲಿಸಿ: ರಾಮನು ಪತ್ರ ಬರೆದನು.
questions.a: ರಾಮನಿಂದ ಪತ್ರ ಬರೆಯಲ್ಪಟ್ಟಿತು.

questions.q: ಆಶ್ಚರ್ಯಾರ್ಥಕ ವಾಕ್ಯವಾಗಿಸಿ: ಈ ದೃಶ್ಯ ತುಂಬಾ ಸುಂದರವಾಗಿದೆ.
questions.a: ಎಷ್ಟು ಸುಂದರವಾದ ದೃಶ್ಯ!

questions.q: ಮಿಶ್ರ ವಾಕ್ಯ ಎಂದರೇನು?
questions.a: ಒಂದು ಪ್ರಧಾನ ವಾಕ್ಯ ಮತ್ತು ಒಂದು ಅಧೀನ ವಾಕ್ಯ ಸೇರಿದ ವಾಕ್ಯ.

lesson.homework: ಹದಿನೈದು ವಾಕ್ಯ ಬದಲಾವಣೆಯ ನಿಯಮಗಳನ್ನು ಉದಾಹರಣೆ ಸಹಿತ ಬರೆಯಿರಿ.

topics.title: The Skeletal System
topics.summary: Major bones: cranium and vertebrae (neck); scapula and clavicle (shoulder); ribs and sternum (thorax); humerus, radius, ulna, carpals, metacarpals, phalanges (fore limb); pelvis (hip); femur, patella, tibia, fibula, tarsals, metatarsals, phalanges (hind limb).
notes: Major bones: cranium and vertebrae (neck); scapula and clavicle (shoulder); ribs and sternum (thorax); humerus, radius, ulna, carpals, metacarpals, phalanges (fore limb); pelvis (hip); femur, patella, tibia, fibula, tarsals, metatarsals, phalanges (hind limb).
Functions: framework and support, movement (with muscles), protection of vital organs, mineral storage, and blood cell production in the marrow.
Joints: fixed/fibrous (skull sutures), slightly movable/cartilaginous (between vertebrae), freely movable/synovial (shoulder, hip, knee, elbow, wrist, ankle).

Hinge joints (knee, elbow) allow flexion and extension; pivot joints (neck) allow rotation; ball-and-socket joints (shoulder, hip) allow flexion, extension, abduction, adduction and rotation; saddle joints (thumb) also allow circumduction.
Exercise makes bones stronger and denser, strengthens joints, improves flexibility and posture, and supports a healthy lifestyle.
Weight-bearing activities such as running and skipping are especially good for bone strength.
outcomes: Identify the major bones of the neck, shoulder, thorax, limbs, spine and hip
State the functions of the skeletal system
Classify joints and describe joint movements, and explain how exercise benefits bones

lesson.hook: Why can you rotate your shoulder in a full circle but only bend your knee one way?
lesson.example: Bowling in cricket uses the ball-and-socket shoulder joint through a wide circle, while the elbow (a hinge) must stay straight.
lesson.activity: Pupils point to and name bones on a partner, then perform one movement at each type of joint and name it.

questions.q: Name the bones of the fore limb.
questions.a: Humerus, radius, ulna, carpals, metacarpals and phalanges.

questions.q: Give three functions of the skeleton.
questions.a: Support, protection of organs and movement (also mineral storage, blood cell production).

questions.q: Which movements does a hinge joint allow?
questions.a: Flexion and extension.

questions.q: Give one example of a ball-and-socket joint.
questions.a: The shoulder (or hip).

lesson.homework: Draw and label a skeleton showing ten bones and three joint types.

topics.title: The Muscular System
topics.summary: Voluntary (skeletal) muscles move bones under our control; involuntary (smooth) muscles work in organs like the stomach; cardiac muscle is found only in the heart and never tires.
notes: Voluntary (skeletal) muscles move bones under our control; involuntary (smooth) muscles work in organs like the stomach; cardiac muscle is found only in the heart and never tires.
Isotonic contraction changes muscle length and moves a joint (a bicep curl); isometric contraction produces force without movement (holding a plank).
Key muscles: latissimus dorsi, deltoid, rotator cuff, pectorals, biceps, triceps, abdominals, hip flexors, gluteals, hamstrings, quadriceps, gastrocnemius, tibialis anterior.
Muscles work in pairs: when the biceps contracts to bend the elbow, the triceps relaxes.
Exercise increases strength, endurance and power, improves neuromuscular coordination and posture, enhances flexibility and reduces injuries.
Warming up prepares muscles; stretching after exercise helps them recover.
outcomes: Distinguish voluntary, involuntary and cardiac muscles, and isometric and isotonic contraction
Identify major muscles used in sport
State the benefits of exercise on the muscular system

lesson.hook: Which muscles do you use to kick a football, and which ones keep your heart beating?
lesson.example: In a football kick the quadriceps straightens the knee while the hamstrings relax, then the hamstrings slow the leg down.
lesson.activity: Pupils perform a squat (isotonic) and a wall-sit (isometric) and name the muscles they feel working.

questions.q: Where is cardiac muscle found?
questions.a: Only in the heart.

questions.q: Distinguish isotonic and isometric contraction.
questions.a: Isotonic changes muscle length and moves a joint; isometric produces force without movement.

questions.q: Which muscle straightens the knee?
questions.a: The quadriceps.

questions.q: Give two benefits of exercise on muscles.
questions.a: More strength and endurance (also better posture, flexibility).

lesson.homework: List the muscles used in three sports you play.

topics.title: The Respiratory System
topics.summary: Air passes through the nose or mouth, pharynx, larynx, trachea, bronchi and bronchioles to the alveoli in the lungs; the diaphragm helps breathing.
notes: Air passes through the nose or mouth, pharynx, larynx, trachea, bronchi and bronchioles to the alveoli in the lungs; the diaphragm helps breathing.
External respiration: breathing in oxygen and out carbon dioxide, with gases diffusing across the thin walls of the alveoli; internal respiration: cells use oxygen to release energy.
Oxygen debt: the extra oxygen needed after hard exercise to remove lactic acid that built up when muscles worked without enough oxygen.
Second wind: a sudden feeling of relief during long exercise when breathing and energy settle down.
Tidal volume is the air breathed in or out in one normal breath; vital capacity is the most air that can be breathed out after the deepest breath in.
Exercise increases tidal volume, strengthens respiratory muscles, improves aerobic endurance and speeds recovery.
outcomes: Trace the pathway of air into the body
Explain external and internal respiration and the terms oxygen debt, second wind, vital capacity and tidal volume
State the benefits of exercise on the respiratory system

lesson.hook: Why do you keep breathing hard for a few minutes after a sprint?
lesson.example: After a 400 m race, heavy breathing repays the oxygen debt and clears lactic acid from the muscles.
lesson.activity: Pupils count breaths per minute at rest and after one minute of skipping, and record recovery time.

questions.q: Name the path of air from the nose to the alveoli.
questions.a: Nose, pharynx, larynx, trachea, bronchi, bronchioles, alveoli.

questions.q: What is oxygen debt?
questions.a: Extra oxygen needed after hard exercise to remove lactic acid.

questions.q: Distinguish tidal volume and vital capacity.
questions.a: Tidal volume is one normal breath; vital capacity is the maximum air breathed out after the deepest breath.

questions.q: Give two benefits of exercise on breathing.
questions.a: Stronger breathing muscles and better aerobic endurance.

lesson.homework: Explain second wind in your own words with an example.

topics.title: The Circulatory System
topics.summary: The heart has two atria (receiving chambers) and two ventricles (pumping chambers); arteries carry blood away from the heart, veins carry it back, and capillaries connect them.
notes: The heart has two atria (receiving chambers) and two ventricles (pumping chambers); arteries carry blood away from the heart, veins carry it back, and capillaries connect them.
Heart rate is beats per minute; stroke volume is blood pumped per beat; cardiac output = heart rate × stroke volume.
Double circulation: the right side pumps blood to the lungs to collect oxygen; the left side pumps oxygen-rich blood to the body.
Blood contains plasma, red blood cells (carry oxygen with haemoglobin), white blood cells (fight infection) and platelets (clotting).

Blood groups A, B, AB and O with Rh factor: O negative can be given to all groups (universal donor), AB positive can receive from all (universal recipient); systolic pressure is during a heartbeat, diastolic between beats.
Regular exercise strengthens and enlarges the heart, lowers resting pulse, raises haemoglobin, reduces heart disease and speeds recovery after activity.
outcomes: Describe the structure of the heart and blood vessels
Explain heart rate, stroke volume, cardiac output and blood circulation
Describe the composition of blood, blood groups, haemoglobin and blood pressure, and the benefits of exercise

lesson.hook: How much blood does your heart pump in one minute during a match?
lesson.example: If heart rate is 70 beats per minute and stroke volume is 70 mL, cardiac output is about 4.9 litres per minute.
lesson.activity: Pupils take their pulse at rest, after jogging and after two minutes of rest, and plot a recovery graph.

questions.q: What is cardiac output?
questions.a: Heart rate multiplied by stroke volume — blood pumped per minute.

questions.q: What does haemoglobin do?
questions.a: It carries oxygen in red blood cells.

questions.q: Which blood group is the universal donor?
questions.a: O negative.

questions.q: How does exercise affect resting pulse?
questions.a: It lowers the resting pulse.

lesson.homework: Draw and label the heart showing its four chambers.

chapters.title: Games and Sports: Psychological and Social Benefits

topics.title: Games and Sports: Psychological and Social Benefits
topics.summary: Games are organised play with rules, often played in teams for enjoyment (hide-and-seek, kabaddi); sports are competitive physical activities with formal rules and governing bodies (athletics, cricket).
notes: Games are organised play with rules, often played in teams for enjoyment (hide-and-seek, kabaddi); sports are competitive physical activities with formal rules and governing bodies (athletics, cricket).
Psychological benefits: confidence, emotional control, competitive spirit, positive attitude, self-esteem, patience and resilience.
Learning to accept winning and losing with grace builds maturity.
Social benefits: cooperation, teamwork, camaraderie, respect for authority and rules, leadership and fair play.
Sport teaches time management by balancing practice with study.
Sportsmanship means respecting opponents, officials and rules, win or lose.
outcomes: Distinguish games and sports
Explain the psychological benefits of games and sports
Explain their social benefits such as teamwork and sportsmanship

lesson.hook: Besides fitness, what has playing in a team taught you?
lesson.example: A captain who shakes hands with the other team after a loss and thanks the umpires shows sportsmanship.
lesson.activity: Pupils share a moment from a game when they learned patience, teamwork or fair play.

questions.q: Distinguish games and sports.
questions.a: Games are organised play for enjoyment; sports are competitive with formal rules and governing bodies.

questions.q: Give three psychological benefits of sport.
questions.a: Confidence, emotional control and resilience.

questions.q: Give three social benefits of sport.
questions.a: Teamwork, leadership and respect for rules.

questions.q: What is sportsmanship?
questions.a: Respecting opponents, officials and rules whether you win or lose.

lesson.homework: Write about a sportsperson you admire for sportsmanship.

topics.title: Cricket
topics.summary: The pitch is 22 yards (20.12 m) long and 10 ft (3.05 m) wide; stumps are 28 in (71.1 cm) high and the wicket is 9 in (22.86 cm) wide.
notes: The pitch is 22 yards (20.12 m) long and 10 ft (3.05 m) wide; stumps are 28 in (71.1 cm) high and the wicket is 9 in (22.86 cm) wide.
The ball weighs 155.9–163 g with a circumference of 22.4–22.9 cm; the bat is at most 38 in (96.5 cm) long and 4.25 in (10.8 cm) wide.
Each side has eleven players; formats are Test (five days), first-class (four days), One Day (50 overs) and T20 (20 overs).
Officials: two on-field umpires, a third umpire, a match referee and two scorers.
Ways of getting out include bowled, caught, leg before wicket, run out, stumped, hit wicket, handled the ball (now obstructing the field), timed out and hit the ball twice.
Skills: batting (on drive, off drive, square cut, leg glance), bowling (in-swing, out-swing, yorker), fielding (catching, long barrier, throwing) and wicket-keeping (footwork, catching, diving).
outcomes: Describe the cricket field, pitch, ball, bat, stumps and players
Explain types of matches, officials and ways of getting out
Describe fundamental batting, bowling, fielding and wicket-keeping skills

lesson.hook: How many ways can a batter be out in cricket?
lesson.example: A yorker pitches at the batter's feet near the crease, making it very hard to hit.
lesson.activity: On the field, pupils practise the long barrier and the forward defensive stroke in pairs.

questions.q: What is the length of a cricket pitch?
Name four ways of getting out.
questions.a: Bowled, caught, LBW and run out.

questions.q: Name the officials in an international match.
questions.a: Two on-field umpires, a third umpire, a match referee and two scorers.

questions.q: What is a yorker?
questions.a: A ball that pitches at the batter's feet near the crease.

lesson.homework: Draw the cricket pitch with its measurements.

topics.title: Football
topics.summary: A team has eleven players including a goalkeeper; a match has two halves of 45 minutes.
notes: A team has eleven players including a goalkeeper; a match has two halves of 45 minutes.
The field is 90–120 m long and 45–90 m wide (international matches 100–110 × 64–75 m); the goal is 7.32 m wide and 2.44 m high.
The penalty spot is 11 m from goal and the penalty area extends 16.5 m; a size-5 ball has a circumference of 68–70 cm.
A player is offside if, when the ball is played to them, they are in the opponents' half and nearer the goal line than both the ball and the second-last opponent.
Fouls lead to direct or indirect free kicks, or a penalty inside the penalty area; yellow cards warn and red cards send a player off.
Skills: passing (short, long, through pass), dribbling, shooting, heading, tackling and goalkeeping.
outcomes: Describe the football field, ball, players and equipment
Explain the main laws: duration, offside, fouls, free kicks and penalties
Describe fundamental skills: passing, dribbling, shooting, heading and goalkeeping

lesson.hook: Why is offside one of the most debated rules in football?
lesson.example: A through pass slips the ball between defenders into space for a teammate running onto it — timing avoids offside.
lesson.activity: Pupils practise inside-foot passing and dribbling through cones, then play a small-sided game.

questions.q: How long is a football match?
questions.a: Two halves of 45 minutes.

questions.q: How far is the penalty spot from goal?
When is a player offside?
questions.a: When nearer the opponents' goal line than both the ball and the second-last opponent as the ball is played to them (in the opponents' half).

questions.q: Name three football skills.
questions.a: Passing, dribbling and shooting.

lesson.homework: Draw a football field and mark its main areas.

topics.title: Hockey
topics.summary: Each team has eleven players; the field is 91.4 m × 55 m; a match has four quarters of 15 minutes.
notes: Each team has eleven players; the field is 91.4 m × 55 m; a match has four quarters of 15 minutes.
Goals are 3.66 m wide and 2.14 m high; the shooting circle extends 14.63 m from the goal.
A goal counts only if the ball is played by an attacker inside the circle.
A penalty corner is given for certain defensive fouls inside the circle; a penalty stroke is a free shot from 6.4 m for a foul that prevents a probable goal.
The ball may be played only with the flat side of the stick; dangerous play is penalised.
Skills: push, hit, flick, scoop, dribble (including the Indian dribble), stopping/trapping, and tackling.
outcomes: Describe the hockey field, ball, stick and players
Explain main rules: duration, shooting circle, penalty corner and penalty stroke
Describe fundamental skills: push, hit, flick, dribble, stopping and tackling

lesson.hook: Why must a goal in hockey be scored from inside the circle?
lesson.example: In a penalty corner, the ball is pushed from the back line to attackers at the top of the circle, who stop it and shoot.
lesson.activity: Pupils practise the push pass and trapping in pairs, then an Indian dribble through cones.

questions.q: How long is a hockey match?
questions.a: Four quarters of 15 minutes.

questions.q: How wide is a hockey goal?
When is a goal valid?
questions.a: When an attacker plays the ball inside the shooting circle.

questions.q: What is a penalty stroke?
questions.a: A free shot from 6.4 m for a foul that prevented a probable goal.

lesson.homework: Draw a hockey field showing the shooting circle and centre line.

topics.title: Basketball
topics.summary: Each team has five players on court; the court is 28 m × 15 m and the ring is 3.05 m high.
notes: Each team has five players on court; the court is 28 m × 15 m and the ring is 3.05 m high.
FIBA matches have four quarters of 10 minutes; a size-7 ball has a circumference of 74.9–78 cm.
Baskets score 2 points, 3 points from beyond the 6.75 m line, and 1 point for a free throw.
Time rules: 24-second shot clock, 8 seconds to cross into the front court, 3 seconds maximum in the opponents' restricted area, 5 seconds to pass when closely guarded.
Violations include travelling and double dribble; personal fouls give free throws or possession, and a player leaves after five fouls.
Skills: dribbling, chest and bounce passes, lay-up and jump shot, rebounding and man-to-man or zone defence.
outcomes: Describe the basketball court, ball and players
Explain main rules: scoring, violations, fouls and time rules
Describe fundamental skills: dribbling, passing, shooting, rebounding and defence

lesson.hook: Why does a basketball team have only 24 seconds to shoot?
lesson.example: A lay-up is a two-step approach and a one-handed shot off the backboard, the highest-percentage shot near the basket.
lesson.activity: Pupils practise chest and bounce passes, then lay-ups from both sides.

questions.q: How high is the basketball ring?
How many points is a shot from beyond the arc?
questions.a: Three points.

questions.q: What is travelling?
questions.a: Moving with the ball without dribbling (taking too many steps).

questions.q: What is the 24-second rule?
questions.a: A team must attempt a shot within 24 seconds of gaining possession.

lesson.homework: Draw a basketball court with the three-point line and restricted area.

topics.title: Volleyball
topics.summary: Six players per side; the court is 18 m × 9 m; the net is 2.43 m high for men and 2.24 m for women.
notes: Six players per side; the court is 18 m × 9 m; the net is 2.43 m high for men and 2.24 m for women.
Rally-point scoring: sets are played to 25 points (the fifth set to 15) with a 2-point lead; a match is best of five sets.
A team may touch the ball three times before sending it over (a block does not count); one player cannot touch it twice in a row.
Teams rotate clockwise when they win back the right to serve.
The libero is a defensive specialist in a different-coloured shirt who cannot serve, spike above net height or block.
Skills: underarm and overarm serve, dig (forearm pass), set (overhead pass), spike (attack) and block.
outcomes: Describe the volleyball court, net, ball and players
Explain the main rules: rally scoring, rotation, three touches and the libero
Describe fundamental skills: serve, dig, set, spike and block

lesson.hook: Why does a volleyball team rotate after winning back the serve?
lesson.example: The classic attack is dig–set–spike: the dig controls the serve, the setter places the ball, the spiker hits it down.
lesson.activity: Pupils practise the forearm dig and overhead set against a wall, then in pairs.

questions.q: How many players does a volleyball team have on court?
questions.a: Six.

questions.q: To how many points is a set played?
questions.a: 25 (the fifth set to 15), winning by 2.

questions.q: How many touches may a team make?
questions.a: Three (a block does not count).

questions.q: What is a libero?
questions.a: A defensive specialist who cannot serve, attack above net height or block.

lesson.homework: Draw a volleyball court and mark the positions of the six players.

topics.title: Badminton
topics.summary: The court is 13.40 m long; 6.10 m wide for doubles and 5.18 m for singles.
notes: The court is 13.40 m long; 6.10 m wide for doubles and 5.18 m for singles.
The net is 1.524 m high at the centre and 1.55 m at the posts.
Rally-point scoring: a game is to 21 points with a 2-point lead (capped at 30); a match is best of three games.
The serve must be hit below the waist with the racket shaft pointing downward, diagonally into the opponent's service court.
A shuttle has 16 feathers and weighs 4.74–5.50 g; its feathers create drag, which slows it sharply.
Strokes: short and long serve, overhead clear, drop shot, smash, net shot and drive; footwork brings the player back to the centre.
outcomes: Describe the badminton court, net, shuttle and racket
Explain the rules of scoring, service and faults
Describe fundamental strokes: serve, clear, drop, smash and net shot

lesson.hook: Why does a shuttlecock slow down so quickly after a hard smash?
lesson.example: A clear sends the opponent to the back of the court; a drop shot then pulls them to the net.
lesson.activity: Pupils practise the high serve and overhead clear, then a clear–drop sequence with a partner.

questions.q: What is the length of a badminton court?
To how many points is a game played?
questions.a: 21, with a 2-point lead (up to 30).

questions.q: How must the serve be hit?
questions.a: Below the waist, diagonally into the opponent's service court.

questions.q: Name three badminton strokes.
questions.a: Clear, drop shot and smash.

lesson.homework: Draw a badminton court showing singles and doubles lines.

topics.title: Human Growth and Development
topics.summary: Growth is an increase in size (height, weight); development is the improvement of skills and abilities — physical, mental, emotional and social.
notes: Growth is an increase in size (height, weight); development is the improvement of skills and abilities — physical, mental, emotional and social.
Stages: infancy (0–5 years), childhood (5–12), adolescence (12–19) and adulthood (19–65 and above).
Adolescence brings rapid growth spurts, puberty and emotional changes, so activity and diet needs rise.
Factors: heredity, environment, gender, nationality (including climate and culture) and nutrition.
Physical activity supports healthy growth, bone strength, coordination and self-confidence.
Every child develops at a different pace; comparisons should be kind and fair.
outcomes: Distinguish growth and development
Describe the stages of human growth and development
Explain the factors that influence growth and development

lesson.hook: Why do some classmates grow taller earlier than others?
lesson.example: Two twins with the same genes may differ in height if one has poorer nutrition — environment matters as well as heredity.
lesson.activity: Pupils list physical, mental and social changes they have noticed between Class 5 and now.

questions.q: Distinguish growth and development.
questions.a: Growth is increase in size; development is improvement in skills and abilities.

questions.q: What is the age range of adolescence?
questions.a: 12 to 19 years.

questions.q: Name three factors affecting growth.
questions.a: Heredity, environment and nutrition.

questions.q: Why is physical activity important during growth?
questions.a: It supports healthy bones, coordination and confidence.

lesson.homework: Write how nutrition and exercise together affect growth in adolescence.

topics.title: Physical Education and Body Types
topics.summary: Physical education is education through physical activity to develop the whole person.
notes: Physical education is education through physical activity to develop the whole person.
Objectives: physical development (fitness, skills), psychological development (confidence, concentration), social development (teamwork, leadership) and emotional development (control, resilience).
Endomorph: rounder body, stores fat easily, often strong — suits activities like weightlifting or shot put.
Mesomorph: muscular, broad shoulders, narrow waist — suits sprinting, gymnastics and many team games.
Ectomorph: slim, long limbs, light frame — suits long-distance running and high jump.
Most people are a mix of types; training and interest matter more than body type alone.
outcomes: Explain the meaning and objectives of physical education
Describe the three body types
Relate body types to sports

lesson.hook: Is physical education only about playing games?
lesson.example: Many marathon runners are ectomorphs: light bodies carry less weight over long distances.
lesson.activity: Pupils match ten sports to the body type that suits them best and discuss exceptions.

questions.q: What is physical education?
questions.a: Education through physical activity to develop the whole person.

questions.q: Name the four objectives of physical education.
questions.a: Physical, psychological, social and emotional development.

questions.q: Describe a mesomorph.
questions.a: Muscular, with broad shoulders and a narrow waist.

questions.q: Which body type suits long-distance running?
questions.a: Ectomorph.

lesson.homework: Write how physical education helps social development.

topics.title: Physical Fitness
topics.summary: Physical fitness is the ability to carry out daily tasks with energy and without undue tiredness, with reserve for emergencies and leisure.
notes: Physical fitness is the ability to carry out daily tasks with energy and without undue tiredness, with reserve for emergencies and leisure.
Components: cardiovascular endurance, stamina, strength, flexibility, power, speed, coordination, agility, balance and accuracy.
Power combines strength and speed (a long jump take-off); agility is changing direction quickly (a badminton player).
Factors: heredity, nutrition, environment, training facilities and methods, illness, self-motivation, emotional stability, lifestyle and posture.
Fitness reduces the risk of disease, improves mood and concentration, and helps performance in study and sport.
Simple tests: shuttle run (agility), sit-and-reach (flexibility), 600 m run (endurance).
outcomes: Explain the meaning and importance of physical fitness
Describe the components of physical fitness
Explain the factors that affect fitness

lesson.hook: Can someone be strong but not fit?
lesson.example: A goalkeeper needs agility to change direction, power to jump, and coordination to catch — several components at once.
lesson.activity: Pupils do a shuttle run and sit-and-reach test, record results, and set one personal target.

questions.q: What is physical fitness?
questions.a: The ability to do daily tasks with energy, without undue tiredness, with reserve for emergencies.

questions.q: What is agility?
questions.a: The ability to change direction quickly and in control.

questions.q: Name four components of fitness.
questions.a: Endurance, strength, flexibility and speed.

questions.q: Give three factors that affect fitness.
questions.a: Nutrition, training and lifestyle.

lesson.homework: Plan a one-week routine to improve two fitness components.

topics.title: Sports Training
topics.summary: Sports training is a systematic process of preparing a sportsperson for better performance through planned exercise.
notes: Sports training is a systematic process of preparing a sportsperson for better performance through planned exercise.
It builds strength and endurance, improves skills and knowledge, motivation and confidence, speeds recovery and makes the body more resistant to injury.
Overload: work harder than usual; progression: increase load gradually; adaptation: the body adjusts to demands.
Specificity: train for the needs of your sport; individuality: plans suit each person; recovery: rest allows adaptation; reversibility: fitness is lost when training stops.
Other principles: variance (vary exercises), frequency, continuity, intensity, active participation and periodisation (dividing the year into phases).
A good plan balances hard days, easy days and rest.
outcomes: Explain the meaning and importance of sports training
Describe the principles of sports training
Apply the principles to a simple training plan

lesson.hook: Why does lifting the same weight every day stop making you stronger?
lesson.example: A sprinter who stops training for two months loses speed and power — reversibility.
lesson.activity: Pupils design a four-week plan for a school athlete, labelling which principle each week applies.

questions.q: What is sports training?
questions.a: A systematic process of preparing a sportsperson for better performance.

questions.q: Explain the principle of overload.
questions.a: The body must work harder than usual to improve.

questions.q: What is reversibility?
questions.a: Fitness gains are lost when training stops.

questions.q: What is periodisation?
questions.a: Dividing the training year into phases with different goals.

lesson.homework: Explain three principles of training with examples from your sport.

topics.title: Safety in Sports
topics.summary: Common injuries: muscle strain, sprained ankle, torn ligaments (ACL, MCL), shin splints, stress fracture, fracture, plantar fasciitis, tennis elbow, low back pain, hip bursitis, concussion, Achilles tendonitis and runner's knee.
notes: Common injuries: muscle strain, sprained ankle, torn ligaments (ACL, MCL), shin splints, stress fracture, fracture, plantar fasciitis, tennis elbow, low back pain, hip bursitis, concussion, Achilles tendonitis and runner's knee.
For strains and sprains, first aid is rest, ice (wrapped, for short periods), compression and elevation, and avoiding further play.
A suspected fracture should be kept still and supported; get medical help — do not try to straighten it.
Any blow to the head with dizziness, confusion or headache may be a concussion: the player must stop and be checked by a doctor before returning.
Prevention: warm-up and cool-down, fitness, correct and well-maintained equipment, knowing the rules, protective gear, rest between workouts, supervision, correct technique and safe facilities.
Pain that does not improve, swelling, numbness or inability to bear weight needs a doctor.
outcomes: Describe common sports injuries and their first aid
Explain how injuries can be prevented
Recognise when an injury needs medical attention

lesson.hook: What should you do in the first minutes after twisting your ankle?
lesson.example: A player who "rolls" an ankle stops, rests, applies a wrapped ice pack, compresses and raises the leg, and sees a doctor if they cannot walk.
lesson.activity: Pupils role-play the first-aid steps for a sprained ankle and list the warning signs of concussion.

questions.q: What are the first-aid steps for a sprain?
questions.a: Rest, ice, compression and elevation.

questions.q: What should be done for a suspected fracture?
questions.a: Keep it still and supported and get medical help.

questions.q: Why must a player with a suspected concussion stop playing?
questions.a: A further blow can be dangerous; a doctor must check them first.

questions.q: Give three ways to prevent injuries.
questions.a: Warm up, use correct equipment and wear protective gear.

lesson.homework: Make a poster on preventing sports injuries in your school.

topics.title: Health Education and Nutrition
topics.summary: Health is complete physical, mental and social well-being, not merely the absence of disease; health education builds habits that protect it.
notes: Health is complete physical, mental and social well-being, not merely the absence of disease; health education builds habits that protect it.
A balanced diet contains carbohydrates (energy), proteins (growth and repair), fats (stored energy), vitamins and minerals (protection and body functions), water and fibre, in the right amounts.
Malnutrition includes undernutrition (too little food or nutrients) and overnutrition (too much, leading to obesity).
Sportspersons need more calories, carbohydrates for energy, proteins for muscle repair, fluids and salts (such as sodium) to replace sweat.
Before activity: a light, carbohydrate-rich meal 2–3 hours earlier; during long activity: water; after: carbohydrates and protein to recover.
Avoid heavy, oily food just before exercise, and drink water regularly.
outcomes: Explain health and the importance of health education
Describe the constituents of a balanced diet and malnutrition
Explain dietary needs of sportspersons and plan meals for activity

lesson.hook: What should you eat before a football match — and what should you avoid?
lesson.example: A pre-match meal of idli with sambar or a banana with curd gives energy without heaviness.
lesson.activity: Pupils plan a one-day menu for a school athlete on match day and check it against the balanced-diet list.

questions.q: What is health?
questions.a: Complete physical, mental and social well-being, not merely absence of disease.

questions.q: What is the role of proteins?
questions.a: Growth and repair of body tissues.

questions.q: Why do sportspersons need extra fluids and salts?
questions.a: To replace what is lost in sweat.

questions.q: What should be eaten before activity?
questions.a: A light, carbohydrate-rich meal two to three hours earlier.

lesson.homework: Make a sample menu for a day of training with reasons for each meal.

topics.title: Careers in Physical Education
topics.summary: Coach: trains athletes and teams; needs knowledge of the sport, teaching skill and coaching certification.
notes: Coach: trains athletes and teams; needs knowledge of the sport, teaching skill and coaching certification.
Physical education teacher: teaches fitness and sports in schools; needs a degree in physical education.
Professional sportsperson: competes at a high level; needs talent, years of training and discipline.
Sports management: organises events, leagues and athletes' careers.
Commentators describe and analyse matches; officials (umpires, referees) apply rules fairly and need certification.
Other options include sports medicine, physiotherapy, fitness training, nutrition and sports journalism.
outcomes: Describe career options in physical education and sport
Identify the skills and qualifications each career needs
Relate careers to personal interests

lesson.hook: Can you make a career in sport without being a professional player?
lesson.example: A cricket fan with good communication skills may become a commentator or a certified umpire.
lesson.activity: Pupils interview the school PE teacher or coach about their career path and share the answers.

questions.q: What does a coach do?
questions.a: Trains athletes and teams to improve performance.

questions.q: What qualification does a PE teacher need?
questions.a: A degree in physical education.

questions.q: Name two careers other than playing.
questions.a: Sports management and commentary (also coaching, officiating).

questions.q: What do officials need?
questions.a: Knowledge of the rules, fairness and certification.

lesson.homework: Write about a sports career you would like and the steps to reach it.

topics.title: Cricket: Skills, Terms and Tournaments
topics.summary: Review: 22-yard pitch, eleven players, formats (Test, first-class, ODI, T20), officials and ways of getting out.
notes: Review: 22-yard pitch, eleven players, formats (Test, first-class, ODI, T20), officials and ways of getting out.

Batting shots: cover drive, straight drive, pull, hook, sweep, reverse sweep, late cut; bowling: in-swing, out-swing, off-cutter, leg-cutter, reverse swing.

Use cricket terminology correctly
Name national and international governing bodies and tournaments

lesson.hook: What is the difference between a maiden over and a dot ball?

topics.title: Football: Skills, Terms and Tournaments
topics.summary: Review: eleven players, two 45-minute halves, pitch and goal sizes, offside, free kicks, penalties, cards.
notes: Review: eleven players, two 45-minute halves, pitch and goal sizes, offside, free kicks, penalties, cards.

Use football terminology correctly

topics.title: Hockey: Skills, Terms and Tournaments
topics.summary: Review: eleven players, 91.4 × 55 m field, four 15-minute quarters, shooting circle, penalty corner and stroke.
notes: Review: eleven players, 91.4 × 55 m field, four 15-minute quarters, shooting circle, penalty corner and stroke.

questions.a: A quick attack before the defence is set.

topics.title: Volleyball: Skills, Terms and Tournaments
topics.summary: Review: six players, 18 × 9 m court, net height, rally scoring to 25, three touches, rotation and libero.
notes: Review: six players, 18 × 9 m court, net height, rally scoring to 25, three touches, rotation and libero.

topics.title: Commercial Activities
topics.summary: Commercial activities are done to earn money (a shopkeeper selling goods); non-commercial activities are done out of love, duty or social service (cooking for family, volunteering).
notes: Commercial activities are done to earn money (a shopkeeper selling goods); non-commercial activities are done out of love, duty or social service (cooking for family, volunteering).

Business: producing or buying and selling goods and services for profit, with risk; profession: specialised services by qualified people for a fee (doctor, lawyer); employment: working for others for a salary or wage.
Industry produces goods: primary (extraction — farming, mining, fishing), secondary (manufacturing and construction) and tertiary (services that support them).
Commerce includes trade and aids to trade that remove hindrances between producers and consumers.
Trade: wholesale and retail, domestic and foreign, and e-commerce/e-trade; aids to trade: transport, banking, advertising, insurance, warehousing and packaging.
Non-profit organisations (charities, clubs, trusts) serve members or society rather than earning profit.
outcomes: Distinguish commercial and non-commercial activities
Explain business, profession and employment
Classify business activities into industry and commerce, and commerce into trade and aids to trade

lesson.hook: Your mother cooks at home and a caterer cooks for a wedding. Which one is a commercial activity?
lesson.example: A farmer grows cotton (primary industry), a mill makes cloth (secondary), trucks and banks help it reach shops (aids to trade), and a shop sells it (trade).
lesson.activity: Pupils classify twenty activities from their neighbourhood as business, profession, employment or non-commercial.

questions.q: Distinguish business and profession.
questions.a: Business earns profit from goods or services with risk; a profession gives specialised services for a fee by qualified people.

questions.q: Give two examples of primary industry.
questions.a: Farming and mining (also fishing).

questions.q: Name four aids to trade.
questions.a: Transport, banking, insurance and warehousing (also advertising, packaging).

questions.q: Give an example of a non-profit organisation.
questions.a: A charitable trust or a sports club.

lesson.homework: Draw a chart classifying commerce into trade and aids to trade with examples.

topics.title: Commercial Organisations
topics.summary: Sole proprietorship: owned and run by one person, who keeps all profit and bears unlimited liability.
notes: Sole proprietorship: owned and run by one person, who keeps all profit and bears unlimited liability.
Partnership: two or more people share capital, profit and management under a partnership deed.
One-person company: a company with a single member and limited liability; LLP: a partnership with limited liability of partners.
Joint stock company: a separate legal entity owned by shareholders, managed by directors, with limited liability.
Cooperative society: formed by members for mutual benefit on the principle of "one member, one vote".

Public sector: departmental undertakings (Indian Railways), public corporations set up by an Act (LIC) and government companies (at least 51% government-owned); joint sector: owned jointly by government and private business.
outcomes: Describe private sector enterprises: sole proprietorship, partnership, one-person company, joint stock company, LLP and cooperative society
Describe public sector enterprises
Explain joint sector enterprises

lesson.hook: Who owns Indian Railways, and who owns the tea shop outside school?
lesson.example: A milk cooperative collects milk from member farmers and shares the profit among them.
lesson.activity: Groups pick a business in town and decide which form of organisation suits it best, with reasons.

questions.q: What is unlimited liability?
questions.a: The owner's personal assets can be used to pay business debts.

questions.q: Give two features of a joint stock company.
questions.a: Separate legal entity and limited liability.

questions.q: What principle does a cooperative follow?
questions.a: One member, one vote.

questions.q: Give an example of a departmental undertaking.
questions.a: Indian Railways (or India Post).

lesson.homework: Compare a sole proprietorship and a joint stock company in a table.

topics.title: Departments of a Commercial Organisation
topics.summary: Production: turns inputs into goods or services efficiently, at the right quality, quantity and cost.
notes: Production: turns inputs into goods or services efficiently, at the right quality, quantity and cost.
Marketing and sales: finds out what customers want, promotes products and sells them to earn revenue.
Finance and accounting: raises and manages money, keeps records and prepares accounts.
Human resources: recruits, trains, pays and looks after employees.
Departments depend on each other — sales forecasts guide production, finance funds production, HR supplies people.
Clear communication and coordination between departments make an organisation effective.
outcomes: Explain the meaning and objectives of the production department
Explain marketing and sales, finance and accounting, and human resources departments
Show how departments work together

lesson.hook: Who in a company decides how many biscuits to make, how to sell them, and who to hire?
lesson.example: If marketing expects festival demand for sweets, production increases output, finance arranges funds and HR hires temporary staff.
lesson.activity: Pupils role-play a meeting of four department heads planning a new product launch.

questions.q: What is the objective of the production department?
questions.a: To produce goods efficiently at the right quality, quantity and cost.

questions.q: What does the HR department do?
questions.a: Recruits, trains, pays and looks after employees.

questions.q: What does the finance department do?
questions.a: Raises and manages funds and keeps accounts.

questions.q: Why must departments coordinate?
questions.a: Because each depends on the others to meet the organisation's goals.

lesson.homework: Draw a chart of a company's departments and their objectives.

topics.title: Communication in Commercial Organisations
topics.summary: Communication is the exchange of information and ideas between a sender and a receiver.
notes: Communication is the exchange of information and ideas between a sender and a receiver.
Process: sender → encoding → message → channel → decoding → receiver → feedback.
It helps in planning, coordination, decision-making, motivation and customer relations.
Methods: letters (formal, recorded), e-mail (quick, can reach many), audio and video conference calls (meetings across places) and social media (reaching customers widely).
The method depends on urgency, formality, cost and need for a record.
Barriers include language, noise, poor listening and unclear messages.
outcomes: Explain the meaning and process of communication
Describe the role of communication in a commercial organisation
Describe methods: letter, e-mail, conference calls and social media

lesson.hook: How would a company tell 500 employees about a new holiday in one hour?
lesson.example: A company uses a video call to discuss sales with branch managers in five cities without travel costs.
lesson.activity: Pupils send the same message by note, e-mail and a spoken chain, and compare speed and accuracy.

questions.q: What is communication?
questions.a: The exchange of information between a sender and a receiver.

questions.q: Name the steps of the communication process.
questions.a: Sender, encoding, message, channel, decoding, receiver and feedback.

questions.q: Give one advantage of e-mail.
questions.a: It is quick and can reach many people at once.

questions.q: How do companies use social media?
questions.a: To communicate with customers widely and quickly.

lesson.homework: Write when a company should use a letter instead of an e-mail.

topics.title: Accounting: Meaning, Terms and Principles
topics.summary: Bookkeeping records transactions; accounting classifies, summarises, analyses and interprets them.
notes: Bookkeeping records transactions; accounting classifies, summarises, analyses and interprets them.
Accounting cycle: transactions → journal → ledger → trial balance → final accounts.
Terms: capital (owner's investment), liability (amount owed), asset (what the business owns), revenue, expense, purchases, sales, stock, debtors, creditors, drawings, debit, credit and discount.
Principles: business entity (owner and business are separate), money measurement, going concern, accounting period, dual aspect, matching and full disclosure.
Dual aspect gives the accounting equation: Assets = Liabilities + Capital.
Accounts help owners know profit or loss and the financial position.
outcomes: Explain accounting and bookkeeping and the accounting cycle
Define basic accounting terms
Explain basic accounting principles and the accounting equation

lesson.hook: If a shopkeeper starts with ₹50,000 and borrows ₹20,000, how much does the shop own in total?
lesson.example: Capital ₹50,000 + loan ₹20,000 = assets ₹70,000 (Assets = Liabilities + Capital).
lesson.activity: Pupils record the effect of six transactions on assets, liabilities and capital in a table.

questions.q: Distinguish bookkeeping and accounting.
questions.a: Bookkeeping records transactions; accounting classifies, summarises and interprets them.

questions.q: State the accounting equation.
questions.a: Assets = Liabilities + Capital.

questions.q: What is the business entity principle?
questions.a: The business and its owner are treated as separate.

questions.q: What are drawings?
questions.a: Money or goods taken by the owner for personal use.

lesson.homework: Explain five accounting terms with examples.

topics.title: Journal, Ledger and Trial Balance
topics.summary: The journal is the book of original entry: date, particulars, ledger folio, debit and credit amounts, with a narration.
notes: The journal is the book of original entry: date, particulars, ledger folio, debit and credit amounts, with a narration.

Traditional rules: personal accounts — debit the receiver, credit the giver; real accounts — debit what comes in, credit what goes out; nominal accounts — debit expenses and losses, credit incomes and gains.
Example: goods purchased for cash ₹5,000 — Purchases A/c Dr, To Cash A/c.
The ledger groups entries by account; each account is posted and balanced (balance c/d and b/d).
A trial balance lists all ledger balances; total debits should equal total credits.
A trial balance that agrees shows arithmetical accuracy, though some errors can still exist.
outcomes: Classify accounts and apply rules of debit and credit
Record transactions in a journal
Post to the ledger, balance accounts and prepare a trial balance

lesson.hook: How does an accountant check that every transaction was recorded correctly?
lesson.example: Rent paid ₹2,000: Rent A/c Dr ₹2,000, To Cash A/c ₹2,000 (nominal: debit expenses; real: credit what goes out).
lesson.activity: Pupils journalise five simple transactions, post them to ledgers and prepare a trial balance.

questions.q: What is a journal?
questions.a: The book of original entry where transactions are first recorded.

questions.q: State the rule for nominal accounts.
questions.a: Debit all expenses and losses; credit all incomes and gains.

questions.q: Journalise: goods purchased for cash ₹5,000.
questions.a: Purchases A/c Dr ₹5,000, To Cash A/c ₹5,000.

questions.q: What does a trial balance show?
questions.a: Whether total debit balances equal total credit balances.

lesson.homework: Journalise, post and prepare a trial balance for five given transactions.

topics.title: Commercial Banks
topics.summary: Commercial banks accept deposits, give loans and advances, and provide agency and utility services.
notes: Commercial banks accept deposits, give loans and advances, and provide agency and utility services.
Savings account: for individuals to save; limited withdrawals; earns interest.
Current account: for businesses with many transactions; no or low interest; overdraft facility possible.
Recurring deposit: a fixed amount deposited every month for a fixed period, with interest.
Fixed deposit: a lump sum kept for a fixed period at a higher interest rate; early withdrawal may attract a penalty.
Banks also offer cheques, drafts, lockers, ATMs and digital banking.
outcomes: Explain the functions of commercial banks
Describe savings, current, recurring and fixed deposit accounts
Choose a suitable account for different needs

lesson.hook: Which bank account suits a shopkeeper who deposits and withdraws many times a day?
lesson.example: A salaried person saving ₹2,000 every month for a trip may open a recurring deposit.
lesson.activity: Pupils match five customers (student, shopkeeper, retired person…) to the most suitable account.

questions.q: Give two functions of commercial banks.
questions.a: Accepting deposits and giving loans.

questions.q: Which account suits a business with many transactions?
questions.a: A current account.

questions.q: Distinguish a recurring and a fixed deposit.
questions.a: Recurring: fixed amount every month; fixed: a lump sum for a fixed period.

questions.q: Which account usually earns the highest interest?
questions.a: A fixed deposit.

lesson.homework: Compare the four types of bank accounts in a table.

topics.title: E-commerce and E-trade
topics.summary: E-commerce is buying and selling goods and services over the internet; e-trade includes online trading of goods, services and securities.
notes: E-commerce is buying and selling goods and services over the internet; e-trade includes online trading of goods, services and securities.
Merits: available 24×7, wide choice, price comparison, home delivery, lower costs for sellers and reach to distant customers.
Demerits: cannot touch or try products, delivery delays, risk of fraud, need for internet access and digital skills, and returns can be difficult.
Types include business-to-consumer (B2C), business-to-business (B2B) and consumer-to-consumer (C2C).
Safe practices: use trusted websites, secure payment, check reviews and return policies, never share OTPs or passwords.
E-commerce has helped small sellers reach national markets.
outcomes: Explain e-commerce and e-trade
State the merits and demerits of online trading
Discuss safe online buying

lesson.hook: Why do people buy phones online but vegetables mostly from the market?
lesson.example: A weaver in a village sells sarees across India through an online marketplace — reach that a local shop could not give.
lesson.activity: Pupils list five merits and five demerits of online shopping from their family's experience.

questions.q: What is e-commerce?
questions.a: Buying and selling goods and services over the internet.

questions.q: Give two merits of online trading.
questions.a: Available 24×7 and wide choice (also home delivery).

questions.q: Give two demerits of online trading.
questions.a: Cannot inspect products and risk of fraud.

questions.q: Give one safe online shopping practice.
questions.a: Never share OTPs or passwords (use trusted sites).

lesson.homework: Write a guide for your family on shopping safely online.

topics.title: Social Responsibility towards the Environment
topics.summary: Businesses use natural resources and create waste, so they have a responsibility to protect the environment.
notes: Businesses use natural resources and create waste, so they have a responsibility to protect the environment.
E-waste is discarded electronic equipment; it contains harmful metals and must be collected and recycled safely by authorised recyclers.
Recycling turns waste into new materials, saving resources and energy.
Afforestation (planting trees) restores forests and absorbs carbon dioxide.
Eco-friendly products use less harmful materials and energy and are biodegradable or recyclable.
Businesses must comply with environmental laws on pollution, waste and emissions.
outcomes: Explain the social responsibility of businesses towards the environment
Describe e-waste management, recycling and afforestation
Explain eco-friendly products and legal compliance with environmental norms

lesson.hook: Where do old mobile phones go when we throw them away?
lesson.example: A phone company that takes back old phones for safe recycling is meeting its responsibility for e-waste.
lesson.activity: Pupils audit e-waste at home and find the nearest authorised collection point.

questions.q: What is e-waste?
questions.a: Discarded electronic and electrical equipment.

questions.q: Why must e-waste be recycled safely?
questions.a: It contains harmful substances that can pollute soil and water.

questions.q: What is afforestation?
questions.a: Planting trees to create or restore forests.

questions.q: Give an example of an eco-friendly product.
questions.a: Cloth or jute bags (or biodegradable packaging).

lesson.homework: Write how a company near your town can reduce its environmental impact.

topics.title: Stakeholders in Commercial Organisations
topics.summary: Stakeholders are people or groups affected by, or able to affect, a business.
notes: Stakeholders are people or groups affected by, or able to affect, a business.
Internal stakeholders: shareholders (owners), employees and employers/managers.
External stakeholders: suppliers, creditors, government and society.
Expectations: owners want profit and growth; employees want fair pay, safety and growth; creditors and suppliers want timely payment.
Government expects tax payment and legal compliance; society expects safe products, jobs and care for the environment.
Balancing stakeholder interests builds trust and long-term success.
outcomes: Explain the meaning and types of stakeholders
Distinguish internal and external stakeholders
Describe the expectations of each stakeholder from a commercial organisation

lesson.hook: Who cares whether a company does well — and why?
lesson.example: A factory that pays wages on time, pays suppliers promptly and treats its waste properly meets the expectations of several stakeholders at once.
lesson.activity: Pupils map the stakeholders of their school canteen and what each expects.

questions.q: What is a stakeholder?
questions.a: A person or group affected by or able to affect a business.

questions.q: Name two internal stakeholders.
questions.a: Shareholders and employees.

questions.q: What do creditors expect?
questions.a: Timely repayment of what is owed.

questions.q: What does society expect from business?
questions.a: Safe products, employment and care for the environment.

lesson.homework: Distinguish internal and external stakeholders with examples.

topics.title: Marketing, Products and Pricing
topics.summary: Marketing is identifying customer needs and satisfying them profitably; it includes research, product design, pricing, promotion and distribution.
notes: Marketing is identifying customer needs and satisfying them profitably; it includes research, product design, pricing, promotion and distribution.
Sales is the transfer of goods to customers for money — only one part of marketing.
Objectives of marketing: satisfy customers, increase sales and market share, build brand image and earn profit.
A product is tangible (a bicycle); a service is intangible, cannot be stored and is produced and used at the same time (a haircut).
Pricing is fixing the value of a product in money; objectives include profit, survival, market share and meeting competition.
The price must cover costs, suit customers and compare well with competitors.
outcomes: Explain the meaning and objectives of marketing and distinguish marketing and sales
Distinguish products and services
Explain pricing and its objectives

lesson.hook: Is selling the same as marketing?
lesson.example: A phone company studies what students want (marketing) before the shop sells the phone (sales).
lesson.activity: Pupils design and price a new school stationery product and explain their pricing objective.

questions.q: Distinguish marketing and sales.
questions.a: Marketing covers identifying and satisfying customer needs; sales is only the exchange of goods for money.

questions.q: Give two differences between a product and a service.
questions.a: A product is tangible and can be stored; a service is intangible and cannot be stored.

questions.q: What is pricing?
questions.a: Fixing the value of a product or service in money.

questions.q: Give two objectives of pricing.
questions.a: Profit and market share.

lesson.homework: Write the objectives of marketing with examples.

topics.title: Advertising and Sales Promotion
topics.summary: Advertising is paid, non-personal promotion of goods, services or ideas by an identified sponsor.
notes: Advertising is paid, non-personal promotion of goods, services or ideas by an identified sponsor.
Merits: informs customers, increases sales, supports mass production and helps new products; demerits: raises costs, may mislead and can encourage wasteful spending.
Publicity is unpaid mention in the media and is not controlled by the company.
Advertising agencies plan, create and place advertisements for clients; social advertising promotes causes (road safety, voting).
Sales promotion gives short-term incentives: discounts, free samples, coupons, contests, exchange offers.
Advertising builds long-term demand; sales promotion boosts immediate sales.
outcomes: Explain advertising, its importance, merits and demerits
Distinguish advertising and publicity, and describe advertising agencies and social advertising
Explain sales promotion and distinguish it from advertising

lesson.hook: Why does a "buy one, get one free" offer last only a few days?
lesson.example: A "wear a helmet" campaign by the government is social advertising.
lesson.activity: Groups create an advertisement and a sales-promotion scheme for the same product and compare them.

questions.q: Distinguish advertising and publicity.
questions.a: Advertising is paid and controlled by the sponsor; publicity is unpaid and not controlled.

questions.q: Give two functions of an advertising agency.
questions.a: Planning and creating advertisements (also placing them in media).

questions.q: What is social advertising?
questions.a: Advertising that promotes social causes.

questions.q: Give two sales promotion techniques.
questions.a: Discounts and free samples.

lesson.homework: Write the merits and demerits of advertising.

topics.title: Consumer Protection and E-commerce
topics.summary: The Consumer Protection Act 2019 set up the Central Consumer Protection Authority and consumer commissions at district, state and national levels, and covers e-commerce and misleading advertisements.
notes: The Consumer Protection Act 2019 set up the Central Consumer Protection Authority and consumer commissions at district, state and national levels, and covers e-commerce and misleading advertisements.
Consumer rights: safety, information, choice, being heard, redressal and consumer education.
Consumer exploitation: adulteration, underweighing, high prices, poor quality, duplicate products and false advertising; awareness helps consumers protect themselves.
E-commerce differs from traditional trade: no physical shop, 24×7 access and digital payment.
E-tailing is online retailing; e-advertising and e-marketing promote products online; e-security protects data and payments.
ERP (enterprise resource planning) software links modules such as finance, HR, sales and inventory in one system.
outcomes: Explain the Consumer Protection Act 2019, consumer rights and consumer exploitation
Explain the importance of consumer awareness
Describe e-commerce, e-tailing, e-advertising, e-marketing, e-security and ERP

lesson.hook: What can you do if an online seller sends a fake product?
lesson.example: A buyer who receives a fake product can complain to the seller and then file a complaint with the consumer commission online.
lesson.activity: Pupils examine product labels for MRP, dates, standard marks and customer-care details.

questions.q: Name four consumer rights.
questions.a: Safety, information, choice and redressal.

questions.q: Give two forms of consumer exploitation.
questions.a: Adulteration and underweighing.

questions.q: What is e-tailing?
questions.a: Retail selling over the internet.

questions.q: What is ERP?
questions.a: Software linking business functions like finance, HR, sales and inventory in one system.

lesson.homework: Write the features of the Consumer Protection Act 2019.

topics.title: Capital and Revenue
topics.summary: Capital expenditure buys or improves fixed assets that benefit the business for many years (machinery, building, vehicle).
notes: Capital expenditure buys or improves fixed assets that benefit the business for many years (machinery, building, vehicle).
Revenue expenditure is for day-to-day running and benefits only the current year (wages, rent, electricity, repairs).
Capital receipts come from capital sources (owner's capital, loans, sale of fixed assets).
Revenue receipts come from normal operations (sales, commission, interest earned).
Deferred revenue expenditure is revenue in nature but large, with benefits over several years (heavy advertising for a new product).
Correct classification is needed for true profit and a true balance sheet.
outcomes: Distinguish capital and revenue receipts
Distinguish capital and revenue expenditure
Explain deferred revenue expenditure

lesson.hook: Is buying a delivery van an expense of this year only?
lesson.example: Buying a machine is capital expenditure; repairing it next year is revenue expenditure.
lesson.activity: Pupils classify fifteen items as capital or revenue expenditure/receipts.

questions.q: Classify: purchase of machinery.
questions.a: Capital expenditure.

questions.q: Classify: payment of wages.
questions.a: Revenue expenditure.

questions.q: Classify: sale of an old vehicle.
questions.a: Capital receipt.

questions.q: Give an example of deferred revenue expenditure.
questions.a: Heavy advertising for launching a new product.

lesson.homework: Distinguish capital and revenue expenditure with five examples each.

chapters.title: Final Accounts of a Sole Proprietor

topics.title: Final Accounts of a Sole Proprietor
topics.summary: Final accounts are prepared at the end of the accounting period from the trial balance.
notes: Final accounts are prepared at the end of the accounting period from the trial balance.
Trading account finds gross profit: sales minus cost of goods sold (opening stock + purchases + direct expenses − closing stock).
Profit and loss account finds net profit: gross profit plus other incomes minus indirect expenses (salaries, rent, advertising).
Balance sheet shows the financial position: assets on one side, liabilities and capital (plus net profit, minus drawings) on the other.
Closing stock is credited in the trading account and shown as a current asset in the balance sheet.
Total assets must equal total liabilities and capital.
outcomes: Explain the trading account, profit and loss account and balance sheet
Prepare final accounts of a sole proprietor from a trial balance
Adjust for closing stock

lesson.hook: How does a shopkeeper know whether the year ended in profit?
lesson.example: Sales ₹1,00,000, opening stock ₹10,000, purchases ₹60,000, closing stock ₹15,000: cost of goods sold ₹55,000, gross profit ₹45,000.
lesson.activity: Pupils prepare a trading account, profit and loss account and balance sheet from a simple trial balance.

questions.q: What does the trading account show?
questions.a: Gross profit or gross loss.

questions.q: How is closing stock treated?
questions.a: Credited in the trading account and shown as a current asset in the balance sheet.

questions.q: Give two indirect expenses.
questions.a: Salaries and rent.

questions.q: What does the balance sheet show?
questions.a: The financial position: assets, liabilities and capital.

lesson.homework: Prepare final accounts from the trial balance given by your teacher.

topics.title: Costs and Budgeting
topics.summary: Fixed costs stay the same whatever the output (rent, salaries); variable costs change with output (flour, packaging); semi-variable costs have both parts (electricity with a fixed charge plus usage).
notes: Fixed costs stay the same whatever the output (rent, salaries); variable costs change with output (flour, packaging); semi-variable costs have both parts (electricity with a fixed charge plus usage).
Direct costs can be traced to a product (raw material, direct labour); indirect costs are shared (factory rent, supervisor's salary).
A budget is a financial plan for a future period expressed in numbers.
Utility: planning, control, coordination and measuring performance.
Types: sales, production, purchase, cash and master budgets.
Forecasting predicts what may happen; budgeting sets targets and plans action based on forecasts.
outcomes: Classify costs by behaviour: fixed, variable and semi-variable
Classify costs by nature: direct and indirect
Explain budgeting, its utility, types of budgets, and compare budgeting and forecasting

lesson.hook: Does a bakery's rent change if it bakes twice as many cakes?
lesson.example: A bakery's rent ₹20,000 a month is fixed; flour cost rises with every extra cake — variable.
lesson.activity: Pupils prepare a simple monthly cash budget for a school club.

questions.q: Give an example of a fixed cost.
questions.a: Rent (or salaries).

questions.q: Give an example of a variable cost.
questions.a: Raw materials.

questions.q: What is a budget?
questions.a: A financial plan for a future period in numbers.

questions.q: Distinguish budgeting and forecasting.
questions.a: Forecasting predicts; budgeting sets targets and plans based on forecasts.

lesson.homework: Classify fifteen costs as fixed, variable or semi-variable.

topics.title: Sources of Finance
topics.summary: The capital market deals in long-term funds; it mobilises savings, channels them into investment and provides liquidity through stock exchanges.
notes: The capital market deals in long-term funds; it mobilises savings, channels them into investment and provides liquidity through stock exchanges.
Shares represent ownership: equity shareholders get dividends after preference shareholders and have voting rights; preference shareholders get a fixed dividend first and priority in repayment.
Debentures are loans to the company; debenture holders are creditors who get fixed interest whether or not there is profit.
Key difference: shareholders are owners with variable returns; debenture holders are lenders with fixed interest and usually security.
Short-term finance from banks: cash credit (borrow up to a limit against security), overdraft (withdraw more than the current account balance) and discounting of bills.
Long-term needs (factory) should be met by long-term funds; working needs by short-term funds.
outcomes: Explain the meaning and functions of the capital market
Distinguish shares (equity and preference) and debentures
Describe short-term sources: cash credit, overdraft and discounting of bills

lesson.hook: How does a company raise ₹100 crore to build a new factory?
lesson.example: A company issues equity shares to build a factory and uses an overdraft to buy raw materials in a busy month.
lesson.activity: Pupils compare a shareholder and a debenture holder in a debate: "Who takes more risk?"

questions.q: What is the capital market?
questions.a: The market for long-term funds.

questions.q: Distinguish shares and debentures.
questions.a: Shares give ownership and variable dividends; debentures are loans with fixed interest.

questions.q: What is an overdraft?
questions.a: Permission to withdraw more than the balance in a current account.

questions.q: Who gets dividend first — equity or preference shareholders?
questions.a: Preference shareholders.

lesson.homework: Explain the functions of the capital market.

topics.title: Recruitment, Selection and Training
topics.summary: Recruitment is searching for and attracting suitable candidates to apply.
notes: Recruitment is searching for and attracting suitable candidates to apply.

Internal sources: promotion and transfer — cheaper and motivating but limit fresh ideas; external sources: advertisements, employment exchanges, campus placement, online portals — wider choice but costlier.
