Selection is choosing the best candidate: screening applications, tests, interview, reference check, medical examination, and appointment letter.
Selection tests: intelligence, aptitude, personality, trade (skill) and interest tests.
Training improves employees' knowledge and skills; objectives include higher productivity, fewer accidents and better morale.
On-the-job training (apprenticeship, job rotation, coaching) happens at the workplace; off-the-job training (lectures, case studies, simulations) happens away from it.
outcomes: Explain recruitment and its internal and external sources
Describe the steps of selection and types of selection tests
Explain training, its objectives and on-the-job and off-the-job methods

lesson.hook: How does a company find the right person out of 500 applicants?
lesson.example: A bank promotes a clerk to officer (internal source) and trains new officers at its staff college (off-the-job).
lesson.activity: Pupils design a recruitment advertisement and a three-step selection process for a school librarian.

questions.q: Give two internal sources of recruitment.
questions.a: Promotion and transfer.

questions.q: Give two external sources of recruitment.
questions.a: Advertisements and campus placement.

questions.q: What is an aptitude test?
questions.a: A test of a candidate's ability to learn a skill.

questions.q: Distinguish on-the-job and off-the-job training.
questions.a: On-the-job is at the workplace; off-the-job is away from it.

lesson.homework: Write the steps of selection in order.

topics.title: Industrial Relations and Social Security
topics.summary: Industrial relations are the relations between employers and employees.
notes: Industrial relations are the relations between employers and employees.
Objectives: industrial peace, higher productivity, workers' welfare and avoiding disputes.
A trade union is an association of workers formed to protect their interests.
Functions: collective bargaining for wages and conditions, protecting jobs, welfare activities and representing workers.
Social security protects workers against risks such as old age, illness and unemployment.
Provident fund: savings from employer and employee contributions; gratuity: a lump sum on leaving after long service; National Pension System: a contributory retirement scheme.
outcomes: Explain industrial relations and their objectives
Explain trade unions and their functions
Explain social security: provident fund, gratuity and National Pension Scheme

lesson.hook: Why do workers form unions?
lesson.example: Through collective bargaining, a union and management agree on a wage rise and safety improvements without a strike.
lesson.activity: Role play: a negotiation between a union and management over working hours.

questions.q: What are industrial relations?
questions.a: Relations between employers and employees.

questions.q: Give two functions of trade unions.
questions.a: Collective bargaining and protecting workers' interests.

questions.q: What is gratuity?
questions.a: A lump sum paid to an employee on leaving after long service.

questions.q: What is social security?
questions.a: Protection of workers against risks like old age, illness and unemployment.

lesson.homework: Write the objectives of good industrial relations.

topics.title: Logistics: Transport, Warehousing and Insurance
topics.summary: Logistics is planning and managing the movement and storage of goods from origin to consumer.
notes: Logistics is planning and managing the movement and storage of goods from origin to consumer.
Transport: road (door-to-door, flexible), rail (cheap for bulky goods over long distance), air (fast, costly) and water (cheapest for heavy goods, slow).
Warehousing stores goods until needed, smoothing supply and demand; types: public, private and bonded (for imported goods before customs duty is paid).
Insurance transfers risk to an insurer for a premium; types: life and general (fire, health, marine).
Principles: utmost good faith, insurable interest, indemnity (except life), contribution, subrogation, causa proxima and mitigation of loss.
Logistics, warehousing and insurance together remove hindrances of place, time and risk.
outcomes: Explain logistics and its classification
Compare modes of transport and explain warehousing and its types
Explain insurance, its types and principles

lesson.hook: How does a mango from Ratnagiri reach Delhi in good condition?
lesson.example: Mangoes travel by refrigerated truck, are stored in a cold warehouse, and the shipment is insured against damage.
lesson.activity: Pupils plan the logistics of sending goods from their town to another state, choosing transport, storage and insurance.

questions.q: What is logistics?
questions.a: Managing movement and storage of goods from origin to consumer.

questions.q: Give one merit and one demerit of air transport.
questions.a: Fast; costly.

questions.q: What is a bonded warehouse?
questions.a: A warehouse for imported goods before customs duty is paid.

questions.q: State the principle of indemnity.
questions.a: The insured is compensated only for the actual loss, not to make a profit.

lesson.homework: Compare the four modes of transport in a table.

chapters.title: Banking: Central Bank, Internet Banking and Fraud

topics.title: Banking: Central Bank, Internet Banking and Fraud
topics.summary: The Reserve Bank of India is the central bank: it issues currency, is banker to the government and to banks, controls credit and keeps foreign exchange reserves.
notes: The Reserve Bank of India is the central bank: it issues currency, is banker to the government and to banks, controls credit and keeps foreign exchange reserves.
Central bank vs commercial bank: the central bank does not deal with the public for profit; it regulates the banking system.
NEFT transfers money in batches; RTGS moves large amounts in real time; IMPS transfers instantly 24×7; mobile wallets store money for quick payments.
A debit card draws from your own account; a credit card borrows up to a limit, repaid later.
Frauds: credit card fraud, false accounting, insurance fraud, intellectual property fraud, internet and cyber fraud.
Safe practices: never share PINs, OTPs or passwords; use secure websites; check statements; report lost cards immediately.
outcomes: Explain the meaning and functions of the central bank and compare it with commercial banks
Describe internet banking: NEFT, RTGS, IMPS, mobile wallets, ATMs, credit and debit cards
Identify financial frauds and safe practices

lesson.hook: What should you do if someone calls and asks for your card's OTP?
lesson.example: A caller claiming to be from a bank and asking for an OTP is a fraud; banks never ask for OTPs.
lesson.activity: Pupils create a poster of five rules for safe digital banking.

questions.q: Name two functions of the central bank.
questions.a: Issuing currency and controlling credit.

questions.q: Distinguish NEFT and RTGS.
questions.a: NEFT works in batches; RTGS transfers large amounts in real time.

questions.q: Distinguish a debit and a credit card.
questions.a: Debit card uses your own money; credit card borrows up to a limit.

questions.q: Give two safe banking practices.
questions.a: Never share OTPs and report lost cards immediately.

lesson.homework: Explain three types of financial fraud and how to avoid them.

topics.title: Government and Environment Protection
topics.summary: The Environment (Protection) Act 1986 was passed after the Bhopal gas tragedy to protect and improve the environment.
notes: The Environment (Protection) Act 1986 was passed after the Bhopal gas tragedy to protect and improve the environment.
Features: it empowers the central government to set standards for emissions and discharges, regulate hazardous substances, inspect and close polluting units, and punish violators.
The Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) advises the government on pollution, sets standards, monitors air and water quality and coordinates State Pollution Control Boards.
CPCB also collects and publishes pollution data and runs awareness programmes.
Businesses must obtain consents, treat waste and meet emission standards.
Compliance protects people, avoids penalties and builds public trust.
outcomes: Describe the features of the Environment (Protection) Act 1986
Explain the functions of the Central Pollution Control Board
Discuss business responsibility for environmental compliance

lesson.hook: Who can stop a factory from polluting a river?
lesson.example: Under the Act, a unit discharging untreated effluent can be ordered to close until it installs a treatment plant.
lesson.activity: Pupils check the air quality index of their city on the CPCB website and discuss what affects it.

questions.q: When was the Environment (Protection) Act passed?
Give two features of the Act.
questions.a: Setting emission standards and power to close polluting units.

questions.q: Give two functions of the CPCB.
questions.a: Setting standards and monitoring air and water quality.

questions.q: Why should businesses comply with environmental laws?
questions.a: To protect people and the environment, avoid penalties and build trust.

lesson.homework: Write how the government protects the environment through laws and agencies.

topics.title: Understanding our Environment
topics.summary: The environment is everything around us — living and non-living — that affects our lives; environmental science studies how humans interact with it.
notes: The environment is everything around us — living and non-living — that affects our lives; environmental science studies how humans interact with it.
Main problems: depletion of resources (water, forests, minerals), pollution of air, water and soil, and extinction of species.
Developed countries consume far more resources per person; developing countries face rapid population growth and poverty — both add to the problem.
The roots are the population crisis (too many people for local resources) and the consumption crisis (too much use per person).
Sustainability means meeting present needs without harming the ability of future generations to meet theirs.
A sustainable society uses renewable resources wisely, reduces waste and shares resources fairly.
outcomes: Explain what environment and environmental science mean
Describe the main environmental problems: resource depletion, pollution and extinction
Explain the roots of the problems and the idea of sustainability

lesson.hook: If everyone on Earth lived like the average person in a rich country, how many Earths would we need?
lesson.example: Refilling a steel bottle instead of buying plastic bottles reduces both resource use and waste — a small sustainable choice.
lesson.activity: Pupils keep a one-day diary of water, electricity and plastic use and identify three changes.

questions.q: What is environmental science?
questions.a: The study of how humans interact with their environment.

questions.q: Name the three main environmental problems.
questions.a: Resource depletion, pollution and extinction of species.

questions.q: What is the consumption crisis?
questions.a: Excessive use of resources per person, mostly in developed countries.

questions.q: What is sustainability?
questions.a: Meeting present needs without harming future generations' ability to meet theirs.

lesson.homework: Write five ways your school can become more sustainable.

topics.title: Living Things in Ecosystems
topics.summary: An ecosystem is a community of organisms interacting with each other and with abiotic factors (sunlight, water, soil, temperature).
notes: An ecosystem is a community of organisms interacting with each other and with abiotic factors (sunlight, water, soil, temperature).
A population is individuals of one species in an area; a community is all populations living together.
Habitat is an organism's "address"; its niche is its "profession" — its role and how it uses resources.

Interactions: predation, competition, parasitism, mutualism (both benefit) and commensalism (one benefits, the other is unaffected); the law of limiting factors says growth is limited by the scarcest need.
Adaptations suit organisms to their environment; natural selection favours helpful traits; co-evolution shapes species together; species can go extinct.
India has biogeographic zones such as the Himalaya, the Thar Desert, the Western Ghats, the Deccan Plateau, the Gangetic Plain, the coasts and the islands, each with typical wildlife.
outcomes: Explain ecosystems, populations and communities
Distinguish habitat and ecological niche
Describe species interactions, adaptation, evolution and biogeographic zones of India

lesson.hook: Why can't a polar bear survive in the Western Ghats?
lesson.example: Bees and flowers show mutualism: bees get nectar, flowers get pollinated.
lesson.activity: Pupils observe a patch of school ground and list biotic and abiotic components and one interaction.

questions.q: What is an ecosystem?
questions.a: A community of organisms interacting with each other and their non-living surroundings.

questions.q: Distinguish habitat and niche.
questions.a: Habitat is where an organism lives; niche is its role there.

questions.q: What is commensalism?
questions.a: An interaction where one species benefits and the other is unaffected.

questions.q: Name two biogeographic zones of India.
questions.a: The Western Ghats and the Thar Desert.

lesson.homework: Give one example each of predation, parasitism and mutualism.

topics.title: How Ecosystems Work
topics.summary: Almost all life depends on the sun: producers make food by photosynthesis; consumers eat producers or other consumers; respiration releases energy from food.
notes: Almost all life depends on the sun: producers make food by photosynthesis; consumers eat producers or other consumers; respiration releases energy from food.
A food chain shows who eats whom; many linked chains form a food web.
Trophic levels: producers, primary consumers, secondary consumers and so on; only about 10% of energy passes to the next level.
Materials cycle: the water cycle, the carbon cycle (humans add CO₂ by burning fuels and cutting forests) and the nitrogen cycle (bacteria fix nitrogen).
Natural cycles are interdependent — changing one affects the others.
Succession is the gradual change of communities: primary on bare rock, secondary after a disturbance such as a forest fire.
outcomes: Explain how energy flows through ecosystems
Describe food chains, food webs and trophic levels
Describe the water, carbon and nitrogen cycles and ecological succession

lesson.hook: Why are there fewer tigers than deer in a forest?
lesson.example: Grass → deer → tiger: if the grass holds 10,000 units of energy, the deer get about 1,000 and the tiger about 100.
lesson.activity: Pupils build a food web on the board from cards of forest organisms and trace energy loss.

questions.q: Why does life depend on the sun?
questions.a: Producers use sunlight to make food that all other organisms depend on.

questions.q: What fraction of energy passes to the next trophic level?
questions.a: About 10%.

questions.q: How do humans affect the carbon cycle?
questions.a: By burning fossil fuels and cutting forests, adding CO₂.

questions.q: Distinguish primary and secondary succession.
questions.a: Primary starts on bare ground; secondary follows a disturbance where soil remains.

lesson.homework: Draw a food web with at least eight organisms.

topics.title: Kinds of Ecosystems
topics.summary: Forests: tropical rainforests (richest biodiversity, threatened by clearing), temperate rainforests, temperate deciduous forests and taiga.
notes: Forests: tropical rainforests (richest biodiversity, threatened by clearing), temperate rainforests, temperate deciduous forests and taiga.
Grasslands: tropical savannas and temperate grasslands (prairies, steppes, pampas); deserts; tundra — threatened by farming, overgrazing and climate change.
Freshwater: lakes, ponds, wetlands (marshes, swamps) and rivers; wetlands filter water and control floods but are drained and polluted.
Marine: estuaries (nurseries for fish), coral reefs (bleached by warming and damaged by pollution) and open oceans (overfishing, plastic).
Polar ecosystems of the Arctic and Antarctic are threatened by warming, melting ice and pollution.
Each ecosystem gives services such as clean water, food, climate regulation and habitat.
outcomes: Describe forests, grasslands, deserts and tundra
Describe freshwater ecosystems and the threats to wetlands and rivers
Describe marine and polar ecosystems and their threats

lesson.hook: Which ecosystem would you protect first if you could choose only one?
lesson.example: Coral reefs cover a tiny part of the ocean floor but shelter a large share of marine species — warming water bleaches them.
lesson.activity: Groups prepare a one-page profile of an ecosystem: climate, typical life, services and threats.

questions.q: Why are tropical rainforests important?
questions.a: They have the richest biodiversity.

questions.q: Give two functions of wetlands.
questions.a: They filter water and control floods.

questions.q: What threatens coral reefs?
questions.a: Warming water (bleaching) and pollution.

questions.q: Name two threats to polar ecosystems.
questions.a: Warming and melting ice (also pollution).

lesson.homework: Compare a desert and a rainforest in a table.

topics.title: Water
topics.summary: Most water is salty; much fresh water is frozen in ice caps; usable surface water and groundwater are limited — aquifers are running low.
notes: Most water is salty; much fresh water is frozen in ice caps; usable surface water and groundwater are limited — aquifers are running low.
Dams store water but can displace people and cause disputes over rivers.
Solutions: desalination, water conservation, rainwater harvesting and careful irrigation.
Point-source pollution comes from a single place (a factory pipe); non-point pollution comes from wide areas (farm run-off).
Nutrients cause artificial eutrophication (algal blooms that use up oxygen); hot water causes thermal pollution; pathogens spread disease; wastewater treatment plants clean sewage.
Ocean pollution comes from rivers, ships and plastic; prevention needs treatment, less plastic and international rules.
outcomes: Describe the world's water resources and solutions to water shortage
Explain freshwater pollution, its effects and treatment
Explain ocean pollution and its prevention

lesson.hook: If most of Earth is covered with water, why do cities run short of it?
lesson.example: A rooftop rainwater harvesting system on a school can collect lakhs of litres in a monsoon.
lesson.activity: Pupils calculate how much rain falls on their school roof in a year (area × rainfall).

questions.q: Why is usable fresh water limited?
questions.a: Most water is salty or frozen, and groundwater is being depleted.

questions.q: Distinguish point and non-point pollution.
questions.a: Point comes from a single source; non-point from wide areas.

questions.q: What is eutrophication?
questions.a: Excess nutrients cause algal blooms that use up oxygen in water.

questions.q: Give two solutions to water shortage.
questions.a: Rainwater harvesting and water conservation.

lesson.homework: Write a plan for saving water at home.

topics.title: Air
topics.summary: Sources: natural (volcanoes, dust storms), domestic burning, vehicles and industry.
notes: Sources: natural (volcanoes, dust storms), domestic burning, vehicles and industry.
Major pollutants: carbon monoxide, oxides of nitrogen and sulphur, ground-level ozone, lead, hydrocarbons, benzene and particulate matter.
Primary pollutants are released directly; secondary pollutants form in the air (ozone, smog); aerosols are fine particles suspended in air.

Thermal inversion traps cool polluted air under warm air (as in Los Angeles); photochemical smog forms when sunlight acts on vehicle pollutants (as in Mexico City); acid rain forms from sulphur and nitrogen oxides.
Impacts: breathing and heart problems, lower crop yields, damage to buildings and economic losses.
The Bhopal gas tragedy (1984) leaked methyl isocyanate from a factory, killing thousands.
outcomes: Describe the causes and major pollutants of air pollution
Explain thermal inversion, photochemical smog and acid precipitation
Describe the impact of air pollution, including the Bhopal gas tragedy

lesson.hook: Why is the air in many cities worst on still winter mornings?
lesson.example: On a calm winter morning, a layer of warm air sits above cold air, trapping smoke near the ground — a thermal inversion.
lesson.activity: Pupils track the air quality index for a week and relate it to weather and traffic.

questions.q: Name four air pollutants.
questions.a: Carbon monoxide, sulphur dioxide, nitrogen oxides and particulate matter.

questions.q: What is a secondary pollutant?
questions.a: A pollutant formed in the air from other pollutants, such as ozone.

questions.q: What is a thermal inversion?
questions.a: A layer of warm air trapping cooler polluted air near the ground.

questions.q: What happened in the Bhopal gas tragedy?
questions.a: In 1984 methyl isocyanate leaked from a factory, killing thousands.

lesson.homework: Write how acid rain affects ecosystems and buildings.

topics.title: Atmosphere and Climate
topics.summary: Photosynthesis and respiration keep oxygen and carbon dioxide in balance; the atmosphere has layers — troposphere, stratosphere, mesosphere and thermosphere.
notes: Photosynthesis and respiration keep oxygen and carbon dioxide in balance; the atmosphere has layers — troposphere, stratosphere, mesosphere and thermosphere.
Climate depends on latitude, air and ocean circulation, local geography and seasons.
Greenhouse gases (CO₂, methane, nitrous oxide, water vapour) trap heat; rising levels cause global warming, changing weather, affecting farming and raising sea levels.
Slowing warming: clean energy, efficiency, forests and less waste.
Ozone in the troposphere is a pollutant; ozone in the stratosphere shields us from ultraviolet rays.
CFCs and similar chemicals thin the ozone layer, increasing skin cancer and harming crops; alternatives to CFCs and the Montreal Protocol have helped it recover.
outcomes: Describe the atmosphere and what determines climate
Explain the greenhouse effect and global warming
Explain ozone depletion and its causes, effects and solutions

lesson.hook: How can a thin layer of gas protect all life on Earth?
lesson.example: A car parked in the sun gets hot inside because glass lets light in but traps heat — like the greenhouse effect.
lesson.activity: Pupils compare two jars in sunlight, one covered with clear film, and record temperatures.

questions.q: Name three greenhouse gases.
questions.a: Carbon dioxide, methane and nitrous oxide.

questions.q: Give two effects of global warming.
questions.a: Rising sea levels and changing weather.

questions.q: Why is stratospheric ozone important?
questions.a: It absorbs harmful ultraviolet rays.

questions.q: What causes ozone thinning?
questions.a: CFCs and similar chemicals.

lesson.homework: Distinguish "good" and "bad" ozone.

topics.title: Soil and Land
topics.summary: Causes of deforestation in developing countries: need for fuel, farmland, cash crops, population pressure, timber demand and grazing.
notes: Causes of deforestation in developing countries: need for fuel, farmland, cash crops, population pressure, timber demand and grazing.
Consequences: soil erosion, floods, changed rainfall, loss of wildlife and more carbon dioxide.
Soil erosion is caused by removing vegetation, overgrazing, overcultivation, clearing slopes, drought, heavy rain and poor farming.
Desertification turns fertile land into desert-like land.
Land pollution: salinisation from poor irrigation, fertilisers, pesticides, toxic and nuclear waste, domestic waste and groundwater contamination.
Healthy land needs vegetation cover, careful farming and proper waste disposal.
outcomes: Explain the causes and consequences of deforestation
Explain soil erosion and desertification
Explain the causes and consequences of land pollution

lesson.hook: What happens to a hillside when all its trees are cut?
lesson.example: On a bare slope, heavy rain washes away the topsoil that took hundreds of years to form.
lesson.activity: Pupils pour water on two trays of soil, one bare and one with grass, and compare the run-off.

questions.q: Give three causes of deforestation.
questions.a: Fuel needs, farmland and timber demand.

questions.q: Give two consequences of deforestation.
questions.a: Soil erosion and floods.

questions.q: What is desertification?
questions.a: Fertile land turning into desert-like land.

questions.q: What is salinisation?
questions.a: Build-up of salts in soil, often from poor irrigation.

lesson.homework: Write how planting trees prevents soil erosion.

topics.title: People and Poverty
topics.summary: Development indicators include per-capita income, housing, disease and nutrition; they show a wide gap between rich and poor countries.
notes: Development indicators include per-capita income, housing, disease and nutrition; they show a wide gap between rich and poor countries.
Poverty exists in developed countries too, but it is deeper and wider in developing countries.
Rural poverty is linked to small landholdings and low farm incomes; urban poverty to slums, informal jobs and high living costs.
The poverty trap: poor people depend directly on natural resources, overuse them, and become poorer as resources decline.
Environmental damage hurts the poor most — they rely on forests, water and soil for their living.
Breaking the trap needs education, jobs, health care and access to resources.
outcomes: Describe world poverty and the gap between developed and developing countries
Distinguish rural and urban poverty
Explain the poverty trap and its effect on the environment

lesson.hook: Why might a poor family cut a forest even if they know it is harmful?
lesson.example: A family with no other fuel cuts nearby trees, the forest thins, and they must walk farther for firewood — a poverty trap.
lesson.activity: Pupils compare two countries using three development indicators from a given table.

questions.q: Name three development indicators.
questions.a: Per-capita income, housing and nutrition.

questions.q: Distinguish rural and urban poverty.
questions.a: Rural poverty is linked to farming and land; urban poverty to slums and informal jobs.

questions.q: What is the poverty trap?
questions.a: Poor people overuse resources, which then decline and make them poorer.

questions.q: Why does environmental damage hurt the poor most?
questions.a: They depend directly on natural resources.

lesson.homework: Suggest ways to break the poverty trap in a village.

topics.title: Urbanisation
topics.summary: Urbanisation is the growth of the share of people living in towns and cities.
notes: Urbanisation is the growth of the share of people living in towns and cities.
Push factors (from villages): few jobs, poor services, low income; pull factors (to cities): jobs, education, health care and hope of a better life.
Manifestations: growth of slums, a large informal sector, pressure on water, transport and housing, and loss of human potential and hope.
Problems: housing shortage, congestion, pollution, loss of farmland and difficulty in providing services.
Rapid, unplanned growth makes these problems worse.
Planning, rural development and smaller towns can manage urbanisation.
outcomes: Explain the push and pull causes of urbanisation
Describe the manifestations of urbanisation
Describe the social, economic and environmental problems of cities

lesson.hook: Why do so many people move from villages to cities every year?
lesson.example: A young farmer moves to a city after crop failure (push) for a construction job (pull).
lesson.activity: Pupils list the push and pull factors for a family who moved to their town.

questions.q: What is urbanisation?
questions.a: The growth in the share of people living in towns and cities.

questions.q: Give two push factors.
questions.a: Lack of jobs and poor services in villages.

questions.q: Give two pull factors.
questions.a: Jobs and better education in cities.

questions.q: Name three urban problems.
questions.a: Housing shortage, congestion and pollution.

lesson.homework: Write about the problems of urbanisation in your nearest city.

topics.title: Agriculture
topics.summary: Modern agriculture often uses monocultures, causing loss of traditional crop varieties.
notes: Modern agriculture often uses monocultures, causing loss of traditional crop varieties.
Heavy use of pesticides and chemical fertilisers pollutes soil and water; over-irrigation depletes groundwater and causes waterlogging and salinity.
Large farm units remove hedges and trees, increase erosion and harm biodiversity.
Food mountains are huge surpluses in some developed countries, often wasted while others go hungry.
The Green Revolution (from the 1960s) used high-yielding seeds, fertilisers and irrigation, making India self-sufficient in food grains.
But it caused soil and water problems and helped richer farmers and irrigated regions more — it was a success with costs.
outcomes: Explain the unsustainable patterns of modern industrialised agriculture
Describe environmental damage from large farm units and food mountains
Evaluate the Green Revolution

lesson.hook: Did the Green Revolution solve India's food problem or create new ones?
lesson.example: Punjab greatly increased wheat and rice output, but its groundwater levels have fallen sharply.
lesson.activity: Class debate: "The Green Revolution was a success."

questions.q: What is a monoculture?
questions.a: Growing a single crop over a large area.

questions.q: Give two problems of heavy fertiliser use.
questions.a: Soil and water pollution.

questions.q: What are food mountains?
questions.a: Huge food surpluses in some developed countries.

questions.q: Give one success and one failure of the Green Revolution.
questions.a: Food self-sufficiency; soil and groundwater damage.

lesson.homework: Write how farming can be made more sustainable.

topics.title: Controlling Air Pollution
topics.summary: Domestic pollution: replacing smoky wood and dung fires with cleaner fuels (LPG, biogas, and kerosene where no better option exists) and improved stoves.
notes: Domestic pollution: replacing smoky wood and dung fires with cleaner fuels (LPG, biogas, and kerosene where no better option exists) and improved stoves.
Industrial controls: energy-efficient devices, clean technologies, filters and scrubbers, tall stacks, zoning industries away from homes, penalties for polluters and subsidies for clean technology.
The Taj Trapezium Zone around Agra restricts polluting industries and fuels to protect the Taj Mahal from discolouration.
Vehicle controls: catalytic converters, cleaner engines, clean fuels such as CNG, emission standards, and regular checks.
Public transport, traffic management and economic measures (parking charges, fuel taxes) reduce vehicle use.
Controls work best when combined and enforced.
outcomes: Describe ways to reduce pollution from domestic cooking
Explain measures to control industrial air pollution, including the Taj Trapezium case
Explain vehicle emission control measures

lesson.hook: How can a city cut air pollution without stopping its factories and vehicles?
lesson.example: Delhi moved its buses and auto-rickshaws to CNG, lowering some pollutants from vehicles.
lesson.activity: Pupils design a clean-air plan for their town with three domestic, industrial and transport measures.

questions.q: How can pollution from cooking be reduced?
questions.a: By using cleaner fuels such as LPG or biogas and improved stoves.

questions.q: What is the Taj Trapezium Zone?
questions.a: A zone around the Taj Mahal where polluting industries and fuels are restricted.

questions.q: What does a catalytic converter do?
questions.a: It converts harmful exhaust gases into less harmful ones.

questions.q: Give two traffic measures to reduce pollution.
questions.a: Better public transport and traffic management.

lesson.homework: Write the advantages of CNG as a vehicle fuel.

topics.title: Addressing Population
topics.summary: Growing populations in developing countries and rising consumption in developed countries both put pressure on resources and climate.
notes: Growing populations in developing countries and rising consumption in developed countries both put pressure on resources and climate.
UN projections expect world population to rise to roughly 9–10 billion by 2050; choices made now shape which future we get.
Demographic transition: from high birth and death rates, to falling death rates (rapid growth), to falling birth rates, to low stable rates.
Strategies: family planning, health care, education (especially of girls), economic development and women-centred human development.
Poverty alleviation through social mobilisation, agricultural development, small-scale industries and human development reduces pressure on the environment.
When women are educated and healthy, families tend to be smaller and healthier.
outcomes: Explain the link between population growth and environmental degradation
Describe the demographic transition
Describe strategies for controlling population and alleviating poverty

lesson.hook: Is the problem too many people, or too much consumption?
lesson.example: Kerala's high literacy and good health care are linked to a low birth rate.
lesson.activity: Pupils plot birth and death rates through the four stages of demographic transition.

questions.q: How is population linked to environmental degradation?
questions.a: More people and more consumption increase pressure on resources.

questions.q: What happens in the second stage of demographic transition?
questions.a: Death rates fall while birth rates stay high, so population grows fast.

questions.q: Give two strategies for controlling population growth.
questions.a: Education of girls and family planning.

questions.q: Why is women-centred development important?
questions.a: Educated, healthy women tend to have smaller, healthier families.

lesson.homework: Write how education can help control population growth.

topics.title: Managing the Urban Environment
topics.summary: Rapid urbanisation is a major challenge; sustainable cities use resources efficiently and limit pollution.
notes: Rapid urbanisation is a major challenge; sustainable cities use resources efficiently and limit pollution.
Planning: efficient land use, energy planning, affordable shelter, public transport, water supply, wastewater and sanitary waste management, and regulated construction.
Rural development (jobs, services) reduces migration to big cities.
Developing secondary (smaller) cities spreads growth and eases pressure on megacities.
Community participation keeps surroundings clean; private enterprises can support city improvement through partnerships.
Incentives and clear rules increase private participation.
outcomes: Explain why sustainable cities are needed
Describe planning for environmental improvement in cities
Explain rural development, secondary cities and community participation

lesson.hook: What would make your town a better place to live in 2040?
lesson.example: Resident welfare associations that segregate waste at source reduce what goes to landfills.
lesson.activity: Groups design one improvement for their neighbourhood and list who must take part.

questions.q: What is a sustainable city?
questions.a: One that uses resources efficiently and limits pollution while meeting people's needs.

questions.q: Give three areas of urban planning.
questions.a: Land use, public transport and water supply.

questions.q: How does rural development help cities?
questions.a: It reduces migration to cities.

questions.q: How can communities help keep cities clean?
questions.a: By segregating waste and keeping surroundings clean.

lesson.homework: Write a plan to make your school campus sustainable.

topics.title: Managing Soil and Land
topics.summary: Erosion control: terracing, contour ploughing, strip cropping, bunds, check dams in gullies, wind-breaks, tree planting and organic manure.
notes: Erosion control: terracing, contour ploughing, strip cropping, bunds, check dams in gullies, wind-breaks, tree planting and organic manure.
Soil and water conservation go together: vegetative and mechanical practices, appropriate cropping patterns, tree and foliage crops.
Land reforms in India aimed to give land to the landless (ceilings, redistribution, tenancy protection).
Integrated rural development and self-help schemes such as social and community forestry improve livelihoods and land.
Combating deforestation: reforestation, energy plantations, harvesting non-timber forest products, alternative livelihoods and changed consumption; controlled grazing (National Forest Policy 1988).
Recycling timber and paper and using alternatives reduce pressure on forests; women and communities play key roles in conservation.
outcomes: Describe soil erosion control and conservation techniques
Explain land reforms and integrated rural development
Describe ways to combat deforestation, manage grazing and find alternatives to timber

lesson.hook: How did farmers on steep hills grow crops for centuries without losing their soil?
lesson.example: Terraces on hill slopes slow run-off and hold soil and water.
lesson.activity: Pupils build a model slope with and without terraces and pour water to compare erosion.

questions.q: Name three soil erosion control methods.
questions.a: Terracing, contour ploughing and wind-breaks.

questions.q: What were land reforms meant to do?
questions.a: Give land to the landless.

questions.q: What is social forestry?
questions.a: Planting trees on common and community land for local benefit.

questions.q: Give one alternative to cutting timber.
questions.a: Recycling timber and paper.

lesson.homework: Write about the role of women in forest conservation (for example, the Chipko movement).

topics.title: Food
topics.summary: Integrated pest management combines biological, cultural and limited chemical control to keep pests below harmful levels.
notes: Integrated pest management combines biological, cultural and limited chemical control to keep pests below harmful levels.
Genetically modified organisms have altered genes for traits like pest resistance; benefits include higher yields, risks include effects on biodiversity and resistance.
Regenerative techniques: mixed cropping, intercropping, crop rotation, agroforestry, polyculture; conservation tillage reduces ploughing to protect soil.
Drip irrigation delivers water directly to roots, saving water; organic manures, green manures and biofertilisers improve soil.
Gene banks store seeds and genetic material to protect crop diversity.
Global food security is limited by unequal distribution more than total production; food aid helps in emergencies but long-term solutions need local farming.
outcomes: Explain sustainable agriculture practices
Describe GM organisms, high-yielding and hybrid varieties, and gene banks
Discuss global food security and food aid

lesson.hook: How can farmers grow more food while using less water and chemicals?
lesson.example: Growing legumes in rotation adds nitrogen to the soil naturally, reducing fertiliser needs.
lesson.activity: Pupils design a small school garden plan using intercropping and composting.

questions.q: What is integrated pest management?
questions.a: Combining biological, cultural and limited chemical methods to control pests.

questions.q: Give one advantage of drip irrigation.
questions.a: It saves water by delivering it to roots.

questions.q: What is a gene bank?
questions.a: A store of seeds and genetic material to protect crop diversity.

questions.q: What limits global food security?
questions.a: Mainly unequal distribution of food.

lesson.homework: Write the advantages and disadvantages of GM crops.

topics.title: Biodiversity
topics.summary: Biodiversity is lost through habitat destruction, overexploitation, pollution, invasive species and climate change.
notes: Biodiversity is lost through habitat destruction, overexploitation, pollution, invasive species and climate change.
Humans are "super consumers" whose actions strain Earth's resources.
Reasons to conserve: economic (food, medicine, materials), ecological (stable ecosystems) and aesthetic (beauty, culture).
In-situ conservation protects species in their habitats — wildlife sanctuaries, national parks and biosphere reserves.
Ex-situ conservation protects them outside — zoos, botanical gardens and gene banks.
Strategies: Wildlife (Protection) Act 1972, Project Tiger 1973, IUCN, the Ramsar Convention (1971), CITES and the Convention on Biological Diversity.
outcomes: Explain why biodiversity is at risk and why it matters
Distinguish in-situ and ex-situ conservation
Describe national and international conservation strategies

lesson.hook: Why should we care if an insect we have never seen goes extinct?
lesson.example: Project Tiger reserves protect tigers and, with them, the whole forest ecosystem.
lesson.activity: Pupils prepare a fact file on a protected area in their state.

questions.q: Give three causes of biodiversity loss.
questions.a: Habitat destruction, overexploitation and pollution.

questions.q: Distinguish in-situ and ex-situ conservation.
questions.a: In-situ protects species in their habitats; ex-situ outside them.

questions.q: When was Project Tiger launched?
What does CITES regulate?
questions.a: International trade in endangered species.

lesson.homework: Write the economic, ecological and aesthetic reasons to conserve biodiversity.

topics.title: Energy
topics.summary: Most electricity still comes from fossil fuels, which are non-renewable and pollute.
notes: Most electricity still comes from fossil fuels, which are non-renewable and pollute.
Nuclear fission splits heavy atoms to release energy; advantages: large power, little CO₂; disadvantages: radioactive waste, high cost and accident risk (Chernobyl 1986).
Nuclear fusion joins light atoms and could provide clean energy in future, but is not yet practical for power.
Alternatives: solar, wind, hydroelectricity, geothermal, biomass, and fuels such as ethanol, methanol, gasohol, CNG and hydrogen.
Energy conservation — efficient appliances, LED lighting, public transport — is the cheapest "source".
A sustainable future mixes clean sources with wise use.
outcomes: Distinguish renewable and non-renewable energy resources
Explain nuclear energy, its advantages, disadvantages and safety concerns
Describe a sustainable energy future with conservation and alternative sources

lesson.hook: What will power our homes when coal runs out?
lesson.example: Replacing ten old bulbs with LEDs cuts a household's lighting electricity use sharply.
lesson.activity: Pupils audit electrical appliances at home and suggest three energy savings.

questions.q: Give two disadvantages of nuclear energy.
questions.a: Radioactive waste and accident risk.

questions.q: Distinguish fission and fusion.
questions.a: Fission splits heavy atoms; fusion joins light atoms.

questions.q: Name four alternative energy sources.
questions.a: Solar, wind, geothermal and biomass.

questions.q: Why is energy conservation important?
questions.a: It reduces demand, pollution and cost.

lesson.homework: Write about India's use of solar energy.

topics.title: Waste
topics.summary: We live in a "throwaway society" producing large amounts of solid waste.
notes: We live in a "throwaway society" producing large amounts of solid waste.
Biodegradable waste (food, paper) breaks down naturally; non-biodegradable waste (plastic, glass, metal) does not.
Landfills bury waste but can pollute groundwater and release methane; incinerators burn waste but can pollute the air.
Better options: produce less waste, reuse, recycle, compost and vermicompost (earthworms turning waste into manure).
Biotechnology uses microbes to break down waste; finding alternatives to harmful materials reduces waste at source.
Segregating waste at source makes recycling and composting possible.
outcomes: Describe solid waste and distinguish biodegradable and non-biodegradable materials
Explain landfills and incinerators
Describe options: reduce, reuse, recycle, compost, vermiculture and biotechnology

lesson.hook: Where does your school's rubbish go after it leaves the gate?
lesson.example: A school that composts canteen waste turns it into manure for its garden.
lesson.activity: Pupils segregate a day's classroom waste into wet, dry and hazardous and weigh each.

questions.q: Distinguish biodegradable and non-biodegradable waste.
questions.a: Biodegradable breaks down naturally; non-biodegradable does not.

questions.q: Give one problem of landfills.
questions.a: They can pollute groundwater (and release methane).

questions.q: What is vermicomposting?
questions.a: Using earthworms to turn organic waste into manure.

questions.q: Why segregate waste at source?
questions.a: To make recycling and composting possible.

lesson.homework: Plan a waste management system for your school.

topics.title: Environment and Development
topics.summary: Global pollution is caused by both developed countries (historical emissions, high consumption) and developing countries (rapid industrial growth); cooperation is needed.
notes: Global pollution is caused by both developed countries (historical emissions, high consumption) and developing countries (rapid industrial growth); cooperation is needed.
Developing countries argue for the right to develop; developed countries stress global limits; debt burdens push poorer countries to overuse resources.
Unfair trade can push poor countries to export raw materials cheaply, harming their environment.
Multinational corporations bring investment, jobs and technology but may move polluting processes to countries with weaker rules.
The Bhopal gas tragedy (1984) at a multinational's pesticide plant showed the human cost of weak safety.
Regulation, liability laws and transparency can make MNCs accountable.
outcomes: Discuss responsibility for global pollution
Explain the link between economic development, trade and environmental degradation
Evaluate the role of multinational corporations, with the Bhopal case study

lesson.hook: Should rich and poor countries share the cost of cleaning the planet equally?
lesson.example: A country selling raw logs cheaply to pay debts may lose forests faster than it earns.
lesson.activity: Debate: "Developed countries should pay more to fight climate change."

questions.q: Who is responsible for global pollution?
questions.a: Both developed and developing countries, in different ways.

questions.q: What is the debt trap?
questions.a: Debt pushes poorer countries to overuse resources to repay it.

questions.q: Give one benefit and one risk of MNCs.
questions.a: Investment and jobs; moving pollution to countries with weak rules.

questions.q: What lesson does the Bhopal tragedy teach?
questions.a: Weak safety and regulation can cause huge human harm.

lesson.homework: Write how MNCs can be made accountable for environmental harm.

topics.title: Towards a Sustainable Future
topics.summary: Countries depend on one another economically and environmentally; global environmental health is a shared responsibility, and fair trade and aid can reduce inequality.
notes: Countries depend on one another economically and environmentally; global environmental health is a shared responsibility, and fair trade and aid can reduce inequality.
The Montreal Protocol (1987) phased out ozone-depleting substances; the Global Environment Facility funds environmental projects.
The Earth Summit (Rio, 1992), the Cairo International Conference on Population and Development (1994) and the Kyoto Protocol (1997, emission cuts) were milestones.
Sustainable development means growth that meets present needs without harming future generations; it looks different for developed and developing countries.
NGOs raise awareness, protect communities and push for better policy.

Satellite remote sensing monitors deforestation, desertification, mining, ozone and helps predict droughts and floods; alternative and biotechnology can support self-sustaining societies and food security.
outcomes: Explain global economic and environmental interdependence
Describe international cooperation: Montreal Protocol, GEF, Earth Summit, Cairo conference and Kyoto
Explain sustainable development, the role of NGOs and technologies such as remote sensing

lesson.hook: How do countries agree to protect the air they all share?
lesson.example: Satellite images show forest loss year by year, helping governments act quickly.
lesson.activity: Pupils make a timeline of international environmental agreements.

questions.q: What did the Montreal Protocol do?
questions.a: It phased out ozone-depleting substances.

questions.q: When and where was the Earth Summit held?
questions.a: Rio de Janeiro, 1992.

questions.q: What is sustainable development?
questions.a: Development that meets present needs without harming future generations.

questions.q: How does remote sensing help the environment?
questions.a: It monitors changes like deforestation and helps predict droughts and floods.

lesson.homework: Write about the role of one environmental NGO in India.

topics.title: Basic Concepts of Economics
topics.summary: Lionel Robbins defined economics as the study of human behaviour as a relationship between ends (wants) and scarce means that have alternative uses.
notes: Lionel Robbins defined economics as the study of human behaviour as a relationship between ends (wants) and scarce means that have alternative uses.
Paul Samuelson described it as how societies use scarce resources to produce valuable goods and distribute them among people.
An economy is the system by which people earn a living through production, exchange and consumption.
Consumers buy goods and services to satisfy wants; producers combine resources to make them.
Households supply labour and other resources and spend income; the government makes rules, provides public goods and collects taxes.
Together these entities decide how scarce resources are used.
outcomes: Define economics using the scarcity and allocation views (Robbins, Samuelson)
Identify economic entities: consumers, producers, households and government
Explain the role of each entity in an economy

lesson.hook: Your family, the corner shop and the government all make economic decisions every day. What are they?
lesson.example: A household earns wages from a factory (producer), spends them at shops, and pays taxes that the government uses for roads.
lesson.activity: Pupils draw a circular flow diagram linking households, producers and government.

questions.q: State Robbins's definition of economics.
questions.a: The study of human behaviour as a relationship between ends and scarce means that have alternative uses.

questions.q: What is an economy?
questions.a: The system through which people earn a living by production, exchange and consumption.

questions.q: What role does the government play?
questions.a: It makes rules, provides public goods and collects taxes.

questions.q: What do households supply?
questions.a: Labour and other resources.

lesson.homework: Compare the definitions of Robbins and Samuelson.

chapters.title: Economic Problems, Growth and Types of Economies

topics.title: Economic Problems, Growth and Types of Economies
topics.summary: Every economy must decide what to produce, how to produce and for whom to produce, and use resources efficiently.
notes: Every economy must decide what to produce, how to produce and for whom to produce, and use resources efficiently.
Economic growth is an increase in a country's output or income; economic development also includes better health, education, living standards and equality.
Developed economies have high income and good infrastructure; developing economies are growing but still face poverty; underdeveloped economies have low income and weak infrastructure.
Capitalist economies rely on private ownership and markets; socialist economies on state ownership and planning.
Mixed economies combine private and public sectors under government regulation, as in India.
The type of economy shapes how the central problems are solved.
outcomes: Explain the central problems: what, how and for whom to produce
Distinguish economic growth and economic development
Classify economies as developed, developing, underdeveloped, capitalist, socialist and mixed

lesson.hook: Why is a country with high income not always a developed country?
lesson.example: A country whose GDP rises while most people lack schools and clinics shows growth without development.
lesson.activity: Pupils classify five countries (from a given data table) as developed or developing, with reasons.

questions.q: Name the three central problems of an economy.
questions.a: What, how and for whom to produce.

questions.q: Distinguish economic growth and development.
questions.a: Growth is rising output; development also includes better living standards and welfare.

questions.q: Give two features of a capitalist economy.
questions.a: Private ownership and the price mechanism.

questions.q: What kind of economy is India?
questions.a: A mixed economy.

lesson.homework: Write the features of a mixed economy with Indian examples.

topics.title: Sectors of the Indian Economy
topics.summary: The Indian economy has three main sectors: agriculture (primary), industry (secondary) and services (tertiary).
notes: The Indian economy has three main sectors: agriculture (primary), industry (secondary) and services (tertiary).
Agriculture provides food, raw materials and jobs to a large share of workers.
Industry makes goods and creates jobs; services (banking, transport, IT, health, education) contribute the largest share of national income.
The sectors are interdependent: industry needs farm raw materials, farmers need machines and fertilisers, and both need transport and banks.
By ownership, sectors are private (owned by individuals) or public (owned by government); by area, rural and urban.
The service sector adds to national income, employment and regional development.
outcomes: Describe the agriculture, industry and service sectors and their interdependence
Classify sectors as private and public, and rural and urban
Explain the importance of the service sector

lesson.hook: How does a farmer depend on a factory and a bank?
lesson.example: A sugar mill buys cane from farmers, uses rail to send sugar to cities, and a bank finances both.
lesson.activity: Pupils trace a product of their choice through all three sectors.

questions.q: Which sector contributes the most to India's national income?
questions.a: The service sector.

questions.q: Give one example of sector interdependence.
questions.a: Industries need raw materials from agriculture.

questions.q: Distinguish public and private sectors.
questions.a: Public is owned by government; private by individuals or companies.

questions.q: Give two examples of services.
questions.a: Banking and transport.

lesson.homework: Write the importance of the service sector in India.

topics.title: Agriculture, Industry and the Ecosystem
topics.summary: Agriculture feeds the nation and employs many, but faces small landholdings, dependence on monsoon and low productivity.
notes: Agriculture feeds the nation and employs many, but faces small landholdings, dependence on monsoon and low productivity.
Agricultural harm: large dams submerge land and habitats and displace people; loss of topsoil and desertification; overuse of fertilisers and pesticides.
Measures: smaller hydropower projects, alternative cropping, grassland conservation, manure, biofertilisers, biopesticides, green manuring and compost.
Industry drives growth and jobs, but mining, factories, power generation, vehicles and urbanisation deface land, cut forests and pollute water and air.
Industrial waste from mines, cement plants, refineries and construction spoils landscapes and harms health and aquatic life.
Measures: efficient and eco-friendly technologies, waste segregation, composting, treating effluents before discharge, and enforcing air standards.
outcomes: Explain the role and problems of agriculture and industry in India
Describe the impact of agricultural and industrial practices on the ecosystem
Describe measures to protect the ecosystem

lesson.hook: Can a country grow more food and build more factories without harming nature?
lesson.example: A cement plant that fits dust filters and treats wastewater reduces its harm to nearby villages.
lesson.activity: Groups prepare a "green plan" for a farm and a factory near their town.

questions.q: Give two problems of Indian agriculture.
questions.a: Small landholdings and dependence on monsoon.

questions.q: How do large dams affect the ecosystem?
questions.a: They submerge land and habitats and displace people.

questions.q: Give two eco-friendly alternatives to chemical fertilisers.
questions.a: Compost and biofertilisers.

questions.q: How can industry reduce water pollution?
questions.a: By treating effluents before discharge.

lesson.homework: Write how industrialisation affects the environment of a city.

topics.title: Infrastructure of the Indian Economy
topics.summary: Infrastructure is the basic structure of services that supports economic activity.
notes: Infrastructure is the basic structure of services that supports economic activity.
Economic infrastructure: transport, power, communication, irrigation and banking — it directly supports production.
Social infrastructure: education, health, family welfare and housing — it improves people's quality of life and productivity.
Good infrastructure attracts investment, creates jobs, reduces costs and connects markets.
Poor infrastructure leads to power cuts, traffic delays, illness, low skills and regional imbalance.
Investment in both types is essential for balanced development.
outcomes: Distinguish economic and social infrastructure
Explain the role of infrastructure in development
Discuss problems caused by poor infrastructure

lesson.hook: Why do factories cluster near highways, ports and power plants?
lesson.example: A new all-weather road lets farmers take vegetables to a city market before they spoil.
lesson.activity: Pupils survey infrastructure in their locality and rate it (roads, water, clinics, schools).

questions.q: Distinguish economic and social infrastructure.
questions.a: Economic supports production (transport, power); social improves quality of life (education, health).

questions.q: Give two examples of social infrastructure.
questions.a: Schools and hospitals.

questions.q: How does infrastructure help development?
questions.a: It attracts investment, creates jobs and reduces costs.

questions.q: Give one effect of poor infrastructure.
questions.a: Power cuts and delays that raise costs.

lesson.homework: Write how better health care improves an economy.

topics.title: Consumer Awareness
topics.summary: Consumers are exploited through underweighing, adulteration, poor quality, high prices, duplicate goods and misleading advertisements.
notes: Consumers are exploited through underweighing, adulteration, poor quality, high prices, duplicate goods and misleading advertisements.
Reasons: lack of information, limited choice, illiteracy and weak enforcement.
Consumer rights: safety, information, choice, being heard, redressal and consumer education.
The consumer protection law (COPRA, now the Consumer Protection Act 2019) sets up consumer commissions for redressal.
The Right to Information Act 2005 lets citizens ask public authorities for information, helping them hold services accountable.
Awareness of food adulteration (for example chalk in flour, water in milk) protects health.
outcomes: Describe the ways consumers are exploited and the reasons
Explain consumer rights and the growth of consumer awareness
Describe legal measures: consumer protection law and the Right to Information

lesson.hook: Have you ever bought something that was not what it claimed to be?
lesson.example: FSSAI's home test: a drop of pure milk on a slanting polished surface flows slowly and leaves a white trail; milk mixed with water runs off quickly without a trail.
lesson.activity: Pupils check packaged items for MRP, weight, dates and standard marks.

questions.q: Give three ways consumers are exploited.
questions.a: Underweighing, adulteration and false advertising.

questions.q: Name four consumer rights.
questions.a: Safety, information, choice and redressal.

questions.q: What is the RTI Act?
questions.a: A law that lets citizens obtain information from public authorities.

questions.q: Why is consumer education important?
questions.a: It helps consumers protect themselves from exploitation.

lesson.homework: Write about the harmful effects of food adulteration.

topics.title: Globalisation
topics.summary: Globalisation is the integration of countries through trade, investment, technology and movement of people.
notes: Globalisation is the integration of countries through trade, investment, technology and movement of people.
Enabling factors: technology (transport, internet, communication) and liberalisation (removing trade barriers).
The World Trade Organization (WTO) aims to reduce trade barriers, set fair trade rules and settle trade disputes.
Multinational corporations (MNCs) set up operations in many countries, bringing investment and technology.
Indian companies benefited by reaching global markets, forming partnerships and becoming MNCs themselves.
Globalisation also raises concerns about competition for small producers and environmental harm, as case studies like Bhopal show.
outcomes: Explain the meaning of globalisation and the factors enabling it
State the objectives of the WTO
Describe the impact of globalisation, including MNCs and benefits to Indian companies

lesson.hook: How many things in your house were made in another country?
lesson.example: Indian IT companies serve clients worldwide — a benefit of globalisation.
lesson.activity: Pupils list ten products at home and find where they or their brands come from.

questions.q: What is globalisation?
questions.a: Integration of countries through trade, investment, technology and people.

questions.q: Name two factors enabling globalisation.
questions.a: Technology and liberalisation.

questions.q: Give two objectives of the WTO.
questions.a: Reducing trade barriers and settling trade disputes.

questions.q: How have Indian companies benefited?
questions.a: They reached global markets and some became multinationals.

lesson.homework: Write the advantages and disadvantages of globalisation for India.

topics.title: Demand and Supply
topics.summary: Demand is the quantity buyers are willing and able to buy at a price in a period; supply is the quantity sellers offer at a price.
notes: Demand is the quantity buyers are willing and able to buy at a price in a period; supply is the quantity sellers offer at a price.

Joint demand: goods demanded together (car and petrol); derived demand: demand for inputs arising from demand for a product (labour for houses); composite demand: a good with many uses (milk for tea, curd, sweets).
Law of demand: other things equal, price and quantity demanded move in opposite directions; law of supply: price and quantity supplied move in the same direction.
Market demand/supply is the sum of individual demands/supplies at each price.
A change in the good's own price causes movement along the curve; other factors (income, tastes, prices of related goods, costs, technology) shift the curve.
Exceptions to the law of demand: Giffen goods, prestige (Veblen) goods, expectations of future price rises, and emergencies.
outcomes: Explain demand, supply and types of demand (joint, derived, composite)
State the laws of demand and supply with individual and market schedules and curves
Distinguish movement along and shift of curves, determinants, and exceptions to the law of demand

lesson.hook: Why do people buy more umbrellas in July even at higher prices?
lesson.example: In the rainy season, umbrella demand shifts to the right — people buy more at every price.
lesson.activity: Pupils build individual schedules for three buyers and add them to get a market demand curve.

questions.q: What is derived demand?
questions.a: Demand for an input that arises from demand for the final product.

questions.q: State the law of supply.
questions.a: Other things equal, quantity supplied rises when price rises.

questions.q: What causes a shift of the demand curve?
questions.a: Changes in factors other than price, like income or tastes.

questions.q: Give two exceptions to the law of demand.
questions.a: Giffen goods and prestige goods.

lesson.homework: Draw and explain a market demand curve from three individual schedules.

topics.title: Elasticity of Demand and Supply
topics.summary: Elasticity of demand measures how quantity demanded responds to a price change; elasticity of supply measures the response of quantity supplied.
notes: Elasticity of demand measures how quantity demanded responds to a price change; elasticity of supply measures the response of quantity supplied.
Percentage method: E = % change in quantity ÷ % change in price.
Types: perfectly elastic, relatively elastic (>1), unitary (=1), relatively inelastic (<1) and perfectly inelastic (0).
Factors for demand: substitutes, necessity or luxury, share of income, number of uses, habit and time.
Factors for supply: time period, cost of production, nature of the good (perishable or durable) and technology.
Simple numerical problems apply the percentage method.
outcomes: Explain price elasticity of demand and supply and their types
Measure elasticity using the percentage method
Explain the factors affecting elasticity of demand and supply

lesson.hook: If bus fares rise 20%, do people stop travelling?
lesson.example: Price of tea rises from ₹10 to ₹12 (+20%), sales fall from 100 to 90 cups (−10%): Ed = 10/20 = 0.5, inelastic.
lesson.activity: Pupils solve five numerical problems and classify each good.

questions.q: Write the percentage formula for elasticity of demand.
questions.a: Ed = % change in quantity demanded ÷ % change in price.

questions.q: Why is demand for salt inelastic?
questions.a: It is a necessity with few substitutes and a small share of income.

questions.q: Give two factors affecting elasticity of supply.
questions.a: Time period and nature of the good.

questions.q: Price falls 10% and quantity rises 20%. What is Ed?
questions.a: 2 — relatively elastic.

lesson.homework: Solve: price rises from ₹50 to ₹60 and quantity supplied rises from 200 to 260. Find Es.

topics.title: Factors of Production
topics.summary: Land (all natural resources) is limited, immobile and varies in fertility; its productivity depends on fertility, location, irrigation and methods.
notes: Land (all natural resources) is limited, immobile and varies in fertility; its productivity depends on fertility, location, irrigation and methods.
Changing land use — migration, industrialisation, shifting cultivation, housing, mining, urbanisation and dams — destroys ecosystems.
Labour is human effort for reward; division of labour (simple, complex, territorial) raises skill and output but causes monotony and dependence.
Reasons for low efficiency of Indian labour: poor health and nutrition, low education and training, poor working conditions and outdated tools.
Capital (machines, tools, buildings) is man-made and depreciates; capital formation depends on the ability and willingness to save and on investment.
The entrepreneur organises factors, bears risk, innovates and drives economic development.
outcomes: Explain land and its productivity, and ecosystem damage from changing land use
Explain labour, division of labour and the efficiency of Indian labour
Explain capital, capital formation and the role of the entrepreneur

lesson.hook: What does it take to set up a small factory?
lesson.example: A garment factory divides cutting, stitching and finishing among workers — division of labour increases output.
lesson.activity: Pupils make paper cups alone, then with division of labour, and compare output.

questions.q: Give two characteristics of land.
questions.a: Limited in supply and immobile.

questions.q: Give two reasons for low efficiency of Indian labour.
questions.a: Poor health and low training.

questions.q: What is capital formation?
questions.a: Increase in the stock of capital through saving and investment.

questions.q: Give two functions of an entrepreneur.
questions.a: Bearing risk and innovating.

lesson.homework: Write how changing land use damages ecosystems, with examples.

topics.title: Market Structures
topics.summary: Perfect competition: many buyers and sellers, identical products, free entry and exit, perfect knowledge; firms are price takers.
notes: Perfect competition: many buyers and sellers, identical products, free entry and exit, perfect knowledge; firms are price takers.
Monopoly: one seller, no close substitutes, barriers to entry; the firm is a price maker.
Monopolistic competition: many sellers with differentiated products, advertising and some control over price.
Product differentiation: making a product seem different through brand, design, packaging or service.
Monopsony: a single buyer (for example, the only employer in a town).
Oligopoly: a few large sellers who watch one another, such as mobile networks or airlines.
outcomes: Describe perfectly competitive, monopoly and monopolistically competitive markets
Explain product differentiation
Explain the meaning of monopsony and oligopoly with examples

lesson.hook: Why do soap companies spend so much on advertising?
lesson.example: Toothpastes are similar, but brands, flavours and adverts make each seem different — monopolistic competition.
lesson.activity: Pupils classify ten Indian markets into market structures with reasons.

questions.q: Give two features of perfect competition.
questions.a: Many sellers and identical products.

questions.q: What is product differentiation?
questions.a: Making a product appear different by brand, design or packaging.

questions.q: What is a monopsony?
questions.a: A market with a single buyer.

questions.q: Give an example of oligopoly.
questions.a: Mobile telecom services (or airlines).

lesson.homework: Compare monopoly and perfect competition in a table.

topics.title: The State and Economic Development
topics.summary: The state promotes development by building infrastructure, providing public services, regulating markets and reducing inequality.
notes: The state promotes development by building infrastructure, providing public services, regulating markets and reducing inequality.
Fiscal policy is the government's use of taxation and spending; monetary policy is the central bank's control of money and credit.
Direct taxes (income tax) fall on the payer and are progressive, but may discourage saving; indirect taxes (GST) are convenient and reach everyone, but can burden the poor.
Types: progressive (rate rises with income), proportional (same rate), regressive (heavier on the poor) and degressive (rises slowly up to a limit).
Public sector enterprises build industries and serve welfare, but some suffer losses, inefficiency and political interference.
Privatisation aims at efficiency, competition, less burden on the budget and better services.
outcomes: Explain the role of the state in development
Explain fiscal policy, direct and indirect taxes, and types of taxes
Explain monetary policy, the role and problems of public enterprises, and privatisation

lesson.hook: How does the government use taxes to build roads and reduce inequality?
lesson.example: Income tax slabs that rise with income are progressive.
lesson.activity: Pupils calculate the tax share of a low and a high earner under progressive and proportional taxes.

questions.q: What is fiscal policy?
questions.a: Government policy on taxation and spending.

questions.q: Give one merit and one demerit of indirect taxes.
questions.a: Convenient to collect; can burden the poor.

questions.q: What is a degressive tax?
questions.a: A tax whose rate rises with income up to a limit, then stays constant.

questions.q: Give two reasons for privatisation.
questions.a: Efficiency and reducing the budget burden.

lesson.homework: Write the role and problems of public sector enterprises in India.

topics.title: Money, Inflation and Banking
topics.summary: Money is anything generally accepted as a medium of exchange; functions: medium of exchange, measure of value, store of value, standard of deferred payments and transfer of value.
notes: Money is anything generally accepted as a medium of exchange; functions: medium of exchange, measure of value, store of value, standard of deferred payments and transfer of value.
Inflation is a sustained rise in the general price level; types: creeping, walking, running and hyperinflation.
Effects: debtors gain and creditors lose; fixed-income groups lose; producers may gain in the short run.
Commercial banks accept deposits, give loans, create credit and provide agency and utility services.
The RBI issues currency, is banker to government and banks, lender of last resort and controller of credit.
Credit control: quantitative (bank rate, repo rate, open market operations, CRR, SLR) and qualitative (margin requirements, credit rationing, moral suasion, direct action).
outcomes: Explain money and its functions
Explain inflation, its types and effects
Describe functions of commercial banks and the RBI, and its credit control measures

lesson.hook: Why does ₹100 buy less today than it did ten years ago?
lesson.example: When the RBI raises the repo rate, loans become costlier and spending slows, helping control inflation.
lesson.activity: Pupils role-play the RBI choosing tools for high inflation and for a slowdown.

questions.q: Give three functions of money.
questions.a: Medium of exchange, measure of value and store of value.

questions.q: Who loses during inflation?
questions.a: Creditors and fixed-income groups.

questions.q: Give two functions of the RBI.
questions.a: Issuing currency and controlling credit.

questions.q: Name two quantitative credit control tools.
questions.a: Repo rate and CRR.

lesson.homework: Distinguish quantitative and qualitative credit control.

topics.title: Commercial Organisations: Terms and Classification
topics.summary: Commerce covers trade and aids to trade; business is any activity for profit; industry produces goods; trade is buying and selling.
notes: Commerce covers trade and aids to trade; business is any activity for profit; industry produces goods; trade is buying and selling.
An organisation is a group working towards common goals; a firm is a business unit; a company is a registered body with a separate legal identity.
By activity: manufacturing, trading and service organisations, grouped into industries such as textiles, FMCG (fast-moving consumer goods), automobiles and IT.
By objective: profit-making (businesses) and non-profit (trusts, NGOs) — both need good management.
By ownership: sole proprietorship, partnership, company, cooperative and public sector enterprises.
Each form differs in control, liability, capital and continuity.
outcomes: Define commerce, business, industry, trade, organisation, firm and company
Classify commercial organisations by activity, objective and ownership
Relate classifications to industry groups such as textiles and FMCG

lesson.hook: Is a biscuit company, a hospital trust and a railway the same kind of organisation?
lesson.example: Soap, toothpaste and biscuits are FMCG — sold quickly, in large volumes, at low prices.
lesson.activity: Pupils classify fifteen local organisations by activity, objective and ownership.

questions.q: Distinguish a firm and a company.
questions.a: A firm is any business unit; a company is registered and has a separate legal identity.

questions.q: What is FMCG?
questions.a: Fast-moving consumer goods sold quickly at low prices, such as soap and biscuits.

questions.q: Why do non-profit organisations need good management?
questions.a: To use resources well and achieve their goals.

questions.q: Name three ownership forms.
questions.a: Sole proprietorship, partnership and company.

lesson.homework: Write the features of three forms of ownership.

topics.title: Natural Resources and their Conservation
topics.summary: Natural resources — air, water, soil, metals, minerals, forests and fuels — support all life and business.
notes: Natural resources — air, water, soil, metals, minerals, forests and fuels — support all life and business.
Depletion causes: overuse, unequal distribution, technological and industrial growth, and population growth.
Human activities have degraded the environment physically, chemically and biologically; intensive farming and mining add to it.
Conservation: find alternatives, reduce waste and promote renewable resources.
Biogas plants produce fuel from dung and waste; solar panels convert sunlight to electricity; wind turbines use moving air; hydropower uses flowing water.
Renewable sources are clean and inexhaustible but can be costly or depend on weather; non-renewables are reliable but pollute and will run out.
outcomes: Explain the importance of natural resources
Explain the causes of resource depletion
Describe conservation practices and renewable energy: biogas, solar, wind and hydro

lesson.hook: What happens to a town when its only river dries up?
lesson.example: A village biogas plant turns cattle dung into cooking gas and leaves slurry that is good manure.
lesson.activity: Pupils build a simple chart comparing four renewable sources on cost, reliability and pollution.

questions.q: Give three causes of resource depletion.
questions.a: Overuse, population growth and industrial development.

questions.q: How does a biogas plant work?
questions.a: Dung and waste decompose without air to produce gas for fuel.

questions.q: Give one advantage and one disadvantage of solar energy.
questions.a: Clean and renewable; depends on sunlight and has high initial cost.

questions.q: What are non-renewable resources?
questions.a: Resources that will run out, such as coal and petroleum.

lesson.homework: Write how your family can conserve water and electricity.

topics.title: Pollution and Eco-friendly Industry
topics.summary: Industrial pollution harms air, water and soil, and damages health and ecosystems.
notes: Industrial pollution harms air, water and soil, and damages health and ecosystems.

Sources: vehicles, industries, burning garbage, brick kilns, industrial waste, offshore oil drilling, thermal pollution, chemical fertilisers, biomedical waste, pesticides and radiation (X-rays, nuclear fallout).
Biomedical waste must be segregated and treated to prevent infection.
Measures: cleaner fuels and technology, filters and treatment plants, waste segregation and recycling, and strict enforcement.
Eco-friendly industrial development meets needs without harming the environment.
Businesses that reduce pollution also save resources and build trust.
outcomes: Explain industrial pollution and environmental degradation
Identify sources of pollution
Describe measures for eco-friendly industrial development

lesson.hook: Where does the smoke from a brick kiln go?
