lesson.example: Hospitals use colour-coded bins to separate biomedical waste for safe treatment.
lesson.activity: Pupils map pollution sources around their school and suggest one remedy for each.

questions.q: Name four sources of pollution.
questions.a: Vehicles, industries, brick kilns and burning garbage.

questions.q: What is thermal pollution?
questions.a: Release of heated water into water bodies, harming aquatic life.

questions.q: Why must biomedical waste be treated?
questions.a: To prevent infection and pollution.

questions.q: Give two measures to control industrial pollution.
questions.a: Filters and effluent treatment plants.

lesson.homework: Write why industries should adopt eco-friendly development.

topics.title: Functioning of a Commercial Organisation
topics.summary: Purchase and stores buys materials at the right price and time and keeps stock safely.
notes: Purchase and stores buys materials at the right price and time and keeps stock safely.
Production turns materials into goods of the right quality and quantity.
Marketing and sales understands customers, promotes and sells products.
Finance raises and manages money; HR recruits, trains and cares for staff.
General administration handles day-to-day office work; the legal department ensures the firm follows laws and contracts.
All departments depend on each other: a failure in one affects the rest.
outcomes: Describe the roles of departments in a firm: purchase and stores, production, marketing and sales, finance, HR, administration and legal
Explain how departments depend on each other
Analyse a simple case study of a firm

lesson.hook: What happens in a company when the purchase department forgets to order raw materials?
lesson.example: If stores run out of packaging, production stops, sales miss deliveries and finance loses revenue.
lesson.activity: Groups study a local firm (bakery, printing press) and map its departments and links.

questions.q: What does the purchase department do?
questions.a: Buys materials at the right price and time.

questions.q: What is the role of the legal department?
questions.a: Ensuring the firm follows laws and contracts.

questions.q: Why must departments coordinate?
questions.a: Because each depends on the others.

questions.q: What does general administration handle?
questions.a: Day-to-day office work.

lesson.homework: Draw a chart showing the departments of a firm and their links.

topics.title: Business Communication
topics.summary: As organisations grow, clear communication becomes essential for coordination and decisions.
notes: As organisations grow, clear communication becomes essential for coordination and decisions.
Verbal communication is written (letters, reports, e-mails) or spoken (meetings, calls); non-verbal uses body language, gestures, tone and expressions.
Written communication is recorded and precise but slower; spoken is quick and personal but may be forgotten.
Skills: listening, speaking clearly, writing well, empathy and giving feedback.
Tools: letters (formal), fax (quick copies of documents, now rare), e-mail (fast, cheap), video conferences (meetings across places), memos (internal notes) and telephone calls.
Choose the tool by urgency, formality, cost and need for a record.
outcomes: Explain the growing relevance of communication in organisations
Compare verbal (written, spoken) and non-verbal communication
Describe skills and tools: letter, fax, e-mail, video conference, memo, telephone

lesson.hook: Can your face say something different from your words?
lesson.example: A manager who says "good job" while frowning sends a mixed message — non-verbal cues matter.
lesson.activity: Pupils give the same instruction by memo, e-mail and phone call and compare clarity.

questions.q: Distinguish verbal and non-verbal communication.
questions.a: Verbal uses words; non-verbal uses body language, gestures and tone.

questions.q: Give one advantage of written communication.
questions.a: It provides a record.

questions.q: What is a memo?
questions.a: A short internal written message within an organisation.

questions.q: Name two skills for effective communication.
questions.a: Listening and clear speaking.

lesson.homework: Compare five communication tools in a table.

topics.title: Accounting: Need, Terms and Records
topics.summary: Accounting records, classifies and summarises transactions to show profit and financial position.
notes: Accounting records, classifies and summarises transactions to show profit and financial position.
Every transaction has two sides: one account is debited and another credited.
Terms: capital, liability, asset, revenue, expense, purchases, sales, stock, debtors and creditors.
The journal records transactions first; the ledger groups them by account.
The cash book records cash receipts and payments; the trial balance checks that debits equal credits.
Accurate records help in decisions, taxes and trust with lenders.
outcomes: Explain the need for accounting
Understand debit and credit and basic terms
Describe records: journal, ledger, cash book and trial balance

lesson.hook: How does a business know how much it owns and owes?
lesson.example: A shop that sells goods on credit to a customer records the customer as a debtor until payment.
lesson.activity: Pupils sort ten items into assets, liabilities, revenues and expenses.

questions.q: Why is accounting needed?
questions.a: To know profit, financial position and to make decisions.

questions.q: Who is a debtor?
questions.a: A person who owes money to the business.

questions.q: What is a cash book?
questions.a: A book recording cash receipts and payments.

questions.q: What does a trial balance check?
questions.a: That total debits equal total credits.

lesson.homework: Explain the accounting terms with examples from a shop.

topics.title: Markets and Marketing
topics.summary: A market is wherever buying and selling takes place — shops, online platforms, catalogues, direct sales and tele-markets.
notes: A market is wherever buying and selling takes place — shops, online platforms, catalogues, direct sales and tele-markets.
Marketing is identifying, anticipating and satisfying customer needs profitably.
Marketing has evolved from production focus, to selling focus, to customer focus and societal focus.
Types of markets include local, national and international; consumer and industrial markets.
Products are tangible (durable or non-durable, consumer or industrial); services are intangible, perishable and inseparable from the provider.
Many offerings combine both, such as a restaurant meal.
outcomes: Define markets and marketing, including non-traditional markets
Describe the stages of marketing and types of markets
Distinguish products and services and their types

lesson.hook: Is a TV shopping channel a market?
lesson.example: A tele-market sells insurance by phone — no shop, still a market.
lesson.activity: Pupils list five non-traditional markets they have seen and what each sells.

questions.q: What is a market?
questions.a: Any place or arrangement where buying and selling take place.

questions.q: Give two examples of non-traditional markets.
questions.a: Catalogues and tele-markets (also online stores).

questions.q: Give two features of services.
questions.a: Intangible and perishable.

questions.q: What is the modern focus of marketing?
questions.a: Customer and societal needs.

lesson.homework: Distinguish products and services with examples.

chapters.title: The Marketing Mix and Product Life Cycle

topics.title: The Marketing Mix and Product Life Cycle
topics.summary: The marketing mix (4 Ps): product, price, place (distribution) and promotion.
notes: The marketing mix (4 Ps): product, price, place (distribution) and promotion.
Product life cycle: introduction, growth, maturity and decline — strategy changes at each stage.
Pricing strategies: skimming (high launch price), penetration (low price to win market share), parity (matching competitors) and cost-plus (cost plus a margin).
Distribution channels: direct (producer to consumer), or through wholesalers and retailers.
Promotion: advertising, sales promotion, personal selling, publicity and direct selling.
A good mix fits the target customer and the product's stage.
outcomes: Explain the marketing mix: product, price, place and promotion
Describe the stages of the product life cycle
Explain pricing strategies and distribution channels

lesson.hook: Why do new phones cost the most in their first month?
lesson.example: A new phone launches with skimming prices; as rivals arrive, prices drop — the product moves from introduction to maturity.
lesson.activity: Pupils plan the 4 Ps for a new school snack.

questions.q: Name the 4 Ps.
questions.a: Product, price, place and promotion.

questions.q: What is penetration pricing?
questions.a: A low price to win market share quickly.

questions.q: Name the stages of the product life cycle.
questions.a: Introduction, growth, maturity and decline.

questions.q: What is a direct channel?
questions.a: Selling from producer straight to consumer.

lesson.homework: Draw the product life cycle and describe each stage.

topics.title: Advertising, Branding and Selling
topics.summary: Advertising is paid, non-personal promotion by an identified sponsor through media such as newspapers, TV, radio, internet and outdoor.
notes: Advertising is paid, non-personal promotion by an identified sponsor through media such as newspapers, TV, radio, internet and outdoor.
A brand is a name, symbol or design that identifies a product; brand loyalty is repeated buying; brand equity is the added value of a strong brand.
Sales promotion gives short-term incentives; advertising builds long-term demand; publicity is unpaid.
Selling process: prospecting, approach, presentation, handling objections, closing the sale and follow-up.
Personal selling is face-to-face and can answer questions directly.
A good salesperson is honest, knowledgeable, courteous, persuasive and a good listener.
outcomes: Explain advertising, its types, media, merits and demerits
Explain branding, brand loyalty, brand equity and brand promotion
Describe sales promotion, personal selling, the selling process and qualities of a good salesperson

lesson.hook: Why do people pay more for a branded product?
lesson.example: Customers who always buy one brand of tea even when others are cheaper show brand loyalty.
lesson.activity: Pupils role-play the selling process for a school product.

questions.q: What is brand equity?
questions.a: The added value a strong brand gives a product.

questions.q: Distinguish advertising and sales promotion.
questions.a: Advertising builds long-term demand; sales promotion boosts short-term sales.

questions.q: Name the steps of the selling process.
questions.a: Prospecting, approach, presentation, handling objections, closing and follow-up.

questions.q: Give three qualities of a good salesperson.
questions.a: Honesty, product knowledge and courtesy.

lesson.homework: Write the advantages and disadvantages of advertising.

topics.title: Accounting Principles and Financial Statements
topics.summary: GAAP are common rules for accounting: entity (business separate from owner), duality (every transaction has two sides), matching (expenses matched with related revenue), money measurement and going concern.
notes: GAAP are common rules for accounting: entity (business separate from owner), duality (every transaction has two sides), matching (expenses matched with related revenue), money measurement and going concern.
A receipts and payments account is a summary of cash received and paid (like a cash book), including capital items.
An income and expenditure account shows only revenue incomes and expenses of the period and gives surplus or deficit.
Non-profit organisations prepare both; the income and expenditure account is like a profit and loss account.
A balance sheet shows assets, liabilities and capital (or fund) on a date.
These statements help members, owners and lenders judge the organisation.
outcomes: Explain generally accepted accounting principles: entity, duality, matching, money measurement, going concern
Distinguish receipts and payments account and income and expenditure account
Explain the balance sheet

lesson.hook: How does a school club show members where its money went?
lesson.example: A club buys a computer: it appears in receipts and payments, but not in income and expenditure (a capital item).
lesson.activity: Pupils prepare a receipts and payments account for a class fund.

questions.q: What is the duality concept?
questions.a: Every transaction has two equal sides — debit and credit.

questions.q: Distinguish receipts and payments account and income and expenditure account.
questions.a: The first records all cash received and paid; the second only revenue incomes and expenses for the period.

questions.q: What does a balance sheet show?
questions.a: Assets, liabilities and capital on a date.

questions.q: What is the going concern concept?
questions.a: The business is assumed to continue in the foreseeable future.

lesson.homework: Explain five accounting concepts with examples.

topics.title: Banking
topics.summary: The central bank (RBI) regulates banks and money; commercial banks deal with the public for profit.
notes: The central bank (RBI) regulates banks and money; commercial banks deal with the public for profit.
Accounts: savings, current, recurring and fixed deposit — each suits different needs.
An account holder uses a passbook (record), cheque book (payments) and pay-in slip (deposits).
Advantages of cheques: safe, convenient, a record; disadvantages: can bounce, can be misused, take time to clear.
A bank may refuse payment if funds are insufficient, the signature differs, the cheque is stale (over three months old), post-dated, altered or the account is closed.
A bank draft is prepaid and guaranteed by the bank, unlike a cheque; ATMs allow 24-hour cash and services.
outcomes: Compare the central bank and commercial banks
Describe types of deposit accounts and documents: passbook, cheque book, pay-in slip
Explain cheques, when banks refuse payment, ATMs and bank drafts

lesson.hook: Why might a bank refuse to pay a cheque?
lesson.example: A cheque signed on 1 January and presented on 15 May is stale and will be refused.
lesson.activity: Pupils fill in a sample pay-in slip and cheque (with made-up details) and identify errors in faulty ones.

questions.q: Distinguish the central bank and a commercial bank.
questions.a: The central bank regulates the system; commercial banks serve the public for profit.

questions.q: Give two reasons a bank may refuse a cheque.
questions.a: Insufficient funds and signature mismatch.

questions.q: Distinguish a cheque and a bank draft.
questions.a: A draft is prepaid and guaranteed by the bank; a cheque depends on the account balance.

questions.q: What is a pay-in slip?
questions.a: A form used to deposit money into an account.

lesson.homework: Write the advantages and disadvantages of cheques.

topics.title: Costs
topics.summary: Cost is the amount spent to produce a good or service.
notes: Cost is the amount spent to produce a good or service.
Direct costs can be traced to a product (cloth for a shirt, a tailor's wages per shirt).
Indirect costs are shared (shop rent, electricity, supervisor salary).
Variable costs change with output; fixed costs stay the same; semi-fixed costs have a fixed part and a variable part.
Knowing costs helps fix prices and control spending.
Total cost = fixed cost + variable cost.
outcomes: Explain the concept of cost
Classify costs by nature: direct and indirect
Classify costs by behaviour: variable, fixed and semi-fixed

lesson.hook: Does a tailor's shop rent rise if she stitches more shirts?
lesson.example: Rent ₹10,000 a month is fixed; cloth at ₹200 per shirt is variable: 100 shirts cost ₹10,000 + ₹20,000 = ₹30,000.
lesson.activity: Pupils classify fifteen costs of a school canteen.

questions.q: Give an example of a direct cost.
questions.a: Raw material used in a product.

questions.q: Give an example of a fixed cost.
questions.a: Rent.

questions.q: What is a semi-fixed cost?
questions.a: A cost with a fixed part and a part that varies with output.

questions.q: How is total cost found?
questions.a: Fixed cost plus variable cost.

lesson.homework: Calculate total cost for 50 and 150 units given fixed and variable costs.

topics.title: Human Resources
topics.summary: HRM manages people: planning, recruitment, selection, training, appraisal, pay and welfare.
notes: HRM manages people: planning, recruitment, selection, training, appraisal, pay and welfare.
Recruitment sources: internal (promotion, transfer) and external (advertisements, placement agencies, campus, online); methods: direct and indirect.
Selection chooses the best candidates through tests and interviews (structured, unstructured, group, panel).
Training is important for productivity, safety and morale.
On-the-job methods: coaching, understudy, "assistant to" positions, job rotation, committee membership and apprenticeship.
Off-the-job methods: internship, vestibule training (a replica workplace), case study, role playing, lectures and sensitivity training.
outcomes: Explain the features, role and functions of human resource management
Describe recruitment sources and methods
Explain selection, interviews and methods of training

lesson.hook: What makes a new employee feel ready for the job?
lesson.example: Airlines train pilots in simulators — a form of vestibule training.
lesson.activity: Pupils design a two-week training plan for a new school office assistant.

questions.q: Give two functions of HRM.
questions.a: Recruitment and training.

questions.q: What is vestibule training?
questions.a: Training in a replica of the actual workplace.

questions.q: Give two on-the-job training methods.
questions.a: Coaching and job rotation.

questions.q: Name two types of interviews.
questions.a: Structured and panel interviews.

lesson.homework: Distinguish recruitment and selection.

topics.title: Public Relations
topics.summary: Public relations (PR) builds and maintains goodwill and understanding between an organisation and its public.
notes: Public relations (PR) builds and maintains goodwill and understanding between an organisation and its public.
Its scope covers customers, employees, investors, media, government and the community.
Elements: human relations (good relationships), empathy (understanding others' feelings), persuasion (convincing through reason) and dialogue (two-way communication).
PR grew from press agentry to a strategic management function using media and digital platforms.
Ethical PR is truthful, transparent and respects the public; unethical spin damages trust.
Business ethics is increasingly important to PR and reputation.
outcomes: Explain the meaning, nature and scope of public relations
Describe elements: human relations, empathy, persuasion and dialogue
Discuss the history, present status and ethics of public relations

lesson.hook: How does a company rebuild trust after a mistake?
lesson.example: A company that recalls a faulty product quickly and apologises openly protects its reputation.
lesson.activity: Pupils draft an honest public statement for a school after a canteen hygiene problem.

questions.q: What is public relations?
questions.a: Building goodwill and understanding between an organisation and its public.

questions.q: Name the four elements of PR.
questions.a: Human relations, empathy, persuasion and dialogue.

questions.q: Why is ethics important in PR?
questions.a: Truthfulness builds long-term trust.

questions.q: Who is the public for a company?
questions.a: Customers, employees, investors, media, government and community.

lesson.homework: Write about the role of PR in a modern business.

topics.title: Environment, Values and Consumer Education
topics.summary: Industrialisation, business units, transport, tourism and mining destroy ecosystems; minerals and non-renewable resources are overused.
notes: Industrialisation, business units, transport, tourism and mining destroy ecosystems; minerals and non-renewable resources are overused.
Energy crisis affects cities (power shortages) and villages (fuel wood scarcity); renewable sources help.
Greenhouse gases cause global warming, with rising seas and extreme weather; acid rain damages crops, lakes and buildings.
Environmental values: fundamental duties, cloth bags, organic manure, clean surroundings, refusing polybags and styrofoam, reusing containers and recycling paper.
Consumer education teaches rights, wise choices and awareness of food adulteration.
Disasters like Bhopal (1984) and Chernobyl (1986) show pollution's human cost; the Chipko movement showed community power to protect forests.
outcomes: Explain ecosystem destruction and resource overuse by business
Explain the energy crisis, greenhouse effect, global warming and acid rain
Discuss environmental values, consumer education, pollution disasters and community movements like Chipko

lesson.hook: Can a single cloth bag make a difference?
lesson.example: In the Chipko movement villagers, many of them women, hugged trees to stop them being cut.
lesson.activity: Pupils run a one-week "refuse the polybag" challenge and report the results.

questions.q: Give two causes of ecosystem destruction.
questions.a: Mining and industrialisation.

questions.q: What is acid rain?
questions.a: Rain made acidic by sulphur and nitrogen oxides from pollution.

questions.q: Give two examples of environmental values.
questions.a: Using cloth bags and recycling paper.

questions.q: What was the Chipko movement?
questions.a: A community movement in which villagers hugged trees to stop felling.

lesson.homework: Write how consumer education protects people.

chapters.title: Concept and Scope of Home Science

topics.title: Concept and Scope of Home Science
topics.summary: Home Science is an applied science with five streams: Foods and Nutrition, Resource Management, Human Development, Textiles and Clothing, and Communication and Extension.
notes: Home Science is an applied science with five streams: Foods and Nutrition, Resource Management, Human Development, Textiles and Clothing, and Communication and Extension.
Foods and Nutrition studies food, health and diet; Resource Management covers money, time, energy and the home.
Human Development studies growth from infancy to old age; Textiles and Clothing covers fibres, fabrics and garments.
Communication and Extension teaches how to share knowledge with families and communities.
The streams combine to improve the quality of life of individuals, families and communities.
Home Science builds life skills and leads to careers in dietetics, design, child care, textiles and community work.
outcomes: Describe the five streams of Home Science
Explain how the streams integrate
Explain the significance of Home Science in daily life

lesson.hook: Is Home Science only about cooking?
lesson.example: Planning a family's weekly meals within a budget uses nutrition, resource management and communication together.
lesson.activity: Pupils list one everyday task for each stream of Home Science.

questions.q: Name the five streams of Home Science.
questions.a: Foods and Nutrition, Resource Management, Human Development, Textiles and Clothing, Communication and Extension.

questions.q: What does Human Development study?
questions.a: Growth and development across the life span.

questions.q: Why is Home Science called multi-disciplinary?
questions.a: It combines knowledge from several sciences to improve daily life.

questions.q: Name two careers linked with Home Science.
questions.a: Dietitian and textile designer.

lesson.homework: Write how Home Science helps a family.

topics.title: Food and its Functions
topics.summary: Food is anything eaten that nourishes the body; nutrients are its useful substances; nutrition is how the body uses food.
notes: Food is anything eaten that nourishes the body; nutrients are its useful substances; nutrition is how the body uses food.
A balanced diet has all nutrients in the right amounts; malnutrition is too little or too much; optimum nutrition is the best level for health.
Functions of food: physiological (energy, growth, protection), psychological (comfort, satisfaction) and social (sharing, celebration, hospitality).
Cookery terms: cutting, chopping, grating, kneading, beating, peeling, stringing, julienne, mashing, cut-and-fold, blending and dusting.
Herbs such as mint, coriander, basil and curry leaves add flavour and nutrients.
Spices such as turmeric, ginger, garlic, cumin and cardamom aid digestion and flavour; they support, but do not replace, medical care.
outcomes: Define food, nutrient, nutrition, balanced diet, health, malnutrition and optimum nutrition
Explain the physiological, psychological and social functions of food
Explain basic cookery terms and the health benefits of common herbs and spices

lesson.hook: Why do festival meals make us feel happy, not just full?
lesson.example: Sharing sweets at Diwali or Eid shows the social function of food.
lesson.activity: Pupils demonstrate three cookery terms (grating, kneading, julienne) with safe tools under supervision.

questions.q: What is nutrition?
questions.a: The process by which the body takes in and uses food.

questions.q: Give the three functions of food.
questions.a: Physiological, psychological and social.

questions.q: What does "julienne" mean?
questions.a: Cutting food into thin matchstick strips.

questions.q: Give two herbs used in Indian cooking.
questions.a: Mint and curry leaves.

lesson.homework: Write the health benefits of five spices found in your kitchen.

topics.title: Nutrients and Deficiency Diseases
topics.summary: Energy-giving: carbohydrates (cereals, sugar) and fats (oil, ghee, nuts).
notes: Energy-giving: carbohydrates (cereals, sugar) and fats (oil, ghee, nuts).
Body-building: proteins (pulses, milk, eggs, meat) and minerals.
Protective: vitamins A, D, E, K, B-complex (thiamine, riboflavin, niacin) and C; minerals calcium, iron and iodine.
Regulatory: water and roughage (fibre) help digestion and body processes.
Deficiencies: vitamin A — night blindness; vitamin D — rickets; vitamin C — scurvy; thiamine — beriberi; niacin — pellagra; iron — anaemia; iodine — goitre; protein-energy — kwashiorkor and marasmus.
A varied diet with cereals, pulses, vegetables, fruits and milk prevents most deficiencies.
outcomes: Classify nutrients by function: energy-giving, body-building, protective and regulatory
State sources and functions of carbohydrates, fats, proteins, vitamins, minerals, water and roughage
Identify deficiency diseases

lesson.hook: Why do some children get night blindness?
lesson.example: Iodised salt has greatly reduced goitre in India.
lesson.activity: Pupils classify foods from their lunch boxes into nutrient groups.

questions.q: Name two energy-giving nutrients.
questions.a: Carbohydrates and fats.

questions.q: Which vitamin deficiency causes night blindness?
questions.a: Vitamin A.

questions.q: What causes anaemia?
questions.a: Iron deficiency.

questions.q: What is the role of roughage?
questions.a: It aids digestion and prevents constipation.

lesson.homework: Make a chart of nutrients, sources, functions and deficiency diseases.

chapters.title: Growth and Development from Birth to Five

topics.title: Growth and Development from Birth to Five
topics.summary: Growth is increase in size; development is increase in skills and abilities.
notes: Growth is increase in size; development is increase in skills and abilities.
Principles: development follows a pattern (head to toe, centre outwards), is continuous, proceeds from general to specific, and each child has an individual pace.
Milestones are skills most children reach around a certain age.
Physical and motor: holding the head up (about 3 months), sitting (about 6 months), walking (about 12 months), running and climbing later.
Language: cooing, babbling, first words around one year, short sentences by two to three years.
Social, emotional and cognitive: smiling, recognising familiar people, playing with others, curiosity and problem-solving grow over these years.
outcomes: Distinguish growth and development
State the principles of development
Describe milestones of physical, motor, social, emotional, cognitive and language development from birth to five

lesson.hook: At what age do most babies take their first steps?
lesson.example: A baby controls its head before it can sit, and sits before it walks — development proceeds from head to toe.
lesson.activity: Pupils make a timeline of milestones from birth to five years.

questions.q: Distinguish growth and development.
questions.a: Growth is increase in size; development is increase in skills.

questions.q: Give two principles of development.
questions.a: It follows a pattern and each child has an individual pace.

questions.q: Around what age do most children walk?
questions.a: About 12 months.

questions.q: What is a developmental milestone?
questions.a: A skill most children achieve around a certain age.

lesson.homework: Observe a young child in your family and note three milestones.

topics.title: Play, Play-schools and Immunisation
topics.summary: Play develops the body, mind, language, emotions and social skills together.
notes: Play develops the body, mind, language, emotions and social skills together.
Choose safe, age-suitable indoor and outdoor play and materials.
Types of play: constructive (building), fantasy (pretend), solitary (alone), cooperative (with others) and creative (art, music).
Play schools: Montessori (self-directed learning with special materials), nursery and kindergarten.
Common childhood diseases: tuberculosis, mumps, measles, chickenpox, diphtheria, pertussis (whooping cough), tetanus, rubella and polio.
Immunisation protects children with vaccines such as BCG (TB), DPT (diphtheria, pertussis, tetanus), OPV/IPV (polio) and MMR (measles, mumps, rubella); following the national schedule is important.
outcomes: Explain the role of play in holistic development
Describe types of play and play materials
Describe types of play schools, common childhood diseases, vaccines and immunisation

lesson.hook: Is play a waste of time for young children?
lesson.example: Building with blocks (constructive play) improves hand skills, planning and patience.
lesson.activity: Pupils design a safe play corner for a nursery with materials for each type of play.

questions.q: Give two benefits of play.
questions.a: Physical development and social skills.

questions.q: What is fantasy play?
questions.a: Pretend play, such as playing house.

questions.q: Which vaccine protects against tuberculosis?
questions.a: BCG.

questions.q: What does MMR protect against?
questions.a: Measles, mumps and rubella.

lesson.homework: Write why immunisation is important for every child.

topics.title: Colour in the Home
topics.summary: Hue is the name of a colour; value is its lightness or darkness; intensity is its brightness or dullness.
notes: Hue is the name of a colour; value is its lightness or darkness; intensity is its brightness or dullness.
The Prang colour wheel: primary (red, yellow, blue), secondary (orange, green, violet) and tertiary colours.
Warm colours (red, orange, yellow) feel lively; cool colours (blue, green, violet) feel calm; neutrals (white, grey, beige) balance; metallics add shine.
Related schemes: monochromatic (one hue in different values) and analogous (neighbouring hues).
Contrasting schemes: complementary, double complementary, split complementary, triad and tetrad.
Living rooms suit lively schemes; bedrooms calm schemes; kitchens light, clean colours.
outcomes: Explain the dimensions of colour: hue, value and intensity
Describe the Prang colour wheel and warm, cool, neutral and metallic colours
Apply related and contrasting colour schemes to rooms

lesson.hook: Why do bedrooms often use soft blues and greens?
lesson.example: A bedroom in shades of blue (monochromatic) feels restful.
lesson.activity: Pupils paint a colour wheel and plan colour schemes for two rooms.

questions.q: What is hue?
questions.a: The name of a colour.

questions.q: Name the primary colours on the Prang wheel.
questions.a: Red, yellow and blue.

questions.q: What is an analogous scheme?
questions.a: A scheme using colours next to each other on the wheel.

questions.q: Which colours feel calm?
questions.a: Cool colours such as blue and green.

lesson.homework: Plan colour schemes for a living room and a study.

chapters.title: Lighting, Energy and Sanitation in the Home

topics.title: Lighting, Energy and Sanitation in the Home
topics.summary: Lighting: general (whole room) and local/task (reading, cooking); direct and indirect; natural and artificial sources.
notes: Lighting: general (whole room) and local/task (reading, cooking); direct and indirect; natural and artificial sources.
Choose adequate lighting: bright task light in the kitchen and study, softer light in bedrooms.
Conserve cooking gas (soak pulses, use lids, pressure cookers), water (fix leaks, reuse) and electricity (LEDs, switch off, efficient appliances).
Sanitation and hygiene inside and outside the home prevent disease.
Waste should be segregated into biodegradable and non-biodegradable, organic and inorganic, plastic, metal and e-waste.
The five Rs — reduce, refuse, reuse, recycle and reinvent — conserve resources.
outcomes: Describe types and sources of lighting and choose lighting for rooms
Explain sustainable use and conservation of cooking gas, water and electricity
Explain sanitation, hygiene, waste segregation and the five Rs

lesson.hook: How much electricity does your home waste in a day?
lesson.example: Cooking dal in a pressure cooker with soaked pulses saves both time and gas.
lesson.activity: Pupils audit energy and water use at home for a day and suggest five savings.

questions.q: Distinguish general and task lighting.
questions.a: General lights the whole room; task lights a specific activity.

questions.q: Give two ways to save cooking gas.
questions.a: Use lids and pressure cookers (also soak pulses).

questions.q: Why segregate waste?
questions.a: To allow recycling and composting and prevent pollution.

questions.q: Name the five Rs.
questions.a: Reduce, refuse, reuse, recycle and reinvent.

lesson.homework: Make a home energy-saving checklist.

topics.title: Fibres: Properties and Uses
topics.summary: A fibre is the basic hair-like unit from which yarns and fabrics are made.
notes: A fibre is the basic hair-like unit from which yarns and fabrics are made.
Natural fibres: cotton (from cotton bolls), silk (from silkworm cocoons) and wool (from sheep's fleece).
Man-made (regenerated) fibre: rayon from wood pulp; synthetic fibres: nylon and polyester from petrochemicals.
Properties: cotton is absorbent and cool; silk is smooth, lustrous and strong; wool is warm and elastic; nylon is very strong and elastic; polyester resists wrinkles.
Burning tests (done by the teacher, with care): cotton and rayon burn like paper leaving soft ash; silk and wool smell like burning hair; nylon and polyester melt into hard beads.
Under a microscope, cotton looks like a twisted ribbon and wool shows scales.
outcomes: Define fibre and classify fibres as natural, man-made and synthetic
Describe origin and properties of cotton, silk, wool, rayon, nylon and polyester
Identify fibres by microscopic appearance and burning tests

lesson.hook: How can you tell silk from polyester without reading the label?
lesson.example: A thread that melts into a hard bead when burnt is synthetic, such as polyester.
lesson.activity: Teacher demonstrates burning tests on small samples with safety precautions; pupils record smell, flame and residue.

questions.q: Give an example of a regenerated fibre.
questions.a: Rayon.

questions.q: Which fibre smells like burning hair?
questions.a: Silk or wool.

questions.q: How does polyester behave in a burning test?
questions.a: It melts and forms a hard bead.

questions.q: Give one property of cotton.
questions.a: It is absorbent and cool.

lesson.homework: Compare the properties and uses of six fibres in a table.

topics.title: Fabric Structure
topics.summary: Yarn is fibres twisted together; fabric is made by weaving, knitting or bonding yarns or fibres.
notes: Yarn is fibres twisted together; fabric is made by weaving, knitting or bonding yarns or fibres.
In weaving, warp yarns run lengthwise and weft yarns run crosswise; the selvedge is the firm edge along the warp.
Plain weave: over one, under one — strong and simple (muslin, poplin).
Twill weave: diagonal lines, durable (denim, gabardine); satin weave: long floats, smooth and lustrous.
Decorative weaves include spot weaves and pile weaves (cut pile like velvet, uncut pile like terry towelling).
Non-woven fabrics like felt are made by bonding fibres; knitted fabrics (hand or machine) interlock loops and stretch, used for sweaters and T-shirts.
outcomes: Define yarn, warp, weft, selvedge and fabric
Describe woven fabrics: plain, twill, satin and decorative weaves
Describe non-woven and knitted fabrics and their uses

lesson.hook: Why does denim have diagonal lines on it?
lesson.example: Denim's diagonal lines come from its twill weave.
lesson.activity: Pupils weave a paper mat in plain and twill patterns.

questions.q: Distinguish warp and weft.
questions.a: Warp runs lengthwise; weft runs crosswise.

questions.q: What is the selvedge?
questions.a: The firm finished edge of a fabric along the warp.

questions.q: Give an example of twill fabric.
questions.a: Denim.

questions.q: How is felt made?
questions.a: By bonding fibres together without weaving or knitting.

lesson.homework: Collect fabric samples and identify their weaves.

topics.title: Communication
topics.summary: Communication is sharing information, ideas and feelings between people.
notes: Communication is sharing information, ideas and feelings between people.
Functions: informing, persuading, expressing feelings, building relationships and solving problems.
Elements: sender, message, medium, receiver and feedback.
Interpersonal communication is between individuals, face to face or through media.
Skills: listening attentively, speaking clearly, reading with understanding and writing correctly.
Good communication strengthens families and communities.
outcomes: Explain the meaning, functions and importance of communication
Describe the elements of communication
Explain interpersonal communication and the skills of listening, speaking, reading and writing

lesson.hook: Why do arguments often start from misunderstandings?
lesson.example: Repeating back what a friend said ("So you mean…") checks understanding — active listening.
lesson.activity: Pupils play a listening game where instructions are passed and checked with feedback.

questions.q: Name the elements of communication.
questions.a: Sender, message, medium, receiver and feedback.

questions.q: What is interpersonal communication?
questions.a: Communication between individuals.

questions.q: Give two functions of communication.
questions.a: Informing and building relationships.

questions.q: Why is feedback important?
questions.a: It shows whether the message was understood.

lesson.homework: Write five tips for being a good listener.

topics.title: Family Budget and Saving
topics.summary: A family budget is a plan of expected income and expenditure for a period.
notes: A family budget is a plan of expected income and expenditure for a period.
Types: surplus (income more than expenditure), balanced (equal) and deficit (expenditure more than income).
Factors: size and composition of the family, stage of the life cycle and socio-economic status.
Steps: estimate income, list needs and wants, allot money to each head (food, rent, education, health, savings), compare and adjust, review.
Saving is keeping part of income for future needs and emergencies — in banks, post office schemes or recurring deposits.
Budgeting helps plan and use limited resources wisely.
outcomes: Explain the concept and importance of a family budget
Describe surplus, balanced and deficit budgets and factors affecting them
Prepare a family budget and explain the importance of saving

lesson.hook: Why do some families run out of money before the month ends?
lesson.example: A family earning ₹40,000 that plans ₹36,000 of expenses and saves ₹4,000 has a surplus budget.
lesson.activity: Pupils prepare a monthly budget for a family of four from a given income.

questions.q: What is a family budget?
questions.a: A plan of expected income and expenditure for a period.

questions.q: What is a deficit budget?
questions.a: One where expenditure exceeds income.

questions.q: Give two factors affecting a family budget.
questions.a: Family size and socio-economic status.

questions.q: Why is saving important?
questions.a: For future needs and emergencies.

lesson.homework: Prepare a budget for a family function within a fixed amount.

topics.title: Kitchen Planning and Home Furnishing
topics.summary: A good kitchen considers aspect (direction), size, colour, ventilation, walls, flooring, work counters, lighting and storage.
notes: A good kitchen considers aspect (direction), size, colour, ventilation, walls, flooring, work counters, lighting and storage.
Layouts: one-walled, corridor (galley), L-shaped, U-shaped and island.
The work triangle links the preparation, cooking and washing centres; a compact triangle saves time and energy.
Modular kitchens use pre-made units that fit the space efficiently.
Home furnishing includes curtains, floor coverings and upholstery; objectives: beauty, expressiveness and functionalism.
Selection depends on use, budget, climate, care and the room's colour scheme.
outcomes: Describe features of a good kitchen and kitchen layouts
Explain the work triangle and modular kitchens
Explain the objectives and selection of home furnishings

lesson.hook: Why do some kitchens feel tiring to work in?
lesson.example: In an L-shaped kitchen, sink, stove and counter form a tight triangle, reducing walking.
lesson.activity: Pupils draw their home kitchen and mark the work triangle, then suggest one improvement.

questions.q: Name three kitchen layouts.
questions.a: One-walled, L-shaped and U-shaped.

questions.q: What is the work triangle?
questions.a: The link between preparation, cooking and washing centres.

questions.q: What is a modular kitchen?
questions.a: A kitchen built from pre-made units that fit the space.

questions.q: Give the three objectives of home furnishing.
questions.a: Beauty, expressiveness and functionalism.

lesson.homework: Plan the furnishing of a living room within a budget.

chapters.title: Growth and Development in Middle Childhood

topics.title: Growth and Development in Middle Childhood
topics.summary: Middle childhood (6–12 years) brings steady growth and development of physical, social, emotional, cognitive and language skills.
notes: Middle childhood (6–12 years) brings steady growth and development of physical, social, emotional, cognitive and language skills.
Physical: steady growth, better coordination and strength; cognitive: logical thinking, reading and reasoning grow.
Social and emotional: friendships deepen; children learn rules and cooperation and manage feelings better.
The "gang age" is when children form close peer groups with shared rules and loyalty.
The family gives love, values and security; the peer group teaches cooperation, competition and belonging; the school builds knowledge, discipline and social skills.
Balanced guidance helps children avoid negative peer pressure.
outcomes: Describe growth and development between 6 and 12 years
Explain the gang age
Explain the roles of family, peer group and school in social development

lesson.hook: Why do children of 9–10 love belonging to a group?
lesson.example: A group of ten-year-olds who form a "club" with a secret handshake shows the gang age.
lesson.activity: Pupils recall their own friend groups at age 9–10 and what they learned from them.

questions.q: What is the gang age?
questions.a: The stage in middle childhood when children form close peer groups.

questions.q: Give one role of the family in middle childhood.
questions.a: Giving love, values and security.

questions.q: What does the peer group teach?
questions.a: Cooperation, competition and belonging.

questions.q: Name two cognitive changes in middle childhood.
questions.a: Logical thinking and reasoning.

lesson.homework: Write the role of school in a child's social development.

topics.title: Learning Difficulties
topics.summary: A learning difficulty is a condition that affects how a child learns particular skills, despite normal intelligence.
notes: A learning difficulty is a condition that affects how a child learns particular skills, despite normal intelligence.
Dyslexia: difficulty with reading, spelling and recognising words.
Dysgraphia: difficulty with handwriting and putting thoughts on paper.
Dyscalculia: difficulty with numbers and mathematical concepts.
ADHD: difficulty with attention, hyperactivity and impulsiveness.
Early identification, patience, suitable teaching methods and acceptance by family, school and peers help children succeed; teasing and labels harm them.
outcomes: Explain the meaning of learning difficulty
Describe dyslexia, dysgraphia, dyscalculia and ADHD
Explain the roles of family, school and peers in acceptance and support

lesson.hook: Why might a bright child still struggle to read?
lesson.example: A child with dyslexia may understand a story well when it is read aloud but struggle to read it alone.
lesson.activity: Pupils discuss how classmates can support someone with a learning difficulty.

questions.q: What is dyslexia?
questions.a: A learning difficulty affecting reading and spelling.

questions.q: What is dyscalculia?
questions.a: Difficulty with numbers and mathematics.

questions.q: Name two signs of ADHD.
questions.a: Difficulty paying attention and hyperactivity.

questions.q: How can peers help?
questions.a: By accepting, supporting and not teasing.

lesson.homework: Write how schools can support children with learning difficulties.

topics.title: Meal Planning
topics.summary: Five food groups: cereals, roots and tubers; pulses and legumes; milk and meat products; fruits and vegetables; sugars and fats.
notes: Five food groups: cereals, roots and tubers; pulses and legumes; milk and meat products; fruits and vegetables; sugars and fats.
Cereals give energy; pulses and milk give protein; fruits and vegetables give vitamins, minerals and fibre; fats and sugars give concentrated energy.
Meal planning is deciding in advance what to cook and serve.
Principles: meet nutritional needs of each member, include variety, suit the budget, save time and energy, and consider likes and customs.
Factors: age, gender, activity, health, income, season, availability of food and family traditions.
Good planning reduces waste and keeps the family healthy.
outcomes: Describe the five basic food groups and their nutritional contribution
Explain meal planning, its principles and importance
Explain factors affecting meal planning

lesson.hook: How can a family eat well without spending too much?
lesson.example: Dal, rice, vegetable curry, curd and a fruit together cover all five food groups.
lesson.activity: Pupils plan a day's menu for a family with a child, a working adult and a grandparent.

questions.q: Name the five food groups.
questions.a: Cereals/roots and tubers; pulses; milk and meat; fruits and vegetables; sugars and fats.

questions.q: What is meal planning?
questions.a: Deciding in advance what to cook and serve.

questions.q: Give two principles of meal planning.
questions.a: Meet nutritional needs and include variety.

questions.q: Give two factors affecting meal planning.
questions.a: Income and age of family members.

lesson.homework: Plan a week's menu for your family using the five food groups.

topics.title: Food Hygiene, Storage and Preservation
topics.summary: Food hygiene means handling food so it stays safe and clean.
notes: Food hygiene means handling food so it stays safe and clean.
Personal hygiene: wash hands, cover hair, keep nails short and avoid handling food when ill; keep the kitchen clean and safe.

Perishable foods (milk, meat, fish, leafy vegetables) spoil quickly and need refrigeration; semi-perishable foods (potatoes, onions, flour) last weeks; non-perishable foods (rice, pulses, sugar) last months in dry containers.
Food preservation prevents spoilage: sun drying, freezing, and using salt, sugar, spices, oil or permitted chemical preservatives.
Pickles use salt, oil and spices; jams use sugar; papads and vadis are sun-dried.
Convenience foods save time but can cost more and may contain more salt, fat and preservatives.
outcomes: Explain food hygiene in purchase, storage, preparation and serving
Classify foods as perishable, semi-perishable and non-perishable and store them correctly
Describe household methods of food preservation and convenience foods

lesson.hook: Why does milk spoil in a day while rice lasts for months?
lesson.example: Mango pickle keeps for months because salt and oil stop microbes from growing.
lesson.activity: Pupils classify twenty kitchen foods into perishable, semi-perishable and non-perishable, with storage methods.

questions.q: What is food hygiene?
questions.a: Handling food so it stays safe and clean.

questions.q: Give two examples of perishable foods.
questions.a: Milk and fish.

questions.q: Name three household methods of preservation.
questions.a: Sun drying, freezing and using salt or sugar.

questions.q: Give one advantage and one disadvantage of convenience foods.
questions.a: Save time; may contain more salt and preservatives.

lesson.homework: Write the rules of hygiene for a school canteen.

topics.title: Selecting Fabrics and Garments
topics.summary: Fabric selection depends on age, gender, occupation, season, occasion, fashion and budget.
notes: Fabric selection depends on age, gender, occupation, season, occasion, fashion and budget.
Cotton suits hot weather; wool suits cold; synthetics are durable and easy to care for.
For ready-made garments, check fit, colour (and colourfastness), workmanship (stitches, seams, buttons), cost and ease of maintenance.
Good workmanship: even, secure stitches, wide enough seams, neat finishing and matching patterns.
Read labels for fibre content and care instructions.
A well-made garment lasts longer and gives better value.
outcomes: Explain factors affecting the selection of fabric
Explain factors in choosing ready-made garments
Apply selection to real purchases

lesson.hook: Why might a cheap shirt cost more in the long run?
lesson.example: Checking that seams are wide and stitches small before buying prevents a shirt from tearing soon.
lesson.activity: Pupils examine two garments and grade them on fit, workmanship and care label.

questions.q: Give three factors affecting fabric selection.
questions.a: Season, occasion and budget.

questions.q: What should be checked in workmanship?
questions.a: Stitches, seams, buttons and finishing.

questions.q: Why read care labels?
questions.a: To know fibre content and how to wash and maintain the garment.

questions.q: Which fabric suits hot weather?
questions.a: Cotton.

lesson.homework: Write a checklist for buying a school uniform.

topics.title: Laundering Clothes
topics.summary: Laundering is washing, drying and finishing clothes to keep them clean and in good condition.
notes: Laundering is washing, drying and finishing clothes to keep them clean and in good condition.
Cotton: can be washed with soap or detergent, rubbed or brushed, and ironed hot; whites may be starched and blued.
Silk: wash gently in lukewarm water with a mild detergent, do not rub or wring, dry in shade, iron on low heat.
Wool: wash in lukewarm water, squeeze gently, avoid hot water and rubbing (which cause shrinking and felting), dry flat in shade.
Synthetics: wash in warm water with detergent, do not wring, drip dry, iron at low temperature.
Starch gives crispness; blue and optical brighteners make whites look whiter; detergents work well even in hard water.
outcomes: Describe household laundering of cotton, silk, wool and synthetics
Explain the use of soaps, detergents, starch, blue and optical brighteners
Follow care labels to prevent damage

lesson.hook: Why did a woollen sweater shrink after washing?
lesson.example: Hot water and rubbing make wool fibres lock together and shrink — felting.
lesson.activity: Pupils prepare a step-by-step washing chart for four fabrics.

questions.q: How should wool be dried?
questions.a: Flat in the shade.

questions.q: Why should silk not be wrung?
questions.a: It can weaken and damage the fibres.

questions.q: What does starch do?
questions.a: Gives crispness to fabrics.

questions.q: What is an optical brightener?
questions.a: A substance that makes whites look whiter.

lesson.homework: Write the steps for washing a cotton shirt and a woollen sweater.

topics.title: Development Terms and Schemes
topics.summary: Gender discrimination is unfair treatment because of gender; women's empowerment gives women equal rights, choices and resources.
notes: Gender discrimination is unfair treatment because of gender; women's empowerment gives women equal rights, choices and resources.
Sex ratio is the number of females per 1000 males; female foeticide and infanticide lower it and are crimes.
Child labour, child abuse and human trafficking violate children's rights; morbidity is illness in a population, mortality is death rate.

Carbon footprint is the greenhouse gas caused by a person's activities; population explosion is very rapid population growth; human capital is people's skills and health; the poverty line marks the minimum income for basic needs.
DWCRA supported groups of rural women for income generation; MGNREGA guarantees 100 days of wage work to rural households.
Ayushman Bharat (PM-JAY) gives health insurance cover to poor families; Ujjwala Yojana provides LPG connections to poor households.
outcomes: Explain development terms such as gender discrimination, women's empowerment, sex ratio, child labour, human trafficking and poverty line
Explain terms such as carbon footprint, endangered species, population explosion and human capital
Describe schemes: DWCRA, MGNREGA, Ayushman Bharat and Ujjwala Yojana

lesson.hook: What do government schemes actually do for a village family?
lesson.example: An LPG connection under Ujjwala replaces a smoky wood stove, protecting women's and children's health.
lesson.activity: Pupils prepare posters on one scheme: aim, target group and benefits.

questions.q: What is sex ratio?
questions.a: The number of females per 1000 males.

questions.q: What does MGNREGA guarantee?
questions.a: 100 days of wage employment to rural households.

questions.q: What does Ujjwala Yojana provide?
questions.a: LPG connections to poor households.

questions.q: What is human capital?
questions.a: The skills, knowledge and health of people.

lesson.homework: Write how women's empowerment helps a family and a nation.
